In animals with a small-diameter intestinal lumen, this procedure may not be feasible. In this case, the forceps are advanced into the intestinal lumen, opened and retracted almost against the tip of the endoscope, and the endoscope tip is deflected obliquely into the mucosa as much as possible to attain as perpen- dicular an orientation as is possible. During this maneuver, it is often impossible to see the mucosa (“red-out”). The tissue samples are obtained by gently pressuring the jaws of the forceps into the mucosa without turning the tip of the instrument away. Except for gastric mucosa in the area of the pylorus, it is not necessary to forcefully tug or jerk the forceps to obtain biopsies. In the antrum, the mucosa separates less easily and thus it is more difficult to obtain adequately sized biopsy samples. To avoid damage to the working channel, it is generally advisable to straighten the endoscope tip as much as possible or at least to let go of the deflecting knobs before retracting the biopsy forceps. This is clearly mandatory if a forceful jerk is deemed necessary. In the stomach, overdistension must be avoided before and while taking samples. Ulcerated areas are sampled at the rim between abnor - mal and normal-looking mucosa. Sampling the crater of an ulcer is avoided as this is risky due to the possibility of per - foration and will not yield a useful pathological result. Masses are biopsied multiple times in the same location with as big a biopsy forceps as possible. The biopsy forceps are pushed a little deeper with each attempt. This will help to obtain superficial mucosal samples and give deep enough samples to increase the possible diagnosis of malig - nancy. With some experience, one can appreciate if a mass is soft or hard – the latter clearly pointing toward a malig - nant mass. Up to 20 biopsy samples are obtained when a neoplasia is highly likely. With rigid endoscopy a perpendicular angle of the biopsy forceps cups to the mucosa can rarely be achieved unless an angulated tip forceps is used. If the forceps are passed through the working channel, it is helpful to cover the port opening with an instrumentation channel cap. The biopsy instrument is passed through the capped hole and advanced out of the sheath until the jaws can be seen in the field of view. The forceps is opened and retracted up to the tip of the sheath. The endoscope is then angled toward the mucosa/mass as much as possible, taking care not to injure the animal by excessive manipulation. The open cups are advanced tangentially into the mucosa and closed as soon as a small mucosal fold has developed at the cup tips. The endoscope is angulated back into the lumen to ascertain that mucosa has been grasped and the biopsy forceps is retracted out through the working channel. To biopsy a mass, the cups are pushed into the tissue, closed, and the biopsy forceps are either retracted through the working channel or removed together with the whole endoscope to retrieve a bigger tissue sample. If an angulated tip forceps is used, this is passed beside the endoscope into the lumen. The lumen has to be sealed around endoscope and forceps. Air is insufflated until the lumen is again visible and the forceps are advanced until the tip can be seen endoscopically. The jaws are opened, the cups are pushed perpendicular into the mucosa/mass, closed, and pulled back out of the patient. After obtaining specimens, the biopsy forceps are removed from the endoscope and the tissue sample is carefully removed from the jaws. Placing the jaws containing the sample into a container filled with isotonic saline and then “washing-off” the sample by shaking the tip of the forceps helps to avoid damaging the edges of the cups (Video 3.3). Similarly, the tissue sample can be rinsed from the cup with a stream of isotonic saline instead of fiddling it out with a needle (Video 3.4). If saline solution is used to remove tissue from the cups, the container with both sample and saline is carefully decanted to remove as much saline as possible directly upon finishing the endoscopic procedure. Formalin is then added to get a 10 : 1 ratio of liquid to tissue (Video 3.5). Other techniques such as placing biopsy specimens on sponge or cucumber slices has been described (Jergens 2013) but teasing the specimen from the cup with a needle has a high risk of damage to the biopsy instrument or the tissue and the authors do not recommend this technique (Ruiz et al. 2016). Careful and thorough manual cleaning of forceps with water and an enzymatic agent are performed shortly after completion of any GI endoscopic procedure. Biopsy forceps are particularly difficult to clean and require autoclaving (i.e. steam under pressure) for effective sterilization due to their complicated mechanical structure. Specimens are sent in fixative to the pathology laboratory rapidly for histopathological examination. Submission of a complete history and macroscopic endoscopy evaluation report to the pathologist is mandatory to obtain best results. Furthermore, tissue samples can be used for other laboratory investigation (i.e. culture, polymerase chain reaction [PCR]) or to create touch imprints for cytological evaluation (Mangelsdorf et al. 2015). The endoscopic evaluation report should accompany the tissue and a pro-forma can be obtained from the WSA VS GI Standardization Group at https://wsava. org/global-guidelines/gastrointestinal-guidelines/. Histopathological evaluation of endoscopic biopsies should be done by a pathologist experienced in GI-pathology (Day et al. 2008; Wilcock and Day 2013). Besides regular his - topathology, other techniques such as PCR for antigen recep - tor rearrangements (PARR) or immunohistochemistry may

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 36 be done on inconclusive tissue samples and several studies have shown that these techniques complement each other (Briscoe et al. 2011; Jergens et al. 2016; Sabattini et al. 2016). 3.2.4 Patient Preparation Food is withheld 12–18 hours before endoscopy of the upper GI tract while water can still be provided up to 2 hours prior to the procedure. In lower GI tract endoscopy, food is withheld for at least 24 hours and preferably up to 48 hours to ensure no further passage of ingesta from the small into the large intestine. If the owner is unable to withhold food (i.e. multiple cat household, pet complaining severely, and outdoor cat), it is advisable to hospitalize the patient prior to the procedure to ensure proper fasting. Normally, the stomach in dogs empties within 12 hours and even quicker in cats (Wyse et al. 2003); therefore, finding retained food in the stomach of a properly fasted animal may give useful information about a possible ana- tomical or mechanical outflow obstruction or gastric motil- ity disorder. In these cases, a significant amount of gastric ingesta may compromise examination since the entire mucosa cannot be visualized (Figure 3.15). Lesions or even foreign bodies might be missed. If necessary, fluid can be aspirated through the working channel, or if too much food is present, it can be aspirated through a separate gas - tric tube alongside the endoscope or removed by flushing the stomach with water via a larger diameter tube. In some instances, it is sufficient to gently turn the animal around the endoscope to visualize the entire mucosa. If a barium contrast study has been performed, upper or lower GI endoscopy is postponed for at least 24 and 72 hours, respectively, to allow complete clearing of the barium from the mucosal surface. Any residual barium is never aspirated through the instrumentation channel as this may adhere to the channel’s inner lining and clog the lumen. For flexible colonoscopy and ileoscopy, removal of all feces from the entire colon is required; in rigid colonoscopy, the descending colon needs to be empty of feces. Fasting and administration of enemas may be sufficient to evacuate almost all fecal material. However, polyethylene glycol-con - taining electrolyte GI lavage solutions (e.g. Klean-Prep, Norgine GmbH; GoLYTELY, Braintree Laboratories) administered on the day before colonoscopy via a naso- esophageal tube prepares the colon significantly better (Richter and Cleveland 1989). Two doses of about 20–30 ml/ kg 1–4 hours apart have been recommended (Leib 2011). Cats and even dogs might vomit during administration of these lavage solutions and aspiration can lead to severe complications (Marshall and Bartels 1998). Therefore, some authors state that the use of oral lavage solution is not appropriate in cats (Sum and Ward 2009). Oral sodium phosphate solution (2–4 ml/kg) might be an alternative to polyethylene glycol-containing electrolyte solutions (Chien- Yuan et al. 2015). While sodium-phosphate solutions seem safe and only rarely cause electrolyte abnormalities (hyper - phosphatemia), they should be used cautiously in animals with overt or early kidney disease (Leib 2011). Warm water enemas (dogs: about 20–50 ml/kg; 50–75 ml/ cat) administered every one to two hours until the water is clear can be effective in cleaning out the colon. A well- lubricated rubber tube is passed gently into the colon no further than the length measured from the anus to the last rib and warm water is slowly infused into the colonic lumen under gravitational feed. Extreme care is taken not to overdistend the colon as this might lead to vomiting, especially in cats. The last enema is applied no later than two hours before the procedure. In one of the authors’ experience, feeding only meat broth (exclusively the liq- uid) to dogs for 48 hours prior to colonoscopy is sufficient to clean out the colon and no enema is needed with this procedure. 3.2 ­echniEue 37 For diagnostic flexible upper GI endoscopy, the patient is always placed in left lateral recumbency. If rigid endoscopy is performed, the patient is placed in sternal recumbency for esophagoscopy and in sternal or right lateral recumbency for proctoscopy and colonoscopy. Left lateral recumbency places the gastric antrum and pylorus uppermost, which significantly improves opening of these structures by insufflated air, allowing any fluid to fall into the fundus (Figure 3.16). Evaluation of the mucosa and passage through the stomach and pylorus are easily possible. In an animal lying in right lateral recumbency, it is much more difficult to clearly identify all parts of the stomach or pass into the antrum. The only exception to this positioning is for placement of a percutaneous gastrotomy feeding tube, which is placed through the left flank in an animal lying in right lateral recumbency (see Section 3.6.2). For flexible colonoscopy, the patient is also placed in left lateral recumbency, so the descending colon lies downward while the transverse and ascending colon is upward. This positioning is helpful to properly open the lumen of the proximal colon by air insufflation and reduces fluid accu- mulation around the ileo-ceco-colic junction. 3.2.5 Anesthesia General anesthesia is required for GI endoscopy and intubation with a cuffed endotracheal tube is mandatory because of the risk of gastroesophageal reflux. The safest anesthetic regime is one familiar to the operator, but inhalation anesthesia is preferable. Even if injection anesthesia is used throughout the procedure, the animal has to be intubated and the cuff inflated at all times. A mouth gag is always inserted for upper GI endoscopy to prevent damage to the endoscope. Spring-loaded mouth gags are not used in cats. These are associated with potential cortical blindness after the procedure due to occlusion of the maxillary artery, as cats lack the inner carotid artery that is present in dogs (Stiles et al. 2012; Barton-Lamb et al. 2013). A chopped down and slightly padded syringe or needle cap has proven sufficient for holding the mouth open. Some anesthetic agents affect intestinal motility and sphincter function making the passage through the cardia and pylorus potentially more difficult (Smith et al. 2004). Atropine and other anticholinergic drugs are not used unless necessary to increase heart rate, as these drugs may alter gastric motility patterns and increase pyloric tone. Pure opioid agonists may also increase pyloric tone and are ideally avoided. Fluid support is given during anesthesia; dehydrated ani- mals need to be rehydrated before anesthesia unless endos - copy needs to be performed as an emergency procedure. In hypoproteinemic patients, colloid administration is consid- ered to ensure reasonable oncotic pressure. Anesthesia monitoring during upper GI endoscopy includes at minimum assessment of heart rate, respiration, and pulse oximetry. Air insufflation is essential in upper GI endoscopy to open the lumen and move the mucosa away from the endoscopic tip. Overinflation of the stomach can cause cardiorespiratory compromise and both endoscopist and assistant should monitor the degree and possible effects of insufflation (Gross et al. 2005). Removal of excessive air via suction pump or – if unavailable – compression of the abdomen in an aboral-to-oral direction is indicated to alle - viate possible complications. 3.2.6 Complications and Contraindications Complications secondary to GI endoscopy are rare and include GI perforation, hemorrhage from blood vessel laceration, and anesthetic complications associated with gastric overdistension causing decreased venous return. A prevalence of perforation of 1.6% in cats and of 0.1% in dogs associated with GI endoscopy has been reported (Irom et al. 2014) while other studies did not mention any complications in large series of upper or lower GI endoscopies. Reasons for perforation can be associated with insertion and manipulation of the endoscope, retrieval of GI foreign bodies (e.g. bones lodged in the esophagus) (Gianella et al. 2009), excessive insufflation, esophageal stricture dilation (Leib et al. 2001; Bissett et al. 2009), and rarely during obtaining biopsies (e.g. from an ulcer pit). Using excessive force when trying to pass a very narrow area is likely the riskiest procedure and even experienced endoscopist may encounter a non-passible pylorus in very small pets. Furthermore, perforation of pre-existing duodenal ulcers during endoscopy is possible. Relative contraindications are inadequately fasted or prepared patients, those not well enough worked-up for their GI signs (extra-intestinal, motility, or functional diseases), and animals with major comorbidities. 3.2.7 Endoscopic Training No one is born a master – to perform GI endoscopy, a veterinarian must not only have knowledge of anatomy, physiology, and what to expect to find, but technical skills are just as important. Like every new technique, this must be learned and practiced to become proficient. Self-training was the mode that GI endoscopy was learned in the early days. Luckily, good teachers and courses with practical hands-on labs are now available throughout the world. Guidelines for training GI endoscopy have been estab- lished in human medicine (Anon 2001) and can be plagia- rized to the veterinary profession. The most important skills that trainees need to become proficient are listed in Table 3.3. In human medicine, over the years, a plethora of endo- scopic simulators have been used (Cohen 2011) with very sophisticated virtual reality endoscopic simulation plat- forms available nowadays that use realistic, procedure- based content to teach cognitive and motor skills training (e.g. AccuTouch simulator). These are interactive systems with tactile feedback that permit learning and practice without putting patients at risk. No such computerized systems are available for dogs or cats. Nevertheless, initial training of endoscopic novices starts in models, going to ex-vivo animal organ simulators and potentially ending in live animal courses. The authors have developed various models used for courses to train practical GI endoscopy. Plastic tubes, bought from any hardware store, can be built together to create a three-dimensional system (Figure 3.17) in which adroitness to use torque of the inser- tion tube by twisting the wrist and proper use of the dials is practiced. Hand–eye coordination is taught and learned. The next step could be to use ex-vivo models. Examples are pig-stomachs with at least 10 cm esophagus and duodenum still attached obtained from an abattoir and freely hung in a box in the same three-dimensional position that the stomach normally lies in a dog/cat in left lateral recum- bency (Figure 3.18). The esophagus is put over a short tube and securely fixed with a string or a clamp. In order to seal the stomach from air leakage, a rubber glove can be used through which the endoscope is pushed (small hole). With this model, normal movement of the endoscope in the

3.3 Esophagoscopy 39 stomach is shown and pyloric intubation is practiced. Obtaining biopsies from all parts of stomach and duode - num can be shown and learned. GI endoscopy can also be learned in freshly euthanized dog cadavers but ex-vivo models have the advantage that trainees can visualize from the outside what they and others are doing with the endo - scope within the stomach. This is not possible in cadavers. Once trainees have internalized the acquired knowledge and have taken the torqueing technique completely to heart, then either live animal models (piglets, dogs) are used (Figure 3.19) or trainees’ practice in pet patients, hopefully initially still supervised. 3.3 Esophagoscopy 3.3.1 Indications, Limitations Common clinical signs which might necessitate an esophagoscopy are retching, dysphagia, regurgitation, and possibly ptyalism; it should be remembered however that differentiating vomiting from regurgitating can be difficult and is often not possible for owners. Plain radiographs of the thorax are always performed in animals with these symptoms and may diagnose a radiodense foreign body or gas/distension around a possible non-radiodense foreign body, megaesophagus, gastroesophageal intussusception, or mediastinal mass. In cases of general dilation of the entire esophagus, the diagnosis of megaesophagus can be made and further workup with diagnostic imaging (con- trast study or endoscopy) is rarely indicated. Additional studies even pose great risks for aspiration pneumonia. Contrast radiographs with liquid contrast (iodine-based or barium) or mixed with food might be indicated in some animals and several abnormalities such as a stricture, radi- olucent foreign body, vascular ring anomaly, gastroesopha- geal intussusception, or tumor can be diagnosed with this modality (Figure 3.20). A swallow study (fluoroscopy) is needed to diagnose functional esophageal motility prob - lems, which can happen in cases of neuromuscular dis - ease, myopathy, dysautonomia, or be idiopathic. Recently, esophageal manometry has been used to give an overall highly informative assessment of pharyngeal and esopha- geal motility disorders (Kempf et al. 2013). Nevertheless, endoscopy might still be indicated if the problem cannot be diagnosed sufficiently and this is the only modality to diag - nose esophagitis. 3.3.2 Procedure The esophagus can be markedly dilated in dogs and cats, unless there are strictures present, thus basically all flexi- ble endoscopes normally used in small animal GI endos - copy can be used (Section 3.1.1). 3.3 Esophagoscopy 41 The cervical esophagus is normally collapsed so a red-out briefly obscures visibility. Insufflation is continued once the UES is passed, but forward motion is halted until the esoph - ageal lumen is visible as a straight tube with a slight bend at the thoracic inlet. The endoscope tip is adjusted into the center of the lumen and the endoscope is advanced through the esophagus in a slow continuous movement with no or very minor resistance. To keep the lumen from collapsing, intermittent or continuous air flow is applied as needed, over-insufflation is avoided. In rare instances, slight trans - cutaneous manual compression of the upper esophagus is needed to prevent escape of insufflated air. Distending the lumen of the thoracic esophagus gener - ally needs minimal insufflation. While passing the endo - scope through the length of the esophagus, the entire mucosal circumference is inspected for mucosal color, tex - ture, and possible pathologic lesions, so as not to confuse these with iatrogenic changes when withdrawing the endo - scope. A fuller investigation is performed on the way back out of the patient. 3.3.3 Normal Findings Normal esophageal mucosa is smooth, glistening, pale pink (Figure 3.22), and superficial mucosal vessels can be seen. Spots of pigmented mucosa may be seen in pig - mented dog breeds such as the Chow Chow and Shar Pei. In the cat, the esophagus is composed of striated muscle in the proximal two thirds and smooth muscle in the distal third (Bremner et al. 1970); the distal part has the appear - ance of circular wavelike ripples, sometimes called the “herring bone” effect (Figure 3.23). The trachea and bifur - cation of the main stem bronchi are usually visible and over the base of the heart (Figure 3.24) pulsation of the aorta can be seen. At the gastroesophageal junction in dogs, the gastric mucosa can often be seen in a serrated fashion protruding into the esophagus; this is called the “z-line” (Figure 3.25). In the cat, there is a slit-like opening that passes obliquely at about a 30° angle through the diaphragm into the stom- ach. The lower or gastroesophageal sphincter (GES) is a high-pressure zone that keeps the stomach closed between swallows. During endoscopy it may be closed or open (Figure 3.26) depending on anesthetic depth. To pass the endoscope into the stomach, the endoscope tip is deflected slightly left and upward. The endoscope is advanced under direct visual inspection with slight pressure and variable air insufflation until the gastric lumen is reached. A short red-out can be seen when passing. Little resistance should be encountered. If forward motion is impeded when enter - ing the stomach, it is usually because the tip has missed the GES. The endoscope is withdrawn and redirected prior to repeat intubation. Biopsies are rarely taken of the esophagus because the mucosa is lined with a stiff and relatively tough squamous epithelium. Masses or ulcerated mucosa, however, are always biopsied. Recently, biopsies taken from the gastroe - sophageal junction during upper GI endoscopy showed that – after a learning curve – adequate biopsies can rou- tinely be taken and up to 25% show histological lesions (Münster et al. 2013). 3.3.4 Abnormal Findings Possible abnormalities found during esophagoscopy are summarized in Table 3.4. Mucosal erythema, irregularity, erosion, and ulceration indicate a mild-to-severe esophagitis (Figure 3.27). Ulcers may appear as oval-shaped shallow lesions with indistinct margins or as deeper lesions with raised and edematous margins. The more severe forms are often located further caudally. Most cases of esophagitis occur from gastroe - sophageal reflux, from injuries secondary to foreign bodies, or from acute or chronic vomiting. Other causes are anes - thesia-related reflux, chemical injuries, drugs (doxycycline, clindamycin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), and

3.3 Esophagoscopy 43 infectious agents (calici virus in cats, pythiosis in dogs) (Gualtieri 2001). Esophageal strictures are characterized by circumfer - ential narrowing, commonly in the exact center of the lumen, which generally cannot be passed (Figure 3.28), depending on the diameter size of the endoscope. Strictures can be single or multiple along the esophagus and the length can be from few millimeters to several centimeters. Strictures occur secondary to injury (e.g. foreign bodies) or severe esophagitis of any cause extending into the submu- cosa or muscular layer of the esophageal mucosa. Healing of these lesions by intramural fibrosis leads to stricture for - mation. It is important not to confuse strictures with diffi- culties to pass the cardia, which might be a problem in some animals. Strictures are most commonly treated with balloon dilation or bougienage (see Section 3.6.2.1) (Palma and Berent 2015b). Rarely, stents can be placed after dilat - ing the stricture but results so far are not satisfactory (see Section 3.6.2.2) (Lam et al. 2013). A technique using endo - scopic electrocautery incisions of the stricture before bal- loon dilation has been proposed (Gualtieri 2001). Rarely, esophageal stenosis looks similar to a stricture but during balloon dilation no indentation of the balloon can be seen (Figure 3.29). An implantable balloon dilation esophagostomy tube has been developed for management of esophageal stric- tures that shows promise. This system allows daily dilation of the stricture without anesthesia. Foreign bodies are readily diagnosed and can in most cases be removed endoscopically (see Section 3.6.1) Figure 3.25 At the cardia, the gastric mucosa can be seen extending into the esophagus. This is called the “Z-line. ” In this dog, the cardia is mostly closed so passing the endoscope will result in a short “red-out. ” Figure 3.26 Examples of open cardia and Z-line in two French Bulldogs. This is a normal finding in many brachycephalic dogs and can also be seen in other dogs, depending on anesthetic depth.

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 44 (Figure 3.30). Foreign bodies can be smooth and poorly traumatizing objects (e.g. balls, meat bits, and toys) or sharp and cutting objects (e.g. bones, fishhooks) that cause hemorrhagic and perforating lesions during obstruction and retrieval. Bones are by far the most common foreign bodies in dogs (>80%) with toys following second place (Lüthi and Neiger 1998); depending on the region of the world, fishhooks can also be commonplace. Seventy to eighty percent of foreign bodies are lodged between the base of the heart and the diaphragm. Smooth foreign bod- ies are poorly traumatizing but can cause marked compres- sive lesions or lesions secondary to their putrefaction. The mucosa can become necrotic and it may also affect the muscular layer. Esophageal foreign bodies should be removed promptly to avoid the risk of necrosis, perfora- tion, or bleeding. 3.3 Esophagoscopy 45 Tumors of the esophagus are rare, accounting for <5% of GI tumors. Primary tumors of the esophagus are polyps, leiomyoma, papilloma, squamous cell carcinoma, osteosar - coma, fibrosarcoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, and leio - myosarcoma. Metastatic tumors are encountered more frequently at this site, most often from lymphatic dissemi- nation of thyroid, mammary, gastric, and bronchogenic carcinoma (Willard 2012). They mostly present as masses protruding into the lumen (Figure 3.31) and tend to be ulcerated and friable. Sometimes esophageal lymphoma may appear simply as a very irregular mucosa with cobble- stoned appearance. A leiomyoma/sarcoma arising from the gastroesophageal junction can sometimes be seen protrud- ing into the lumen (Figure 3.32). Dogs from endemic regions might have a granulomatous mass protruding into the lumen due to Spirocerca lupi (Figure 3.33) (Lobetti 2014). Untreated, this granuloma may transform into an esopha- geal carcinoma. Besides spirocercosis, granulomas might also arise due to Pythium insidiosum infection (Patton et al. 1996). Extraluminal compression can be either due to a mass in the mediastinum (lymphoma, cyst, thymoma) or a vascu- lar ring anomaly (e.g. persistent right aortic arch). While in the former bulging of the mucosa with cranial dilation is visualized, the latter often has a typical band crossing the esophagus with a cranial diverticulum (Figure 3.34). Protrusion of gastric rugal folds into the esophagus is the hallmark of a gastroesophageal intussusception (Figure 3.35). 3.3 Esophagoscopy 47 tion of the stomach can be attempted (Shibli et al. 2014). Hiatal hernias are occasionally diagnosed by endoscopy. They appear as a ballooning of the distal esophageal wall into the esophageal lumen. The ballooning often occurs at the same rate as respiration – this can be provoked by occluding the endotracheal tube until a forceful inspiration results in visualization of the stomach moving through the hiatus. A condition called cardial incompetence has been proposed to occur in dogs when the cardia is partially or completely open during esophagoscopy and the gastric cavity can be directly seen from the esophagus (Gualtieri 2001). It is more likely that this is a normal variation depending mainly on the anesthetic protocol used and depth of anesthesia. Traumatic esophageal perforation is possible resulting commonly from dog or cat bites. Fistulae can be congeni- tal or acquired – congenital ones mostly communicating with the respiratory tract (esophagotracheal, esophagob - ronchial, and esophagopulmonary). Acquired fistulae are more common than congenital fistulae and often result from pointed foreign body ingestion, chronic ulcerative lesions, or complicated esophageal surgery (suture). During endoscopy, perforation and fistulae are rarely seen and contrast studies are better able to make a diagnosis. In fistulae with the respiratory tract, foamy material may be seen coming from the opening, depending on the area involved. Generalized dilation and hypomotility of the entire esophagus is the definition of a megaesophagus . It has to be differentiated from localized esophageal dilation which can be frequently observed proximal to obstructive disor - ders. However, early cases of megaesophagus might have only segmental dilation which may become generalized with time. In addition, not all dogs with abnormal esopha- geal motility progress to megaesophagus. Idiopathic meg - aesophagus may be congenital or acquired. In some dog breeds (Great Dane, German Shepherd, Irish Setter, Golden Retriever, Labrador Retriever, Greyhound, Newfoundland, and Shar Pei) a familial predisposition is reported, while in others (Miniature Schnauzers and Fox Terriers) an autoso - mal dominant inheritance trait has been discovered (Schönfelder et al. 2011). In cats, megaesophagus is uncom- mon. The acquired adult-onset form is most commonly idi- opathic (>70%) or secondary to other systemic disorders, especially those causing neuromuscular dysfunction. Megaesophagus is commonly diagnosed on plain or con- trast radiographs and esophagoscopy is rarely indicated or might even be contraindicated due to the high risk of aspira- tion pneumonia during induction or recovery from anesthesia. Froth, fluid, and fermenting food might be seen in megaesophagus together with signs of esophagitis (Figure 3.36). Furthermore, it might be dif- ficult to pass through the GES as the endoscope might be diverted into some blind ending folds, or a diverticulum. 3.4 Gastroscopy and Duodenoscopy 3.4.1 Indications, Limitations Upper GI endoscopy is used to find structural abnormali- ties of the gastric and duodenal mucosa – for this, endo- scopically obtained biopsies are paramount, even if no gross abnormalities can be seen (see Section 3.2.3). Besides diagnostic endoscopy, gastric foreign body removal (see Section 3.6.1), feeding tube placement (see Section 3.6.2), or balloon dilation of an esophageal stricture (see Section 3.6.2.1) are common therapeutic indications. Diagnostic gastroscopy is always performed in conjunction with enteroscopy (endoscopy of upper small intestine) and possibly even ileoscopy (see Section 3.5.2) (Procoli et al. 2013). Recently, it was shown that duodenal biopsies do not always match ileal biopsies and obtaining biopsies in both parts of the small intestine will help to better tailor the treatment. Typical indications for which upper GI endoscopy may be helpful are chronic vomiting and chronic diarrhea, nau- sea and hypersalivation, hematemesis, melena, chronic abdominal pain, and possibly anorexia. 3.4 ­GastrasropyGand D rndarasropy 49 only followed by gastroscopy if there is a high index of sus - picion of a gastric foreign body which will then be removed endoscopically. If diagnostic imaging finds markedly thick - ened gastric or duodenal wall, endoscopy is also warranted even if signs are acute. Functional problems and motility abnormalities cannot be diagnosed by upper GI endoscopy and neither can systemic and metabolic diseases. Therefore, a very thorough clinical workup of dogs and cats prior to gas - troduodenoscopy is mandatory . Hematology, biochemistry, and abdominal imaging (radiographs or preferably ultra- sonography) are the minimum database but other tests may be indicated as well. Potential tests which may need to be run depending on signalment, history, geographic location, physical examination findings, and results from the minimum database are listed here: urinalysis, fecal examination for parasites (including Giardia antigen, Cryptosporidia , and T. foetus PCR test) and viruses, pancre - atic lipase, TLI, cobalamin and folate concentration, ACTH-stimulation test, thyroxin concentration or other endocrine tests, bile acid stimulation test, ammonia toler - ance test, heartworm tests in cats in endemic areas, dietary trials, and contrast studies. If marked gastric wall thicken- ing is seen on abdominal ultrasound, ultrasound-guided FNA may be helpful to obtain a diagnosis of gastric tumor without anesthesia and endoscopy (Marolf et al. 2015). Once metabolic diseases (renal, hepatic, and endocrine), drugs, or toxins have been ruled out as the cause of the clinical symptom, clinicians need to decide which step to take next. Since endoscopy is rarely indicated for acute problems, unless diagnostic imaging clearly points toward a structural problem, there is often sufficient time to first perform dietary or medical trials before upper GI endos - copy is performed. Deworming with a broad-spectrum anthelmintic also working against Giardia spp., dietary tri- als, or giving gastric protective drugs (proton pump inhibi- tors, sucralfate) are done to rule out parasitism, dietary hypersensitivity, or nonspecific gastritis. If vomiting or hematochezia/melena starts shortly after NSAID adminis - tration, gastroscopy will merely show petechial bleeding or erosions, rarely ulcers, but this would be anticipated so endoscopy should be postponed and medical therapy started. Only if the pet does not respond adequately, endos - copy is indicated to find possible other problems causing the symptoms. In conjunction with abdominal ultrasound, upper GI endoscopy is a very useful tool. Limitations for endoscopy are clearly that not all parts of the small intestine can be visualized, unless push-endos - copy (see Section 3.7.2) is used which can reach far into the ileum. Contrast studies may be helpful in some of these instances, e.g. when motility problems are suspected. 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 50 The merit of follow-up upper GI endoscopy has not been proven and dogs with IBD will often have similar macro - scopic and histologic findings after several weeks of appro - priate therapy as they did prior to therapy (Walker et al. 2013; Schmitz et al. 2015). In order to monitor these patients, it is likely better to repeat the CCECAI (Allenspach et al. 2007) score at regular intervals than to repeat the endoscopic procedure with repeated biopsies. Whether repeated endoscopy is needed to assess therapeutic success in animals with gastric or intestinal lymphoma, peptic ulcers or even granulomatous gastritis has not been proven and needs to be discussed in earnest with the owners. It is likely that clinical signs and laboratory tests (C-reactive protein, serum protein, cobalamin-concentration, etc.) as well as repeated ultrasound are more helpful to assess ther - apeutic success (Güssow et al. 2016). 3.4.2 Procedure A full examination of all areas of the stomach and upper duodenum is performed in every patient and all landmarks are identified properly. Even when therapeutic endoscopy is performed, it is wise to check all accessible areas in order not to miss something. Inflammatory conditions are often diffuse with various parts of small intestine and stomach involved but this is not always the case. Upon observing gastric ulcers, one needs to assess if peptic ulcers are also seen in the duodenum. Finally, even when a foreign body has been successfully removed endoscopically, the clini- cian needs to investigate why the small animal has ingested the foreign body in the first place (pica, allotriophagia) and an inflammatory process in the small intestine might explain this. The endoscopist needs to be familiar with the luminal gastric anatomy to successfully maneuver the endoscope through the stomach, obtain retroflexed views of the fun- dus and cardia, advance around the lesser curvature/ incisura angularis into the antrum, and traverse the pyloric canal into the duodenum (Figure 3.37). The stomach is only briefly examined on the way in so as to note the gross appearance; full examination and taking of biopsies is done after duodenoscopy as prolonged insufflation and examination of the stomach stimulates pyloric closure and makes intubation more difficult. It is important to know the important landmarks to facilitate orientation. The most important landmark is the incisura angularis which divides the corpus (commonly on top in a patient lying in left lateral recumbency) from the antrum (commonly on the bottom). Rugal folds tend to have a longitudinal orientation that can be followed toward the antrum and pylorus.

3.4 ­GastrasropyGand D rndarasropy 51 Upper GI endoscopy is performed with a flexible endo - scope (see Section 3.1.1). The diameter and length dictate how easy the pylorus can be passed. No studies have inves - tigated endoscopic diameter, body weight, and success of pyloric intubation but as a general rule, intubation in mid- dle to large breed dogs can be accomplished with almost any diameter and length is the restricting factor. Here the endoscope should be 140 cm or longer, especially in giant breed dogs. In dogs from 5 to 10 kg, an endoscope with 8–9 mm diameter and 100–140 cm length will commonly allow pyloric intubation and the same is true for large cats. In small patients, the diameter needs to be even smaller (7.5–8 mm) but now the length is no longer a concern. In very small animals, one might need to use a bronchoscope instead of a gastroscope. The disadvantage is that there will only be two-way tip deflection so left/right movement must now be completely made via torque of the insertion tube. Air insufflation needs to be done via the instrumentation channel either with an attached syringe or an air bulb. It was possible to pass the pylorus in 9 of 10 pet ferrets (weight 0.72–1.34 kg) with a 5.5 mm videobronchoscope with a 5.3 mm diameter insertion tube and a 60 cm working length (Devaux et al. 2016). For patient preparation and anesthe - sia, see Sections 3.2.4 and 3.2.5. After passing the GES (see Section 3.3.3) and before attempting to advance the endoscope into the stomach, air is insufflated until the lumen is visible. In small dogs and cats, insufflation can be achieved in mere seconds. If the stomach does not distend, the cause might be a blocked air/water channel port, reflux of air through the esopha- gus, or gastric wall disease that prevents mucosal disten- sion. The degree of gastric distension is judged by increased flattening of the folds, with a completely smooth mucosa seen at maximal insufflation. Generally, the least disten- sion necessary to pass the endoscope through the stomach is when the rugal folds are separated and begin to stretch. This allows orientation and identification of gross lesions (ulcers, foreign bodies, and masses) while avoiding overd- istension which is detrimental to the movement of the dia- phragm possibly leading to serious cardiopulmonary compromise. Minimal distension of the stomach at this stage also reduces the likelihood of pyloric contraction making passage through into the duodenum considerably easier. It also reduces the occurrence of paradoxical move - ment where a loop of insertion tube pushes the greater cur - vature away and results in the tip of the insertion tube moving further away from the pylorus as the endoscope is inserted. Once orientation is achieved, the endoscope is advanced along the greater curvature by lifting the tip upward and pushing it gently forward using rotational torque if neces - sary. With the patient in left lateral recumbency and the endoscope held in the conventional manner, the view is predictable. In order to reach the antrum an important landmark is the incisura angularis (Figure 3.38). By lifting the tip and advancing the endoscope, the incisura comes into view almost automatically. Sometimes the tip has to be deflected down again slightly. The antrum is below the incisura, while the cardia is above it and can be viewed by increased retroflexion of the tip. 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 52 will become visible and the incisura angularis at the 12-o’clock position will eventually disappear (Figure 3.39). In cats, the angle of the lesser curvature may be very acute, and a slide-by technique might be necessary to pass into the antrum. This slide-by technique can be used to advance around tight flexures in the stomach or intestine. Using this technique the endoscope tip is deflected in the direction required to follow the lumen and as the deflected tip impinges on the outer radius of the gastric/intestinal bend, a red-out is seen. If this red-out seems to be moving, it is generally safe to advance until the next straight part, in this case the antrum, can be visualized. With this maneuver mucosal damage can occur, leading to linear streaks of hyperemia or mucosal hemorrhage. Another method to avoid such artifacts is to pre-deflect the tip within the body of the stomach and then advance into the antrum. The biggest and most common mistake when trying to advance into the antrum and intubate the pylorus is overd- istension. With increased intraluminal pressure the stom- ach assumes a round shape, the antral opening is flattened, and antral contractions are stimulated. It becomes difficult to enter the antrum and to find the pylorus. In this case, air must be aspirated and the maneuver to advance into the antrum is repeated with a less-inflated stomach. Another major mistake is to try to intubate the pylorus with two people, one holding the handpiece and the other person holding the insertion tube. The endoscopist must be standing (not sitting) in front of the patient’s mouth, hold- ing the handpiece of the endoscope with the left hand and the insertion tube with the right hand. Coordinated movement of up/down knob, torque technique with wrist movement of the left hand, and some pressure on the inser- tion tube with the right hand together with continuous or intermittent air insufflation in a fairly empty stomach will almost always lead to successful intubation of the pyloris. To intubate the pyloric canal, the pylorus is always kept in the center of the endoscopic field of view. As the pyloric position changes with respiratory movement and peristal- sis, small adjustments by up/down deflection and insertion tube rotation (torque) may be necessary. The aim is to con- tinually move forward while readjusting and keeping the pylorus in the center of view. During intubation of the pylorus, red-out frequently occurs and it often is easiest to aim at the darkest area which usually is the lumen. Air insufflation is continued either constantly (larger breed dogs) or intermittently (smaller breed dogs, cats) during passage of the pyloric canal. Nevertheless, the field of view is often blurred. The assistant monitors for overdistension and respiratory compromise. Furthermore, increased vagal tone might happen when the pylorus is manipulated. This is a rather infrequent occurrence but may lead to the need for pharmacologic intervention in rare instances (e.g. atro- pine 0.01–0.02 mg/kg iv; glycopyrrolate 0.005–0.01 mg/kg iv). Often the endoscope tip can be directed into the pyloric canal by turning it slightly left and up (both wheels in counterclockwise direction) while advancing forward gradually. Once the tip is inside the pyloric canal, vision is blurred as the pyloric wall closes around the tip. In many patients, there will be a color change from cream/apricot (antrum, pylorus) to a peach, fawn, or “macaroni and cheese” color once the duodenum has been reached. Due to some bile, a greenish color may also be seen. The normal pylorus has significant variation in its appearance due to individual patient anatomy, muscle tone, and the extent of gastric insufflation (Figure 3.40). In some cases, the pylorus may be open and passage is achieved quite easily. However, in most patients, the pylorus is closed tight and offers significant resistance to endoscope passage. Even finding the pyloric opening is sometimes difficult when pooled fluid, a tissue fold, or a mucosal rosette obscures the entrance. In dogs, the pyloric canal may be at an obtuse angle in relation to the antrum. As the endoscope is advanced through a narrow area, considerable force may be generated against the pylorodu- odenal junction; it may be necessary to have the assistant hold the patient’s body in a stable position. In some cases, the tip cannot be aligned properly to the pyloric opening. It can still be possible to advance the endoscope by putting the tip against the peripyloric wall and gently pushing the insertion tube forward. The tip often deflects into the pylorus as the area of the orifice stretches by the advance of the insertion tube. The amount of pressure one dares to use is a matter of experience and judgment. An experienced endoscopist recognizes a situation in which it is unlikely that the pylorus can be passed. It is difficult to pass an endoscope of >9 mm outer diameter through a pylorus of animals <5 kg; however, a 9 mm diameter endoscope or smaller can usually be passed. 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 54 Tonkinese), a smaller endoscope of <8 mm is preferred (Tams 2011). Drugs given to decrease pyloric tone and ease passage of the endoscope are not useful (Matz et al. 1991). If the pylorus cannot be passed, the following tech - niques might help. First, the clinician makes sure that the animal has not been turned from right to left recumbency during the start of anesthesia as this might cause some rotation on the stomach making the passage into the antrum very difficult. Second, if the pylorus is at an oblique angle or otherwise obscured, turning the pet to dorsal recumbency while the endoscope remains in place might help. Once the pylorus has been passed, the animal is then turned back to the left lateral position. Third, over - inflation of the stomach during multiple attempts to enter the pylorus often happens and removal of air via suction is helpful. Fourth, using a biopsy instrument as a guide wire (Seldinger technique) is often used by inexperienced endoscopists. The authors do not advocate this technique as it may seriously harm the duodenum and tempt the cli - nician to repeat it later again. If used by an experienced endoscopist in an animal with tightly closed pyloric canal, the biopsy instrument should only be advanced a few cen - timeters into the duodenum and immediately be retracted into the instrument channel as soon as the tip of the endo - scope passes into the pyloric canal. Troughs in the cranial duodenal mucosa from the force of the biopsy instrument are commonly seen with this technique and must be rec - ognized as an iatrogenic problem (Figure 3.41). It must be remembered that traversing the pyloric canal may be dif - ficult but with expertise, this is possible in virtually all dogs and cats if an appropriate endoscope is used. However, inexperienced clinicians should give themselves a time-limit (e.g. passing pylorus in less than 20 minutes) and if they do not succeed, either ask a colleague to help or take blind upper intestinal biopsies. If the lumen of the duodenum is not clearly visible after passing, the pylorus insufflation may be necessary to dis - tend the intestinal lumen. Further gentle advance usually provides a view into the descending duodenum, seen as a straight tunnel. In some cases, minor forward or backward adjustments are needed to free the tip from the mucosa. If these maneuvers do not provide a clear view of the intesti- nal lumen, the endoscope is retracted under constant insufflation until a view can be obtained. No forward move - ment is attempted without clear visualization and no force is ever used. The endoscope can usually be advanced easily through the descending duodenum toward the caudal duodenal flexure. Depending on the length of the endoscope and the size of the animal, the ascending duodenum and the proxi- mal jejunum may be reached. Variable degrees of insuffla- tion are required to maintain luminal distension and a clear view of the mucosa. As there is already a bend in the endoscope’s insertion tube in the stomach, forward move - ment in the descending duodenum can, in some cases, be facilitated by withdrawing the endoscope slightly, thereby reducing the loop in the stomach. This procedure is most helpful in large to giant breed dogs when little insertion tube is left to push forward. Forward movement is some - times accelerated at this point and great care has to be taken not to move the tip against the mucosal surface. While the insertion tube is slowly advanced, the intestine is closely examined for mucosal surface appearance and obvi - ous lesions. 3.4 ­GastrasropyGand D rndarasropy 55 tube can be rotated around its longitudinal axis via the torque technique. After reaching the pelvic flexure of the duodenum, the duodenum ascends a short distance before reaching a ven- trally directed bend. This bend is the juncture between the duodenum and jejunum. Gradual advance of the endo - scope can be continued as long as the lumen can be viewed clearly, and no resistance is met. Because the curves of the intestine move easily, only minor adjustments in tip deflec- tion are required. In some animals, the loop in the stomach cannot be straightened and the pyloric resistance remains high preventing further advancement past the pelvic flex - ure of the duodenum. Sometimes massaging the intestinal loops transabdominally relaxes intestinal musculature and may help to facilitate further examination. As soon as resistance is met, the endoscope is retracted. At this point, the mucosa is closely examined and biopsies are taken during retraction of the endoscope (see Section 3.2.3). Following examination and biopsy of the duodenum, a complete examination of the stomach is done by inspecting first the antrum, then the greater curvature up to the incisura, followed then by inspecting the cardia and fun- dus. To examine the cardia and fundus, the endoscope is retroflexed (Figure 3.42). This retroversion maneuver, or “J-maneuver,” provides a view of the inside of the cardia and the fundus of the stomach. In cats, the J-maneuver is started when the endoscope is at the middle part of the gas - tric body opposite the incisura angularis. The tip is lifted up (counterclockwise deflection of inner control knob) and the endoscope is advanced further into the stomach. By deflecting the tip up almost completely, the cardia comes into view. In this retroflexed view, the endoscope entering the stomach can be seen. Sometimes this maneuver extends the GES and air will leak into the esophagus necessitating further air insufflation to provide adequate distension. For close-up views of the cardia, the endoscopist’s right hand retracts the insertion tube thereby pulling the tip toward the mucosa. By applying rotational movement to the insertion tube using rotational torque of the whole endoscope with the handpiece and turning the outer deflection knob for a lateral view, a circumferential examination of the proximal stomach can be accomplished. While the endoscope is ret - roflexed slowly, the mucosa is further inspected. Leaving the tip in the proximal stomach and turning the deflection controls into a neutral position, the body of the stomach is viewed. Alternatively, by advancing the endoscope while the tip is still deflected, an additional view of the proximal stomach is provided. After complete inspection of the gas - tric mucosa, an adequate number of biopsies are taken from the various parts of the stomach (see Section 3.2.3). After completion of the procedure, the duodenum and stomach are completely deflated using suction. If there is gastric content (bile, liquid, and food) in the esophagus, this needs to be aspirated or lavaged to prevent aspiration during recovery from anesthesia and to prevent esophagitis with possible stricture formation (see Section 3.3.4). The animal is supervised closely during recovery and the endotracheal tube removed as late as possible. 3.4.3 Normal Findings The initial view on entering the stomach is of rugal folds of the stomach’s greater curvature (Figure 3.43a). During this initial examination of the stomach, it is important to note the gross appearance of the rugal folds, the ease with which the gastric wall distends during insufflation, and if fluid or ingesta is present. The mucosa of the normal stomach is pale pink and the rugal folds separate and stretch easily (Figure 3.43b). 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 56 esophagus. If the stomach is still completely or partially collapsed, the mucosa lies close to the tip and view is quite limited. If an animal has been properly fasted, the stomach is completely empty. A small amount of liquid is not con- sidered abnormal, large amounts of liquid, especially bil- ious fluids, may suggest reflux of intestinal fluid into the stomach. This finding may occur in animals that have been treated with enemas, which have a gastric motility or duo - deno-gastric reflux disorder, or an intestinal obstruction. As bile is irritating to the gastric mucosa, it may appear red- dened in cases of significant gastric biliary retention. Small amounts of fluid do not need to be removed for proper evaluation of the stomach but if moderate-to-larger amounts of fluid obscures the view of the mucosa, this needs to be aspirated. Alternatively, the animal can be gen- tly turned on its back to move the fluid to another position while inspecting the concealed part of the mucosa. Then the animal is put back in left lateral recumbency. The key landmark in the stomach is the incisura angula- ris which separates the body from the antrum (Figures 3.38 and 3.39). In animals in left lateral recumbency, the antrum will be seen below and the fundus/body above. The antrum lacks rugal folds, but commonly peristaltic waves propa- gate toward the pylorus. The pylorus is easily identified at the end of the antrum and it has a variety of appearances. In dogs, it is often off center and shows a variety of folds (Figure 3.40). The pylorus can persistently be closed or be in variable degrees of dilation; sometimes bile colored reflux from the duode - num is observed. Occasionally, the location can be difficult to identify because of peristaltic waves, antral masses, or fluid obscuring the view. Pyloric folds are extremely rare in cats and the pylorus is usually straight at the end of the antrum (Figure 3.40f). Once the junction of the pylorus and the duodenum is reached, the mucosal color changes from pale pink to pink - ish red. The color of the normal duodenal and jejunal mucosa is cream to slightly reddish pink (Figure 3.44) and the presence of villi gives it a velvety to villous appearance. Peyer’s Patches (aggregated lymphoid nodules) can routinely be seen in the normal canine duodenal mucosa showing a shallow central crater of around 2–3 cm diame - ter (Figure 3.44a). Peyer’s patches are not as readily identi- fiable in cats, although aggregated lymphoid nodules do occur. The major duodenal papilla, which represents the combined opening of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, is located close to the convex curve formed by the antrum, pylorus, and proximal duodenum. It is generally a round to oval disc, 1.5–2 mm in diameter, and appears almost white against the surrounding reddish mucosa (Figure 3.45). Dogs have a major and minor duodenal papilla and sometimes both can be seen, opposing each other. As the endoscope is retracted through the proximal duodenum and pyloric canal, this area is closely inspected as it typi- cally has not been viewed on the way in. Pyloric ulcers or tumors can be detected during this examination. 3.4.4 Abnormal Findings Dogs and cats with gastritis often have gross mucosal abnormalities, either focally or diffusely throughout the entire gastric mucosa. Acute gastritis can be due to drugs (NSAID, steroids, antibiotics, and others), dietary indiscretion, ingestion of plant material, “stress” or any severe disease, and hypoten- sion. Normally, endoscopy of the stomach in these patients is not necessary and symptomatic therapy with a proton pump inhibitor, sucralfate, an antiemetic drug and dietary management is all that is required (Neiger 2009). Endoscopic views of acute gastritis may be completely nor - mal or might show mild-to-severe erythema, petechial bleeding, and/or erosions, especially in the antrum (Figure 3.46). Lesions may be focal but more often multifo - cal or generalized throughout the entire stomach (Figure 3.47). Dogs with acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS) undergoing upper GI endoscopy show normal gastric mucosa but macroscopic findings in the intestinal tract show hyperemia, increased mucosal friabil- ity, hemorrhage, and erosions (Unterer et al. 2014). Chronic gastritis is part of the IBD complex. As in acute gastritis, the mucosa often looks normal but may appear irregular, friable, or show petechial or larger areas of erythema or hemorrhage (Figure 3.48). Again, the lesions can be localized or generalized. For this reason, tak - ing endoscopic biopsies of both normal and abnormal areas of the stomach for histopathological examination is mandatory for all animals undergoing diagnostic gastric endoscopy. Since a Helicobacter -infection has not been shown to have any pathologic role in dogs and cats (Simpson et al. 2000), further diagnostic steps to diagnose these bacteria are not indicated. When biopsies are taken, it is important to get them from the rim and not from the center, first because of the inherent risk of perforating the stomach and second because histology of biopsies from the center only reveals necrosis and may fail to diagnose underlying neoplasia. Tumors in the stomach can either be benign, such as polyps, gastric adenomas or leiomyomas, or malignant such as adenocarcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, carcinoid, or GI stromal tumor (GIST) (Figure 3.50) (Bray and Neiger 2011). While benign tumors generally are smooth and small, malignant tumors tend to be irregular with a potentially ulcerated mucosa (peptic ulcers). Malignant gastric tumors tend to occur at the entrance into the antrum on the lesser curvature and may extend from the pylorus all along the greater or lesser curvature. Some tumors may be difficult to biopsy during gastroscopy if they are completely submu- cosal or if they are scirrhous and full-thickness biopsies are required. Potential abnormal findings in the duodenum are simi- lar to the stomach, i.e. abnormal-looking mucosa with increased friability, granularity, areas of focal bleeding, and erosions (Figures 3.51–3.53) (Table 3.6). In the duodenum, small whitish spicules can sometimes be seen which often indicate lymphatic dilation (Figure 3.54). Differentiation between lymphoplasmacytic IBD and small-cell lymphoma in cats is difficult and should be con- firmed by immunohistochemistry (Briscoe et al. 2011) or molecular clonality assays (Sabattini et al. 2016). This might be a primary pathology, but is more commonly identified secondary to gastritis or other inflammatory GI conditions. 3.5 Colonoscopy/Ileoscopy 3.5.1 Indications, Limitations As mentioned in indications of upper GI endoscopy, colo - noscopy is also used to find structural abnormalities of the colonic mucosa. Typical clinical signs in which colonos - copy is indicated are chronic large bowel diarrhea, hema- tochezia, tenesmus, or increased mucus on normal feces. Abnormal digital rectal findings might also be evaluated more closely with endoscopy and subsequent biopsies. Rarely, constipation or obstipation may need colonoscopy if an intraluminal mass or obstruction causing the consti- pation is seen on diagnostic imaging. Large bowel diarrhea, which is the most frequent reason for colonoscopy, will present with very frequent defecation but only small amounts, with increased urgency to defe - cate (tenesmus), fresh blood, and excess mucus. In cats, vomiting is also a common problem when large bowel dis - ease is present. Weight loss is an uncommon complaint in both species, unless the animal shows anorexia or a colonic tumor is present. Most animals with large bowel diarrhea do not need a colonoscopic procedure to obtain a diagnosis and to treat appropriately. A structured and logical workup might

Tumor recurrence after surgery or response to chemotherapy in lym - phoma is probably better investigated ultrasonographically. Indications for ileoscopy are similar to those for upper GI endoscopy (see Section 3.4.1). Vomiting is seen in up to 30% of cats with distal small intestinal or large intestinal problems thus taking biopsies from the ileum is attempted in all small animals in which upper GI endoscopy is indi- cated (Scott et al. 2011; Procoli et al. 2013). Therapeutic colonoscopy is used for balloon dilation of rectal strictures (Webb et al. 2007), laser ablation of colonic or rectal tumors, stenting of colonic strictures (Berent 2015), and rarely foreign body retrieval. The most important limitation for colonoscopy and ile - oscopy are functional diseases, motility abnormalities, or dietary problems. Also extraintestinal structural diseases or a disease process in the muscularis mucosa that cannot be reached with endoscopically taken biopsies. 3.5.2 Procedure The colon is a straight tube with some bends, so the tech- nique to learn colonoscopy is often quickly mastered. It is important to properly prepare the patient and use an appropriate endoscope, either flexible or rigid is available. Furthermore, most colonic diseases are diffuse throughout the entire colon, so taking biopsy samples only from the descending colon may be sufficient to reach a diagnosis. 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 66 performed to ensure that a rectal mass or stricture is not missed. The endoscope is well lubricated up to a length of about 20 cm and inserted 1–2 cm into the rectum. Air insuf- flation is started while an assistant closes the perianal tissue tightly around the insertion tube to prevent air leak - age. Enough air is insufflated to extend the rectal and colonic lumen, so that the colon is seen as a “tunnel” and the colonic mucosal folds straighten. An inability to dis - tend the lumen may indicate severe fibrosis with chronic inflammation, the presence of a stricture, or inadequate closure of the anal canal. With intermittent or constant air insufflation (as needed) the endoscope is slowly advanced as far as possible up the colon. The tip of the endoscope is kept in the center of the lumen by turning the inner angu- lation knob and rotational torque of the endoscope. No or only minor resistance should be encountered. If the center of the lumen cannot be seen, the endoscope is slowly with- drawn while more air is insufflated until the mucosa is vis - ible again. A partial fold separates the rectum from the descending colon but straightens almost completely with air insufflation. As the endoscope is advanced through the descending colon, the mucosa is inspected and lesions noted. The flex - ure at the junction of the descending colon to the trans - verse colon represents an approximate 90° change in direction upward (from left to right) but may also be less distinct and less than 90° in cats. To enter the transverse colon, the tip of the insertion tube is advanced almost against the mucosa of the flexure’s outer curve. Air is insuf- flated and the tip deflected gradually up while the endo - scope is advanced until the 90° bend is achieved. Visualization might be lost for a brief moment until the transverse colon is entered and distended by insufflation. In most cats, insufflation of the descending colon leads to distension of the complete large intestine. Once the endo - scope is in the transverse colon, the tip is straightened and centered in the middle of the lumen. It is then advanced slowly up to the flexure marking the beginning of the ascending colon. The endoscope should slide easily along the mucosa in most dogs. In cats, the intestinal tract is very pliant and thus manual support of the endoscope insertion tube from the outside by abdominal wall manipulation may be needed in some instances. If the lumen of the transverse colon is not visible, slight rotational torque and angulation of the outer deflection knob will often help. The transverse colon is very short (dog: 5–8 cm; cat 2–4 cm) and the flexure to the ascending colon looks similar to the flexure between descending and transverse colon. Advancement around this flexure is similar to the tech- nique utilized to navigate into the transverse colon, but the tip must now be deflected caudally. The ascending colon is equally short (dog: 3–6 cm; cat 1–2 cm) and at the end the ileocolonic sphincter enters in a star-like opening adjacent to the caecocolonic junction (Figure 3.57). 3.5 Colonoscopy yIleoscopy 67 Once the end of the colon is reached, one can see both the ileocolonic sphincter and the caecocolonic junction (Figure 3.57). In some dogs, the caecocolonic junction may be difficult to recognize as it is commonly open and does not appear like any junction at all. In others, it may be partly or mostly closed. In cats, the caecocolonic junction is also difficult to recognize as the cecum is just a very small blind ending sack at the end of the ascending colon. The ileocolonic sphincter is commonly easy to recognize in dogs as it protrudes like a small volcano into the lumen of the colon. This sphincter is commonly closed but may be open and can then be easily passed. In cats, the ileocolonic sphincter appears as a small mucosal fold. The cecum should be entered in dogs and visualized in cats where it is quite small. As the cecum may contain mucus and chime, it may have to be flushed to visualize the mucosa. Biopsies can easily been taken from the cecum. In middle-to-large breed dogs, it is often possible to enter the ileum (ileoscopy) to assess the mucosa and take ileal biop- sies. Due to the small ileocolonic sphincter, ileal intubation is rarely possible in cats and small breed dogs, unless using a pediatric gastroscope (<6.0 mm insertion tube diameter). If it is attempted, extreme caution is warranted to prevent colonic rupture. If necessary, blind biopsies can be col- lected from the ileum (Figure 3.58). The biopsy forceps is carefully advanced through the sphincter, opened in the ileum, gently advanced until some resistance is felt, the cups are closed, and the biopsy is retrieved. Inspection of the colonic mucosa is performed and biop- sies are taken as the endoscope is retracted. At the end of the procedure, the endoscope is completely withdrawn; evacuation of air in the colon is achieved by cessation of anal compression. In cats, insufflation of the large intestine can result in distension of the small intes - tine and ultimately of the stomach, leading to potential respiratory distress. If overdistension of the stomach has occurred, it can be relieved by passing a tube into the stomach and evacuating passively or by attaching the tube to a suction pump. During recovery from anesthesia the animal is supervised closely and extubated as late as possi- ble, as some animals, especially cats, tend to vomit. Gastric evacuation makes vomiting much less likely. 3.5.3 Normal Findings The colonic mucosa is pale pink, smooth and glistening, and submucosal blood vessels can usually be seen through- out the entire colon (Figure 3.60). Pale patches of lymphoid follicles with a diameter of 2–3 mm and small central depression are commonly present. Hyperemia should be carefully interpreted as it can occur secondary to warm water enemas, trauma from the rubber tube and endo - scope, or mucosal inflammation. Depending on the patient preparation (see Section 3.2.4), very little to large quantities of feces is present (Figure 3.60). A small amount of liquid is commonly present in the most dependent part of the colon and this can be suctioned out via the working channel. If fecal material is adhering to the mucosa, one may try to flush it off, but this will commonly result in large quantities of liquid in the lumen obstructing the view. Vigorous flushing may be accomplished with a large (60 ml in dogs, 20 ml in cats and small dogs) syringe with warm water attached to the working channel. If this is not successful, specialized pumps may need to be used. 3.5.4 Abnormal Findings Large intestinal disease commonly results in large bowel diarrhea or constipation. It must be remembered that vom- iting is another frequent complaint in cats with large bowel disease (Batchelor et al. 2013). Furthermore, hematochezia can be due to local problems in the large intestine or ano - rectal disease and must be differentiated from generalized coagulopathies. As mentioned, a thorough investigation for systemic diseases is warranted for all these problems prior to endoscopy. The most common abnormal large intestinal disease is some form of colitis. This can be limited to the colon or be part of IBD of the entire intestinal tract. Macroscopic appear - ance can range from fairly normal to a marked irregular, granular appearance, with friable, thickened mucosa and lymphoid hyperplasia. Similar to stomach and duodenum, an endoscopic disease activity score for the mucosal appear - ance of the colon has been proposed looking at friability, granularity, and erosions (Figures 3.61–3.63) (Slovak et al. 2015). The submucosal blood vessels are no longer vis - ible. Hyperemia to mucosal hemorrhage may be seen. In rare cases, erosions or ulcerated mucosa may be present (Figure 3.64). The macroscopic view cannot be differentiated

3.5 Colonoscopy yIleoscopy 69 from histiocytic ulcerative colitis (Figure 3.65), an uncom - mon form of colitis that is seen mostly in young dogs of various breeds (Boxer, French Bulldogs, Beagles, etc.) due to an infection with special invasive Escherichia coli . Rare causes of colitis, e.g. due to histoplasmosis, pythiosis, or protothecosis all look similar in endoscopy. Furthermore, the abnormal mucosa can undoubtedly be grossly m istaken as neoplasia thus it is essential to collect an adequate n umber of biopsies and not overinterpret the gross visual picture. Colonic tumors, especially lymphoma, can look identical to inflammatory colitis and must be differentiated by histo - pathology often with immunohistochemistry for a defini- tive diagnosis. Other large intestinal masses can be benign polyps or malignant tumors including adenocarcinoma and leiomyosarcoma, all being more focal and the latter often invading the lumen with an irregular proliferative appearance (Figure 3.66). Polyps can be broad based or pedunculated – since malignant transformation (Valerius et al. 1997) is possible, they are removed surgically with their mucosal attachment or via snare or electrocautery (Tsukamoto et al. 2012; Coleman et al. 2014). Obtaining diagnostic biopsies might be difficult in tumors as superfi- cial samples will often only reveal inflammation. It is imperative that multiple biopsies are obtained from the same location to reach representative neoplastic tissue. Other findings include fecal parasites (whipworms) (Figure 3.67), ileocolic or ileocecal intussusception (often diagnosed via ultrasound prior to endoscopy), or rectal stricture. This includes mainly removal of foreign bodies from the esoph- agus and stomach, feeding tube placement, and stricture dilation. Due to the fastidious feline eating behavior, GI foreign bodies are much less common in cats compared to dogs.
