3.6 ­herapeutic leeii le GI Endoscopy 73 the entire GI tract without causing any harm. Even pointed objects (needles, etc.) do not necessarily get stuck and may just be an incidental finding on an abdominal radiograph (Pratt et al. 2014). Nevertheless, foreign objects may get stuck almost anywhere in the GI tract and removal is needed. This can be achieved noninvasively via fluoroscopy or endos - copy, as long as the foreign object lies in the esophagus, stomach, or colon. The choice whether fluoroscopy or endoscopy is used depends mostly on availability and experi - ence of the veterinarian. Which technique is used often has evolved over time in a given clinic. Success rates are similar with both techniques being in the range of 85–90%. The most important aspect of successful retrieval is experience of the veterinarian and the personnel. Other factors, such as size of the patient, type of object, or length of time since for - eign body has been ingested are less important regarding success but they are crucial regarding complication during and after removal. Whether an object needs removal or can remain and pass naturally depends on various parameters. Foreign objects stuck in the esophagus always need removal by a veterinar - ian. This is not necessarily an emergency procedure but can be achieved within the next half day. Exceptions to this are if the animal is in pain, there is respiratory distress, if there is a very large object, or one which can easily perforate the esoph - agus (vertebral bones, etc.). Stones and other round objects in the stomach might be vomited if an emetic drug is given. Apomorphine hydrochloride in dogs (0.03 mg/kg given IV or IM or into the conjunctival sac and then rinsed off with saline when the object has been expelled) or xylocaine hydrochlo - ride in cats (1.1 mg/kg i.m. or s.c.) can be tried. Other round or blunted objects may pass spontaneously. If symptoms are mild and intermittent, one can take a “wait-and-see” approach with intermittent control-radiographs to monitor for success or possible complications such as intestinal obstruction. Endoscopy for foreign body removal from the esophagus and stomach is performed identically to diagnostic endos - copy. Before the procedure is initiated, however, the endoscopist must evaluate if the procedure can be performed successfully by assessing the type (sharp ends, needle, and ball) and size of the foreign object, the availa- ble retrieval instruments, as well as their own experience. Foreign bodies which can rarely be removed endoscopi- cally include large/wide hairballs, rubber objects having been in the stomach for prolonged periods of time, very large round objects (stone), or fishhooks with three barbed hooks. Foreign bodies in the intestine which are rarely removable endoscopically include thread or cloth passing the pylorus, both of which pose a major risk of intestinal plication during removal attempts (Hobday et al. 2014). It is clinically unwise to attempt object retrieval for prolonged periods of time which could be removed via exploratory surgery (potentially even without opening the stomach) in a fraction of the time. Diagnostic GI endoscopy is generally done as a one- person procedure and only obtaining biopsies is easier with a helping hand. With endoscopic foreign body retrieval this is the same. The endoscopist manipulates the endoscope and grasping instruments with one hand each and the helping hand only opens the retrieval instruments upon command. Even when long foreign body retrieval prongs are used alongside the endoscope, it is often easier if one person manipulates both, endoscope and prongs. The small movements necessary to visualize the object and grab it can rarely be communicated adequately between two peo - ple. Furthermore, the risk to damage the endoscope with the prongs is markedly reduced if only one person operates the instrument. Endoscopic foreign body removal is in general much quicker than surgery in the hands of an experienced clini- cian, requiring normally less than 30 minutes after anes - thesia has been induced. Other advantages of endoscopy over surgery are minimal-invasiveness and rapid discharge from the clinic. Owners must be made aware of potential complications (anesthesia related, unsuccessful procedure, and esophageal perforation) and thus should provide con- sent to surgical intervention during the same anesthesia in these instances. In those animals with severe esophagitis or perforation post foreign body removal, a temporary gas - trostomy feeding tube placement should be strongly con- sidered (see Section 3.6.2) and ideally is discussed with the owner prior to performing the procedure. Foreign body removal instruments can either pass through the working channel or are pushed alongside the Figure 3.67 Whipworms (­richuris vulpis) in a six-year-old German Shepherd dog with chronic large bowel diarrhea and a protein-losing enteropathy.

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 74 endoscope. Rat-tooth, alligator-jaws, multi-prong forceps, basket forceps, and snares (Figure 3.8) are available for 2.8 mm working channels and some even for as small as 2.0 mm working channels. While it is not necessary to have all of these available, with one type of prong and one type of grasper most objects can be successfully grasped and removed. The choice of the instrument lies mainly in the hands of the endoscopist and sometimes different instruments will need to be tried to grasp the object satis - factorily. It is of paramount importance that no foreign object is ever pulled into the working channel of the endo - scope and that the endoscope is not damaged by the prongs if used alongside the insertion tube . Foreign body prongs used alongside the endoscope have a much better grip - ping strength with the endoscope used only to visualize the foreign object. These must be small enough to pass alongside the endoscope without traumatizing the esoph - agus. A very long and sturdy instrument has recently become commercially available and may help ease the removal of more complicated foreign bodies (Figure 3.9). Another instrument which can be used in a similar man - ner is laparoscopic grasping forceps but it is often too short in middle-to-large breed dogs to reach the distal esophagus or stomach. A plastic overtube (e.g. old endotracheal tube cut to size, gastric lavage tubes) which acts to protect the mucosa and endoscope during the removal of sharp and pointed objects (e.g. needles, fish - hooks) is also helpful. The endoscope is introduced through the tube and the object pulled into the lumen of the tube (Figure 3.68). The endoscope, object, and tube are then removed as one unit. 3.6.1.1 Esophageal Foreign Body Removal Between 60 and 75% foreign objects stuck in the esophagus are lodged between the heart base and the diaphragm, another 20–35% are stuck over the heart base and the reminder in the cervical region (Lüthi and Neiger 1998). The most common type of foreign bodies in dogs will be some type of bony structure (70–90%) or a toy (Figure 3.30) (Gianella et al. 2009). In cats, sewing needles are also possible. Fishhooks can regularly be found but the fre - quency depends on geographical location (Figure 3.69). Interestingly, irrespective of all published case series, the terrier breeds are markedly over represented with around 40% of all esophageal foreign bodies found in these breeds. The West Highland White Terrier is over represented among them and 12–15% of all esophageal foreign bodies are found in this breed alone. Owners will often be aware of the possibility of an esophageal foreign body causing clinical signs such as retching, gagging, odynophagia, dys - phagia, or regurgitation. Differentiation between regurgi- tation and vomiting is commonly not possible for owners so they just report that the animal is “sick” and it will be up to the clinician to ask the pertinent questions to localize the problem. Since owners often see the animal “eating” a foreign body, most dogs present within hours after inges - tion. However, sometimes signs are vague, ingestion has not been observed, and esophageal foreign bodies have been reported to be present for over one month (Gianella et al. 2009). Other signs less commonly reported are drool- ing, anorexia, lethargy, fever, or coughing with the latter two occurring especially if there is aspiration pneumonia. In cases of esophageal perforation with subsequent medi- astinitis, pleuritis, and pyothorax, the animal may present in septic shock. Since needles and fishhooks may still have a thread or line attached, careful sublingual inspection is performed during the clinical examination. The thread or line should never be cut or pulled on until the foreign body has been removed, irrespective of the technique. Thoracic radiographs are often diagnostic for esophageal foreign bodies since most are radiodense. It is important to also obtain cervical radiographs (Figure 3.69). Careful inspection for pneumomediastinum and/or fluid accumu- lation may indicate potential esophageal perforation. Some obstructing foreign bodies are not radiodense. An air-filled esophagus cranial to such an object might give some indi- cation. Contrast studies with nonionic, iodinated contrast agents (diluted 1 : 1 with water, 10–15 ml for cats, 10–60 ml for dogs) given with a syringe may show the obstruction (Figure 3.20b). The authors prefer this type of contrast agent over barium if endoscopy is anticipated to take place, since barium aspirated into the endoscope might adhere and clog the working channel. 3.6 ­herapeutic leeii le GI Endoscopy 75 The procedure of endoscopic foreign body retrieval is similar to diagnostic esophagoscopy (see Section 3.3.2) with the animal lying in left lateral recumbency, so the esophagus is situated above the aorta. Careful inspection of the mucosa for potential foreign body-related injury is done during air insufflation. In cases of a perforated esoph- agus, respiratory compromise may occur and should be anticipated. Once the foreign body has been visualized, it is gripped firmly with a foreign body grasper or forceps. One needs some ingenuity to find the best instrument and the best place to grab the foreign object. Pushing a snare or wire basket behind the object and then slowly closing the instrument might help to seize the foreign body. The endo - scope is never used to push the object as this may harm the instrument and the esophagus. Bony foreign objects tend to be deeply seated in the mucosa and are not easily dislodged (Figure 3.70). Furthermore, muscular spasm often impacts the bone even more. Depending on the duration the foreign body has been present and its size, the esophagus may be lacerated and foam, blood, or food may be seen cranial to the foreign body (Figure 3.71). Before retrieval, the bone must be dis - lodged from the mucosa. Air insufflation through the endoscope may help, especially when someone manually (a) (b) (c) (d) Figure 3.69 Esophageal fishhook removal: (a) a lateral radiograph of a nine-year-old St. Bernhard Mountain dog with a fishhook in the cranial esophagus; (b) a ventrodorsal radiograph of the same dog clearly defining the fishhook; (c) the fishhook in this patient can be clearly seen during endoscopy and was successfully removed with a technique using a tube over the endoscope to protect both endoscope and esophageal mucosa; (d) another patient, an eight-year-old Jack Russel T errier, with a fishhook in its esophagus.

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 76 compresses the upper esophagus from the outside; unfor - tunately, there is high risk that air will pass into the stom- ach causing gastric overdistension and respiratory compromise. Once well visualized, the bone is firmly grabbed with a grasping forceps, ideally one used alongside the endoscope and not through the working channel, as this will allow a much better grip. Now slight but sturdy torqueing of the grasping forceps should take place to ply the bone free from the mucosa. Torqueing is applied in alternating clockwise and counterclockwise rotation with slowly increasing force. The goal is to completely free the bone from the esophageal mucosa. The amount of force required is difficult to describe and one must use enough force to free the foreign object but not too much so as not to cause perforation. As soon as the bone can move and rotate to some degree, the endoscope is removed and the grasping forceps with bone is retracted or the grasping forceps with grasped bone is removed under visual supervision with the endoscope a little ahead of the forceps. If a grasping instru- ment through the working channel is used, it is best to also use a plastic overtube so the bone can be pulled as close to the endoscope as possible without causing any damage (Figure 3.68). The endoscope, tube, and grasping forceps are all removed as one. Pointed objects are initially pushed or pulled out of the mucosa, most times in an aboral direction, with grasping instruments to dislodge them from the mucosa and then the pointed tips are grabbed and pulled toward the endoscope. A two-tube technique to dislodge fishhooks without use of an endoscope has been described (Tams and Spector 2011) and should be tried first in animals with a fishhook embedded in the esophagus or stomach. While some traction is needed, it must be remembered never to use force to remove a foreign object. Rarely, the foreign object is lost just before passing the UES and in these cases it may be possible to remove the object with a long curved grasping forceps under laryngoscopic control or by hand in large dogs. Deflating the endotracheal cuff or even extubation might be necessary in small animals with large foreign bodies to maneuver them through the UES. After removal, the esophagus is inspected for mucosal damage due to both the lodgement of the object as well as its removal (Figures 3.27d and 3.70). Moderate-to-marked esophagitis is treated with liquid oral sucralfate (1/4 to 1 g/animal q8h) and a gastric protectant (proton pump inhibitors, e.g. omeprazole 1 mg/ kg q12h) for one week. Analgesic drugs are given if needed. Repeated thoracic radiographs are indicated to look for pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax if moderate- to-marked mucosal damage is seen. If present, parenteral antibiotics are given. Surgical intervention is rarely needed for a perforated esophagus as most heal rapidly (two to four days) without major complications. Steroids to avoid stric- ture formation are most likely not helpful. In severe cases, a gastrostomy feeding tube (see Section 3.6.2) should be considered. Repeat endoscopic surveillance at a later time to visualize the healing process of a damaged mucosa is not indicated as repeated anesthesia is more likely to cause harm and clinical signs will be sufficient to point toward possible stricture occurrence. Strictures are uncommon complications (see Section 3.6.2.1) but have been reported in up to 20% of cases with successful endoscopic removal (Juvet et al. 2010). 3.6.1.1.1 Gastric Foreign Body Removal Not all visible gastric foreign bodies are the cause of symptoms and they are sometimes seen serendipitously during diagnostic imaging. 3.6 ­herapeutic le eiile GI Endoscopy 77 gastric foreign object ingestion in their pet (Hayes 2009). Almost all types of foreign objects are possible, stones, corn cobs, tree cones, peach or other fruit pits, toys, metal objects, needles, etc., and there are an infinite variety of things that dogs swallow (Figure 3.55). Foreign objects in the stomach of cats are less common but normally they need removal. As described for esophageal foreign bodies, terrier breeds are over represented to have gastric foreign objects (Hayes 2009). There is no predisposition for age or gender. The most important clinical sign of dogs and cats with a gastric foreign body is vomiting. Depending on the type and location, there may be signs of complete obstruction with projectile vomiting shortly after eating. In others, vomiting might occur intermittently or even rarely and be independent from food intake. Gastric foreign bodies might also cause other clinical signs, with or without vomiting, such as anorexia, abdominal pain, lethargy, or diarrhea. In large breed dogs, gastric foreign bodies are a risk factor for GDV (de Battisti et al. 2012). Perforation is possible, albeit rare, and will result in signs of peritonitis. The peritonitis may be localized if the hole, where the foreign body passed through, is sealed by omentum and no further gastric content leaks into the peritoneal cavity. Rarely, systemic signs due to gastric foreign bodies are present, such as hemolytic anemia with ingestion of zinc (Weingart and Kohn 2009), or neurological signs with ingestion of lead objects or alkali- containing batteries. Diagnostic imaging is the hallmark test to find gastric foreign bodies. While radiodense objects are readily seen, radiolucent objects are less easy visualized. Taking abdominal radiographs in right and left lateral recumbency will increase the chance to find foreign bodies (Harness and Biller 2015). Abdominal ultrasound often finds non- radiodense objects and is done prior to any contrast study. Contrast studies with air (negative gastrogram) are some - times diagnostic, especially if a cloth-type foreign body (socks, slip, etc.) in the antrum is suspected. Nonionic iodi- nated contrast agents can be used and are preferred over barium, should gastroscopy be planned within the next 24 hours. Endoscopy is sometimes done in an animal with chronic vomiting without any prior diagnostic imaging procedure, especially in case of financial constraints by the owners. This might not be “state of the art,” however obtaining GI biopsies in such a case is better than just giv - ing steroids. In such a case, a foreign body might be found fortuitously and it is removed endoscopically if possible. Since this foreign body might or might not be the cause of the clinical signs, performing a complete endoscopy with visualization of duodenum and entire stomach as well as obtaining biopsies is paramount in order not to miss something. While radiodense foreign bodies are easily seen on abdominal radiographs, finding them endoscopically in the stomach full of food might be less easy (Figure 3.55e). In animals that have eaten a short while ago or when food can clearly been seen on the radiograph, the clinician needs to decide whether it is prudent to wait until the food has passed into the duodenum or if foreign body retrieval should take place now. In the former case, there is the risk that the foreign body will also pass into the duodenum and be no longer retractable endoscopically. In the latter case, it might be virtually like searching for a needle in a haystack. As mentioned previously, it is unwise to search and try to remove a foreign body endoscopically in a stomach full with food when this could be done in a fraction of time with fluoroscopy or laparotomy. While endoscopy for gastric foreign body removal is started in left lateral recumbency, it may be necessary to rotate the animal to dorsal or even right lateral recumbency should visualization or grabbing of the object be difficult. This is commonly the case when the object lies in the fundus directly adjacent to the cardia so the endoscope sometimes passes by the foreign object and grabbing is not possible when the animal is on its left lateral side. The foreign object dictates the type of removal instru- ment that is used. Sharp objects are removed as previously discussed for esophageal foreign bodies. Using a rubber tubing sleeve over the endoscope can assist with retrieval and protect the mucosa of the stomach and esophagus from lacerations (Figure 3.68). Stones or rubber objects are grabbed with a basket or a prong forceps. Pulling them through the cardia may be difficult. It is easiest to have the object as close to the endoscope as possible. Pulling both as a single unit slowly, with intermittent/simultaneous insufflation will eventually assist with removal. With an air-filled stomach, an assistant can push from the outside in an aboral to oral direction on the stomach and at the same time the endoscopist pulls the endoscope with the foreign object through the LES. In some instances when a foreign object is grabbed with an instrument going through the working channel, but cannot be pulled through the LES, pushing a grasping instrument alongside the endoscope into the stomach and “open” the LES by opening the grasping jaws might help. Passing the UES might also be difficult and deflating the endotracheal cuff or even extubation may be necessary. 3.6.1.2 Duodenal Foreign Body Removal It is very uncommon to be able to grab and remove foreign bodies from the duodenum. These objects need surgical removal as many complications are possible, such as perfo - ration and intussusception. They may also just be too large or too far advanced to properly grasp for safe removal.

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 78 3.6.1.3 Colonic and Rectal Foreign Body Removal Most foreign objects that have found their way into the colon will be passed normally with feces. Rarely, pointy objects, such as sewing needles will have a risk of perforat- ing the descending colonic or rectal mucosa and it might be safer to quickly grab and remove them endoscopically instead of “wait-and-see” while taking intermittent radiographs. 3.6.2 Feeding Tube Placement It is now well accepted that enteral feeding should happen early in all patients since improved survival, benefits to immunological parameters, and enhanced barrier function have been reported (Marks 2013). Force feeding, appetite stimulation, or tube feeding are all possible in anorectic dogs or cats. Pharmacologic stimulants may be tried initially in animals with short-term decreased food intake. Mirtazapine (3.75–30 mg/dog q24h, 1/4 of a 7.5 mg tablet/ cat q72h) or cyproheptadine hydrochloride (dog: 0.2 mg/kg p.o. q12h; cat: 1–2 mg p.o. q12-24h) may stimulate eating, but will often not result in adequate caloric intake if a severe underlying condition is present. Similarly, force feeding does not often provide adequate food intake and may create food aversion, has the risk of aspiration pneumonia, and potentially erodes the human–animal bond. Furthermore, neither technique is useful in dys- phagic patients or those with motility abnormalities. Feeding via enteral feeding tubes circumvents these problems plus it can be used to administer drugs or aspirate gastric contents, depending on the type of tube used. For short-term feeding or if anesthesia is not possible, nasoesophageal feeding tubes are used. These have a small diameter so a special diet is necessary to be delivered. Furthermore, they should not be left in place for a pro- longed period of time (>7 days) and the tube may be regur- gitated during vomiting. Esophagostomy feeding tubes are a bit wider in diameter and thus easier to use, placement is still easy but anesthesia is necessary. If a problem in the esophagus is present, they are not used. Gastrostomy feed- ing tubes are commonly used in patients that need longer term feeding and in which a versatile tube is helpful. Gastrotomy tubes can be placed percutaneously during laparotomy. PEG technique is used most commonly but also a blind percutaneous technique, for example, via ELD applicator, has been described. Feeding tubes are indicated in all patients that have not eaten for three days or which were inappetent for seven days or more and in which decreased caloric intake is anticipated to occur in the next days. Animals with feeding difficulties (fractured jaw, oral neoplasia, esophageal disease, etc.), animals with common metabolic disturbances (renal, hepatic, endocrine, pancreatic, neoplastic, etc.), and cachectic animals that do not eat adequate amounts of food may also be candidates for feeding tube placement. PEG tubes have multiple advantages inasmuch as com- mercial food and special diets for specific diseases (e.g. chronic kidney disease, liver problems) can be administered, the daily caloric requirement is easily met, most oral drugs can be given through the tube (avoid crushing tablets with coating to resist gastric acidity), and the time for feeding is much reduced, not only in a hospital setting but also at home. PEG tubes are not placed when only short-term usage is anticipated (<7 days), in animals that are not good anesthetic candidates or when complications such as wound healing or severe coagulopathy are present. Whether permanent PEG tubes should be placed in animals with megaesophagus is unclear. The major drawback of PEG tubes is the cost of the tube (especially commercial kits) and of endoscopic placement. There are two types of PEG tubes available, commercial kits (from human medicine) which contain all materials for quick placement and “home-made” kits which are cheaper but more cumbersome and therefore time consuming. With both kits, the placement is very quick (commonly <10 minutes) and takes place the same way. A “guide wire” of suture material is pushed via a needle through the abdominal and gastric wall into the gastric lumen, grabbed endoscopically and pulled out through the esophagus and the mouth, the PEG tube is then attached and pulled via the “guide wire” into place. Furthermore, low-profile PEG tubes, also called buttons (Figure 3.72), are available as replacement of the initial tubes or to be placed at the beginning. Commercial PEG tubes are either silicone or polyure- thane and can withstand gastric acidity for the animal’s Figure 3.72 Various forms of low-profile feeding tubes, also called buttons. Some have an inflatable balloon while others have an internal flange.

The authors use both sizes depending on the size of the patient. The internal flange (bumper) is different between different brands but all are suitable for pets. The commercial kits con- tain – besides the feeding tube with conical end – the fol- lowing material, which is also needed in “home-made” kits: a large over-the-needle catheter (16G), double looped strong suture material (long enough to extend from mouth to side of abdomen, 70–100 cm), scalpel blade, material to fix the feeding tube on the skin outside of the abdomen (clips or suture), and an adaptor for a feeding syringe (Figure 3.73). Other materials needed for PEG tube place - ment are an endoscope with some type of retrieval instru- ment (rat tooth or snare), gauze squares, and possibly a body (pet-shirt) to keep the animal from self-trauma and tube auto-removal. 3.6.2.1 Procedure Endoscopy for PEG placement is similar to diagnostic gastroscopy but the animal lies in right lateral recumbency. If a full diagnostic endoscopy with biopsies is needed, this is done prior to PEG tube placement with the animal in left lateral recumbency; the animal is then turned over into right lateral recumbency for PEG tube placement. The left flank caudal to the ribs is clipped generously and surgically prepared (Figure 3.74a). After introducing the endoscope into the stomach, sufficient air is insufflated to push the gastric wall against the abdominal wall and displace abdominal organs (spleen, intestine). In cats or small dogs not too much air is used. Next the site of the tube placement is chosen by both seeing the transillumination from the endoscopic light through the body wall (Figure 3.74b) and by gently pushing the sterile sheath of the over-the-needle catheter or a finger with sterile glove into the prepared site on the flank at the desired location (Figure 3.74c); this will show as an indentation in the stomach endoscopically (Figure 3.74d), and the site can be adjusted by observation of the indentation with the endoscope. The best place for PEG placement is at the junction between the body and antrum. From the outside, this normally translates into few centimeter caudal to the last rib and ventral to the vertebral column (Figure 3.74). Next, the endoscope is withdrawn just to the cardia in order to prevent its accidental punc- ture. The over-the-needle catheter is pushed through the abdominal and gastric walls at about a 45° angle forward in the direction in which the indentation in the stomach was seen best (Figure 3.74f). Then, as soon as the catheter can be seen endoscopically (Figure 3.74g), it is pushed a little bit into the stomach and the stylet is removed (Figure 3.74h), the suture material is fed into the stomach and grabbed with the endoscope using a preplaced grasper (not a biopsy forceps) (Figure 3.74i). The suture material is pulled together with the endoscope out of the mouth (Figure 3.74j) and the gastrostomy tube is attached to the suture (Figure 3.74k). In commercial kits, there are two loops which are threaded over each other (Figure 3.74l) without knotting. The suture material entering the abdominal and gastric wall is now pulled (Figure 3.74m) and with it the attached feeding tube. The conical end will appear in the flank (Figure 3.74n) where a very small (1–(2) mm) inci- sion only in the skin is needed to pull the tube into place (Figure 3.74o). It is important that the skin incision is just big enough to pull the feeding tube through and the open- ing remains tight. In some animals, especially cats and small dogs, no incision at all is necessary. The inner flange remains in the stomach adjacent to the mucosa (Figure 3.74p). If there is too much distance between the gastric wall and the peritoneum, potential seepage of gas - tric content into the abdominal cavity and subsequent peri- tonitis could occur. If there is too much pressure, pressure necrosis of the mucosa could result. It is important to pull the inner flange snug but not too tight into the mucosa. Most commercial PEG tubes have clips to fix the tube and no suturing is needed (Figure 3.74q). The conical end is cut off to the correct length (depending on animal size) (Figure 3.74r) and the remainder of the fittings, including a syringe adaptor port, is attached according to the manu- facturer’s instructions (Figure 3.74s). A final endoscopic examination just before recovery is not really needed but might be a good way to counterbalance possible litigations; a picture with the inner flange in the appropriate position is taken (Figure 3.74p). An outer flange is created from tubing and the feeding tube is secured on the outside with Chinese finger-trap suture (Figure 3.75e) (Neiger et al. 2013). 3.6.2.2 Tube Management Once in place, the site is lightly wrapped with occlusive dressing, a body or stretch netting is commonly sufficient and a buster collar rarely needed. Daily cleaning of the stoma with warm water and iodine cream is important but enteral or parenteral antibiotic treatment is not needed either during placement or when the tube is in place and when no signs of inflammation/infection are seen. Feeding can be started 12–24 hours after placement. Control radiographs are not needed unless there is undue discomfort, increased temperature, or other signs of perito - nitis. In this case, a plain radiograph or giving iodinated contrast agent via the PEG tube might be helpful. It must be remembered that many animals will have mild pneumo - peritoneum shortly after PEG placement. Feeding is started initially with half of the daily calorie requirements and after one day, the full amount can be given. In animals with complete anorexia for seven days or longer, increasing the amount of food should happen over a longer period to avoid refeeding syndrome. In the first days, the animal is given five to six meals but after four to five days feeding can be reduced to three meals daily. It is important, however, to leave a new PEG tube for a minimum of 10–14 days, in animals with wound-healing problems even longer (up to 21 days), in order for proper stoma formation. If accidental loss happens within 48 hours of placement, the animal is carefully observed for signs of peritonitis. No immediate replacement is indicated in these animals. If accidental removal happens between 2 and 10 days post placement, replacement should take place in less than 4 hours to decrease the risk of disrup - tion of stoma formation. But even if loss takes place >10 days after placement, replacement of a new PEG tube needs to happen within 8–12 hours since the stoma will quickly seal and can no longer be seen. Replacement with low-profile devices (buttons) can be considered (Figure 3.72). The advantage of low-profile PEG tubes is, due to their compact design no external retention mechanism or sutures and no dressings are needed (Figure 3.76a). If a pet-body shirt should still be in place depends on the temperament of the animal (Figure 3.76b). Some replacement low-profile PEG tubes have a mushroom-tip which is stretched with an enclosed metal stylet to advance the elongated tip through a proper stoma. Other low-profile tubes have a balloon tip which is insufflated after pushing through the stoma to keep the tube in place. Newer low-profile PEG tubes can also be placed not just as a replacement of “normal” PEG tubes but as a one-step primary procedure (e.g. EndoVive One-Step Button, Boston Scientific) (Whittemoe and Bartges 2011). There are three ways for PEG tube removal: (i) in large breed dogs (>35 kg), the outer part is cut at the level of the abdominal wall and the flange on the inside is left to pass naturally in the feces. Since these tubes are made of mate- rial that remains soft even if left in the stomach for many months, there is an extremely low risk of an obstruction; (ii) in animals less than 20 kg, the internal flange must be retrieved endoscopically if it is cut at the level of the skin as the inside flange of commercial kits is commonly too big to pass naturally. During endoscopy, the internal part is grabbed tightly and securely first, before severing the tube; (iii) the PEG tube may also be removed percutaneously by traction on the tube. Depending on the inner flange/ button, a stylet may help to stretch and narrow it for easier retrieval. If no elongation of the flange is possible, percutaneous retrieval best takes place during anesthesia. With any of the removal techniques no further action is needed as the stoma will close within 8–12 hours. It may be prudent to keep the stoma covered with a pet-body shirt for esthetic purposes. 3.6.3 Stricture Dilation Esophageal strictures are a sequel of mucosal inflamma- tion of the esophagus that is deep enough to reach the mus- cularis mucosa. Healing may then result with intramural fibrosis and subsequent stricture formation (Figure 3.28). Common causes in dogs are chronic vomiting, post anes- thesia, ingestion of caustic agents, or post foreign-body retrieval. In cats, the most common reasons are ulcero- genic drug formulations and its retention within the esoph- agus, (e.g. doxycycline and clindamycin) or foreign body trauma (trichobezoar) (Adama-Moraitou et al. 2002). 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 84 Animals with esophageal strictures present with similar signs as all animals with esophageal problems. Sometimes a clue can be found during history taking (previous anes - thesia, drugs, removal, or foreign bodies, etc.). In general, it takes between one and four weeks after an insult has occurred for a stricture to form and to cause clinical signs. Diagnosis can be made by radiographic contrast studies, including fluoroscopy, or endoscopically. Differentiating a stricture from a tumor may be difficult radiographically. On endoscopy, a stricture presents as roundish circumfer - ential narrowing due to a fibrotic band that is sometimes whitish in color (Figure 3.28). If the stricture has recently formed, surrounding inflammation is often seen (see Section 3.3.4), but normal esophageal mucosa may also be present. The diameter varies from large enough to still be able to pass with a gastroscope to very small openings and in few cases the opening is not easily seen. Strictures can be very short, only a few millimeters long with only a thin ridge of fibrotic tissue, but they may also be up to 15 cm long. Depending on the underlying cause, single or multiple strictures can be present and, if the first stricture cannot be passed with the endoscope, additional caudal strictures are only sometimes seen in the distance or not seen at all. Most strictures are located in the intrathoracic esophagus but up to 20% can also be found in the cervical portion. There are multiple ways to treat strictures of the esopha- gus. While bougienage has been described (Sherding and Johnson 2011), it has largely been replaced by balloon catheter dilation, a procedure that is safe and with a success rate of up to 90% (Harai et al. 1995; Melendez et al. 1998). No parameter (duration, diameter, length, location, and cause) has been found to influence success or potential complications of stricture dilation. The balloon is placed into the stricture, then dilated slowly causing radial stretch- ing and tearing. This procedure results in few complica- tions if performed carefully. The most serious complication, esophageal perforation, has been reported to occur in around 5% of cases. Other potential treatment options are resection and anastomosis or salvage esophageal stenting (see Section 3.6.2.2). This procedure is either performed with endoscopic or fluoroscopic guidance. The former allows for assessment of the mucosa before and after the procedure but exact place - ment of the balloon into the stricture is more difficult. Therefore, it is best to combine both procedures together, assess the stricture before and after dilation visually by endos - copy but use fluoroscopy to place the balloon correctly. Endoscopic esophageal stricture dilation is performed as any diagnostic esophagoscopy with the animal under anesthesia and in left lateral recumbency. Since stricture dilation is a painful procedure, it is wise to use a morphine derivative for induction and continued for at least 24–48 hours afterward. Under endoscopic control, first a guide wire is placed through the stricture and the balloon catheter is placed over the wire alongside the endoscope into the stricture (Figure 3.77). There are balloon catheters available that can be used through the working channel; however, these are expensive and single-use only. Reused cardiac balloon catheters are cheap and very effective. The required length is commonly 6–10 cm, the diameter depends on animal size, from about 0.4–2.5 cm (Figure 3.78). Multiple balloons must be available, gradually increasing in diameter and length. Once within the stricture, the endoscope is withdrawn a few centimeters, the balloon inflated with a liquid (better than air) using a syringe or pump connected to a pressure gauge, up to the maximum pressure permitted for the balloon (Figure 3.79), kept in place for one to two minutes and then deflated. Correct placement is easiest under fluoroscopy, since a “waist” in the balloon with subsequent disappearance can be seen. Use a 1 : 1 mixture of contrast material and saline if fluoroscopy or radiography is utilized. Endoscopic visual inspection after the procedure should show some tears and bleeding (Figure 3.80). Without these signs, the dilation was probably not wide enough or the balloon slipped and the procedure must be repeated. There are no clear protocols about the diameter and length of balloon catheter usage. Diluted iodinated con- trast agent flushed into the esophagus is used to measure the diameter and length of the stricture(s) during fluoros - copy. A marker-catheter is placed to adjust for magnifica- tion. With endoscopy, one can “guestimate” the stricture diameter by placing a biopsy forceps against the stricture. A conservative approach is initially using a balloon about 2–4 mm wider than the stricture. In general, at least 1 cm of balloon length needs to be cranial and caudal of the stricture. The dilation is then repeated with a larger balloon, but caution must be used to avoid too forceful dilation and potential esophageal rup - ture. A balloon that is 50–100% larger than the stricture lumen has also been suggested to be used (Sherding and Johnson 2011). Generally, sequential dilations with gradu- ally larger balloons (2 mm increments) are used to get a balance between best opening with least mucosal tears. Other strictures in the esophagus are dealt with the same way as the first stricture. Ideally, at least a 10 mm balloon is used on all strictures so a gastroscope can pass into the stomach and visually assess the entire esophagus. Cats and small dogs generally can tolerate balloons 6–12 mm, while large breed dogs can tolerate a balloon width of 20–30 mm. To prevent stricture re-formation, the procedure is repeated twice weekly until there is no significant stricture visible endoscopically. The median number of dilation ses - sions is around three to five, depending on the study. Re-dilation when regurgitation reoccurs is another, albeit often less successful approach in the long run. After bal- loon dilation, the animal is treated for severe esophagitis with oral liquid sucralfate, a proton pump inhibitor, an antiemetic drug, and soft food (see gastric foreign body removal for doses). There are no studies showing that pred- nisone/prednisolone will help to prevent stricture forma- tion. In severe cases, endoscopically guided intralesional injection of triamcinolone (0.4 mg/kg) into the cranial edge of the stricture until a bleb is formed is probably more justi- fied. Endotherapy injection needles are available that can pass down the working channel of the endoscope. These injections should be made before balloon dilation is antici- pated. In animals with moderate-to-severe tears of the esophagus, placement of a gastrostomy feeding tube (see Section 3.6.2) is considered. Otherwise, the animal is fed with soft food 12–24 hours after the procedure. Life- threatening major tears are a rare occurrence (4–9%) and will result in mediastinitis with potential tension pneumo - thorax. Surgical repair is needed but carries risk of further stricture formation. In cases with recurrent stricture formation even with fre - quent re-ballooning (>8 times), placement of a self- expandable stent can be considered (see Section 3.6.2.2) (Glanemann et al. 2008; Battersby and Doyle 2010). 3.6.4 Stent Placement Stenting means placement of a stent into a narrowing. In the GI tract, this procedure has been used in esophageal stric - tures (most commonly benign strictures, but also due to a malignant obstruction) and obstructions in the colon/ rectum. Stenting an esophageal stricture is clearly a salvage pro - cedure. So far only few dogs and cats have been described (Glanemann et al. 2008; Battersby and Doyle 2010; Lam et al. 2013). Various stents have been used, including bio - degradable stents, self-expanding metallic stents, self- expanding plastic stents, and both uncovered and covered stents (Figure 3.81). Stents did improve dysphagia score immediately, but complication was common and often severe. Excessive gagging and hypersalivation was a fre - quent problem described by owners. In a report of nine dogs, stent migration occurred in three and recurrence of strictures after stents migrated or absorbed (biodegradable) in six (Lam et al. 2013). Therefore, esophageal stenting at the moment is considered a salvage procedure for cases with unsuccessful dilation with multiple attempts or if owners cannot afford multiple dilations. To place a stent in the esophagus, the following material must be available: balloons to dilate the stent (see Section 3.6.2.1), marker-catheters for sizing, guide wires, and, of course, stents. Biodegradable stents made from poly - dioxonone suture material as well as self-expandable stents are commercially available (e.g. Infiniti Medical or Boston Scientific). Covered stents have a higher risk of migration but a lower risk of re-obstruction. Initially, the procedure is the same as for esophageal balloon dilation but the stricture is not completely dilated. This can be performed when the stent is in place, but is not usually necessary. Ideally, fluoros - copy and endoscopy equipment are available at the same time. Some stents need to be sutured in place, so the cervical area needs clipping and surgical scrubbing. Exact step-by- step techniques how to place stents in the esophagus are described elsewhere (Palma and Berent 2015b).

3.7 Ad d itional ­echniEues in GI Endoscopy 87 3.6.5 P olyp Removal Polyps are quite rare and often incidental findings seen dur - ing endoscopy. It describes a circumscribed lesion protrud- ing from the GI mucosa. They can be pedunculated, sessile, or have a large base. Unless located at a sphincter or causing an obstruction, most polyps in small animals are clinically silent. In human medicine, it is well known that colonic polyps are precancerous and this has also been described in dogs. Therefore, not only do polyps causing clinical signs need to be removed but others need at least careful monitor - ing and if growth is seen, endoscopic or surgical removal should be discussed. Canine polyps in the GI tract are mainly found in the rectum (Figure 3.66d), rarely in the stomach (Figure 3.50a), and exceedingly rare in duodenum, esophagus, colon, and ileum. In cats, an adenomatous duo - denal polyp type is reported (Daure et al. 2017). Endoscopic polypectomy is considered the treatment of choice for GI polyp removal. To remove pedunculated polyps, a polypectomy snare and an electrocautery unit are needed. The snare is passed through the working channel of the endoscope and placed over the polyp. After confirming that no GI mucosa has been grabbed, the snare is gently closed until a mild color change of the polyp indicates a mild degree of ischemia. After tightly closing the snare, it is pulled toward the lumen of the organ to eliminate contact with the mucosa, when properly positioned the electrocautery current is activated, and the polyp is excised. Inspection of the cautery site for burns and completeness of removal is performed. This technique is mainly used for small polyps (<3 cm diameter) while larger polyps are excised in multiple smaller pieces. If a polyp is closely located to a sphincter (e.g. pylorus), is very large or sessile, complete surgical excision through the surrounding healthy mucosa is performed. A technique called mucosectomy can be used for removal of metaplastic/ dysplastic areas of the mucosa (Gualtieri 2013). 3.7 Additional T echniques in GI Endoscopy Newer techniques of minimal invasive diagnostic and ther- apeutic endoscopic procedure are constantly being devel- oped and used in human medicine. These techniques are then adopted in the veterinary field, sometimes with a short or long lag phase. The subsequent additional techniques have been described in dogs and/or cats, sometimes in healthy research animals, and sometimes in client-owned pets with clinical problems. Overall, the techniques are not widely used and improvement of the techniques will invariably happen in the future. Even newer endoscopic applications are developed at increasing speed, so the reader will need to keep an open mind for novelties on the horizon. 3.7 .1 Capsule Endoscopy Capsule endoscopy (CE) is a noninvasive endoscopic imaging technique that has been used for over a decade in human patients. The major advantage of CE is its nonin- vasiveness; not even an anesthetic procedure is required. Furthermore, if well prepared, the entire GI tract can be visually assessed. In veterinary medicine, the technique has mainly been used to assess anthelmintic efficacy of novel drugs – this way, dogs are no longer euthanized to evaluate drug effectiveness but the anthelmintic burden can be checked in vivo (Alice et al. 2015). Recently, CE has been used to detect mucosal lesions in dogs with GI bleed- ing (Davignon et al. 2016). The capsule did not pass the stomach in three of eight dogs, despite prokinetic drug administration. Lesions identified by CE were considered to represent a significant source of GI hemorrhage in four of seven dogs with active bleeding. Animals are fasted as for regular endoscopy. Several commercial capsule endoscopic systems are available (Olympus America, Infinity Medical, Given Imaging, etc.). The system generally contains an Endo Capsule that has no motor function and hence travels along the GI tract entirely through natural peristaltic waves. The camera is located in a plastic shell (about 11 × 26 mm) that encases a CCD chip camera, multiple light-emitting diodes, a battery, and a transmitter. The animal is fitted with multiple exter- nal antennae with an attached recorder unit. Data emis- sions are received by the external antennae that are positioned against the body wall, saved in the recorder unit, and later downloaded onto the workstation for analysis. Battery life is about eight hours. The capsule endoscope is then administered orally followed by about 5 ml of water. So far, CE has only been performed in dogs >5 k g. Major drawbacks are that no biopsy can be taken so the technique at the moment is useful only for visual inspection of the mucosa. Furthermore, obstruction by a capsule is possible needing surgical intervention. 3.7.2 Double Balloon Endosc opy With traditional endoscopy, it is not possible to progress fur - ther than a few centimeters into the jejunum using the oral approach, or a similar distance into the ileum via the anal approach. Double balloon endoscopy (DBE) was first used in human medicine in the beginning of the twenty-first cen- tury. The equipment consists of a 200 cm endoscope (exter - nal diameter 9.4 mm) and a 145 cm overtube (diameter

3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy 88 13.2 mm), both of which have a latex balloon attached to the tip. The two balloons are inflated and deflated in an alter - nating sequence to allow the endoscope to progress (push- ing phase) or fold the explored intestine behind the balloons (pulling phase). Due to the size of the endoscope, animal size is a limiting factor and a minimum forelimb length of 18 cm is recommended to successfully perform oral DBE. Oral DBE can be successfully done, if patient size is taken into account, in about 80–90% of dogs with an insertion depth of 287 ± 36 cm (Sarria et al. 2013a). Anal DPE was successful in nine dogs weighing 23 ± 2 kg and being able to insert the endoscope 212.2 ± 12.7 cm from the anus. This was estimated to assess about 45% of the total length of the small intestine (Sarriá et al. 2013b). Thus, DBE can be help - ful in diagnosing localized lesions in the jejunum, and bowel pathologies that are diffuse or that change depending on the affected section of the small intestine, such as irrita- ble bowel disease or lymphangiectasia. 3.7 .3 Confocal Endomicroscopy GI confocal endomicroscopy is an endoscopic modality that permits simultaneous wide field of view and real-time microscopic imaging of the mucosa. This is achieved either by integration of a confocal microscope into a conventional flexible endoscope, or with confocal mini-probes that can be passed through an endoscopic biopsy channel. Chromoendoscopy permits detailed evaluation of the mucosal surface while other modalities (i.e. endocytoscopy and confocal endomicroscopy) go deeper within the intes - tinal wall to visualize the submucosal architecture and single cells. In vivo confocal endomicroscopy has been recently used for cellular and subcellular imaging of gastric and intestinal topography in healthy dogs (Sharman et al. 2013, 2014), but animals with GI signs haven not been analyzed yet. 3.7.4 Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (NOTES) is a novel technique when a flexible endoscope is intro - duced through a natural orifice (stomach, vagina, bladder, bowel, and esophagus) into a body cavity (abdomen, thorax) to perform procedures (biopsy, splenectomy, falloptian tube ligation, etc.) under visual inspection. Dogs have been used extensively to demonstrate various tech- niques such as transgastric ovariectomy, transcolonic abscess drainage, and many others (Freeman et al. 2009; Moustarah et al. 2013). NOTES procedures require a collaborative team of an experienced gastroenterologist, manipulating the flexible endoscope and a surgeon experienced in laparoscopic surgery. The anesthetist must be aware of potential problems with air insufflation. The exact step-by-step pro - cedure is described in detail elsewhere (Freeman 2011). 3.7.5 Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a procedure used to image the biliary and pancreatic ductal system. It is performed with a combination of endoscopic and fluoroscopic procedures. The main indication in dogs is to assess animals with posthepatic icterus. In humans, biliary obstruction due to choleliths, tumors, papillary stenosis, pancreatitis, and biliary tract inflammation are investigated. ERCP can even be used therapeutically to extract choleliths, place drainage tubes and stents, or perform sphincterotomy and papillectomy. Few reports using ERCP are available in dogs and cats, mainly in healthy animals as feasibility studies (Spillmann et al. 2005a, b, 2011). To perform ERCP , a special side-view (90°) duodeno - scope is needed. With this endoscope, ERCP was success - fully possible in about 70% of dogs weighting >10 kg. Using a pediatric duodenoscope, cats >4 kg can undergo the pro - cedure. Guide wires and catheters to intubate the duodenal papilla as well as contrast agents are needed. Finally, the ERCP procedure needs fluoroscopic technique availability to visualize and record filling of the pancreatic and biliary tract. The exact step-by-step procedure is described in detail elsewhere (Spillmann 2013). 3.8 Care and Cleaning of GI Endoscopic Equipment To ensure long instrument life and minimize maintenance cost, endoscopes and endoscopic accessory instruments need to be treated with great care. Besides proper and care - ful handling, thorough cleaning, disinfection, and storage will significantly prolong the instruments life and usability. User-related damage is often caused by inappropriate han- dling and/or cleaning practices (Table 3.7). By thoroughly training selected staff in endoscope care, a veterinary prac- tice will benefit from the routine use of a quality endoscope for many years, and only minimal repairs will be required. It is recommended to post a laminated reference guide and supply list (Table 3.8) for the specific endoscope model used in the practice in a convenient location to help expe - dite the cleaning procedure. With a practical guide, a full cleaning of a flexible endoscope takes about 15–20 min- utes. Although cleaning and disinfection of a flexible

Immediately before the next procedure, the endoscopes and valves are reassembled, a leakage test is per - formed, and the endoscope is tested for proper function. 3.8.5 Sterilization or High-Level Disinfection The ideal situation would be that flexible endoscopes, as semi-critical devices, are heat sterilized or autoclaved. This is not possible because of their complexity and fragility. Thus, a chemical sterilization process or high-level disin- fection is deemed appropriate. Most high-quality endo - scopes may be sterilized/disinfected using ETO gas sterilization or low-temperature disinfection in a glutaral- dehyde solution. The specific manufacturer’s instructions are consulted before an endoscope is soaked in glutaralde - hyde or gas sterilized. During gas sterilization of flexible endoscopes, attachment of the pressure compensation cap is required to prevent damage. That same cap must be removed during a soaking procedure so that fluid damage is prevented. One system for soaking of flexible endoscopes is to use a plastic tubing system attached to the wall (Figure 3.88). A 2%, 14-day, low-surfactant glutaraldehyde solution such as Cidex® (by Johnson & Johnson, Cilag GmbH International) or MetriCide® (Metrex Research, Orange CA, USA) is usually recommended for low-temperature disinfection. Glutaraldehyde solutions can also be bought as 28- and 30-day solutions, but these contain surfactants, which reduce the surface tension of the solution, making it wetter than water, thus allowing the disinfectant to penetrate into small cracks and crevices. However, the rinse water may not penetrate these small cracks and therefore may leave a residue that can build up over time when small particles of organic matter contact the resid - ual glutaraldehyde. After soaking for the appropriate time in the glutaraldehyde solution according to the manufacturer’s recommendations, usually 20–45 min - utes at 20–25 °C for high-level disinfection while sterili - zation takes up to 10 hours, the instrumentation is thoroughly rinsed with sterile water, dried with sterile towels, and then laid out on a sterile drape ready for endoscopy. Accessory instrumentation that enters sterile sites must also be sterile. Most instrumentation not containing opti - cal parts are autoclavable. Camera heads have not been autoclavable in the past but are now available in autoclav - able models. For all endoscopic equipment, it must be verified with the manufacturer which cycles and temper - atures are allowed. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 4.1 Introduction Rhinoscopy allows easy direct visual and physical access to the nasal cavity (Figure 4.1), nasopharynx, and frontal sinuses for examination, diagnostic sample collection, most therapeutic procedures, and for most operative proce - dures. Initially, rhinoscopy was used primarily as a diag - nostic tool replacing the need for exploratory open surgical rhinotomy. As operative rhinoscopy has been developed, open surgical rhinotomy has been replaced with this mini- mally invasive approach. Because nasal diseases have simi- lar signs and symptoms, diagnosis is difficult without direct visual examination of the nasal cavity. Lack of accessibility to the nasal cavity for direct examination makes evalua- tion, diagnosis, and treatment difficult. Prior to successful application of rhinoscopy, full surgical exposure of the nasal cavity was required for anything but the most limited examinations. Morbidity associated with surgical exposure of the nasal cavity for diagnostic purposes is excessive. This is especially true when compared with rhinoscopy. Effective rhinoscopy requires irrigation with large quanti- ties of liquid. When irrigation was added to the protocol for rhinoscopy, it changed this procedure from being ineffec- tive due to inability to establish a clear visual field into the most effective approach to the nasal cavity. Dry rhinoscopy without fluid irrigation has been suggested and may be applicable to certain disorders but is limited to those condi- tions without exudate or bleeding (Oechtering et al. 2016a). Signs and symptoms of nasal disease include sneezing; mucoid, mucopurulent, bloody, or mixed nasal discharge; epistaxis; pain; facial distortion; and nasal airway obstruc- tion. These findings are variably seen with a variety of nasal diseases and of them none are specific. Facial distor - tion or swelling is indicative of neoplasia and nasal pain suggests fungal infection, but neither can be relied on for a diagnosis. Adequate examination of the nasal cavity is therefore vital to establish a diagnosis. Effective rhinoscopy is essential for assessment of the nasal cavity but cannot be relied on by itself to provide a diagnosis in all cases. A protocol was developed that com- bines procedures necessary to provide consistent success in establishing accurate diagnoses in cases of nasal disease. History, physical examination, computed tomography (CT), culture and sensitivity, rhinoscopy, histopathology, fungal serology, and allergy screening may all be necessary. The sequence of events in diagnostic evaluation of the nasal cavity is also important, otherwise essential diagnos - tic information can be altered or destroyed. With a complete and sequential approach to chronic nasal disease using rhinoscopy, successful diagnoses have been achieved in over 90% of cases without surgical explo - ration. The high diagnostic yield is primarily attributed to five things: performing rhinoscopy, using rhinoscopy as part of a complete diagnostic evaluation rather than as a technique by itself, using irrigation during rhinoscopy to enhance visualization, using rigid telescopes rather than flexible endoscopes, and using large rigid biopsy forceps to obtain large deep biopsies. CT was suggested as a preferred first-line procedure for diagnosing nasal tumors over rhinoscopy, but this study only looked at cases with a confirmed diagnosis of neopla- sia skewing the results (Fink et al. 2015). To provide an accurate answer to this question, it would be necessary to look at all cases of nasal disease and compare the diagnos - tic accuracy of the two procedures. Blind biopsy has also been suggested as equal in accuracy to rhinoscopy-guided biopsy (Harris et al. 2014) but this is only true for very large nasal masses as small lesions are easily missed. Blind biopsy that returns a diagnosis of non-neoplastic disease leaves the question, was the lesion missed or is this truly Timothy C. Rhinoscopy is essential to accurate diag - nosis of nasal disease (Rösch et al. 2019). Treatment of nasal disease with rhinoscopy has become the standard of care. There is no longer a need for the trau- matic and painful procedure of open rhinotomy from either a dorsal or ventral approach. In most cases, operat - ing times are much shorter with rhinoscopy, morbidity is less, pain is dramatically reduced, and recovery is much faster and easier than it is with an open rhinotomy. 4.2 Indications A complete diagnostic approach to nasal disease, includ - ing rhinoscopy, is indicated when there is acute severe dis - ease, chronic disease, when nasal disease is unresponsive to treatment, or when we need more information than we can get with a less invasive technique. Persistent severe sneezing that has not responded to initial conservative treatment warrants diagnostic evaluation of the nasal cav - ity even when the condition is of short duration. Profuse epistaxis even if not life threatening is another acute con - dition where a complete systematic approach to diagnosis is indicated including evaluation to rule out possible sys - temic etiologies. Acute conditions requiring complete nasal diagnostic evaluation are unusual, but they do occur. Reverse sneezing, commonly associated with nasopharyn - geal disease, is also an indication for rhinoscopy. The most common indication for rhinoscopy is chronic unresolved disease that has not responded to treatment and when a diagnosis has not been established. Common presenting complaints associated with nasal disease include sneezing, reverse sneezing, nasal discharge, epistaxis, partial or complete nasal obstruc - tion, difficult or noisy breathing, coughing, gagging or choking, rubbing or scratching at the nose or face, ulcera - tion of the rhinarium, facial or nasal pain, facial swelling or distortion, nasal or oral odor, and knowledge of foreign body inhalation or ingestion (Tables 4.1 and 4.2). Nasal disease may also be manifested systemically with nonspe - cific symptoms of malaise, lethargy, poor appetite, weight loss, and unkempt hair coat. Initial evaluation of patients with systemic symptoms is directed at differentiation of the primary disease process. Determining if the nasal symptoms are an indication of primary nasal disease with secondary systemic involvement, or if the nasal signs are secondary to systemic disease is important in directing the course of the diagnostic evaluation. 4.2 Innications 101 obtained during an ongoing evaluation is required to make this differentiation. Diagnostic approach to nasal disease is divided into three segments (Table 4.3). The initial phase includes those stud- ies and procedures that are done in the awake patient. History, physical examination, blood tests including blood chemistries, CBC, and coagulation assessment; and tho - racic imaging may all be necessary. Progression through this portion of the protocol is required to determine that primary nasal disease exists, complete nasal workup is indicated, and the patient is an acceptable candidate for general anesthesia. The second phase requires general anesthesia and is focused on the nasal cavity, frontal sinuses, and nasophar - ynx. For years, nasal radiographs were the standard of care for imaging of the nasal cavity but have been replaced with the far more sophisticated technique of CT (Auger et al. 2016; Auler et al. 2015; De Rycke et al. 2003; Friling et al. 2014; Lefebvre et al. 2005; Saunders and van Bree 2003; Saunders et al. 2003, 2004; Uosyte et al. 2015; Vansteenkiste et al. 2014). Dental radiographs are indi- cated if dental disease is suspected as a possible cause of the nasal disease. After imaging, nasal culture sample col- lection is performed prior to rhinoscopy. If cultures are not indicated after rhinoscopy has been performed, the sam- ples are discarded. Rhinoscopy is performed last after imaging and culture sample collection. The third phase is undertaken if a diagnosis is not estab - lished with the first two phases. At this time, allergy test - ing, viral cultures, fungal serology, open surgical exploration of the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses, and additional systemic evaluations are indicated. Allergy test - ing is the only commonly performed testing in this group. Open exploratory rhinotomy is no longer an accepted diagnostic procedure. The last open rhinotomy performed by the author was for a chronic rhinitis in a working police dog that did not have a diagnosis after repeated diagnostic procedures including multiple rhinoscopies. An open rhi- notomy was performed with total turbinectomy and all the removed tissue was sent for histopathology. No additional information was obtained with surgery, an etiology was not established, and there was no improvement in the patient. Physical examination is first directed at determining if the nasal cavity is the site of the primary disease process. Attention is then directed at determining the extent, location, and character of the nasal disease. Character and side or sides of nasal discharge is determined. Some dogs and cats will lick discharge away from their nose, so absence of discharge at the time of examination does not exclude nasal disease. Ulcerations on or around the external nares are significant and can be an extension from the primary disease, secondary due to irritation and licking, and can be from systemic disease. Patency of the nasal passages is determined by evaluating an area for condensation on a microscope slide when held just in front of the nares, holding a tuft of hair or thread rostral to the external nares and observing movement with inha- lation and exhalation, or by occluding one nares and observing for dyspnea or increased nasal airway sounds on auscultation. Facial or rostral nasal pain or sensitivity is evaluated. The entire nasal and facial area is carefully palpated and visualized for swellings, distortion, or soft areas due to bone lysis. The nasal cavity and pharyngeal area are auscultated and percussed for differences in density. Otoscopy is performed looking for possible masses, foreign bodies, or middle ear involvement. This is especially important in cats due to the incidence of nasopharyngeal polyps. Cats presenting with ear tumors other than polyps are also candidates for nasal cavity assessment. Oral cavity examination is carefully per - formed, and the upper dental arcade is inspected for dis - eased, damaged or infected teeth and gums, masses or swellings, soft areas of bone lysis in the hard palate, and injuries. If oral examination cannot be completed suc- cessfully in the awake patient, sedation may be employed, or the examination may be completed after anesthesia is induced. The eyes are inspected for visual symmetry, function, and are palpated for resistance to caudal dis - placement. Pharyngeal and pre-scapular lymph nodes are assessed. Examination of the patient to this point will, in most cases, provide sufficient information to establish an ordered rule out list of nasal diseases (Table 4.4), systemic diseases if indicated, and to direct the course of further evaluation. 4 Rhinoscopy 102 4.3 Instrumentation A video endoscopy system with a video camera, monitor, and light source are needed to perform rhinoscopy. See Chapters 1 and 2 for details on this equipment. Rigid endoscopes and sheaths used for rhinoscopy (Table 4.5) include a 1.9 mm diameter arthroscope, a 2.4 mm arthroscope, a 9.5 Fr diameter one-piece cystoscope or operating telescope, and the 2.7 mm diameter multipur - pose rigid telescope (MPRT, Figure 2.26). These telescopes have a viewing angle of 30°. The 1.9 and 2.4 mm diameter arthroscopes have a length of 10 cm and are used with arthroscopy sheaths. The arthroscopy sheaths for the 1.9 and 2.4 mm telescopes do not have a working channel, hav - ing a working length of 8.5 cm, lock to the telescopes, and have 1 Luer irrigation port. The 9.5 Fr cystoscopy/operating telescope is a 1-piece instrument with an integral telescope and sheath having an outer diameter of 9.5 Fr, a working length of 14 cm, 2 Luer ports with stopcocks, and a 3 Fr working channel (Figure 2.31). The 2.7 mm MPRT has a length of 18.0 cm and is used with either an arthroscopy sheath or an operating/cystoscopy sheath (Figure 2.30). An arthroscopy sheath for the 2.7 mm telescope with an out - side diameter of 4.0 mm, a working length of 13.5 cm, a sin- gle Luer attachment with a stopcock for fluid irrigation locks to the telescope, and does not have a working chan- nel (Figure 2.30). The cystoscopy or operating sheath for the 2.7 mm MPRT has an outer diameter of 14.5 Fr (oval shaped with dimensions of 4.0 mm × 5.5 mm), a working length of 15 cm, 2 Luer irrigation ports with stopcocks, locks to the telescope, and has a 5 Fr biopsy channel (Figure 2.30). The sizes of these three telescopes with their sheaths are well suited for rhinoscopy allowing examination of the full range of small animal patients. The 2.7 mm MPRT with its two cannulas is the most commonly used telescope for rhi- noscopy and works well in most cats and dogs. Very small dogs and cats are examined more easily with the 1.9 mm diameter arthroscope but its short length makes it inade - quate for larger patients. The 9.5 Fr one-piece cystoscope also works well for smaller patients and is long enough for most large dogs. For some giant breeds of dogs, the length of the 9.5 Fr 1-piece telescope and the 2.7 mm MPRT are inadequate for complete examination of the nasal cavity and nasopharynx. Occasionally, a longer telescope is required. The 4.0 Cystoscope (Figure 2.26) with one of its sheaths (Figure 2.35) is effective in giant breed dogs. A pri- mary advantage of all these instruments is the capacity for continuous high-flow irrigation during rhinoscopy to allow a clear visual field for examinations. The primary advantages of arthroscopy sheaths over those with working channels is that they are smaller, round rather than oval, and therefore are easier to pass through the nasal cavity. The primary disadvantage of their use is that they do not have an instrument or working channel. Biopsy, other sample collection, and operative procedures are performed by passing biopsy forceps or other instru- mentation outside and parallel to these sheaths. Diode laser fibers are used exclusively with sheaths with working channels to provide accurate positioning of the laser fiber tip. Small flexible fiberoptic endoscopes are also used for rhi- noscopy. Bronchoscopes, pediatric bronchoscopes, flexible cystourethroscopes, and other small flexible endoscopes in the 2.5–5.0 mm diameter range are applicable. These small flexible instruments allow retrograde examination of the nasopharynx and caudal portions of the nasal cavity with some endoscopists indicating advantages in this applica- tion over rigid instrumentation. Rigid instrumentation placed from the rostral approach is effectively passed into the nasopharynx in almost all cases eliminating the need for flexible endoscopes. Flexible instruments may permit examination of the caudal nasal cavity but have the disad- vantage of limited or no ability to irrigate during examina- tion which will impair visibility. They also have the disadvantages of small instrument working channel size, and the 180° flexion required for access makes manipula- tions more difficult. Examination performed with rigid telescopes is superior to that which is performed with flex - ible endoscopes. An extensive array of instrumentation is available for rhinoscopy, sinoscopy, pharyngoscopy, and laryngoscopy in humans but many are not well suited for application in small animals because of differences in size and anatomy. Most operative instruments are too large for application in small animal practice. Smaller rigid telescopes and instru- ments are applicable in size or design but are very similar to the recommended telescopes and instruments. Thus, they do not provide any advantage over the listed equip - ment. The extent of irrigation necessary for rhinoscopy in animals is not employed in humans so the endoscopes are not designed with this need in mind and many do not pro - vide for sufficient fluid flow. With the recommended sheaths, continuous irrigation, which is essential for effec- tive rhinoscopy, can be employed during the entire procedure. In addition to the above endoscopic instrumentation, a diode Laser is essential for effective operative rhinoscopy procedures. Advantages of diode lasers are that they work in a liquid medium and the laser beam is directed through a flexible Quartz fiber ideally suited to the working chan- nels of telescope sheaths. A 30–50-W laser is recommended with settings in the higher range use for tissue ablation. Most diode lasers have the potential to produce continuous or pulsed energy with the continuous energy setting used almost exclusively for removing nasal tissue. The flexible quartz fibers used to transmit the laser beam into the nasal cavity are available in sizes ranging from 400 to 1000 (Table 4.7) microns with fibers of 600–1000 μm used most commonly for nasal tissue ablation. 4.4 Preparation of the Patient A significant percentage of chronic nasal disease cases are in geriatric patients and appropriate preanesthetic assess - ment is indicated consisting of history, physical examina- tion, blood chemistry profile, CBC, UA, coagulation parameters, thoracic radiographs, and EKG. There is also a segment of younger patients who demonstrate signs of significant systemic disease indicating a need for similar preanesthetic evaluation. Young healthy patients may not require as extensive an evaluation. After completion of a general preanesthetic patient appropriate assessment and that portion of the nasal specific diagnostic protocol not requiring anesthesia, the patient is anesthetized for the remainder of the nasal workup. A surgical plane of general anesthesia is required for imaging and for rhinoscopy. The nasal cavity is very sensi- tive and sedation or a light plane of anesthesia is inade - quate to allow examination, imaging, sample collection, or operative procedures. If a surgical plane of anesthesia has not been achieved, violent sneezing is induced during rhi- noscopy causing increased trauma to the patient’s nasal cavity and possible damage to instrumentation. Palatine or infraorbital nerve blocks are used for all but the simplest rhinoscopy to decrease the depth of general anesthesia required and for pain management. General anesthesia is required for diagnostic nasal CT to allow adequate positioning and to maintain immobility during the procedure.
