Proper positioning for nasal radiographs cannot be achieved without anesthesia. Culture sample collection without risk of patient trauma and with minimal risk of sample contamination also requires general anesthesia. Some patients are higher anes - thetic risks and care is taken, but with the currently avail- able anesthetics, appropriate supportive treatment, and with adequate monitoring the risk is minimized. Stress to the patient is less with appropriate anesthesia than with sedation and physical restraint. Time savings and increased quality of diagnostic information is enhanced beyond the risk involved in most cases. An anesthetic regimen is used for rhinoscopy that is safe for the type of patient involved, allows adequate depth and analgesia to prevent sneezing during rhinos - copy, does not require an excessive recovery period or result in excitability during recovery, and provides ade - quate postoperative analgesia. An extensive variety of effective anesthesia protocols and drugs are currently in use and the specific program is based on patient needs, the above requirements specific for rhinoscopy, and on preference of the individual practice. The variability is too great and is continually changing making a specific list of drugs unnecessary. Patients are fasted for 12 hours prior to anesthetic induc- tion but water is allowed during this interval. Preanesthetic medications are administered to reduce anxiety and provide preemptive pain management. An indwelling intravenous catheter is placed, and supportive fluid ther - apy is initiated. Anesthesia is induced with a short-acting or reversible intravenous anesthetic, a cuffed endotracheal tube is placed, and the cuff is inflated. A watertight tra- cheal seal is essential to prevent tracheal aspiration of fluid used for nasal irrigation during rhinoscopy. Anesthesia maintenance is with either an inhalant anesthetic or a CRI. Appropriate monitoring including EKG, blood pressure, pulse oximeter, and capnometer are initiated. 4.5 T echnique An appropriate sequence of procedures is important to pre - vent deletion or distortion of information by previous diag - nostic techniques. Under anesthesia, the oral cavity is examined carefully with particular attention being paid to the maxillary teeth, gums, hard and soft palates, caudal pharyngeal area, and to the nasopharynx. The soft palate is retracted rostrally with an ovariohysterectomy hook or other soft tissue retractor to allow evaluation of the caudal nasopharyngeal area. A CT of the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses is the first diagnostic procedure performed after the above examination. Scanning range for the CT extends from immediately rostral to and including the rostral sur - face of the nasal planum to the caudal margin of the osse - ous bulla. Including the rostral surface of the nasal planum allows measurement of distance from this landmark for future radiation therapy when that treatment is indicated. Evaluation of the CT is performed prior to proceeding with rhinoscopy. Following CT, bacterial and fungal culture samples are obtained. Rhinoscopy is performed as the last procedure in the protocol. If rhinoscopy is performed first, the fluid used for irrigation, bleeding induced by the proce - dure, and tissue removed for biopsy or treatment change the imaged appearance of the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses (Uosyte et al. 2015). Rhinoscopy not only intro - duces fluid density into the nasal cavity but also onto the hair and skin outside the nasal cavity. Fluid and bleeding also alter the bacterial or fungal population in the nasal cavity. Performing CT prior to rhinoscopy is also important to assess the location and extent of lesions for direction of rhinoscopic examination to areas of interest. Collection of culture samples is also done after the CT is performed because sample collection techniques that induce nasal bleeding can alter radiographic appearance. Appropriate samples are collected during rhinoscopy for histopathology and if fungal colonies are seen, fungal culture samples are collected by biopsy of the colonies. If specific gross find- ings establish a diagnosis, or exclude any of the rule outs, samples that are not needed are discarded and costs of these tests are eliminated without decreasing the potential for successful diagnosis. If there are no conclusive find- ings, all of the collected samples are submitted. This approach is more economical for the client and safer for the patient than re-anesthetizing the patient for a second rhinoscopy to obtain additional samples. 4.5.1 Radiographic Imaging CT has replaced radiographs as the procedure of choice for imaging of the nasal cavity (Auger et al. 2016; Auler et al. 2015; De Rycke et al. 2003; Fink et al. 2015; Friling et al. 2014; Lefebvre et al. 2005; Saunders and van Bree 2003; Saunders et al. 2003, 2004; Uosyte et al. 2015; Vansteenkiste et al. 2014). Compared with the information obtained with a CT, radiographs are inadequate. CT is per - formed as the initial procedure after induction of anesthe - sia. Radiographs are the initial diagnostic procedure performed after the patient is anes - thetized. A series of four to six radiographic views are needed to adequately image the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses. Attention to detail that achieves well-positioned radiographs can provide important information whereas poorly positioned images border on being worthless. The first view is a straight lateral projection of the nasal cavity extending from the rostral tip of the nares to the cau- dal end of the soft palate, and from the frontal sinuses dor - sally to and including the hard palate and teeth ventrally (Figure 4.5). A sec- ond lateral film is taken at a higher exposure to adequately image the nasopharynx because this area will be underex - posed on the initial film (Figure 4.7). Passage of a culture swab into the nasal cavity can induce bleeding that will change the appearance of radiographs. Culture samples are collected before rhinoscopy. Passage of the endoscope into the nasal cavity could potentially cause bacterial contamination. Reduction in bacterial pop - ulation caused by copious saline irrigation used during rhi- noscopic examination is a more likely consequence than the chances for bacterial contamination. Either action pro - duces a change in the bacterial population in the nasal cavity. Two techniques have been used for nasal culture sample collection. One uses culture swabs that are passed through surgically prepared external nares. A second uses a cathe - ter that is passed through the nares and a nasal wash is performed. For the first technique, the external nares are surgically prepared with alternating povidone iodine or chlorhexidine and alcohol scrubs. A culture swab or prefer - ably a micro swab is passed through the nares into the nasal cavity as far as it will go easily or to the level of known pathology based on CT findings. The other technique uti- lizes a small-diameter (3 or 5 Fr) catheter, syringe, and ster - ile saline. The catheter is placed into the nasal cavity and the nasal cavity is irrigated with saline followed by aspira- tion. This technique is similar to that used for transtracheal wash sample collection. Part of this sample is submitted for cytological evaluation if indicated. Both techniques are acceptable and provide adequate samples for bacterial and fungal cultures. The validity of nasal culturing has been debated due to the wide variety of normal bacterial flora (Clapper and Meade 1963; Dorn et al. 2017; Tress et al. 2017) and the possibility of secondary bacterial growth unrelated to the primary disease process. The validity of listed normal bac- terial flora can be questioned because of the ability of dogs and cats to mask signs of nasal disease until an advanced stage is reached. Unless all the dogs and cats used for estab - lishing what is considered normal received a complete diagnostic nasal evaluation including rhinoscopy, their “normal” status at the time of sample collection is subject to question. A significant growth of a pathogenic organism is an indi- cation for treatment even if the identified bacteria are not the primary etiology of the nasal disease. Secondary infec- tions impact the ability to treat the primary etiology. 4.5.3 Rhinoscopy After all the above procedures have been completed, rhi- noscopy is performed. The patient is placed in lateral recumbency with its head on an absorbent towel and the rostral end of the nose extending over the edge of the table. The mouth is held open to allow easy fluid egress. Fluid flow through the nasal passages, nasopharynx, and oral cavity is facilitated by this positioning improving visualiza- tion during the procedure. Either lateral recumbent posi- tion is acceptable but if the condition being evaluated is unilateral, the diseased side is usually placed on the down- side. Chances for contamination of the normal side are minimal due to the copious quantities of irrigant employed and easy access for drainage through the external nares and nasopharynx. Alternate positioning with the patient in ventral recum- bency has been utilized and is recommended by many endoscopists (Saylor and Williams 2011). This position is less effective than lateral recumbency as it interferes with fluid flow. For this position, the head and neck are typically placed on a towel or positioner. This position compresses the caudal nasopharynx and pharynx closing the lumen of these structures thus obstructing fluid flow. A well-sealed tracheal airway is essential during rhinos - copy and an endotracheal tube with an inflated cuff is always employed. Effectiveness of the tracheal seal is always retested after CT has been performed and culture samples collected, immediately prior to initiation of irriga-

4.5 Techniiue 109 tion for rhinoscopy, even if adequacy of cuff inflation was tested at the time of intubation. Table height is adjusted to allow the investigator to sit or stand comfortably during the procedure. A waste container is placed under the table directly below the rostral end of the patient’s nose to catch runoff irrigant. If the examiner is seated, their knees are covered with absorbent towels or waterproof drape material. Large quantities of irrigation solution are used (up to 4 l) during examination. If ade - quate preparation is not made, the examiner and surround- ing area become soaked. Irrigation used for rhinoscopy employs arthroscopy or cystoscopy sheaths with their Luer connection ports attached to a standard intravenous administration set and containers of physiologic saline solution or any other crys - talloid solution that does not contain glucose. Arthroscopy and cystoscopy sheaths are ideally suited for rhinoscopy because the design application for arthroscopy and cystos - copy requires similar fluid irrigation. Fluids containing dextrose are not recommended because cleanup after the procedure is difficult. The fluid container is placed as high above the patient as is convenient, usually about 70 cm, and the intravenous drip set control is opened fully. Fluid flow is then controlled with the endoscope sheath stopcock as it is more convenient for the operator. With completion of the above preparation, rhinoscopy is begun. Fluid flow is initiated, and the endoscope is passed into one of the external nares. If a bilateral disease process is present, the side examined first is not of importance. If unilateral disease is present, the normal side is usually evaluated first to minimize changes induced by fluid, exu- date, and blood from examination of the abnormal side. Careful examination of a normal nasal cavity will produce only limited bleeding and will not have a significant impact on findings in the abnormal side. The order of examination is not critical, and specifics of an individual case may indi- cate examination of the involved side first. If the patient is positioned in lateral recumbency with the normal side uppermost, the risk of contamination of the normal side to the extent that examination is affected is minimal. A systematic approach to examination of the nasal cavity is taken to ensure visualization of all accessible areas (Video 4.1). Identification of all normal anatomic struc- tures and turbinates by name is not required. Many of the disease processes seen in the nose produce destruction, dis - tortion, or replacement of the turbinates and identification of normal structures is not possible. Depending on the size of the patient, a variable extent of the nasal cavity is exam- ined. In larger patients, a greater percentage of the nasal cavity is accessible for examination. The entire nasal cavity cannot be examined endoscopically with either rigid instrumentation, flexible endoscopes, or both. A signifi- cant portion of the nasal cavity can however be examined even in small dogs and cats. The size, shape, contour, and relative number of turbi- nates are evaluated. The presence of blood, blood clots, inflammation, foreign bodies, masses, fungal colonies, and exudate is assessed, and the character of any exudate is evaluated. The area of nasal cavity involvement is deter - mined, if involvement is generalized or localized, and if there is unilateral or bilateral disease. If localized, the site and extent are defined. If there is unilateral involvement with neoplasia or with mycotic infection, the nasal septum is evaluated for penetration to the opposite side. In the presence of copious exudate, extensive irrigation may be required before adequate examination can be carried out. Irrigation through the endoscope cannula is sufficient to clear the nasal cavity for examination in almost all cases. Additional irrigation or vigorous flushing with a syringe may occasionally be required when copious or thick exudate is present. If an examination is initiated and the nasal cavity cannot be cleared adequately, the endo - scope is removed and a large quantity of saline is forcefully flushed thorough the nasal cavity. For small dogs and cats, a 12–20 cc syringe is used and for larger dogs, a 60 cc cath- eter tip syringe is employed. Three to five syringes full are flushed into each side of the nasal cavity. The endoscope is reintroduced, and examination is again attempted. This procedure is repeated until the nasal cavities have been cleaned adequately for evaluation. Bleeding does occur during rhinoscopy. With the irriga- tion technique described previously, the quantity of hem- orrhage is rarely sufficient to interfere with examination. With high-flow rate irrigation, the examination is done through the stream of clear irrigant and any blood is forced out of the field of view. Occasionally there is profuse bleed- ing after obtaining biopsies that may make further exami- nation or sample collection more difficult. For this reason, the entire examination is performed before biopsy samples are taken. Increasing the rate of fluid flow by elevation of the fluid container or by placing the solution under pres - sure has occasionally been needed to complete sample col- lection. Bleeding induced by rhinoscopy has not produced sufficient blood loss to endanger patients. In 37 years and over 650 procedures, only one dog has required a transfu- sion following rhinoscopy, one dog required reintroduction of anesthesia with use of a hemostatic powder (HemaBlock ®) to control bleeding (Figure 4.12), and one dog required reintroduction of anesthesia for a short period with no fur - ther bleeding after recovery. Biopsy samples are collected after a complete examina- tion has been performed on both sides of the nasal cavity. Arthroscopy cannulas do not have a biopsy channel, so biopsy forceps are passed into the nasal cavity beside and

This procedure works for most cases allowing accurately placed sample collection (Figure 4.13). Rostral lesions and conditions with turbinate destruction that pro - vide an open cavity for manipulation make this technique easier. It is more difficult to position biopsy forceps and biopsy lesions located further caudally and smaller lesions using this technique. This technique is sometimes difficult and may be frustrating for the beginner but with increased experience, proficiency of sample collection increases. Both systems have advantages and disadvantages. The external parallel tech- nique allows larger biopsy samples to be taken but is more difficult to perform. 4.5 Technii ue 111 Multiple biopsy samples are harvested to increase the quantity of tissue available for histopathology and to sam- ple multiple tissue sites. For multiple sample collection, the endoscope position can be maintained, and the biopsy forceps removed and reinserted for each sample, or both the endoscope and biopsy forceps are removed and rein- serted together for each biopsy. The choice of technique may in some cases be dictated by the location or size of the lesion, by bleeding or exudate, or by patient size and conformation. Tumors are sometimes covered with organized hemato - mas and if inadequate biopsies are taken, accurate results are not obtained. Sufficient tissue sample size, with adequate sample depth, from multiple sites is required to minimize diagnostic errors. In generalized inflammatory processes, multiple samples are taken from different areas throughout the nasal cavity. The gross appearance of the mucosa may not be changed significantly to differentiate between normal and diseased tissue. Biopsy samples are taken in all cases to define mild or moderate inflammatory processes. Any areas of inspissated exudate are sampled for histopathology along with any areas suspicious for fungal colonies. Tumors are effectively debulked with rhinoscopy. Initial attempts at nasal tumor removal endoscopically were aimed at re-establishing a nasal airway when there was complete obstruction due to a tumor mass. This has pro - gressed over time to complete tumor removal and total tur - binectomy. Using a combination of biopsy forceps (Figure 4.2), larger nasal forceps (Figure 4.3), arthroscopy rongeurs (Figure 4.4), and the diode laser (Figure 4.16) tis - sue is removed. Biopsy forceps or arthroscopic rongeurs ranging in size from 2.0 to 5 mm are used to remove tissue both under endoscopic guidance and blindly. When bleed- ing obscures visibility, then the laser is used to cauterize and vaporize tissue until the char obscures tissue identifi- cation. At this point biopsy forceps are used again to remove tissue. This cycle is repeated until turbinectomy is complete, the extent of residual tissue cannot be accurately determined, or bleeding has been sufficient to reduce PCV toward 20%. When total turbinectomy cannot be completed at one surgery, then, if indicated, a second procedure is per - formed in two to four weeks. Tumor removal using rhinoscopy is not the only therapy recommended but has made open rhinotomy an obsolete procedure. With all cases of nasal tumors diagnosed with rhinoscopy, consultation with an oncologist is recommended for radiation and/or chemotherapy as indicated. Debulking at the time of initial diagnostic rhi- noscopy is typically performed as much as can be com- pleted as one procedure. Additional treatment depends on tumor type, location, size, and client preference. Many cli- ents elect repeat rhinoscopy rather than radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Nasal tumor debulking with rhinoscopy also attempts to follow the premise used throughout oncol- ogy of cytoreduction as part of a complete cancer manage - ment protocol. If foreign bodies are found, they are removed with appro - priate forceps. A pair of 6″ alligator forceps works well in most cases. If the foreign material is small, it can be removed rostrally through the external nares. Foreign bod- ies that are too large to remove rostrally must be pushed caudally through the nasopharynx for removal. Foreign bodies may be multiple, so the entire nasal cavity is care - fully assessed. Culture samples taken prior to rhinoscopy are usually submitted when foreign bodies are found but biopsies are generally not taken. If there is doubt about concurrent disease, biopsies are taken and submitted. An attempt is made during examination to therapeutically flush all of the exudate out of the nasal cavity. As part of a complete examination of the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx and pharyngeal areas are examined. Complete filling of the nasopharynx with irrigation fluid may not occur creating an air–liquid interface that interferes with visualization. When this occurs, irrigation is discontinued, and examination is performed through air. Frequently, intermittent irrigation is used to clean the telescope lens and remove blood or exudate to maintain a clear visual field. In most medium-to-large-sized dogs, without large bilateral nasal masses, the rigid 2.7 mm diameter MPRT is passed through the nasal cavity and into the nasopharynx by insertion through the external nares. In smaller dogs and in cats, 2.7 mm instrumentation cannot always be manipu - lated through the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx and a 1.9 mm telescope is required. If a 1.9 mm endoscope is not Figure 4.16 A 1000 μm laser fiber used to vaporize tissue and control bleeding during tumor debulking with rhinoscopy guidance.

4 Rhinoscopy 112 available for these smaller cases, other options for examina- tion are employed. Nasopharyngeal examination is per - formed with a small flexible endoscope passed through the mouth and flexed around the caudal margin of the soft pal- ate. The caudal portion of the nasopharyngeal area is also examined through the open mouth by retracting the soft palate rostrally using a tissue retractor (spay hook). This technique allows adequate assessment of the area in some cases. If exudate is present, irrigation is employed for removal to allow examination. The endoscope is used for irrigation and to assist visualization beyond what can be seen by direct examination. Another technique employed for nasopharyngeal examination utilizes percutaneous puncture in the area employed for pharyngostomy tube placement. This allows direct access to and complete exami- nation of the nasopharynx and caudal nasal cavity. With availability of both 1.9 and 2.7 mm instrumentation, these alternate techniques have been infrequently required and are inferior to passage of rigid instrumentation from the rostral approach into the nasopharynx. When rhinoscopy has been completed, the pharyngeal area is cleaned to remove fluid, debris, and blood clots. The external nares and pharyngeal area are monitored for excessive bleeding. Patient recovery is allowed to be slow and quiet with minimal stimulus. Sedatives are used as needed. Narcotic induction agents, if used, are not reversed unless systemic complications warrant a more rapid recov - ery regime. Intravenous fluids are administered during anesthesia and recovery. It is strongly recommended that these patients be hospi- talized for the night after the procedure even if they are adequately recovered from anesthesia for release. The stimulus and excitation produced by reunion with their owner and release from the hospital frequently induces epistaxis when they are sent home on the same day as the procedure. Post rhinoscopy epistaxis has not been suffi- cient to be a risk for the patient, but epistaxis combined with sneezing and excitement can cause considerable anxi- ety for the owner. If patients are allowed to rest quietly overnight after rhinoscopy, epistaxis is rare. Nasal biopsy sample collection has been recommended with multiple other routes and techniques. These tech- niques are unpredictable in their results and have an unac- ceptably low yield of diagnostic material. Cytologic samples are obtained by irrigation of the nasal cavity and collection of the effluent. Solid tissue samples from tumors or frag - ments of fungal colonies are sometimes dislodged by force - ful irrigation of the nasal cavity. Needle aspiration and needle biopsy procedures are effectively employed for sam- ple collection from tumors that have penetrated bone and are palpated through the skin or hard palate. Rostral or caudal approaches to the nasal cavity for needle aspiration or needle biopsy require blind placement with no control of the location of sample collection. Blind catheter biopsy collection using a stiff polypropylene catheter cut to pro - duce a sharp cutting edge and passed into the external nares with multiple jabbing motions to cut cores out of tumors has the same disadvantages as needle aspirate and needle biopsy techniques. With generalized inflammatory processes, with extensive tumors, or large fungal colonies, this approach may produce diagnostic samples. Small tumors or fungal colonies can be missed, and inflamma- tory histopathology findings cannot be differentiated between an accurate diagnosis or a missed lesion. Adequate samples may be obtained from large lesions, but smaller ones may be missed. Foreign bodies, dental disease, and other conditions may also be missed. Rhinoscopy is supe - rior to these techniques as it allows direct visualization of the nasal cavity providing for gross diagnosis and selection of appropriate sites for sample collection. Biopsy forceps are accurately placed with direct visualization to obtain samples of representative tissues greatly enhancing accu- racy of histopathology results. Multiple samples taken from the same biopsy site or multiple biopsy sites are pos - sible. Fungal colonies are biopsied to assist in identifica- tion of fungal species both by histopathology and culture. Fungal cultures grown from biopsy samples of fungal colo - nies taken with rhinoscopy produce a high rate of success - ful growth on laboratory media when compared with samples taken by irrigation and by culture swab collection. Ability to see lesions for biopsy with rhinoscopy and its low morbidity and mortality make rhinoscopy the procedure of choice for nasal biopsy sample collection. Surgical exploration of the nasal cavity may also be used for diagnostic sample collection. This is a procedure of last resort. Direct visualization is achieved with open surgical exploration of the nasal cavity allowing gross diagnosis prior to sample collection and accurate sample site selec- tion but its morbidity far exceeds that of rhinoscopy. Exploratory rhinotomy is not recommended unless all other approaches have failed to produce a diagnosis. Since rhinoscopy was added to the diagnostic protocol for chronic nasal disease, surgical exploration has only been performed once in over 650 cases spanning a 37 year period, and in that case surgery did not provide any additional informa- tion beyond what was obtained with rhinoscopy. 4.5.4 Frontal Sinoscopy The frontal sinuses are examined endoscopically directly through the nasal cavity with the rostral approach in some cats and dogs. Loss of turbinates from a disease process facil- itates access to the frontal sinuses from the nasal cavity. Most cases require access percutaneously by trephining a 5–10 mm

If significant pathology is present, fluid irrigation must be employed for adequate visualization. When irriga - tion is used, the diameter of the trephine hole is made large enough to allow free flow of irrigant out around the endo - scope cannula. The normal communication of the frontal sinus with the nasal cavity may be occluded when signifi - cant pathology is present so the only place for fluid egress is around the endoscope. If biopsies are taken, the trephine hole is made large enough to allow passage of biopsy instru - mentation beside the endoscope. If there is generalized pathology, where the location of the sample is not critical, a smaller hole is used, and biopsies are taken blindly without endoscopic visualization. Therapeutic debridement of fron - tal sinus pathology, such as fungal colonies, tumors, or bone sequestrum, is accomplished through this approach. A large number of different nasal tumor types occur originating from any tissue type found in the nasal cavity or metastasizing from other sites. A series of 100 consecutive nasal neoplasia cases (Table 4.9) revealed 19 different histopathologically defined tumor types. These have included 11 different kinds of sarcomas, 5 different types of carcinomas, and 3 varieties of benign tumors. The location of tumors is highly variable as is their color, shape, contour, and con - sistency. There is very poor correlation between gross appearance and histopathologic tumor type with a few exceptions. The majority of nasal tumors are surrounded by mucoid or mucopurulent exudate that is relatively easy to remove with endoscopic irrigation. Some tumors are surrounded by active bleeding (Figure 4.52), fresh blood on the surface of visible tumors (Figure 4.53), or blood clots from previous bleeding episodes. The amount of organization of resulting blood clots affects their appearance and ranges from freshly formed bright red obvious blood clots (Figure 4.54) to chronic well-organ - ized tissue like structures that cannot be grossly differen - tiated from tumor tissue (Figure 4.55). Selective biopsy of this tissue is required for identification. All stages of blood clot maturation are seen in nasal tumor cases and multiple stages are seen in individual patients represent - ing different bleeding episodes. Early maturation pro - duces rounded clots with persistent red coloration seen without visible tumor tissue (Figure 4.56) or adjacent to visible tumor tissue (Figure 4.57). Nasopharyngeal polyps in cats are characteristically pink (Figure 4.115) or white (Figure 4.116) with a roughened, lobulated, or irregular surface and variable vascularity. They are also dark purple (Figure 4.117) or greenish purple with mottled areas of white (Figure 4.118). Combinations of appearances may also be seen in one polyp. They have vari - able friability with internal tissue color resembling outer sur - face coloration. Nasopharyngeal polyps in cats are generally unilateral in their origin but frequently produce bilateral signs by producing partial or complete nasopharyngeal air - way obstruction. Using rhinoscopy, the stalk of feline naso - pharyngeal polyps is sometimes seen as it exits from the eustachian tube (Figure 4.119). Nasopharyngeal polyps can frequently be visualized, biopsied, or removed by rostral retraction of the soft palate (Figures 4.115 and 4.117). Nasopharyngeal polyps are easily removed with rhinoscopy by applying traction using biopsy forceps or by pushing on the polyp with the endoscope or with biopsy forceps. Retracting the soft palate rostrally provides access to the eus - tachian tube in cats for endoscopic examination (Figure 4.120) and for removal of the eustachian tube (Figure 4.121) and middle ear portions of polyps (Figure 4.122). The eustachian tube is usually enlarged secondary to the presence of the polyp stalk and access to the middle ear is possible with a 1.9 or smaller rigid endoscope and with 2.0 or smaller biopsy forceps. Nasopharyngeal polyps are easily differentiated from other types of nasopharyngeal tumors because polyps have a narrow base of attachment that is easily broken, and all other tumor types have a wide base of attachment that is not breakable to allow complete removal. The shape of nasal tumors is influenced by nasal cavity shape and the anatomy of the turbinate structures. Large tumors are more commonly associated with extensive turbinate changes, but this is dif- ficult to appreciate via endoscopy because of lack of space for examination. The entire extent of a tumor of any appre - ciable size is also difficult to assess, again due to lack of space for examination. Signs seen with Aspergillus infections in dogs include unilateral or bilateral mucopurulent nasal discharge, pain on palpation of the rhinarium, ulceration of the nares, and obstruction of the airways (McCarthy 2002). A variable quantity of fungal material may be found. The amount of mucopurulent exudate is typically exten- sive (Figure 4.156), being more than that seen with most other nasal diseases. It is commonly thicker than with other nasal disease (Figure 4.157), is seen adherent to and obscuring fungal colonies (Figure 4.158), or extending into the contralateral nasal passage (Figure 4.159). In unilateral involvement, there may be significant bilateral mucopuru- lent discharge even in the absence of identifiable bilateral fungal colonies. Discharge sometimes contains blood but there is rarely extensive bleeding or blood clots. Inflammatory, granulomatous, and fibroplastic responses associated with chronic fungal infections result in turbinate destruction and distortion. In mild or relatively acute cases, there will be more distortion than destruction. Early mild destruction may not be obvious, but examination may seem easier than in a normal dog because of increased space between turbinates (Figure 4.160). Distortion first becomes evident as mild changes in turbinate shape (Figure 4.161), loss of turbinate height with thickening (Figure 4.162), or loss of turbinate bulk (Figure 4.163). With progression of disease, there is additional loss of turbinate mass and fur - ther distortion (Figure 4.164) with the ethmoidal turbinates taking on a crumpled shrunken appearance (Figure 4.165). With further changes, turbinates appear unsupported as cartilage is lost and they may seem to float in the fluid stream coming from the endoscope (Figure 4.166). The end - point of this destructive process is an empty nasal cavity with irregular turbinate remnants and lined with inflam - matory tissue (Figure 4.167). The primary indication of frontal sinus involvement is a concentration of thick mucopurulent exudate dorsally in the caudal or caudola- teral aspect of the nasal cavity that is draining from the frontal sinus (Figures 4.180, 4.182, 4.197, and 4.198). This exudate drainage is usually unilateral, and no other disease process is evident. In these cases, CT will show increased density partly or completely filling the involved frontal sinus. Involvement may appear as generalized increased fluid density of the entire cavity or more commonly as an irregular increased density on the floor of the frontal sinus. These cases may be evaluated further by frontal sinoscopy with access via trephination of the frontal sinus or occa- sionally via the nasal cavity (Figure 4.191). Fungal colonies in the frontal sinuses are generally large and easily seen with exudate under the colonies but not covering them (Figures 4.193 and 4.195). There is typically a contralateral response to frontal sinus infections with thickening and hyperemia of the mucosa, exudate, and no visible fungal colonies (Figure 4.199). Fluid irrigation may or may not be required for examina- tion of the frontal sinus in the presence of fungal infection. If there is extensive exudate in the frontal sinus, irrigation is required. If the frontal sinus is air filled with a dry fungal mass on its floor, then irrigation may not be required. The procedure is started dry and irrigation is added if needed. Nasal fungal colonies are removed with irrigation, suc- tion, and biopsy forceps using the same technique as for tumor debulking and turbinectomy (Figure 4.200). Frontal sinus procedures performed through the nasal cav - ity use the same technique as is used for fungal colonies in the nasal cavity. Removal of frontal sinus fungal colonies through a dorsal trephine approach is performed using irri- gation, suction, repeated biopsies, and curettage, with use of stone baskets if the colonies are firm enough to come out in one piece (Figure 4.201). Complete colony removal is the goal and is usually achieved (Figure 4.202). Medical management of fungal infections is instituted after removal of fungal colonies at the same anesthesia or at a later time (Burrow et al. 2013, Sharman et al. 2012). Frontal sinus and nasal cavity tube placement is performed at the time of frontal sinoscopy if the medical protocol includes extended treatment. The most successful manage - ment of nasal Aspergillus infections performed by the author involved use of Enilconazole instilled in implanted tubes one to two weeks. Treatment at the same time as fun- gal colony removal using Clotrimazole irrigation over a one-hour period requires occlusion of the nasopharynx to prevent leakage into the pharynx. A Foley catheter is placed through the nares and nasal cavity into the naso - pharynx and the bulb is inflated. The position of the cath- eter and adequate bulb inflation is confirmed endoscopically (Figure 4.203). Many drugs and treatment protocols have been used for treatment of nasal Aspergillus with variable success rates. The underlying cause of nasal and frontal sinus Aspergillus sp. infections is not known but contributing factors are suspected. Foreign bodies have been found in some cases with Aspergillus colonies or positive fungal cul- tures (Figures 4.204 and 4.205). Foreign material is not found in most cases but with the time frame from possible exposure to diagnosis, it is possible that the foreign mate - rial is destroyed by the fungus or dissolved by nasal fluid or exudate. Hyposensitization injections combined with environmental allergen exclusion has been very encouraging in these cases. There is a tremendous amount that is not known about allergic rhinitis in dogs and cats. Considerable research is needed to study this condition and define its properties and management (Mueller et al. 2018). It must be remembered that with allergies, the location of the presenting symp - toms does not necessarily indicate the site of allergen expo - sure. This is understood with allergic dermatitis and its relationship to food allergies with management using exclusionary diets. The same relationships have not been applied to other body systems. Gastrointestinal symptoms can be associated with inhaled allergens and respiratory signs can be associated with food allergies. Another misun- derstanding is that there is rarely only one allergen involved in allergic disease. There is the concept of “total allergen load” meaning that it is a combination of multiple aller - gens that exceed a threshold to produce clinical disease. From this concept, management is directed toward reduc- ing any and all allergen exposure to reduce the total aller - gen load to below the threshold for the individual patient. This involves reducing the exposure to all allergens, not just those that produce the strongest reaction with allergy testing. Many of our patients, and ourselves, have subclini- cal allergy exposure most or all of the time. When allergen overload occurs due to an increase in a single allergen, the subclinical state becomes clinical. With reduction in the total allergen load, this single allergen overload exposure may not reach the threshold to become clinical or may be less severe. In the context of allergic rhinitis, a clinical episode may be due to an inhaled allergen but could also be due to an ingested allergen. Allergic rhinitis management involves reduction in exposure to all allergens and medica- tions plus hyposensitization. 4.7.4 Nasal Foreign Bodies Nasal foreign bodies in dogs and cats are uncommonly seen in referral practice. When foreign bodies are found, they are removed under endoscopic visualization using foreign body removal forceps (Figure 4.235) designed for endoscopic application or with alligator forceps of appropriate length. Smaller foreign bodies are removed rostrally by retraction with forceps. Larger for - eign material must be pushed caudally through the naso - pharynx into the pharynx for removal. Large bone foreign bodies have been found in the nasopharynx that were lodged firmly in place between the bone of the hard palate and the vomer dorsoventrally or between the palatine bones laterally. Considerable force may be required for their removal. If a foreign body is pushed into the nasopharynx, rostral retrac - tion of the soft palate may be required to locate and remove the foreign material from this area. Vigorous irrigation is employed after foreign body extraction to remove residual exudate and minimize the chance of persistent inflammation or infection. All foreign bodies encountered during rhinos - copy performed by the author were removed endoscopically (excluding orthopedic implants). Surgery could potentially be required for multiple foreign bodies or those that are fixed in place and cannot be dislodged with the endoscope. Reaction of nasal tissue to foreign bodies is similar to what is seen with other causes of rhinitis occasionally with severe changes mimicking fungal infections. These find- ings support the theory that fungal infections may start from a nasal foreign body. 4.7 .5 Rhinitis Secondary to Dental Disease Rhinitis secondary to dental disease is a disappearing entity in small animal practice due to improved dental care, but is Figure 4.235 Removing a nasal foreign body with standard alligator forceps. Dental disease causes unilateral or bilateral rhinitis with unilateral or bilateral clear watery, mucoid, mucopurulent, or purulent discharge. Nasal infec- tion and inflammation originate from periapical abscesses, severe gingivitis associated with bone erosion around tooth roots, and oronasal fistulas involving any maxillary or pre - maxillary teeth. The most common teeth involved are the upper canine teeth, the upper fourth premolar, and the upper first molar because of their size and root configura- tion. Involvement can, however, include any or all of the upper dental arcade on one or both sides. Exudate in the nasal cavity of dogs with rhinitis second- ary to dental disease is very characteristic in close proxim- ity to the involved teeth (Figure 4.236), but varies in quantity and appearance throughout the remainder of the nasal cavity mimicking exudate seen with other rhinitis etiologies. Discharge from the external nares is usually mild, clear, and watery or mucoid even in the presence of severe dental involvement and rhinitis. The appearance and amount of exudate does not seem to be related to the severity of the dental disease. Character of exudate may be more mucoid than purulent or mucopurulent when com- pared with the extent of dental disease present and the amount of exudate seen with other nasal inflammatory processes. Exudate found in the ventrolateral nasal cavity associated with areas of dental involvement is very charac- teristic and specific to rhinitis induced by dental disease (Figure 4.236). Exudate in the area of dental disease is white, thick flocculent material that is well delineated from the surrounding more fluid exudate in the remainder of the nasal cavity. This material is basically the same inspis - sated purulent material seen in the oral cavity around tooth roots with severe periodontal disease. When irrigated vigorously, the exudate breaks off in discrete chunks. Tissue under the areas of the exudate is inflamed, hypere - mic, and ulcerated showing the full range of changes seen with other inflammatory diseases of the nasal cavity. A change specific to dental disease caused rhinitis are cyst- like structures (Figure 4.237) over involved tooth roots when penetration has not occurred. Roots of involved teeth are generally not seen in the endoscopic field. In many cases, flow of irrigant is seen in the oral cavity coming from around involved teeth. Probing around the roots of involved teeth may reveal loss of bone between the root and the nasal cavity. Direct communication between the oral and nasal cavities is found in many cases. Extraction of involved teeth will result in resolution or nasal discharge and rhini- tis. Oral nasal fistulas may result following removal of these involved teeth and surgical closure is required or rhi- nitis persists. Dental disease is always considered as a cause of nasal discharge in older, especially smaller breed, dogs that have significant dental disease. It is not ruled out in larger dogs, or in dogs without significant obvious dental disease or gingivitis. Roots of the maxillary teeth are assessed care - fully on nasal radiographs, dental radiographs, or CT. Teeth are examined carefully under anesthesia for evidence of gingivitis, bone recession, periapical abscesses, and frac- tured teeth (Figure 4.238). Rhinoscopic examination is then directed at these areas. Enlargement of bone in the area of tooth roots may indicate dental disease but without penetration into the nasal cavity or accumulation of exu- date, these teeth are not the ones causing the rhinitis. Bacterial culture samples are submitted when dental dis - ease is diagnosed but submission of fungal cultures is optional. Biopsies of the involved areas of nasal mucosa are taken and may be sent or saved for future submission if Figure 4.236 Undisturbed exudate adjacent to an abscessed tooth root in a dog with rhinitis secondary to dental disease. History, signs, and symp - toms are similar to other nasal diseases with no specific indications of this pathology. Thromboembolism is com- mon in cats and specifically in those with myocardial dis - ease presenting clinically as an aortic saddle thrombus or less frequently as more proximal aortic lesions and as renal, mesenteric, coronary, cerebral, and brachial artery occlu- sions. Microthromboembolism also occurs in all these arte - rial divisions that are clinically undetected with lesions frequently seen as an incidental finding in the kidneys. Nasal turbinate infarction is simply another presentation of this disease process. Lesions occur bilaterally, unilater - ally, and focally. Cats typically present with unilateral or bilateral nasal discharge with variable nasal airway obstruction that is unresponsive to treatment. Radiographs and CT findings are variable and are not helpful in establishing a diagnosis. Rhinoscopy in cases of turbinate infarction reveals white completely avascular tissue (Figure 4.239) or pale tissue with decreased vascular supply indicating partial vascular occlusion (Figure 4.240). Varying degrees of dis - tortion (Figure 4.241) and destruction (Figure 4.242) are seen depending on severity and chronicity of the infarct. There is little or no bleeding with biopsies (Figure 4.243) or with telescope contact (Figure 4.244) even where there is significant turbinate damage (Figure 4.245). Exudate seen with turbinate infarction is mucopurulent in charac - ter typical of that seen with many nasal diseases (Figure 4.246). The adenoids in people are lymphoid tissue on the dorsal wall of the nasopharynx and are also called the nasopharyngeal tonsils. Dogs and cats have an area of lym- phoid tissue on the dorsal wall of the nasopharynx that is essentially the same structure as the adenoids in people. This structure has not been identified as a named anatomic structure in animals and is hereby named the “CANENOIDS” in dogs and the “FELENOIDS” in cats. When not inflamed or enlarged, this area is not easy to identify (Figures 4.33, 4.35, and 4.36). Chronic mani - festations following acute viral rhinitis in cases can present with nasopharyngeal polyps or as chronic sinusitis. Viral rhi - nitis in dogs was common prior to widespread use of effective distemper vaccines. Chronic rhinitis in dogs and cats has not been documented to be viral in etiology. Secondary bacterial infections can become established as a chronic sequela of viral rhinitis. Without common application of viral cultures this is a difficult diagnosis to make or rule out. 4.7.13 Bacterial Rhinitis True bacterial rhinitis is not considered to be a primary or final diagnosis in cases with chronic nasal disease. Cases of bacterial rhinitis would be expected to respond well to antibiotic therapy and would not become part of the chronic nasal disease group that is presented for the type of nasal evaluations discussed here. An insufficient number of cases have been seen to define signalment, history, physical findings, imaging, or appearance with rhinoscopy. It is unknown if this is an inherited condition, a developmental condition, or an acquired abnormality. Two cases of nasal vascular dyspla- sia have been documented with histopathology out of 669 procedures in 545 patients examined with rhinoscopy over a 37 year period. One in a 14-year-old neutered male West Highland White Terrier (Figure 4.294) and the other case was a 12-year-old neutered male Schipperke (Figure 4.295). In these patients, the blood vessels appeared enlarged, tor - tuous, and increased in number. There also appeared to be loss of turbinate bulk and loss of cartilage support (Figure 4.296). Over this period of time, it is acknowledged that other cases may have occurred but were not recovered in searching for cases with this disorder. A literature search did not find reports of this abnormality. 4.7.15 Epistaxis Epistaxis, hemorrhage from the nasal cavity, needs to be differentiated from blood staining of a nasal discharge. Epistaxis is not a diagnosis but is a sign of nasal disease or systemic disease and may be due to a variety of conditions with a wide variety of origins. True epistaxis is most com- monly seen with nasal neoplasia and with systemic coagu- lopathies. Epistaxis is a cardinal sign of hypertension in man but has not been defined as such in the dog or cat. Blood-stained discharges, whether watery, mucoid, mucop - urulent, or purulent, are seen with almost all of the condi- tions producing chronic nasal discharge. Neoplasia, severe mycotic rhinitis, and foreign bodies will demonstrate blood more frequently, but this finding is too variable to use as a diagnostic criterion. Differentiation between a systemic bleeding disorder and local nasal pathology is critical prior to performing a nasal workup with rhinoscopy. Epistaxis due to nasal tumors can be profuse but is localized to the nasal cavity. Recent studies in Europe (Oechtering et al. 2016a, b; Schuenemann and Oechtering 2014) have determined that this approach is inadequate to maximize long-term resolution of upper airway obstruction in many brachiocephalic dogs. Patient selection for proce - dures beyond the traditional triad has not been fully determined. Geographic differences between Europe, North America, and other parts of the world in upper air - way abnormalities of brachiocephalic dogs have not been studied. In consideration of these comments and the information provided by the European studies, evalua - tion of the upper airways of brachiocephalic dogs beyond the old standard is recommended to answer these ques - tions and use the answers to improve the results for our patients. In addition to the previous standard for preoperative evaluation of physical assessment, thoracic radiographs, preoperative CBC and BCP , and EKG recommendations include a nasal CT study. Information from the CT is used to determine if partial turbinectomy is indicated in addi- tion to the standard surgical triad. A name change for everted lateral saccules to “laryn - goceles” has also been suggested by our European col - leagues. In the human literature, “laryngocele” refers to a congenital anomaly of an air sac outside of the larynx communicating with the airway and producing an out - ward bulge in the neck or a benign dilation of the laryn - geal saccule protruding into the airway (Lancella et al. 2007). Everted lateral saccules in brachiocephalic dogs are similar to benign dilation of the laryngeal saccule in people but the opposite of this description for laryn - goceles producing an outward projection is completely dif - ferent. In one way, this condition in dogs is similar to that in people but the term in people encompasses multiple and more complex entities. A change in the approach to upper airway revision sur - gery currently practiced by the author in brachiocephalic dogs is elimination of everted lateral saccule, or laryn- gocele resection. Almost all complications associated with brachiocephalic upper airway revision are due to laryngeal swelling following everted lateral saccule resection and almost none of the complications are associated with soft palate resection or stenotic nares correction. Postoperative recovery of cases with this approach has been easier and smoother than when everted lateral saccule resection was performed and there has been no detectable difference in long-term results. Follow-up bronchoscopy assessment of the larynx in a small number of patients when anesthe - tized for other procedures that have had upper airway revi- sions without everted lateral saccule resection has revealed that in many cases lateral saccule eversion has resolved. This is thought to be due to reduced upper airway resist - ance produced by stenotic nares correction and soft palate resection. An insufficient number of cases have been per - formed to determine the incidence of everted lateral sac- cule resolution with this procedure and also to answer the questions about proper case selection for leaving the everted lateral saccules in place or when resection is still indicated. Rhinoscopy of brachiocephalic dogs reveals a variable degree of airway interference due to excessive turbinate bulk for the size of the nasal cavity. This is visible as contact between turbinates leaving no airway space (Figures 4.315 and 4.316) and this occurs throughout the nasal cavity interspersed with areas having adequate interturbinate airways (Figure 4.317). Cases of nasopharyngeal stenosis involving a nasal workup with rhinoscopy have been adults with probable acquired disease, but many are sufficiently chronic that an etiology is difficult to confirm. Vomiting or regurgitation with gas - tric acid contamination of the nasopharynx is a possible etiology of this disease but in many cases cannot be docu- mented. One case in an adult dog did develop a naso - pharyngeal stenosis shortly after an episode of severe vomiting. Presentation of nasopharyngeal stenosis cases are typi- cally for respiratory signs due to airway obstruction but are also seen for nasal discharge. Discharge is usually bilateral and mucoid or mucopurulent due to underlying primary rhinitis, secondary rhinitis, rhinitis due to the same etiol- ogy as the stricture, discharge due to interference with nor - mal nasal mucus flow caused by the stricture, or a combination of these reasons. Imaging of the nasal and nasopharyngeal areas with CT is very helpful in localizing the level of airway obstruction to the nasopharynx and developing a plan for surgical or endoscopic management. CT is also necessary for measur - ing the area of length of the stenosis and diameter of the normal nasopharynx when stent placement is being considered. The nasal cavity in cases of nasopharyngeal stenosis ranges from normal to severe rhinitis with any or all of the turbinate changes seen with other causes of chronic rhini- tis. There is also a variable amount of exudate in the nasal cavity from a minimal amount to extensive mucoid or mucopurulent material interfering with rhinoscopy. Irrigation and suction are used to remove exudate and improve visualization. All cases of nasopharyngeal stenosis that have been seen were chronic in both dogs and cats. The stricture in cats have been either short with a thin wall of tissue causing the obstruction without any visible lumen through the stric- ture (Figure 4.322), a longer area of stenosis tapering to a blind pouch (Figure 4.323), with a variable-sized commu- nicating lumen through the stricture from a very small hole (Figure 4.324) to a larger residual lumen that is clearly visible (Figure 4.325), obscured by exudate (Figure 4.326), or occluded with unidentified material (Figure 4.327). Inflammatory nodules (Figure 4.328) and inflammatory polyps (Figure 4.329) are occasionally seen with naso - pharyngeal stenosis. These are inflammatory mass lesions that are histologically benign but have malignant behavior. A report of 13 cases in dogs indicated signalment, history, physical findings, and imaging compatible with malignant neoplasia (Burgess et al. 2011). Age range was from 7 to 15 years, both males and females, and a wide range of breeds. All dogs in this series were presented with clinical signs including unilat - eral or bilateral nasal obstruction, mucopurulent dis - charge, and recurrent epistaxis. CT imaging revealed soft tissue, contrast-enhancing masses with destruction of the nasal turbinates, invasion into the frontal sinus and retroorbital space, and intracranial extension. Patients that were evaluated with rhinoscopy revealed a well-encapsu- lated, highly vascular soft tissue mass. Cytology when per - formed showed some features supportive of malignancy but histopathology did not support this diagnosis. Vascular proliferation, lympho-suppurative inflammation of well- demarcated masses with intact epithelium lining expan- sile, moderately cellular areas having proliferative fibrocollagenous stroma, and variably sized, shaped, and sometimes inconspicuous vascular profiles. No mass-asso - ciated turbinate bone was identified. Spindle cell prolifera- tion and vessel formation were more prominent than inflammation. Inflammatory characteristics included edema, mild neutrophilic infiltrate, minimal lymphocytic infiltrate, and without areas of necrosis. Surgery, dorsal rhinotomy, was performed in six of the dogs in this report with one postoperative death due to blood loss, three died of unrelated diseases within four years with no clinical indication of recurrence, one was alive at nine months with no further follow-up, and one had recurrence at two Figure 4.345 Irregular turbinates with loss of bulk and support. Some of the charac- teristics are compatible with this diagnosis including pre - senting signs, imaging appearance, and some of the histopathology descriptions. Incompatible characteristics include some of the histopathology but most importantly the rapid recurrence of significant lesions in both cases and the need for repeated debulking to maintain an airway. Recurrences are not reported with angiofibromas in people and were only documented on one of the 13 cases reported in the only published multiple case report in dogs (Burgess et al. 2011). The lack of sufficient follow-up in that publica- tion with most of the cases left untreated and undocu- mented causes of death does not provide for comparison of results from that case series with the biologic behavior in these two cases. Additional information is needed to con- firm that these are comparable to angiofibroma in people and justify using this name. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 5.1 Introduction Small animal bronchoscopy has been an integral part of respiratory veterinary medicine since the early 1970s. Performed by experienced veterinarians, bronchoscopy is invaluable in the diagnosis of a variety of respiratory disorders. In addition to its application in diagnostics, bronchoscopy has been used therapeutically, as well as in the determination of a patient’s overall prognosis. 5.2 Equipment Both rigid and flexible endoscopes have been used for bronchoscopy in small animals. Rigid bronchoscopes have been used in human medicine for over 100 years. Since Ikeda introduced the flexible fiberscope in 1967, use of flexible endoscopes gradually increased and are now the most commonly used instruments for both veterinary and human bronchoscopy. Flexible endoscopes have many advantages over rigid endoscopes: versatility allowing one scope to be used for a variety of veterinary endoscopic procedures and improved maneuverability providing an increased viewing area within the tracheobronchial tree. There are also disadvan- tages when compared to rigid endoscopes: increased initial cost, greater repair costs, decreased durability with greater flexibility leading to more breakage, less suction, less instru- mentation capability as biopsy channel size is generally smaller, and depending on the type of flexible endoscope decreased image quality especially of concern with fiber scopes as opposed to video chip scopes. Despite these limi- tations, the versatility, maneuverability, and increased view - ing area have made flexible endoscopes the preferred bronchoscopic instrument. Species differences, for example, in the length and diam- eter of an animal’s airways, result in certain limitations for using one endoscope as a “veterinary bronchoscope.” I cur - rently use two different size bronchoscopes, 5.0 and 3.7 mm diameter. These two endoscopes allow for bronchoscopic evaluation in patients weighing from 2 kg to over 75 kg and have enough versatility to be used in other endoscopic pro - cedures, such as a rhinoscopy and cystoscopy. A major limitation for bronchoscopy in large dogs is the limited length (55 cm) of a “human” bronchoscope. The one bron- choscope that has been made specifically for use in veteri- nary medicine 1 is 5.0 mm in diameter and 85 cm in length, sufficient to use in all but the very largest dogs. In those giant breed animals, a pediatric gastroscope can be suc- cessfully used for bronchoscopy. Good used endoscopes are often available from local hospitals or endoscopic support and sales companies. 5.2.1 Equipment Care and Cleaning Flexible endoscopes are delicate, expensive instruments, and are handled and cared for with the utmost care. Improper handling such as forceful insertion or bending of the scope and forceful forceps insertion, or improper cleaning and sterilization by soaking instruments that cannot be totally immersed such as those that need to be gas sterilized, may result in instrument damage and expensive repair costs. Equipment sterility is often hampered by humidity; Pseudomonas spp. favor damp environments and this is a common contaminant of respiratory equipment. Ethylene oxide, steam, hydrogen peroxide, and cold soak - ing techniques have been successfully used to sterilize endoscopes and biopsy equipment. It is wise to ensure that all users understand the manufacturer’s approved use, care, and cleaning recommendations for these instruments. 5.3 Indications and Contraindications of Bronchoscopy Bronchoscopy may be used for diagnostic, therapeutic, and prognostic purposes (McKiernan 1989; Ford 1990; Roudebush 1990; Johnson and Vernau 2011; McKiernan 2000). Diagnostic bronchoscopy is used to obtain visual information concerning the airways including compres - sion, obstruction, dynamic collapse, and dilation. Samples are obtained using bronchoscopy for cytology, culture, and occasionally for biopsy. Visualization combined with test results help to establish a specific etiologic diagnosis. Bronchoscopy is useful therapeutically, especially for removal of airway foreign bodies (Leal et al. 2017; Lotti and Niebauer 1992; Johnson 2001). It is also very helpful in determining prognosis when nonreversible structural or mucosal changes are recognized in the airways. Other than risks associated with anesthesia required for the procedure, I do not feel that there are any absolute contraindications to bronchoscopy in veterinary medicine. The clinician must weigh any risks presented by the patient such as anesthesia, bleeding, hypoxemia, and cardiac arrhythmias vs. the benefits of information potentially obtained from the procedure. The endoscopist must have sufficient training and an experienced team to enable the procedure to be safely and quickly performed. Roudebush (1990) summarized the clinical indications and potential contraindications for bronchoscopy, a modification of which is outlined in Table 5.1. 5.4 Anesthesia for Bronchoscopy Insertion of an endoscope into an animal’s airway results in the stimulation of protective reflexes, which may include sneezing, head shaking, paroxysmal coughing, and airway constriction or bronchospasm. General anesthesia is necessary to control these reflexes during bronchoscopy in order to prevent trauma to the patient and at the same time protect the endoscope from potential damage during the procedure. Information obtained from bronchoscopy which aids in establishing a definitive diagnosis and long-term prognosis overrides concerns for general anesthesia in almost all cases. Availability of newer, short acting, and reversible injectable anesthetics has allowed bronchoscopy to be performed with good safety in almost all patients. This form of anesthesia is particularly beneficial because it not only provides adequate anesthesia for the procedure but also allows for relatively rapid patient recovery, which is an important factor in geriatric patients and especially in those with malacic airways. There are a variety of satisfactory anesthetic protocols that are used for bronchoscopy. Selection of a particular protocol is based on preanesthetic evaluation of the patient’s condition and size, the bronchoscopic purpose at hand (e.g. a routine diagnostic vs. a prolonged foreign body removal procedure), as well as the veterinarian’s familiarity with the anesthetic agent(s). Patient movement must be controlled as it makes bronchoscopy more difficult or impossible. The ideal anesthetic provides good patient restraint, has minimal cardiorespiratory effects, is either reversible or of short duration, and allows for a rapid and smooth recovery period. Administration of a bronchodilator prior to bronchos - copy is recommended (Kirschvink et al. 2005) to minimize bronchospasm induced by the procedure and ideally is Figure 5.1 Flexible endoscopes: a 3.7 mm and a 5 mm bronchoscope with three 7.9 mm gastroduodenoscopes properly stored hanging in a storage cabinet for security and to allow them to fully dry following cleaning. There are risks with this form of anesthesia; care must be taken to ensure that air trapping does not occur as the result of the endoscope being placed inside the endotracheal tube as it can significantly increase the resist - ance to air flow into and especially out of the lungs. Lung barotrauma resulting in pneumothorax can result from the insufflation of anesthetic gas or oxygen while not allowing for an adequate volume of gas to be exhaled. All cats and many dogs are too small to allow the bron- choscope to be passed through an endotracheal tube and therefore either jet ventilation (Johnson 2001; Goudra et al. 2015) or injectable anesthesia is used for bronchos - copy in these patients. I prefer to use injectable anesthesia in all small animal patients. Oxygen supplementation prior to induction is recommended, using a face mask, as hypox - emia is common in many of these patients. Flexible endo - scopes will not allow for artificial ventilation and hence supplemental oxygen is administered using one of two techniques. The most common technique used delivers oxygen via a catheter (a soft 3–8 Fr urinary catheter works well for this purpose) passed alongside the bronchoscope and into the lower trachea (Figure 5.4). These catheters are never inserted past the carina to avoid potential lung perfo - ration. The second technique uses bias flow of oxygen (1–2 lpm) through the biopsy channel of the bronchoscope when it is not actively being used for biopsy or lavage pur - poses (Figure 5.5). Once the bronchoscopy procedure is completed, I recommend intubating these patients to pro - vide oxygen during anesthesia recovery. Many bronchoscopy patients are older and may have chronic cardio-pulmonary disease(s), including valvular insuffi- ciency, small airway obstruction, and hypoxemia. Significant decreases in P a O 2 have been reported during bronchoscopy in human medicine. Although the magni- tude and frequency of this problem has not been assessed in veterinary medicine, if similar changes occur, there is a potential for significant hypoxemia to develop. The com- bined cardiopulmonary effects of general anesthesia, mucosal stimulation, and any induced hypoxemia could easily result in cardiac arrhythmias or worse in these patients (Roudebush 1990; Leiten et al. 2016). Sternal recumbency is the preferred position when per - forming bronchoscopy in cats and dogs. Not only is this position easier to maintain and more familiar to veterinar - ians, but it also minimizes any possible gravitational influ- ences on the airways, as well as on cardiorespiratory function. To avoid confusion, endoscopic photographs, training manuals, and endobronchial maps (Amis and McKiernan 1986) are studied and clearly understood. 5.5 Bronchoscopic T raining A good bronchoscopist must be able to easily maneuver the scope for efficient viewing of the tracheobronchial tree and collection of specimens with minimal risk to the patient due to unnecessarily prolonged anesthetic times or mucosal trauma. The bronchoscopist must have a good understand - ing of normal endobronchial lung anatomy as well as mucosal and dynamic airway changes to be able to diagnose abnormalities and diseases. The differentiation or recogni - tion of normal from what is abnormal is obviously a subjec - tive one. Experience and practice will greatly improve the ability to detect lesions at an early stage of disease. Canine endobronchial anatomy differs from the human anatomy. In 1986, Amis and McKiernan described the normal endo - bronchial anatomy and proposed terminology for the dog which has proven reliable and a useful aid or “endoscopic map” during clinical bronchoscopy (Figure 5.6). Similar endoscopic maps have been proposed for use in cats (Caccamo et al. 2007). Bronchoscopic training models can be prepared from lungs collected from cadavers. The use of these dried lung models (McKiernan and Kneller 1983) and a good understanding of normal endobronchial anatomy ensures that beginners have the opportunity to safely develop the manual dexterity and anatomic recognition skills that are critical to becoming a competent bron - choscopist. These endoscopic maps are also very helpful in correlating radiographic lesions to endoscopic findings and vice versa, in localizing lesions, and for recording the loca - tion in writing of lesions, biopsies, or photographs for future comparison and reference. Endoscopy short courses are available through some veterinary schools and at various national meetings. The clinician must pursue some form of specialized training prior to using bronchoscopy as a diag - nostic tool. Bronchoscopic findings and visual changes in the res - piratory mucosa are difficult to describe or depict through line drawings or black and white photography. The reader is encouraged to review normal canine endobronchial anatomy, to consult texts and color photographs of endo - scopic findings from healthy as well as diseased animals when beginning to learn bronchoscopy (Venker-Van Haagen 1979; Venker-van Haagen et al. 1985; Amis and McKiernan 1986; McKiernan 1989; Ford 1990; Roudebush 1990; Brearley et al. 1991; Padrid and McKiernan 1999; McKiernan 2005). 5.6 Bronchoscopic Procedure All necessary bronchoscopic supplies and equipment are made ready before starting the procedure to minimize anesthetic time and maximize the benefits of the bronchoscopy. Mouth gags, an oxygen delivery system, endotracheal tubes, biopsy forceps, preloaded lavage syringes, and cytology slides are laid out for easy access (Figure 5.7). The bronchoscope is clean and ready for use; anesthetic monitoring equipment is turned on and ready, and image capture equipment is calibrated and white bal- anced prior to induction. Consultation with the anesthesiologist is done prior to the procedure with review of the planned endoscopic procedures including diagnostic steps to be performed, possible interventional techniques, and use of a laser, or Figure 5.5 Oxygen supplementation is provided during bronchoscopy by connecting to the biopsy channel of the bronchoscope (arrow) when the channel is not being used for biopsy or lavage purposes.

5 Bronchoscopy 200 other indicated steps (Goudra et al. 2015). As the animal is being induced, the setup is finalized by connecting any monitoring equipment and ensuring proper sternal posi- tioning for the procedure. Dental mouth gags are placed as soon as they are tolerated in order to protect the endoscope during the procedure. Topical anesthetic (1–2% lidocaine) may be applied or sprayed onto the pharyngeal/laryngeal mucosa if desired at this time. Topical lidocaine is also rec- ommended to reduce coughing and bronchospasm due to the procedure (Wahidi et al. 2011; Goudra et al. 2015). Supplemental oxygen is administered as previously described. A systematic examination of both the upper and lower airways is performed when doing a bronchoscopy. By using injectable anesthetics and without intubation a thor - ough evaluation of the oropharynx and larynx is possible to note changes in the anatomy, the mucosa, and the intrinsic function or motion of the larynx during quiet breathing. Following comple - tion of the bronchoscopy, patients are administered sup - plemental oxygen by intubation or a face mask until fully recovered from anesthesia. 5.7 Normal and Abnormal Bronchoscopic Findings After the larynx is evaluated and using the endobronchial “map” (Figure 5.6), the bronchoscope is inserted down the cervical trachea and into the intrathoracic trachea noting any abnormalities in shape, dynamic caliber changes or collapse, as well as mucosal disorders including secretions, erythema, edema, masses, or other lesions. The carina is evaluated for abnormalities such as widening, compres - sion, or mucosal infiltration before sequentially evaluating all the lobar bronchi with as many segmental and subseg - mental bronchi as possible. The extent of this examination varies based on both patient and endoscope size. If time and anesthetic depth allow, retroflex examination around the soft palate is performed to evaluate the nasopharynx and choanae as the bronchoscopy is being completed. As the endoscope is passed through the glottic lumen (Figure 5.8), C-shaped cartilaginous rings are normally vis - ible through the mucosa and beneath the tracheal submu- cosal capillary network (Figure 5.9). When this capillary bed is not clearly visible (Figure 5.10), it implies to the endoscopist that there is either some degree of superficial mucosal edema or cellular infiltration present. The shape of the trachea is noted, with healthy dogs and cats of most breeds having a nearly circular-shaped cervical and intrathoracic trachea (Figure 5.11). Segmental hypoplasia may be encountered, most often in toy breed dogs near the thoracic inlet. Dorsoventral, and rarely lateral, flattening of the trachea is common in toy breed dogs (Figure 5.12). The location, length of involved segment, as well as the severity of the collapse (Grade 1–4) are noted and are critically important when anticipating placement of tracheal stents (Sura and Krahwinkel 2008). Brachycephalic breeds commonly suffer from tracheal hypoplasia that often affects the entire length of their tra- chea that is diagnosed and documented radiographically (Harvey and Fink 1982). Endoscopically, tracheal hypo - plasia is detected by noting overlapping ends of the tra- cheal rings, a misshapen and narrowed tracheal lumen (Figure 5.13), and often excess secretions foamed into a froth in the trachea (Figure 5.14). Many of these breeds have been shown to have a high incidence of bronchial col- lapse and in one study, a total of 94 bronchial stenosis sites were noted in 35 of 40 brachycephalic dogs (DeLorenzi et al. 2009). Normal canine and feline airways have a monopodial branching system and there is a gentle, smooth tapering of the airways into the periphery (Figure 5.15). Changes in the size and shape of the tracheobronchial tree may be focal or generalized and include intraluminal strictures Figure 5.7 All necessary equipment is set out ahead of time in preparation for the bronchoscopic procedure. Johnson and Pollard (2010) reported that approximately 50% of respiratory cases evalu- ated with bronchoscopy were found to have greater than 50% collapse of one or more airways. The dorsal tracheal membrane is viewed as a longitudi - nal strip of muscle joining the ends of the “C” shaped tra - cheal rings (Figure 5.22). In the normal animal, the tracheal membrane is stretched relatively tightly so that there is little if any redundancy or visible protrusion with collapse into the airway during breathing. Small dynamic airway caliber change may be noted during respirations but the airways will not completely collapse in the healthy animal even during a forceful expiratory maneuver such as coughing. Excessive airway narrowing is commonly observed in animals with tracheal and bronchial collapse (bronchomalacia) which are conditions with altered struc - tural integrity of cartilaginous support of the airways (Figure 5.23). Note that the mucosa may appear too white due to light reflection when the scope is too close to the surface. The normal mucosa has a slight glistening appearance due to the presence of a thin layer of fluid (the “sol”) on its sur - face. Excessive fluid accumulation within the mucosa (edema) is readily apparent as it imparts a gelatinous appearance to the epithelial surface (Figure 5.25). Generalized mucosa hyperemia due to inflammatory changes with increased vascularity is a common finding in chronic respiratory diseases. Since animals undergo bron- choscopy due to disease concerns, care must be taken when interpreting appearance of the tracheobronchial mucosa to not accept this hyperemia as normal. Small polypoid mucosal nodules (Figure 5.26) are commonly encountered in cases of chronic bronchitis in dogs. These are not to be mistaken for neoplastic nodules. The left principal bronchus exits the trachea at a slightly sharper angle compared to the right principal bronchus which is more in direct line with the trachea (Figure 5.6). Although the lung and bronchial epithelium appear to respond to irritation in limited ways, grossly visible changes may not be pathognomonic for any specific disease (Haschek 1986). Samples from the airways are therefore needed to establish an etiology or specific diagnosis. Whether gross bronchoscopic abnormalities are noted or not, samples are obtained for culture and cytology with occasional samples for histopathologic evaluation. Airway cytology has been the principal method of evaluating lower airway disease in veterinary medicine. Specimens have been collected by various methods including transtracheal or transoral wash (TTW), bronchial brushing, or bron- choalveolar lavage (BAL). BAL is performed by specifically wedging a bronchoscope or catheter into a distal airway. These different methods of sample collection require dif- ferent evaluative criteria since the cells obtained represent or come from varying portions of the airways.
