The technique is “blind” since a spe - cific lobe cannot be selectively examined as with the bron- choscopic BAL technique, nor can a specific lesion or lobe on a radiograph be selectively assessed. Most often the catheter will end up in one of the caudal lung lobes. Bronchoscopy allows direct visualization of the airways and specific selection of the site for BAL sample collection. The cells from BAL fluid (BALf) are thought to represent the distal small airways and interstitium of the lung (Hawkins et al. 1990). BAL is the only lung sampling tech- nique for which normal differential cell counts have been established and standardized; Table 5.2 summarizes normal BAL differential cell counts from dogs and cats. BAL is the preferred method of sampling the lower airways of dogs and cats. To perform a BAL and collect BALf, the bronchoscope is first gently wedged into a segmental or smaller bronchus. The specific BAL lobe and bronchus site is selected based either on previous chest radiographs or gross visual find- ings during the initial bronchoscopic examination. If how - ever no site is clearly identified as being affected, BALf is obtained from both of the “middle” lung lobes, or more accurately the right middle lobe and the caudal portion of the left cranial lobe. Once the scope is in a wedged position, warm, sterile saline is instilled into the airway via the suc- tion channel of the endoscope or using a sterile washing pipette inserted through the biopsy channel (Figure 5.42). The liquid is immediately aspirated using the same syringe and gentle hand suction (Figure 5.43). Ideally, the proce - dure is repeated twice in each lobe or site. Suction traps may also be used to collect the BALf. The volume instilled for a BAL varies depending on the size of the patient; ali- quots of 10–20 ml/dog or ~2 ml/kg for cats are commonly used. The sites are evaluated individually with total cell counts and a cytospin for dif- ferential cell counts. Differences in BALf analyses obtained from different lobes have been noted (Ybarra 2012). The predominant cell in all species is the alveolar mac- rophage (70+), with usually less than 3–8% of all other cell types. An exception occurs with the cat which may have up to 20%+ eosinophils and still be considered healthy (Figure 5.44). Many pathologists interpret this macrophage predominance in the BALf cell differential as “granuloma- tous” in nature. This is based on the large percentage of macrophages but this is incorrect as the macrophage is the most common normal cell distally in the lung. Cultures from the lower airways are critical in establish - ing a specific diagnosis and in selecting an appropriate anti - biotic based on sensitivity results. Obviously, upper airway contamination must be avoided. The finding of either squa - mous epithelium and/or the large bacterium Simonsiella spp. (Figure 5.45) both of which are common to the oral cavity confirms upper airway contamination, and caution must be used in the interpretation of any BAL results. Obtaining culture samples through an endoscope is con- troversial owing to the opportunity for sample contamina- tion both from the oral cavity as well as from an improperly cleaned endoscope channel. Guarded catheters 3 are avail- able and help decrease the potential for upper airway con- tamination of a BAL sample obtained with flexible endoscopy. Unfortunately, the cost of these catheters has 3 Microbiology Specimen Brush, Medi-Tech, Watertown, MA. been an impediment to their routine use in veterinary medicine. Over the years, a technique for obtaining BALf for cul- tures and cytology has been used without requiring special catheters. Once the initial gross (visual) evaluation of the lower airway is complete, the endoscope is removed from the patient and cleaned by alternating suctioning of the endoscope channel with sterile saline and air immediately prior to performing the BAL. Results have indicated (Peeters et al. 2001) that this technique allows for the col- lection of samples for both cytology and culture void of upper airway contamination. This technique assumes proper endoscope sterilization prior to use. When multiple sites from multiple lung lobes have been sampled, the BALf collected may be combined for a quan- titated culture. Disposable sterile microbiology loops 4 are available to perform quantified cultures and are both inex - pensive and easy to use if cultures are to be plated out in practice. These loops are calibrated to contain 0.01 ml and the resultant colony count is multiplied by 100 to obtain the CFU (colony-forming units)/milliliter of BAL or other fluid (Figure 5.46). Most bronchoscopists recommend per - forming aerobic and Mycoplasma cultures, but rarely anaerobic cultures. It has recently been reported that aero - bic bacterial cultures of 1.7 × 10 3 colony-forming units are required in canine BALf in order to differentiate infection vs. airway colonization (Peeters et al. 2001). Culture results which only report “light growth” are held in suspicion when trying to determine true lower airway infection. 4 Disposable Inoculation Loops (0.01 ml), American Diagnostics, Pendleton, IN. 5.9 Sum mary 213 Gram stain cytology is very helpful in the interpretation of culture results; the presence of 2 intracellular bacteria in any of 50 HPF fields was associated with true infection. Regardless of collection technique, microbiological results must always be interpreted in light of the cytology obtained from the same site for the most accurate interpretation. Although their specific role in small animal clinical res - piratory disease is still uncertain, technology advance - ments have allowed for the easy detection of Mycoplasma spp. Using specialized transport media (e.g. Amies media) or PCR technology based on either the actual BALf or con- centrated cytospin smears, combined with overnight ship - ment to selected laboratories, Mycoplasma can easily be detected in BALf. The clinical significance of positive Mycoplasma samples obtained from the lower airways remains controversial. Mycoplasma spp. are normal inhab - itants of the oropharynx in small animals. Mucosal biopsy samples may be obtained when definite changes are seen or when a mass lesion is visualized (Figure 5.35). Samples obtained with endoscopic forceps are typically small and interpretation may be difficult. When biopsy is performed, multiple specimens are taken if feasible to give the pathologist a greater chance of making a diagnosis. One of the biopsy samples may be gently touched to a glass slide for cytologic evaluation while wait - ing for the results from histopathology. Due to differences in the mucosa, the diagnostic return from bronchial mucosal biopsy is relatively low or often nonspecific, espe - cially when compared to endoscopic gastrointestinal mucosal biopsies. The routine use of transbronchial biopsy techniques, using a Wang biopsy needle or biopsy forceps, has not been well established in veterinary medicine. If a bronchial mucosal biopsy is being used to diagnose pri- mary ciliary dyskinesia, a similar biopsy of the nasal mucosa is evaluated to help differentiate secondary changes due to chronic lower airway disease. Bronchoscopy is generally a safe procedure and assum- ing routine anesthetic precautions are taken, lacks any serious complications. There are a number of potential complications that have been associated with bronchos - copy in human medicine but most of these are uncommon with bronchoscopy in dogs and cats. In people, the list of potentially serious complications includes those associated with anesthesia (e.g. anesthetic reaction, arrhythmias, hemodynamic issues, endotracheal tube trauma, and hypoventilation), effects of the bronchoscopic procedure itself (e.g. bronchospasm, bleeding, bacteremia, pneumo - thorax, and hypoxemia), and those that occur following completion of the procedure (e.g. fever, infection, and new pulmonary infiltrates) (Leiten et al. 2016). Table 5.1 is a list of indications, contraindications, and potential complica- tions of bronchoscopy in dogs and cats. The most serious complications I have encountered were in patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmo - nary disease and specifically those with severe malacic changes and airway collapse (Figure 5.23). These animals may develop exercise or stress-related hypoxemia follow - ing bronchoscopy especially during recovery from anes - thesia. Dogs that present with a chronic history of coughing with or without severe expiratory effort (an abdominal push) while breathing at rest should be consid - ered at high risk during anesthetic recovery. Close patient monitoring (heart rate, oxygen saturation, depth of breath - ing) is imperative throughout the procedure and recovery. Great care is taken in choosing an anesthetic protocol, which allows for a non-excitable, slow anesthetic recovery. Topical lidocaine may be used pre-, during, and post- bronchoscopy to minimize coughing and potential airway collapse during and following the bronchoscopy proce - dure (Wahidi et al. 2011). In anticipation of potential problems, it is imperative that the veterinary bronchoscopist be prepared for all even- tualities. This means that he or she must have a clear understanding of patient risk factors, limitations of the equipment being used, and have both the knowledge as well as all drugs and equipment necessary to treat any of these complications should they develop. 5.9 Summary There is no question that bronchoscopy, including BALf cytology and quantitated airway culture, is the gold stand- ard for diagnosis of lower respiratory tract diseases in small animals. Potential limitations to bronchoscopy are the availability of experienced bronchoscopists and the necessary equipment as well as concerns for general anesthesia and owners’ financial abilities. Despite these concerns, bronchoscopy is considered the diagnostic test of choice in any case with significant, and especially chronic, lower respiratory tract disease in the dog and cat. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 6.1 Introduction Cystoscopy is the most underutilized diagnostic technique in small animal veterinary practice today. Appropriate application of cystoscopy will completely redefine our understanding of lower urinary tract diseases, and once it reaches its full potential, its use will exceed that of gastro - intestinal endoscopy. Transurethral cystoscopy (TUC) has been an integral part of urology in human medicine for over 200 years and was one of the earliest endoscopic pro - cedures performed (Bozzini 1806). Compared with other diagnostic techniques, TUC has been ignored in veterinary medicine. Lower urinary tract disorders comprise a signifi- cant number of diseases diagnosed and treated in small animals, yet TUC has been, until recently, rarely used in veterinary medicine despite the readily available cost- effective instrumentation. TUC is also one of the easiest endoscopic techniques to learn and perform. Cystoscopy in male and female dogs was first reported by Vermooten in 1930 as a technique used in research (Vermooten 1930), and additional human medical research applications were reported in female dogs (Barringer 1947). TUC in dogs was described in 1966 with a discussion of pos - sible clinical application (Ensor 1966). Clinical diagnostic application of cystoscopy in small animals began appearing in the literature in the 1980s and was largely concentrated on female dogs (Biewenga and van Oosterom 1985; Cooper et al. 1984; McCarthy and McDermaid 1990; Senior and Sundstrom 1988; Stone et al. 1983). In the same period, cys - toscopy in male dogs was described transurethrally (Cooper et al. 1984; McCarthy and McDermaid 1986), using perineal urethrostomy or percutaneous perineal puncture (Brearley et al. 1988; Cooper et al. 1984), prepubic percutaneous puncture (McCarthy and McDermaid 1986), and more recently a laparoscopic-assisted approach (Rawlings 2007; Rawlings et al. 2003). Clinical use of cystoscopy was not reported in cats until 1986 (McCarthy and McDermaid 1986) as a prepubic percutaneous technique. Ureteral catheteriza- tion in female dogs under TUC guidance was initially described in 1966 (Ensor 1966) but did not gain acceptance until interventional radiology was added to the technique. The first reported therapeutic application of urinary endos - copy was percutaneous nephroscopy for stone removal (Donner 1987), which was later evaluated using electrohy - draulic shock wave lithotripsy for bladder stone removal in dogs (Adams and Senior 1999). The author’s experience has evolved over 35 years in private small animal surgical referral practice where cys - toscopy has dramatically improved the quality of medicine available and has been not only economically feasible but also financially rewarding. Cystoscopy has many advantages over other diagnostic techniques. The most important is that cystoscopy provides noninvasive direct visualization of the vaginal vestibule, vagi- novestibular junction, vaginal body, cervix, external cervical os, urethral orifice, urethra, bladder, and ureteral ostia. Visualization of these structures, even where accessible by surgery, is far superior with cystoscopy because of the magni- fication provided by the telescopes, excellent lighting, a clear visual field, and lack of distortion that occurs with cystotomy or other surgical entry methods into the urinary tract. TUC has been performed in a wide range of male and female dogs and cats using the currently available instru- ments. Prepubic percutaneous cystoscopy (PPC), percuta- neous perineal cystoscopy, and laparoscopic-assisted cystoscopy (LAC) are also used to evaluate the bladder and proximal urethra where TUC is not possible due to an inad- equate selection of available instrumentation, owing to urethral pathology, or when operative procedures are indi- cated that are beyond the scope of transurethral access. 6 Cystoscopy 218 Data on the procedures performed by the author have been collected since 1983 and led to the development of the diagnostic techniques and operative procedures presented in this chapter. PPC was the first technique used to evalu- ate the bladder with endoscopy but has largely been replaced with TUC and more recently with LAC. During this 37-year period, 1008 cystoscopy procedures were per - formed on 897 cases (Table 6.1). TUC was performed in 494 female dogs whose weights ranged from 2.3 to 102 kg, 166 male dogs from 2.7 to 79 kg, 61 female cats, 34 male cats, and 69 male cats during or immediately after perineal ure - throstomy. PPC was performed to evaluate 19 male dogs varying in size from 5.9 to 41 kg, 4 female dogs from 19 to 34 kg, and 11 male cats. LAC then replaced PPC and was used to examine 22 female dogs from 2.3 to 31 kg, 113 male dogs from 2.7 to 43 kg, 10 female cats, and 17 male cats. Addition of LAC allows a minimally invasive approach for almost all bladder surgery and has made traditional open cystotomy an obsolete procedure. Diagnoses in this series of procedures are listed in Table 6.2. 6.2 Cystoscopy Indications Any and all signs, symptoms, laboratory results, and imaging findings suggesting lower urinary tract disease are indications for cystoscopy. TUC is also indicated in asymp - tomatic older dogs from breeds at risk for developing TCC. Various urinary tract pathologies are diagnosed with cys - toscopy (Table 6.2) and most if not all surgical diseases of the bladder can be corrected with one of the cystoscopy approaches better than with open surgery. Any lesion that originates in or penetrates the mucosa into the lumen are visualized, their extent evaluated, and biopsies taken with cystoscopy. Chronic inflammatory changes are observed, the area of involvement defined, and biopsies taken for his - topathology; when indicated, biopsies are taken for mucosal cultures (Sycamore et al. 2014). Masses in the bladder, urethra, and vagina are noted, their extent evalu- ated, and biopsies taken, and many operable lesions are removed (McCarthy 2003). Small cystic and urethral cal- culi are removed transurethrally therapeutically; these are used as diagnostic samples for stone analysis. Larger stones are crushed with hand instruments or exploded with elec- trohydraulic and laser lithotripsy for transurethral removal. Medium-sized stones are removed intact with PPC and large intact stones are removed with LAC with visualiza- tion better than with traditional open cystoscopy. TUC is the procedure of choice for assessment of urinary tract trauma as the entire urinary tract can be easily and quickly assessed by visualizing the vaginal vestibule, urethral ori- fice, urethra, and bladder, and the kidneys and ureters by examining the clear urine from both ureters. TUC is also the procedure of choice for diagnosis and definition of ectopic ureters as well as for the correction of intramural lesions. Bladder diverticula are assessed effectively with cystoscopy. However, cystoscopy is limited to lesions that are visible within the lumen of the vagina, urethra, and bladder, those that involve the mucosa, and the ureteral openings. Any chronic or acute urinary tract disease not resolved with initial treatment is an indication for cystoscopy (Table 6.3). 6.2 Cystoscopy Innications 219 technique for urinary tract evaluation. Veterinarians should pose the question “WHEN is cystoscopy indicated in the management of lower urinary tract diseases?” and not based on whether cystoscopy is indicated. 6.2.1 Chronic Cystitis Cystitis that has not responded to initial conservative med- ical treatment and the lack of a definitive diagnosis by less invasive techniques are indications for cystoscopy. The time in case management when cystoscopy is indicated cannot be stated with uniformity and will vary from patient to patient. In pursuing a diagnosis, cystoscopy is consid- ered along with ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced radiography. However, cystoscopy consistently provides more information about the lesions within the lumen of the bladder and urethra compared with those obtained with contrast radiographic studies or ultrasonography. Biopsies taken from the urethra, vagina, and bladder using cystoscopy have a higher diagnostic yield than less invasive techniques (Childress et al. 2011). 6.2.2 Hematuria Persistent low-grade hematuria or acute severe hematuria is an important indication for cystoscopy. Multiple etiolo - gies of hematuria are ruled out with endoscopic evaluation and the origin of the bleeding is localized. In older female dogs, a common cause of chronic nonresponsive hematu- ria is neoplasia. Masses are found, defined, and biopsied more easily and earlier with cystoscopy than with other diagnostic tools. Renal bleeding is localized by evaluation of urine characteristics as secreted from the ureters. The involved kidney or kidneys are determined, and with ureteral catheterization, specific samples are collected. Bladder wall hemorrhage is diagnosed, and appropriate biopsies taken to establish an etiology. 6.2.3 T enesmus or Stranguria Straining to urinate is a frequent sign of cystitis and urethritis but may also be due to other causes such as neo - plasia, cystic calculi, urethral calculi, prostatic disease, and urethral obstruction due to strictures or non-urologic diseases. Cystoscopy and urethroscopy are used in the dif- ferentiation of etiologies. In managing urethral transitional cell carcinomas (TCCs), the urethra in female dogs pre - senting with chronic signs of lower urinary tract disease should be assessed, as early diagnosis results in better out - comes. A case in point is an eight-year-old female Dachshund that presented with straining and difficulty urinating. Cystoscopy revealed a small urethral TCC in situ that was removed surgically. This dog was asymptomatic for three years after surgery. This is an individual case and does not imply that surgical removal is an effective treat - ment in all cases. However, most TCCs in dogs (98%) are diagnosed when they are invasive with many having exten- sive areas of urethral and bladder involvement, thereby making resection impossible (Fulkerson and Knapp 2015; Knapp et al. 2014). This case simply illustrates the impor - tance of cystoscopy for early diagnosis. Another case is a 10-year-old West Highland White Terrier that presented with a vaginal discharge. Vaginoscopy was performed to assess the vaginal discharge, with cystos - copy as an ancillary procedure. A 2 mm diameter TCC lesion was found in the bladder, which was removed with 5 Fr biopsy forceps for obtaining a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and to debulk the lesion. The bed of the lesion was ablated with a diode laser. Preanesthetic urinalysis and abdominal ultrasound were both normal in this patient. A veterinary bladder tumor antigen test (V-BTA) was nega- tive. Reexamination of the bladder in this dog was repeated at 6-month intervals with repeat laser ablation as indicated. The dog was tumor-free at 18 months. 6.2.4 Increased Frequency of Urination Pollakiuria is a sign of lower urinary tract disease but may also be an indication of polyuria. Cystoscopy is beneficial in establishing an etiology of lower urinary tract disease or ruling out its involvement as the cause of the increased fre - quency of urination. 6.2.5 Urinary Incontinence Urine dribbling, particularly in younger female dogs, is a sign that warrants endoscopic assessment of the lower Table 6.3 Indications for cystoscopy. 6 Cystoscopy 220 genitourinary tract. A common cause of incontinence in younger female dogs is ectopic ureters. The vagina, ure - thra, and trigone area of the bladder are accurately and eas - ily assessed using TUC. Magnification provided by endoscopy allows the ureteral openings to be found any - where in the lower urinary tract, and their pathology is defined and categorized. Urethral deformities are com- monly found in patients with ectopic ureters, and these are accurately defined. Hydroureters are frequently associated with ectopic ureters and are assessed because the endo - scope can be passed into the dilated ureters in many cases. The prognosis for ectopic ureter correction is not associ- ated with the location of entry of the ureters into the lower urinary tract or to visible ureteral and urethral pathology. Accurate cystoscopic evaluation is essential to preoperative assessment in planning operative procedures (Samii et al. 2004). Radiographic examination for ectopic ureters by excretory urography can in some cases establish a diag - nosis, but accurate placement of the ureteral openings and an understanding of urethral pathology is difficult at best (Cannizzo et al. 2003). Ultrasound evaluation of ureteral and urethral pathology is also less rewarding compared with cystoscopy in defining abnormal ectopic ureteral anatomy and is also hampered by the pelvis. Contrast radi- ology and ultrasound are very helpful in defining renal and proximal ureteral abnormalities that cannot be seen with TUC. Open surgical assessment of abnormal ureteral anat - omy is extremely difficult as ectopic ureters can traverse the full length of the urethral wall up to the opening of the urethral orifice or into the vagina. Ectopic ureters com- monly enter the exterior surface of the bladder wall through a normal location and pass caudally variable distances within the urethral wall before opening into the urethral lumen. At surgery it may only be possible to determine that the ureter enters the bladder wall at a normal location, but it can be very difficult to locate ureteral openings or exten- sive dissection may be required to fully define ureteral and urethral pathology. For these reasons TUC is the procedure of choice for the evaluation and diagnosis of urinary incon- tinence in young female dogs, as well as for the correction of intramural ectopic ureters in female dogs. TUC is one of the minimally invasive options for ectopic ureter correc- tion in male dogs. Incontinence in older female dogs is due to various causes, both urinary and non-urinary in origin. Assessment of the lower urinary tract is essential to gain a complete under - standing of incontinence and to rule out specific pathology such as urethral tumors. TUC is also used in the submucosal injection of bulking agents to manage incontinence. Urinary incontinence in male dogs is far less common than compared with that in females. Ectopic ureters do occur and are typically associated with incontinence or recurrent urinary tract infections. TUC using a small flexible fiberoptic or video endoscope is effective in diag - nosing ectopic ureters in male dogs that are large enough to allow passage of the endoscopes. PPC or LAC is also used to diagnosing ectopic ureters in smaller male dogs or if flexible instruments are not available. Correction of ectopic ureters in male dogs is also performed transure - thrally, but it is far more difficult than in females. LAC and PPC are effective minimally invasive approaches for cor - rection of ectopic ureters in male dogs. 6.2.6 Ureteroceles Ureteroceles are an uncommon abnormality that occurs when the intramural portion of a normally placed or ectopic ureter dilates to form a cyst-like structure in the bladder or proximal urethra (Rogatko et al. 2019). These are easily visible with cystoscopy as well as with ultrasound or contrast urogra- phy. Correction of ureteroceles requires techniques and instrumentation similar to those used for ectopic ureters. 6.2.7 Alteration of the Urinary Stream Changes in the size and shape of the urine stream are an indication of urethral pathology including prostatic disease, calculi, strictures, proliferative urethritis, and neoplasia. These conditions are easily assessed with TUC except in very small patients. 6.2.8 Trauma As mentioned in previous sections, TUC is the procedure of choice for the evaluation of urinary tract trauma in female dogs and cats. Availability of small flexible endo - scopes has expanded trauma indications for TUC, thus including male dogs. Significant trauma to the entire uri- nary tract can be effectively ruled out with TUC. Contusions, mucosal tears, penetrating lacerations, blad- der ruptures, and ureteral or kidney trauma are evaluated. Integrity of the kidneys and ureters is determined by obser - vation of clear urine excreted from both ureters. The absence of urine or presence of significant hematuria is an indication for further upper urinary tract assessment. A review of cystoscopic findings in 36 consecutive cases with pelvic fractures evaluated by the author revealed a 92% incidence of urinary tract trauma (Table 6.4). This com- pares with a 39% incidence of urinary tract trauma in 100 consecutive cases with pelvic fractures diagnosed with contrast radiography (Selser 1982). Ultrasound is also an effective method for evaluating urinary tract trauma cra- nial to the pelvis. A large percentage of cases of urinary tract trauma are managed conservatively by maintaining

Evaluation of the urinary tract in pelvic fracture cases is performed as a separate procedure or at the time of anes - thesia for orthopedic reconstructions. If bladder trauma requiring surgery is found at this time, the orthopedic pro - cedure is delayed, and the urinary system reconstructed. The time and expense involved in endoscopic evaluation of the traumatized urinary tract is less than that required for ultrasound examination or radiographic assessment either by excretory urography or by cystourethrography. If small flexible instrumentation is not available for evaluation of male dogs, then ultrasound or positive contrast cystoure - thrography is employed. Normal appearing micturition does not rule out significant urinary tract compromise. Interest in more effective assessment of the urinary tract in pelvic fracture cases occurred after two patients who were able to stand and urinate clear urine normally developed uroabdomen a week after pelvic fracture reconstruction. Both these patients had puncture wounds of the bladder that were small enough to allow normal urination while urine leaked slowly into the abdomen. The common occur - rence of urinary tract damage in caudal abdominal and pelvic trauma, and the severe consequences of delayed diagnosis, both to the patient and for the client in terms of accurate cost estimation and prognostication, make accu- rate assessment of urinary tract damage critical. 6.2.9 Cystic and Urethral Calculi Cystic and urethral calculi may cause tenesmus, hematuria, chronic nonresponsive cystitis, and alteration of the urine stream, all of which are indications for cystoscopy. The presence of calculi that are considered incidental findings on radiographs taken for other reasons is also an indication for cystoscopy. When cystic calculi are diagnosed radio - graphically or by palpation, cystoscopy may be performed to obtain stone samples for analysis along with mucosal biopsies for histopathology and culture. Appropriate medical and dietary therapy is then employed for dissolva- ble calculi based on accurate knowledge of stone composi- tion. Surgery is thus avoided. Therapeutic removal of smaller stones transurethrally is done using foreign body graspers, biopsy forceps, or stone removal baskets, by irriga- tion and suction, or by hydropropulsion. Larger stones require crushing or lithotripsy prior to removal and can also be accessed for removal with LAC or PPC. 6.3 Instrumentation for Cystoscopy A wide variety of endoscopes is available for use to perform cystoscopy in small animal patients. Rigid human cysto - scopes are made in multiple sizes, from 1.9 to 4.0 mm, which are applicable for TUC in almost all female dogs and cats (Figure 2.26). To perform TUC in the vast majority of female dogs, the 2.7 mm MPRT is the telescope of choice (Figure 2.30 and Table 6.5) although a new telescope (2.9 mm in diameter, 30 cm long) may replace this old standard. For female cats and for the smallest female dogs, a 9.5 Fr one-piece cystoscope is the best choice (Figure 2.31 and Table 6.6). The 4.0 mm cystoscope is recommended for larger female dogs greater than approximately 25 kg (Figures 2.26, 2.35, and Table 6.6). These three telescopes are all that are needed to provide transurethral access in female patients in small animal practice. The one-piece 9.5 Fr (2.6 mm × 3.8 mm) cystoscope is an exception because the telescope and sheath are incorporated into one piece. Bridges are a standard component of cystoscopes intended for adult humans and are used to connect the 4.0 mm cystoscope to their sheaths (Figure 2.35). Straight bridges are available with no instrument access port for examination only or with up to three instrument access ports. Channels in cystoscopy bridges and sheaths allow passage of flexible instrumentation from 3 Fr with the smaller systems up to one 12 Fr instrument or multiple smaller instruments for the larger bridge sheath combina- tion for the 4.0 cystoscope. Smaller telescope sheaths for cystoscopy do not have a bridge and the sheath connects directly to the telescope (Figure 2.30). Instrumentation for obtaining biopsies, correcting ana- tomic abnormalities, removing stones, performing litho - tripsy, removing tumors or polyps, and dilating strictures are available in sizes that can be used with these telescopes in small animal patients (Figure 2.41 and Table 6.7). 6.3 ­InstrumIst stiI itr CnsinsioC 223 Continuous flow cystoscopy systems are a recent addi- tion to the armamentarium for TUC in small animal prac- tice. These systems provide simultaneous inflow and outflow of fluids and facilitate more complex and time- consuming procedures (Figure 6.1 and Table 6.8). A con- tinuous flow sheath system is available for use with the 4.0 mm diameter telescope, but not for the 2.7 mm MPRT, for the one-piece 9.5 Fr cystoscope, or for the 1.9/2.1 mm telescope. To perform continuous flow cystoscopy in smaller patients, additional telescopes are required. The smallest is the 2.0 mm diameter telescope with a 30° viewing angle and a length of 26 cm. A new continuous flow cystoscopy system is available with a 30 cm long, 2.9 mm diameter telescope that may replace both the 2.0 and 4.0 mm systems. Continuous flow sheaths are not needed until prolonged complex operative procedures requiring continuous flow cystoscopy are encountered. Continuous flow sheath systems have an inner and an outer coaxial cannula to allow simultaneous fluid inflow and fluid outflow. Continuous flow is not needed for most diagnostic procedures and for simple operative procedures, except when treatment progresses to more complex and prolonged operative procedures. Techniques using the standard sheaths that cause bleeding or produce smoke or other debris require repeated emptying and refilling of the bladder with fresh fluid to maintain a clear visual field, which can now be achieved uninterrupted with the con- tinuous bidirectional flow system. Fluid inflow is through the inner cannula and outflow is through the outer coaxial cannula. Maintaining a clear visual field with this system facilitates completion of complex procedures with less bladder trauma, less operator stress, less operating time, and increased operative accuracy. Traditional unidirectional systems use a single sheath that only allows flow in one direction at a time (Figure 2.35). These sheaths typically have two Luer fluid connection ports with stopcocks, but both are connected to the lumen of the single sheath and do not allow continuous bidirec- tional flow. Flow at any one time is either into the bladder or out of the bladder. Inflow and outflow lines are con- nected to the ports, and the inflow stopcock is opened so flow is allowed to fill the bladder; when the bladder is ade - quately distended, the inflow stopcock is closed; when the visual field is too cloudy, the outflow stopcock is opened to drain the bladder, and stopcock position is switched to refill the bladder with clear fluid. The 30° viewing angle of telescopes has been found to be the optimum angle for rigid cystoscopes used for transure - thral procedures in small animal applications. This angula- tion greatly increases the area that can be examined because with rotation of the telescope, structures are visi- ble that are not directly in line with the axis of the instru- ment. Thirty degrees also has minimal visual disorientation compared to greater angles. Additional telescopes are avail- able with angles ranging from 0° to 120° (Figure 2.27). Blunt obturators are available for use while passing the cystoscopy sheaths into and through the urethra during a blind passage technique rather than by direct visualization. This technique is employed in human medicine but has not been used by the author in small animal patients. The obturators are therefore not needed. In small animal practice, resectoscopes have been used most com- monly for transurethral removal of bladder and urethral tumors. Another application has been for LAC correction of ectopic ureters and ureteroceles in male dogs. Resectoscope systems include a working element that con- trols the movement of an electrode in and out of the cysto - scope sheath, sheaths of various sizes with either unidirectional or continuous bidirectional flow, and differ - ent unipolar or bipolar cutting or coagulating electrodes (Figure 6.5 and Table 6.11). The resectoscope system for the 2.7 mm MPRT is monopolar with a working element, a 13 Fr unidirectional flow sheath with an 11 cm working length, and a selection of various monopolar electrodes. The 4.0 mm cystoscope resectoscope system includes a working element, 24–28 Fr unidirectional or continuous flow 20 cm working length sheaths, and monopolar and bipolar electrodes. The 2.9 mm diameter, 30 cm long tele - scope resectoscope system has a working element, 15–22 Fr unidirectional and bidirectional sheaths with a 20 cm working length, and both monopolar and bipolar elec- trodes. Resectoscope systems work best with 0° or 12° tel- escopes but will work with 30° telescopes. Diagnostic and operative TUC to this point has used 30° telescopes and this angle of view is used to avoid the expense of purchas - ing additional telescopes. The arthroscopy sheaths for the 2.7 mm MPRT or other smaller arthroscopes are occasionally used for TUC if the 9.5 Fr one-piece cystoscope is not available and for patients that are too small for the 2.7 mm cystoscope. Arthroscopy sheaths have the primary advantage of having a smaller diameter relative to the cystoscope sheath size, as it facili- tates transurethral examination of smaller female dogs and female cats and male cats during or after perineal urethros - tomy surgery has been performed. The primary disadvan- tage of using arthroscopy sheaths for cystoscopy is that they do not have an instrument channel. Arthroscopy sys - tems that are used for PPC and LAC include the telescope, cannula, sharp trocars, second puncture cannulas with their trocars, and rigid instrumentation for obtaining biopsies, removing stones, tumors and polyps, and dilating strictures. Rigid telescopes have limited applications for TUC in male dogs and cats. The distal straight portion of the ure - thra of some giant male dogs has been examined with small rigid telescopes. Male cats have been examined tran- surethrally with a 1.0 mm diameter semirigid telescope and with either the 9.5 Fr diameter cystoscope or the 2.7 mm MPRT with the arthroscopy cannula during or after a per - ineal urethrostomy has been performed. The three sizes of cystoscope systems effectively cover the size range of patients seen in small animal practice. The 4.0 mm telescope and its cannulas have been used for TUC in female dogs larger than 40 lb. 6.3 ­InstrumIststiI itr CnsinsioC 227 6.3.3 Instrumentation for T ransurethral Cystoscopy in Male Cats A semirigid telescope is used for TUC in male cats. This telescope is a 1.0 mm diameter (3.0 Fr) instrument with a 20 cm length and 0° viewing angle (Figure 2.26 and Table 2.2). It has been used primarily for TUC in male cats and has also been used occasionally for examination of the distal urethra in very small male dogs. This endoscope does not have a working channel. The image is transmitted through a fused silica bundle giving excellent image qual- ity for the size of the telescope. The fused silica bundle is a semirigid construction allowing the scope to be used with- out a cannula because mild bending of the instrument will not cause damage. It cannot be bent like a flexible endo - scope. Easy and effective examination of the urethra is pos - sible with excellent image clarity and sufficient light for photographic or video documentation. Examination of the bladder is more difficult because this endoscope is not flex - ible and does not have distal tip deflection control. This limitation can be overcome by external manipulation of the bladder to move areas of the wall in front of the endo - scope’s field of view. Light transmission is adequate for close up direct observation of the bladder wall, but photo - graphic and video documentation capability is limited. Samples of generalized bladder disease can be taken by passing small biopsy forceps transurethrally, without the endoscope in place, to obtain blind mucosal biopsies for histopathology and for cultures. Localized lesions have been sampled by combining transurethral placement of this endoscope with a prepubic percutaneous puncture for passing biopsy instruments. This telescope is supplied as an optical Veress pneumop - eritoneum needle for other applications. The needle is 2.1 mm in diameter with a working length of 17.5 cm and has a spring loaded blunt inner cannula in the needle. 6.3.4 Instrumentation for Prepubic Percutaneous Cystoscopy Instrumentation systems for PPC include rigid telescopes, cannulas with sharp trocars, second puncture cannulas with trocars, and operative instrumentation. 6.3.4.1 T elescopes The most commonly used rigid telescope for PPC is the 2.7 mm diameter 30° MPRT with a working length of 18.5 cm (Figure 2.30 and Table 6.5). This telescope with the arthroscopy sheath, protection sheath, and laparoscopy cannula/trocar works well for PPC in all but the largest or smallest patients. Other telescopes that have been used include 5.0 mm 0° or 30° laparoscopes with 30 cm working length (Figure 2.26 and Table 2.2) and 1.9 mm or 2.4 mm diameter 30° arthroscopes with 10.0 cm working lengths (Figure 2.26 and Table 4.4). The 2.7 mm diameter multipur - pose rigid telescope is used effectively for PPC in almost all small animal patients with the two smaller arthroscopes working well in cats and in very small dogs, while the 5.0 mm diameter laparoscopes allow more light transmis - sion and with their longer working length facilitate examination in larger dogs. 6.3.4.2 Sheaths Sheaths used with these telescopes for PPC do not have an instrument channel and are circular rather than the oval shape of the TUC cannulas. Outside diameters range in size from 8.4 Fr (2.8 mm) for the 1.9 mm arthroscope cannula and 9.6 Fr (3.2 mm) for the 2.4 mm arthroscope cannula (Table 4.4), 12 Fr (4.0 mm) for the 2.7 mm MPRT arthroscopy and laparoscopy cannulas (Figure 2.30 and Table 4.4), and 6.0 mm for the laparoscopy cannula used with the 5.0 mm laparoscopes (see Chapter 8). Arthroscopy cannulas connect and lock directly to the endoscope with- out an adaptor or bridge and do not have instrument ports or channels. Laparoscopy cannulas for use with the 2.7 mm multipurpose telescope and the 5.0 mm laparoscopes do not lock to the telescope but slide freely on the telescope. A valve and gasket system of the laparoscopy cannulas prevents leakage when the telescope is not in the cannula and around the telescope when the telescope is in the cannula. A protection sheath is strongly recommended to support the 2.7 mm MPRT when used with the laparoscopy cannula. Arthroscopy and laparoscopy cannulas are ideally suited for PPC. All these cannulas have single or double Luer connectors for fluid instillation. 6.3.4.3 Sharp T rocars and Blunt Obturators Sharp trocars are available for the arthroscopy and laparos - copy cannulas and are used to penetrate the abdominal and bladder walls for PPC. The arthroscopy trocars lock directly to the cannulas and laparoscopy trocars slide freely into the cannulas. Blunt obturators are also available for the arthroscopy and laparoscopy cannulas and are used to replace cannulas if they are displaced out of the portals during procedures. 6.3.4.4 Second Puncture Cannulas (See Chapter 8) Separate trocars and cannulas are used to obtain access to the bladder as a second puncture when performing PPC for sample collection, stone removal, or operative procedures. A second portal is required because the primary telescope cannulas do not have biopsy channels. These cannulas can also be used as a single percutaneous puncture when TUC

6 Cystoscopy 228 is performed for visualization using cannulas without a biopsy channel. Arthroscopy and laparoscopy cannulas in 2.5, 3.5, 6, and 11 mm diameters are used. These cannulas have a sharp trocar for abdominal wall and bladder pene - tration. Blunt obturators are also available for these can- nulas and are used to replace a cannula if positioning in the bladder is lost during procedures. Laparoscopy cannu- las have a valve to prevent fluid leakage and collapse of the bladder when an instrument is not in the cannula and a gasket to form a seal around the instrumentation when instruments are in the cannula. Arthroscopy cannulas have a gasket but do not have a valve system to prevent leakage. 6.3.4.5 Operative Instrumentation Rigid biopsy forceps from laparoscopy and rhinoscopy are used including 5 mm diameter and 3.0 mm laparoscopy biopsy forceps with apposing cups, 5 mm diameter punch biopsy forceps with cutting jaws, and rigid 2.0 mm diame - ter apposing cup arthroscopy biopsy forceps (Figures 2.42, 4.1, and Table 4.5). Rigid grasping forceps from laparos - copy are used in 5.0 mm diameter (see Chapter 8) and 3.0 mm diameter sizes (see Chapter 8). Arthroscopy ron- geurs and grasping forceps in various sizes also work well for grasping stones. 6.3.5 Instrumentation for Percutaneous Perineal Cystoscopy in Male Dogs Percutaneous perineal access to the proximal urethra and bladder in male dogs has been described using a C-arm for imaging of the urethra at the ischial arch for initial needle placement. Lack of access to a C-arm does not eliminate use of this procedure in practice. Identification of the urethral lumen at the ischial arch can also be accomplished using ultrasound or observation of the urethral lumen at the point of needle insertion with a flexible cystourethroscope. Creation of the perineal access port uses an 8 Fr Foley catheter, 18 gauge 15 cm trocar needle, a 0.035″ hydro - philic weasel wire, a 0.035″ Amplatz super stiff guide wire, serial dilators (4, 8, 12, and 16 Fr), and a 16 Fr teara- way introducer set (Table 6.13). The 2.7 mm MPRT with the 14 Fr cystoscopy/operating sheath or the 9.5 Fr one-piece operating cystoscope is used for examination and operative procedures. 6.3.6 Instrumentation for Laparoscopic- Assisted Cystoscopy LAC is a two-phase procedure using different instrument sets and techniques for the two separate parts. Instrumentation for the laparoscopy portion of the proce - dure are covered in the laparoscopy chapter and will be listed but not repeated in detail in this chapter. Laparoscope, portal cannula, and instrument size are based on patient size. A 0° laparoscope, a telescope cannula, an operative portal cannula, and a Babcock grasping forceps are the only instruments needed for this portion of the procedure. Instrumentation for the cystoscopy portion of the proce - dure include an appropriate size 30° telescope, cystoscopy/ operating cannulas with biopsy channels, arthroscopy or laparoscopy cannulas without biopsy channels, and rigid or flexible operative instrumentation. 6.3.6.1 T elescopes Two rigid telescopes are typically needed for LAC, a 0° lapa- roscope for the initial laparoscopy portion of the procedure and a second telescope with a 30° angle of view for the cys - toscopy portion of the procedure. In some smaller patients the 2.7 mm MPRT with its selection of sheaths and cannu- las is used for both portions of the procedure (Figure 2.30 and Table 6.5). In larger patients the 4.0 mm 30° cystoscope (Figure 2.35 and Table 6.6) has been used for both portions of the procedure with 5 mm laparoscopy trocar-cannulas (see Chapter 8). The laparoscope most commonly used for LAC is the 5 mm diameter 0° 30 cm long telescope but any size telescope will work depending on patient size. For the cystoscopy portion of the procedure the 2.7 mm 30° MPRT is the most commonly used telescope with the 4.0 cystos - copy system used in large dogs and the 9.5 Fr one piece tel- escope used in very small dogs and in cats. Other telescopes that have been used for LAC are 1.9 and 2.4 mm diameter 30° arthroscopes. Telescope selection for either phase of LAC is based on patient size and instrument availability. 6.3.6.2 Flexible Cystourethroscopes (Figure 2.10 and T able 6.12) In male dogs the Flex-XC or fiber optic cystourethroscopes are used in normograde insertion from the bladder par - tially into or completely through the urethra to examine for lesions or residual stones. 6.3.6.3 Cannulas and Sheaths Cannulas and sheaths used with these telescopes for LAC are divided into the two categories, those used for the Table 6.13 Materials needed to establish a urethral percutaneous perineal portal. Cystoscopy sheaths are most commonly used for the cystoscopy portion of the procedure, but arthroscopy can- nulas have also been used. Laparoscopy cannulas are not recommended because they do not cover the length of the telescope and are harder to maintain in the bladder for fluid irrigation. Each type has advantages and disadvan- tages with cannulas that lock to the telescope having more advantages than disadvantages when compared to laparos - copy cannulas. Arthroscopy and laparoscopy cannulas are smaller than cystoscopy sheaths and do not have an instru- ment channel. This requires that all operative instruments be passed besides the telescope, thus increasing the diffi- culty of the procedure but allowing use of larger instru- ments. Cystoscopy cannulas have an instrument channel making procedures easier but smaller instruments must be used that fit through the instrument channel. In many cases both types of cannulas are used for different stages of the procedure. 6.3.6.4 Operative Instrumentation Rigid instruments are passed through the bladder incision rather than through an operative cannula, and this expands the instrument list to include many minimally invasive surgery and standard open surgery instruments. Large cra- nial bladder tumor resection, when indicated, is performed by exteriorizing the involved portion of the bladder and excising the tumor with standard open surgery instru- ments. Laparoscopy biopsy forceps (see Chapter 8) are used for biopsy and resection of bladder tumors. These biopsy instruments also work well as graspers for removing bladder and proximal urethral stones. Laparoscopy grasp - ing forceps in 5, 10, and 3 mm are used to remove stones (see Chapter 8). Various size arthroscopy rongeurs and graspers are also effective for removing stones. Flexible instruments listed for TUC passed through cystoscopy/ operating sheaths (Figure 2.41 and Table 6.7) are also used for LAC. 6.3.7 Instrumentation for Lithotripsy Lithotripsy has been rarely used in small animal practice due to the cost of equipment and increased use of mini- mally invasive approaches to all levels of the urinary tract for stone removal. With the introduction of LAC, all calculi, even the largest, can be removed without open surgery. The advantage of transurethral or LAC for stone removal without breaking the stones into smaller fragments is that there are fewer stone fragments to remove from a single stone to a variable number of defined stones. The advantage of lithotripsy is that stones can be removed through the ure - thra without any incisions. The disadvantage of lithotripsy in addition to cost is that many small stone fragments are created requiring removal of many more individual pieces. This can be time consuming. Any fragment left behind, even if not large enough to cause irritation or urethral obstruction, is a nidus for new stone formation. It is the author’s opinion that it is faster, easier, and less traumatic to remove a single large stone using LAC rather than breaking the stone into many small fragments and removing all frag - ments transurethrally. The number of stones that cannot be managed with transurethral or LAC removal is very few. The primary indication is urethral calculi in male dogs that are lodged in the urethra and cannot be hydropropulsed into the bladder. Since learning effective hydropropulsion there has been one urethral calculus in a male dog that the author could not dislodge and propel back into the bladder for LAC removal. Four different technologies are used for lithotripsy: rigid stone crushing hand instruments, pneu- matic lithotripsy, shock wave lithotripsy, and laser litho - tripsy. Each has advantages and disadvantages. Rigid hand instruments have the advantage of least cost as most are used with the 4.0 mm, 30°, 30 cm long telescope. Various crushing jaw forceps designs are available with integrated sheath forceps combinations. The smallest sheath diameter is 24 Fr (8 mm), which is too large for many small animal patients, and is the primary disadvan- tage of this technique. Shock wave lithotripsy is the least invasive stone fractur - ing approach and uses external shock waves to break up stones that are then allowed to pass naturally or are removed with transurethral techniques. The disadvantages of this approach are cost, and small kidney size compared to the large design criteria for the human kidney. Applications of this technique have been reported in small animals, but the technique has not become a standard procedure. Ultrasonic and pneumatic lithotripsy use straight rigid probes that can pass through the straight operating channel of operating cystourethroscopes, ureterorenoscopes, or percutaneous nephroscopes. Ultrasonic systems use a transducer to create vibration in the range of 26 000 Hz. Pneumatic systems use compressed air to transmit mechan- ical energy through a transformation element that drives a probe placed in contact with the stone similar to a jackham- mer at 12 Hz. Both systems are effective and have the advan- tages of simplicity, safety, and having telescopes that are effective in the size range of our patients. Disadvantages are the cost of the units and the need for additional telescopes

6 Cystoscopy 230 with straight operating channels that will accommodate the probes used with these systems. Laser lithotripsy using Holmium laser technology is the most recent addition to the armamentarium for breaking up calculi. Laser energy is applied for lithotripsy at 4–8 Hz with 0.5–1.7 J of energy using laser fibers ranging from 230 to 600 μm. Both single use and reusable fibers are available. The greatest advantage of this technology is that energy is transmitted through flexible fibers that can be passed through flexible endoscopes and through the curved work - ing channel of cystoscopy sheaths currently in use in small animal practice. The other advantage is that the Holmium laser can be used for soft tissue procedures allowing a wider application of this unit beyond lithotripsy. The dis - advantage of laser lithotripsy is equipment cost, which could be resolved by the gradual decreasing cost of lasers and the increased use of lasers for soft tissue procedures. Unfortunately less expensive diode lasers do not work for lithotripsy. Application of endoscopes for cystoscopy is not limited to those listed here. There is an almost endless variety of options available as any small diameter rigid telescope sys - tem or small flexible fiber optic or video endoscope with adequate length and capability for fluid or air passage through the scope can be employed. An important consideration in employing cystoscopy, or any endoscopic procedure, in private small animal practice is the ability of the veterinarian to adapt and utilize an indi- vidual endoscope for different procedures other than that for which it was designed. An excellent example of this is the 2.7 mm diameter MPRT that was originally designed as an arthroscope and has been used for TUC, PPC, rhinos - copy, frontal sinoscopy, otoscopy, bronchoscopy, thoracos - copy, laparoscopy, fistuloscopy, anal sacoscopy, endoscopy of bite wounds and lacerations, endoscopic examination of cavitated or cystic tumors, ocular examinations, and arthroscopy. Its wide-ranging application is the reason for its designation as a multipurpose rigid telescope. This makes the economics of endoscopy not only feasible but financially rewarding. 6.4 T echniques for T ransurethral Cystoscopy 6.4.1 Patient Preparation General anesthesia is recommended for TUC and required for PPC or LAC. A standard preanesthetic fast is employed. Preanesthetic evaluation prior to anesthesia is based on patient age and medical needs. If a urinalysis and culture have not been done recently, samples are collected prior to cystoscopic examination as fluid irrigation used for the procedure will invalidate urinalysis and culture results. TUC has traditionally been performed as a clean tech- nique with protocols to prevent urinary tract contamina- tion employed. In female dogs and cats the peri-vulvar area of long-haired animals is clipped, but this has not been necessary for short-haired patients. The peri-vulvar area is cleaned to remove any exudate or debris, but an aseptic surgical scrub is not done and draping of the patient has not been employed. In male dogs the end of the prepuce is clipped if needed. The prepuce is flushed, and the tip of the prepuce is cleaned to remove any exu- date or debris. The tip of the penis is exposed by retraction of the prepuce and the tip of the penis is cleaned as would be done for passing a urinary catheter. Prepuce retraction is maintained until the endoscope is at its deepest point of insertion. When an aseptic technique is required, it is used for TUC. Patient positioning preferred by the author for females is either right or left lateral recumbency as this is the easiest position to place dogs and cats under anesthesia. Ventral and dorsal recumbent positions are utilized by many endoscopists. The ventral recumbent position has the advantage of placing anatomic structures in an upright ori- entation but positioning the patient is more difficult and the tail is in the way of telescope manipulation. Dorsal recumbency mimics the position used for human cystos - copy and makes ureteral catheterization easier, but patient positioning is more difficult than lateral recumbency. In male dogs and cats either lateral recumbent position or dorsal recumbency has been used. All these positions work and the one selected is strictly a matter of personal preference. PPC and LAC are performed using standard aseptic sur - gical technique with patients in dorsal recumbency. For PPC the ventral abdomen is clipped, scrubbed, and draped as would be done for a cystotomy. When LAC is planned an adequate sterile field is prepared to allow placement of an umbilical telescope portal in addition to the operative por - tal over the apex of the bladder. In female dogs, female cats, and male cats, an indwelling urinary catheter is placed prior to draping. In male dogs the bladder is catheterized as an aseptic procedure after draping is completed. Sterile instrumentation is employed, and the surgical team is properly attired for aseptic technique. All techniques use liquid to distend the urethra and blad- der to create a visual space for examination and to perform procedures. Intermittent or continuous flow is used to main- tain distention and a clear visual field. A liter container of sterile saline or Ringers solution is placed approximately 40 cm (5–80 cm) above the patient and is connected to the endoscope irrigation port with a standard intravenous fluid

Most diag - nostic procedures and many interventional procedures are performed in a short period of time and with a limited amount of instrumentation. The technique employed in female dogs and cats by this author differs in several major aspects from that which has been reported by other endoscopists (Brearley et al. 1988; Cooper et al. 1984; Rawlings 2009; Morgan and Forman 2015). Patients are placed in lateral recumbency, aseptic preparation and drap - ing are not employed but clean technique is used, passage of the endoscope is done with direct visualization using continuous liquid irrigation, and the vulva is held closed distending the vaginal vestibule until the urethral orifice is identified and entered. Without distention or with minimal distention the urethral papilla is a prominent wide vertical ridge of tissue especially in the dog (Figure 6.10). Air embolism is a potential complica- tion when room air is employed for bladder distension, and this danger is avoided by limiting the amount of air to that which opens but does not pressurize the bladder. Rupture of the bladder is a very rare complication of cystoscopy but can occur with marked over distension or if there is significant bladder wall pathol- ogy. In his 37-year experience, the author experienced a bladder rupture that occurred very early in the cystoscopy timeline when an air distention technique was performed using the insufflation pump for gastrointestinal endoscopy. Do not use the gastrointestinal endoscope insufflation pump for air distention of the bladder . Tearing of the mucosa but with the seromuscular layers remaining intact is more common occurrence with microscopic mucosal tears caus - ing bleeding (Figure 6.24) that interferes with examination but does not cause observable morbidity in the patient. This form of damage is more common in bladders with sig - nificant chronic inflammation that have secondary fibrous tissue formation preventing normal bladder wall stretching. The entire urethra and bladder wall are evaluated with a 30° angle of view telescope. The urethra is evaluated for tumors, calculi, ectopic ureteral openings, strictures, con- tusions, mucosal lacerations, and wall penetrations or dis - ruption. The bladder mucosa is evaluated for contour, texture, and color. Blood vessel number, size and configu- ration are assessed. The entire bladder is examined for the presence of tumors, calculi, diverticula, mucosal tears, and bladder wall lacerations or penetrations. Both ureteral openings are located in the trigone area of the bladder and are examined for anatomic position, configuration, and for the flow and character of urine (Video 6.2). 6 Cystoscopy 240 6.4.3 T ransurethral Cystoscopy in Male Dogs TUC is easily performed in male dogs with appropriate instrumentation. A wide range of different sized dogs can be examined with the FlexXC video urethroscope, or the older fiber optic version, as there is little correlation between dog size and urethral size. Dogs as small as 3.5 kg have been examined with this endoscope, but its insertion is occasionally not possible in dogs as large as 30 kg. If there is a question of urethral size, the urethra is tested by passage of an 8 Fr catheter and if this catheter can be passed, then the urethroscope will pass. This test can be done prior to anesthesia or referral to determine if TUC is possible in the patient. If the urethra is too small other options are discussed with the client prior to referral or prior to anesthesia. With the patient under general anesthesia, the prepuce is retracted exposing the tip of the penis to allow cleaning and endoscope introduction into the urethra. To minimize bladder and urethral contamination, the tip of the penis is cleaned prior to passage of the endoscope and prepuce retraction is maintained until the endoscope is in the blad- der at its deepest point of insertion. An alternative is to clip, surgically prepare, and drape the prepuce to perform an aseptic procedure. Prior to introduction of the endo - scope, a urethral catheter is passed, and the bladder emp - tied. This proved to be easier and faster than emptying the bladder through the endoscope because the small diameter of the operating channel of these small flexible endoscopes makes it difficult and time consuming to adequately remove all the urine. Continuous fluid irrigation is employed to provide urethral distension for examination and to allow endoscope passage under direct visualization. Liquid irrigation is done by attaching an intravenous fluid administration set to the operating channel port of the endoscope and using sterile saline or Ringers solution (Figure 6.6). Air or carbon dioxide is also used when indicated. Examination of the urethra is done as the endoscope is being advanced into the urethra and again as it is being withdrawn ( Video 6.4). Visualization of the urethra during insertion is done both to look for pathology and to assist in passage of the endoscope by visually following the dis - tended urethral lumen. A more careful and complete ure - thral examination is carried out as instrumentation is being withdrawn to ensure that nothing is missed. The distal penile urethra initially appears when collapsed as a flat - tened tube (Figure 6.43) becoming a smooth round tube when distended (Figure 6.44). Resistance to the passage of the endoscope tip may be encountered in some male dogs at the caudal end of the os penis as this is normally the nar - rowest point of the urethra (Figure 6.45). If any difficulty is encountered, then stay sutures are placed to facilitate the procedure and to minimize trauma to the penis and urethra. The tip of the penis is cleansed with an anti - septic solution prior to passage of the endoscope. The ini- tial thought for this technique occurred while performing cystocentesis in a cat. If we can collect urine by cystocente - sis, why can we not puncture the bladder with a small endoscope and see the inside of the bladder? Searching endoscope catalogs revealed that 10 mm telescopes were placed into human bladders using a suprapubic approach. This technique was then applied to small animal patients from cats to large dogs. The discussions about interstitial cystitis in cats came from a picture taken using this tech- nique (McCarthy and McDermaid 1986). This technique has largely been replaced with LAC, but it still has applica- tions and a hybrid modification with a combination of PPC, and capture of the bladder wall without laparoscopy has been used. 6.4.5.1 The Original T echnique The original procedure worked well for bladder examina- tion and for simple manipulations such as biopsies or sin- gle stone removals but does not work well for more complicated procedures. Maintaining bladder distension, preventing leakage into the abdomen, and maintaining portal placement was difficult when more complex proce - dures were undertaken using more than one portal. A surgical plane of general anesthesia is required for PPC. Once this has been achieved, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency and is clipped, prepared, and draped for aseptic surgery in the same manner that would be employed to perform an open cystotomy. The bladder is catheterized, emptied, and the urethral catheter is fixed in place. Sterile soft red rubber urinary catheters and Foley catheters have been employed. The bladder is filled with sterile saline, Ringers solution, or Ringers lactate solution until it is moderately distended and can be easily palpated through the abdominal wall. This can be achieved by con- necting the urinary catheter to an intravenous fluid admin- istration set so that continuous fluid flow can be maintained (Figure 6.67) or in smaller patients a three-way valve with a syringe is attached to allow intermittent injection of fluid. The first technique works better in larger dogs and the lat - ter is better in smaller dogs and in cats because it allows more precise control of fluid flow reducing the risk of blad- der overdistention. The bladder is filled until it is easily pal- pated and firm but not hard, so it is easily stabilized for trocar penetration. The surgeon and patient are appropri- ately prepared for aseptic surgery and the patient is draped to allow exposure of the distended bladder. If a single puncture is to be performed, a small skin incision is made on the ventral midline over the most prominent portion of the bladder (Figure 6.68). For double puncture, required for sample collection, two incisions are made equidistant from the midline and far enough apart to allow instrument triangulation (Figure 6.68). A double puncture technique is required because the instruments lack biopsy channels. The endoscope cannula with a sharp trocar in place is pushed through the abdominal and bladder walls with continuous gradually increasing pressure and oscillating rotation until the bladder lumen is entered. Instrumentation is held perpendicular to the bladder wall at the penetration site during this maneuver (Figure 6.69). For a single punc- ture the cannula will be vertical. For a double puncture, if the bladder is kept on the midline, the cannula is angled Figure 6.67 Irrigation setup for prepubic percutaneous cystoscopy with a container of sterile saline, Ringer’s, or lactated Ringer’s solution and with an IV administration set connected to the telescope sheath fluid stopcock.

6 Cystoscopy 248 until it is perpendicular to the abdominal and bladder walls at the point of penetration (Figure 6.69a) or the bladder is shifted laterally directly under the incision to be used for endoscope placement in which case the cannula will be vertical during placement (Figure 6.69b). Once the tip of the trocar cannula assembly has entered the bladder lumen forward movement is stopped to prevent penetration of the opposite bladder wall. This is easily accomplished in larger patients, since their bladders are of sufficient size to allow an adequate margin of safety for trocar entry but becomes more difficult and critical in smaller dogs and in cats where bladder size allows little room for error. If the trocar is inserted too far damage can occur to the bladder mucosa, bladder wall, and structures outside the bladder. Damage to the mucosa alone is not desirable but has not been found to be detrimental to the patient. This can, however, make examination more difficult because bleeding will cloud irrigation fluid and interfere with examination. If the oppo - site bladder wall is penetrated fluid leakage occurs, making it difficult to maintain bladder distention for examination or for placement of the second puncture instrumentation. Penetration of the opposite bladder wall is avoided but may not be significant for the patient because this hole will seal in the same time frame as the desired puncture site. Significant damage to structures outside the bladder that are detrimental to the patient can occur if the trocar pene - trates beyond the opposite bladder wall. This time inter - val was established by convention and has not been studied to determine the actual time period that decompression must be maintained to insure bladder puncture closure. This procedure is set up and started with the same protocol as for PPC. The bladder is distended and pal- pated through the abdominal wall to determine the opti- mum location for portal placement. The bladder is decompressed, and a small midline abdominal incision is made. The bladder is re-distended, and the incision mar - gins are retracted to allow visualization of the bladder. Stay sutures are placed in the bladder wall and a portion of the bladder wall is exteriorized. A small cystotomy incision is made between the stay sutures. The telescope and instru- mentation are passed through the cystotomy incision and the operative procedures are performed using the same techniques as for LAC. When procedures in the bladder have been completed, the cystotomy and abdominal wall incisions are closed with standard open technique. 6.4.5.3 Diagnostic Sample Collection The trocar cannula system used for this technique does not have an operating channel and biopsy or operating instru - mentation is passed through a separate cannula rather than through an operating channel of the telescope sheath. These cannulas must also be round to provide a tight tissue seal so fluid leakage is prevented. Rigid rather than flexible instru - ments are used and the techniques for sample collection are more like techniques used for laparoscopy than for those previously described for other cystoscopy procedures. Rigid biopsy forceps and grasping forceps are used for biopsies and removing bladder stones. Instrument size is dependent on the size of the second or operating cannula placed at the beginning of the procedure and are typically 2–5 mm diameter instruments. Biopsies are done with the same technique used for liver biopsies with laparoscopy. Stone removal uses rigid grasping forceps for larger stones and smaller stones are removed with suction (Figure 6.72). 6.4.6 T echnique for Laparoscopic-Assisted Cystoscopy LAC is the newest addition to our armamentarium for addressing lower urinary tract disease. This technique pro - vides access to the bladder and proximal urethra for diag - nostic and operative procedures. This technique is superior to any other approach to the bladder including open sur - gery. The primary applications of LAC are removal of tumors and calculi in the bladder and proximal urethra that cannot be accessed with TUC. LAC has the advantages of being a minimally invasive approach causing less trauma with resultant decreased pain and faster recovery. These advantages are desirable and sought after by clients especially when multiple cystic calculi removal procedures are required. The most impor - tant advantage of LAC is that visualization using this approach is dramatically superior to that of open surgery. This technique is more effective and is easier to perform than PPC, which it has essentially replaced. The advan- tages of LAC have made traditional open surgical cystot - omy an obsolete procedure. LAC requires general anesthesia and aseptic technique. Dorsal recumbency is employed with the monitor at the foot of the operating table, the surgeon on one side of the patient, and the assistant on the other side (Figure 6.73). The bladder is catheterized and emptied using a standard urethral catheter. The ventral abdominal wall is clipped, prepared, and draped for aseptic technique similar to what would be used for a cystotomy, but with more cranial expo - sure to allow placement of an umbilical telescope portal. Sterile minimally invasive surgery instruments are used. An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated with carbon dioxide. In female dogs and cats, the bladder is visualized and an operative portal is placed on the midline over the apex of the bladder (Figure 6.74). In male dogs, the opera- tive portal is placed on the midline immediately cranial to the prepuce if the bladder apex is accessible from this location. If the bladder apex is not far enough cranially to reach this location, the portal is placed in a modified para- median position on either side of the prepuce. The skin and subcutaneous incision is paramedian, the prepuce is retracted away from the side of the incision to expose the linea alba, and the portal is placed through the linea alba on the midline. This position for the portal is much easier to use than a portal placed through the rectus abdominis muscle and its separate fascia layers. The bladder has a ten- dency to be trapped in between the fascia layers creating a two-chamber bladder. The apex of the bladder is grasped with forceps and elevated to the abdominal wall at the operative portal site (Figures 6.75 and 6.76). Samples removed during operative removal of masses and calculi are submitted to confirm a diagnosis, but this is not the primary purpose of these procedures. Surgical procedures use all the previously discussed instrumentation and techniques. 6.4.7 Photodynamic Diagnostics with Cystoscopy Enhancement of diagnostics with fluorescence is an addition to our armamentarium to improve early diagno - sis of TCC. This technique is also used for managing TCC after diagnosis to find and ablate small lesions that are not visible with standard white light. Compounds are administered intravenously or placed in the bladder prior to cystoscopy that accumulate in tumor tissue. The selected light wavelengths cause the administered compound to fluoresce, highlighting the tumor tissue (Figure 6.100). 6.5 Normal Endoscopic Anatomy of the Lower Urinary T ract 6.5.1 T ransurethral Cystoscopy in Female Dogs and Cats: Vagina Vaginal anatomy is included in the discussion of TUC in female dogs and cats because of the integral nature of the two procedures. The vaginal vestibule is transited and examined as part of finding the urethral orifice to proceed with cystoscopy. The endoscope is also passed into the vagi- nal body as part of the TUC to minimize the chance of missing any pathology. This part of the procedure typically takes less than a minute, when vaginal body findings are normal, and occasionally, finds important pathology. Presentation of vaginal anatomy and abnormal findings does not intend to replace or interfere with Chapter 7 and may be redundant but it is included for completeness. Beginning at the vulvar opening, the vaginal vestibule is the first structure seen and, with dilation, the urethral papilla seen as a variably elevated ridge of tissue, the exter - nal urethral orifice seen as a vertical slit or round opening on the midline in the center of the urethral papilla, and the vaginovestibular junction seen as a narrowed circumferen- tial band of tissue with the opening into the vaginal body (Figures 6.7–6.10). Variability in the appearance of the ure - thral papilla is anatomic but is mostly due to the extent of dilation produced by fluid distention with the vulvar open- ing held closed. With minimal vaginal vestibule distention, there is a better appreciation of the normal appearance of the urethral papilla (Figures 6.10 and 6.101). The clitoris and clitoral fossa are present on the caudal floor of the vestibular fossa just inside the vulvar labii. Pathology of the clitoris and clitoral fossa is rare. The great - est significance of these structures relative to cystoscopy is that the endoscope is passed too far ventrally or at a horizontal angle and ends up being trapped in the clitoral fossa. This is a common error for beginners when they are learning cystoscopy. The clitoral fossa mucosa has a dis - tinct appearance with multiple small fixed irregular mucosal ridges (Figures 6.111 and 6.112). The clitoris is located on the craniodorsal margin of the clitoral fossa as a “V” shaped structure pointing ventrally into the fossa (Figure 6.113) and is an excellent landmark for orientation when initiating TUC. Passage of the endoscope dorsal to and past the external urethral orifice through the vaginovestibular junction (Figures 6.8–6.11, 6.102, and 6.103) seen as a distinct nar - rowing that is also referred to as the cingulum. The term cingulum, from the Latin meaning belt or girdle, is not used to identify this structure in anatomy texts (Evans and de Lahunta 2013) but applies this term to identify a group of nerve fibers in the brain and in descriptions of dental anatomy. The term vaginovestibular junction is a more accurate term for this structure although cingulum is descriptive of the narrowing of the lumen at this level of the female reproductive tract (Figure 6.114). When the cystoscope is passed through the vaginovestib - ular junction, the vaginal body is seen as a round relatively straight smooth tubular structure in spayed female dogs (Figure 6.115) with variably visible mucosal vasculature (Figure 6.116). Multiple longitudinal mucosal ridges are present in intact female dogs (Figure 6.117) that vary in size and shape with stages of the estrus cycle. Variable-sized vaginal mucosal ridges are also seen in spayed dogs with ovarian remnants (Figure 6.118) and in spayed dogs being given estrogen containing drugs (Figure 6.119). A promi - nent ridge of tissue is found on the dorsal wall of the cranial portion of the vaginal body, the dorsal median fold (Figure 6.120), that extends to the cranial end of the vaginal body and includes the cervix (Figure 6.121).
