Mucosal indenta - tions or diverticula are not common in the urethra of female dogs and cats, and when seen are usually small and single (Figure 6.131) or are multiple and small (Figure 6.132). The significance of these small diverticula is unknown, but their importance is the same as for the vaginal crypts in that they need to be differentiated from the openings of ectopic ure - ters. Rarely, there are larger diverticula associated with ectopic ureters that require exploration with laser transec - tion of their free intraluminal wall (Figure 6.133). When the bladder is first entered, it is typically fully dis - tended due to fluid inflow during passage of the cystoscope through the urethra and visibility is obscured by cloudy urine (Figures 6.15–6.19). After draining cloudy urine and when refilling with clear liquid is initiated to open the bladder, the mucosa is initially seen as a pink ridged (Figure 6.134), irregular (Figure 6.135), or smooth (Figure 6.136) surface without visible blood vessels. At a moderate level of distention, the bladder mucosa is smooth without ridges or corrugations but there may be indenta- tions from surrounding structures (Figure 6.136) or folds of bladder wall (Figure 6.137) and variable appearance of blood vessels. With further distention, blood vessels are easily visible under the mucosa (Figure 6.138) and their branching pattern is easily defined (Figure 6.139). Blood vessels are relatively straight without convolutions or tor - tuosity, appearing to be in the mucosa, and are not raised. The ureteral openings are found dorsolaterally on both sides of the trigone area of the bladder. They change posi- tion and configuration with bladder distention. In dogs with a collapsed or minimally distended bladder, they are close to the midline and to the junction of urethra and bladder appearing as straight longitudinal or slightly oblique slits on papillae (Figures 6.134 and 6.140). With increasing distention, the ureteral stomas are further away from the junction of the bladder and urethra, further apart with only one typically visible at a time, the ridge caudal to the papilla flattens to disappear, the papilla decreases in size, and the ostia continue to appear as straight or slightly curved slits with a thickened free margin (Figure 6.141). Some of these are easily diagnosed and corrected whereas others are difficult to identify or if identified are difficult to man- age. Bacterial cystitis may be diagnosed and the organism identified, but with recurrent or persistent infection, the underlying reason for inability to permanently resolve the problem can be elusive. Cystoscopy provides us more infor - mation to address this scenario than any other diagnostic modality. Magnification produced by endoscopes greatly improves our ability to define inflammatory lesions. The urethra is lined with the same endothelium as the bladder and inflammation commonly occurs in the urethra in com- bination with cystitis or as an independent process. 6 Cystoscopy 270 6.6.1.1 Interstitial Cystitis An example of the advantages of cystoscopy over other diagnostic techniques is introduction of interstitial cystitis as a diagnosis and its inclusion in our understanding of feline lower urinary tract disease based on a picture taken using PPC and its publication on the use of this technique (Figure 6.152) (McCarthy and McDermaid 1986). This was picked up by Dr. Tony Buffington and Dr. Dennis Chew and became the “new paradigm” of feline lower urinary tract disease (Buffington 1994, 2011; Buffington et al. 1996, 1999; Chew et al. 1996; Hague et al. 2013; Kullmann et al. 2018; Lavelle et al. 2000; Stella et al. 2013; Westropp and Buffington 2002; Westropp et al. 2019). This not only created an avenue for research to better under - stand feline lower urinary tract disease in cats but also established cats as a naturally occurring disease model for studying interstitial cystitis in people (Buffington 2004; Hague et al. 2013; Westropp and Buffington 2002). This is a poorly understood extremely complex disease that proba- bly involves the interaction of multiple etiologies and many different therapies that work inconsistently in some patients some of the time. There have been extensive stud- ies and publications on interstitial cystitis in both the human and veterinary fields, but further discussion of this subject is beyond the scope of this publication. The diagnostic appearance of the bladder pathognomonic for interstitial cystitis are small red areas of the mucosa called “glomerulations.” They appear like petechia and actually are small areas of hemorrhage in the urothelium, secondary to tearing of fibrosis with bladder distention. Since the first case was examined using PPC in 1984, this disease has been diagnosed using all cystoscopy approaches in symptomatic and asymptomatic male and female cats and dogs. Female dogs are overrepresented in these images illustrating interstitial cystitis because TUC is more commonly performed on female dogs than in any other group and larger telescopes are used to produce better pic- tures. Glomerulations associated with interstitial cystitis have a widely varied appearance with scattered lesions with uniform distribution and size (Figure 6.152), a mini - mal number of lesions (Figure 6.153), lesions of different sizes (Figure 6.154), focal clusters of lesions (Figure 6.155), solid sheets of lesions (Figure 6.156), lesions that appear chronic (Figure 6.157), and lesions in the urethra (Figure 6.158). Close up magnified images appear both like petechial hemorrhages (Figure 6.159) and like clusters of small blood vessel proliferation (Figure 6.160). Glomerulations have also been seen in patients with other lower urinary tract diseases including cystic calculi, TCCs, urachal diverticula, inflammatory polyps, recessed vulvas, and chronic cystitis of other etiologies. 6.6.1.2 Follicular Cystitis Follicular cystitis is distinguished from “unspecified” cysti- tis by the presence of nodules or follicles of inflammatory Figure 6.152 Glomerulations with scattered uniform distribution and size in an 11-month-old spayed female Golden Retriever with interstitial cystitis plus a urachal diverticulum and a recessed vulva. In veterinary medicine, we use everything but cystoscopy in our diagnostic protocols. Cystoscopy is the gold standard in human medicine and it needs to achieve this status in vet - erinary medicine. The other issue facing veterinarians is that patients are not presented for urinary tract evaluation until they become symptomatic and this means that we are already too late. Presenting signs of TCC can be very similar to uri- nary tract infections and calculi. Many patients are treated for UTI for variable periods of time before diagnostics pro - ceed beyond a urinalysis further delaying diagnosis. This delay is fueled both by client reluctance to do more and veterinary inertia. To improve our treatment results, we need to find a way to diagnose TCC earlier, preferably prior to onset of any signs of symptoms. Performing cystoscopy as a free-standing procedure is expensive. Performing cys - toscopy when patients are under anesthesia for other pro - cedures reduces the cost into the “cheap” range. The author recommends TUC in all female dogs of susceptible breeds when they are under anesthesia for other procedures, such as dentistry. Since bladder and urethral tumors occur most frequently in female dogs, this makes cystoscopy a particularly useful diagnostic tool. Bladder and urethral tumors are less com- monly seen in male dogs and are rarely seen in cats (Fulkerson and Knapp 2015). The caudal two thirds of the vagina including the caudal portion of the vaginal body, the vaginovestibular junction, and the vaginal vestibule are formed from the vaginal plate, a solid tubercle arising from the urogenital sinus, and degeneration of the center of the vaginal plate occurs to form the vaginal lumen. From this, it seems that deformities at the vaginovestibular junction are a failure of degeneration of the vaginal plate to form the vaginal lumen. This understanding of the source of developmental abnormalities is confused by ectopic ureters because the trigone of the bladder and ureters of the female are formed from the paramesonephric ducts. Ectopic ureters that open into the vagina commonly open at the vaginovestibular junction with otherwise normal appearing anatomy (Figures 6.345–6.347) or complex and bizarre deformities including ectopic ureter openings (Figure 6.348). Is our terminology inaccurate or is the embryology of the canine female reproductive tract misunderstood? 6.6.4.2 Ectopic Ureters and Ureteroceles TUC was first used for diagnosis of ectopic ureters by the author in 1984. It was determined that ectopic ureters are more easily defined with more accuracy using TUC than with any other diagnostic modality including exploratory surgery. This opinion has held up over the years even with introduction of ultrasound, CT using contrast, and contrast fluoroscopy. Abnormalities are commonly more than just misplacement of the ureteral openings and may involve abnormal development of the entire urethra, ure - ters, trigone, and vagina. Openings of the ectopic ureters are found anywhere in the lower urogenital tract caudal to their normal openings in the bladder. Ureteral pathol - ogy can be unilateral or bilateral. There is massive hematuria of renal origin that is not associated with coagulopathy, trauma, neoplasia, or renal calculi. Typically seen in young large breed dogs, it is most commonly a unilateral disease but is also seen bilater - ally. Most cases have no definable gross or histopathologic source of hemorrhage. Historically with unilateral disease, the recommended treatment was nephrectomy of the involved kidney (Hawthorne et al. 1998; Hitt et al. 1985; Kaufman et al. 1994; Stone et al. 1983). Recent advances in interventional endoscopy and radiology have made new kidney preserving options available by controlling the source of bleeding with sclerotherapy, laser ablation, or electrocautery or by selective renal arterial embolization (Adelman et al. 2017; Berent 2013, 2016; Di Cicco et al. 2013; Gallagher 2018; Weisse 2015). With either technique, determining the correct kidney is critical. This is especially true with nephrectomy as the removal of the correct kidney is critical to successful treat - ment and patient survival. Determining which kidney is involved is difficult at surgery as the involved kidney appears grossly normal. Cystoscopy makes identification of the involved side easy, quick, and accurate when per - formed at the time of nephrectomy or associated with renal sparing techniques. Cystoscopy using any of the described approaches allows direct magnified observation of the ureteral ostia providing identification of the involved kidney by seeing blood com- ing from that ureter (Figure 6.416) and normal urine com- ing from the ureter of the contralateral normal kidney (Figure 6.417). Transabdominal cystoscopy has been used at the time of nephrectomy after an abdominal incision has been made to confirm the side for nephrectomy (Figure 6.418) when that treatment procedure has been elected. Idiopathic renal hematuria is the most common cause of renal hematuria, but other primary diseases of the kidney occur causing bleeding from kidney or ureteral lesions and presenting similar signs. The most common intervention is ablation of urachal diverticula considered to be a potential cause of chronic or recurrent cystitis. They occur commonly in both male and female dogs and cats. They can be a nidus for bacterial growth that is not subjected to normal urine exchange that is part of the mechanism that controls bacterial population of the bladder. Diagnosis of urachal diverticula is very easy with TUC, and they appear as a small pinpoint or indenta- tion in the bladder mucosa at the apex (Figures 6.391– 6.400). With addition of the diode laser to our surgical armamentarium, correction of urachal diverticula has become an easy transurethral procedure requiring mini- mal time and with minimal side effects or complications. Treatment involves ablation of the diverticulum using a diode laser fiber passed through the operating channel of the cystoscope sheath (Figure 6.419). With the laser fiber protruding into the visual field from the operating channel, it moves with the tip of the cystoscope so that its position is easily controlled. The diode laser fiber is used in a contact mode in most procedures where the tip of the fiber is actu- ally in contact with the tissues (Video 6.8). Urachal diver - ticula ablation is one of the few situations where the fiber is used in a noncontact mode where it is kept a few millim- eters away from the tissue (Figure 6.420) (Video 6.9). This is just one patient and does not provide a statistical support for this approach to treatment but does provide a reason to pursue early diagnosis of TCC. Multiple protocols have been considered, but none have been pursued at this time. A reasonable approach that needs investigation is performing TUC in female dogs above a certain age from susceptible species whenever they are under anesthesia for another procedure. Endoscopic intervention for management of vaginal tumors is also rarely indicated because of the low incidence of vaginal lesions. When vaginal masses requiring removal are found, endoscopy is the procedure of choice for diagnosis and resection. Transitional cell carcinoma lesions in the vagina are usually small, do not interfere with function, and their significance is overshadowed by bladder and urethral lesions. Because of these reasons, removal is rarely indi- cated. Vaginal fibromas (Figure 6.298) and hyperplasia masses (Figures 6.301, 6.302, 6.304, and 6.305) are resected effectively with vaginoscopy using laser resection (Figures 6.299 and 6.300) or a polypectomy snare (Figures 6.303 and 6.306). Transmissible venereal tumors (Figures 6.291–6.295) when seen are also amenable to exci- sion with vaginoscopy (Figures 6.296 and 6.297) for debulk - ing in conjunction with chemotherapy. 6.7 .3 Minimally Invasive Urolithiasis Management Our ability to manage urolithiasis in small animal practice has advanced drastically in the last decade with develop - ment of the ability to dissolve more types of stones plus introduction of minimally invasive approaches for the removal of calculi using interventional and operative endoscopy alone or combined with interventional radiol- ogy (Lulich et al. 2016). These advances have made tradi- tional open surgery for stone removal, an obsolete technique at all levels of the urinary tract. The only indica- tion for an open cystotomy is if the stones cannot be dis - solved and if the client refuses referral for an interventional or minimally invasive surgical approach. Dissolution of struvite uroliths has been the standard of care for years, but other stone types have not been consid- ered to be dissolvable until more recently (Lulich et al. 2016). Methods for dissolving urate and cystine cal- culi are now available. Consideration of medical manage - ment of these stones is currently recommended if they are not at risk for causing obstruction or other complications. When not dissolvable because of stone type, failure of dis - solution techniques to eliminate stones, or high risk of complications, then interventional techniques for stone removal are indicated. One of the requirements of urolith dissolution is ade - quate urine flow to remove dissolved stone components from the urinary tract and to maintain transfer of material from the solid stone into liquid surrounding the stone. If this does not occur, a saturated or supersaturated state exists around the stone stopping the dissolution process. Cystoscopy in this situation reveals a visible viscous or sludge-like material in the bladder. A case example was presented that had multiple suspected struvite stones in

Hydropropulsion has also been used in male dogs with acceptable results but does not work in male cats unless a perineal urethrostomy has been per - formed. Hydropropulsion does not work if there are any stones too large to pass through the urethra. If lithotripsy is available, then the removal of stone fragments with hydro - propulsion after stone fragmentation is possible. Hydropropulsion technique involves filling the bladder with sterile liquid, elevating the head of the patient as much as possible, and expressing the bladder. This is very easy in small dogs and in cats when it is possible to suspend the patient in a vertical position. Large dogs are more dif- ficult, and a tilt table is needed. In female dog and cats, this technique has been com- bined with TUC to facilitate bladder filling, to determine stone size, to confirm that all stones have been removed, and to examine the lower urinary tract for other diagnoses. General anesthesia is required for hydropropulsion to pro - vide adequate relaxation for effective bladder expression. With the patient under anesthesia, cystoscopy is performed providing easier and faster access to the urethral orifice, and irrigation used for cystoscopy fills the bladder with liq- uid (Figure 6.472). The cystoscope is removed and hydro - propulsion is performed. After hydropropulsion, the cystoscope is reinserted to evaluate the efficacy of urolith removal (Figure 6.473). The procedure is repeated until cystoscopy reveals that all calculi have been removed (Figure 6.474). Cystoscopy is also used to examine the vagi- nal vestibule, urethra, and bladder for any abnormalities. Additional diagnoses with this technique have included urachal diverticula, vaginal webs, cystitis, polyps, and TCC. Hydropropulsion for stone removal in male dogs is less effective and more difficult than in females due to their long, narrow, curved urethra. Hydropropulsion for stone removal does not work in male dogs for calculi stuck in the urethra as this confirms that the stone is too large to pass through the urethra. In many patients it is faster with less anesthesia and operating time to perform LAC to remove large stones in one piece than to preform lithotripsy and then to remove many small fragments. Availability of lithotripsy instrumentation is required for transurethral removal of large stones, and without this equipment LAC is indicated. The technique for LAC, percutaneous prepubic cystos - copy, and the hybrid combination of these two techniques is presented with laparoscopy and with diagnostic proce - dures. The procedure for removing cystic calculi for thera- peutic indications is the same as for removing stones for diagnostic purposes, and LAC is not used to retrieve stones for strictly diagnostic reasons. Urethral surgery where stones get stuck, at the caudal end of the os penis, is contraindicated and avoided unless there is no other option. Since learning how to properly perform retrograde hydropropulsion in male dogs 25 years ago, there has only been one case requiring urethrotomy, and all other calculi have been successfully flushed back into the bladder. Retrograde hydropropulsion in male dogs requires a sur - gical plane of anesthesia. Sedation is inadequate. Complete relaxation of the patient is required to relax the urethra and eliminate urethral spasm at the stone site and in the proxi- mal urethra. A urethral catheter is passed to the level of the lodged stone, and the catheter is connected to a 60 cc cath- eter tip syringe filled with saline, saline with KY Jelly, saline with lidocaine, or a combination of all three. A watertight seal is created around the catheter by digital pressure applied to the penis by an assistant or a tourniquet at the tip of the penis. An assistant does a digital rectal examination and compresses the pelvic urethra to produce occlusion. The syringe is held with one hand on the tip to hold the catheter to keep it from coming off the syringe, and the other hand is on the plunger. Strong force is applied to the syringe plunger, and when maximum pressure is achieved, the assistant releases digital pressure on the pel- vic urethra. In almost all cases this works on the first attempt. Occasionally a second attempt is required. Common mistakes are sedation rather than a surgical anes - thesia and being tentative about the amount of pressure applied. If a flexible urethroscope is available, the success of hydropropulsion is evaluated with TUC. This also allows evaluation of the urethra where the stone was lodged for the extent of damage and to determine if stricture is a con- cern (Figures 6.222, 6.224, and 6.226). Do not skip endo - scopic urethral evaluation based on patient size because the Flex-XC video urethroscope has been passed in patients as small as 5 kg. If an 8 Fr urethral catheter will pass, so will the urethroscope. The caudal end of the os penis can also be visually accessed with small ridged endoscopes. Stone removal from the bladder is then completed using LAC. Particular attention is paid to residual calculi in the pelvic urethra (Figures 6.98, 6.99, 6.323, 6.324, 6.328, and 6.329) because hydropropulsed calculi are commonly deposited in the area where the urethral diameter increases, allowing liquid to flow past the stones. All three approaches have indications, advantages, disad- vantages, limitations, and failures. Some patients require all three before full continence is achieved, and some are still incontinent even after all three have been used. The approach to each case is a combination of patient needs, client needs or desires, and available treatment options. Collagen injections to add bulk to the urethral wall has been a standard treatment in human medicine for many years with sufficient success for its continued use, but there is also a sufficient failure rate, so other options are continu- ally being investigated. The same situation is present in small animal practice. Transurethral injection of collagen is the least invasive approach to incontinence management beyond medical management. Multiple human products have been used in dogs with reasonable success for up to about two years when reinjection is indicated to maintain continence. A veterinary product was developed but was removed from the market. This product has been reintro - duced, but results have not been reported. An alternative approach using a radiofrequency probe has been tested and shows some promise but is not yet on the open market. Another approach is looking at stem cell injections. This has produced encouraging results in people, especially in men incontinent after prostatectomy. Artificial urethral sphincter or hydraulic occluder implantation is a totally different concept for managing urinary incontinence that has produced excellent results but also has its own set of problems, disadvantages, and complications. At this time there is no ideal product or technique to solve the problem of urinary incontinence in female dogs. The technique for bulking agent injection is similar for all products. TUC is performed most commonly with the 2.7 mm MPRT and cystoscopy sheath. Special long needles that pass through the operating channel of the cystoscope sheath are available and are obtained from the injection material suppliers. The 9.5 Fr one-piece cystoscope can be used for small patients, and the 4.0 cystoscope with a dedi- cated injection sheath can be used in large dogs. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 363 The use of endoscopy in reproduction of domestic carni- vores has increased in recent years. On one hand, this is because of specialization of the field and on the other hand, it is due to optimization of the use of endoscopes. This instrumentation is becoming more common in small animal clinics. Vaginal endoscopy is used both as a diagnostic tool and to perform intrauterine procedures such as artificial insemination. In addition, since endoscopy is a noninvasive technique, it presents several advantages when compared to surgical procedures. For effective use of endoscopy in small animal reproduction, it is necessary to have a good knowledge of the anatomy of the reproductive tract, skill performing the procedure, and the necessary instrumentation. The uses of endoscopy in reproduction will be described in this chapter. 7.1 Canine Vaginal Anatomy Endoscopic examination of the vagina in the bitch is part of a complete reproductive evaluation. There are some details of vaginal anatomy that must be understood to facilitate performing endoscopy. The vagina of the bitch is very long, extending from the vestibule to the cervix. It is difficult to state an average vaginal size since the length is related to body weight and reproductive status. Neutered animals have significantly shorter vaginas than intact bitches of similar body weight (Gregory et al. 1999). The length of the vagina varies from 10 cm up to 30 cm depending on breed and body size. The vestibule is approximately 2–6 cm long (Wilson 2001, 2003). The position of the vagina is unique, with an oblique or sloped passage of the vestibule from the vulva to the vagina (Figure 7.1). The vestibulo-vaginal junction (VVJ) is an annular, smooth, narrow, somewhat elastic, transverse ridge, and is palpable by digital examination. The urethral meatus opens at the urethral tubercle, which is located on the floor of the cranial vestibule approximately 1 cm caudal to the VVJ (Evans and Christensen 1993; Wilson 2001). The vagina is characterized by the presence of longitudinal mucosal folds that are highly influenced by the hormonal status of the bitch. A distinct fold of tissue, the dorsal medial fold (DMF), is present on the dorsal wall at the cranial end of the vagina (Pineda et al. 1973). The DMF extends cranially to the cervix and can be used as a guide to localize the cervix. The cervix has the appearance of a tubercle of many folds (Figure 7.2) sitting in an angled position (45–90°) in relation to the vaginal floor (Roszel 1992). This area may be narrower especially in maiden and small breed bitches. Even though the cervical tubercle differs in size and in shape (Wilson 2003), it is easily identified with endoscopy at the end of the DMF. The opening of the cervix, the cervical os, varies in position among bitches and depending on reproductive status. The fornix, a blind-ended region located cranio-ventrally to the external cervical os, is the most cranial portion of the vagina. Introduction of any instrument into the canine vagina requires attention to the anatomy, with a vertical vector in the beginning followed by a horizontal approach after passing the pelvic floor. 7.2 Instrumentation The first report of using an endoscope to visualize the post- uterine reproductive tract was done by Lindsay (1983) using a rigid pediatric telescope (Karl Storz SE & Co. The shunt system is a large Foley catheter (36 Fr), which comes in two lengths: 16 and 21 cm (MOFA, Inc.) with a balloon at the end. Inflation of the balloon simulates the events of natural mating and seals the vagina. Continuous air insuf- flation pressure may lift the cervix, improving visualization of the os. The introduction of the shunt is similar to intro - duction of the TCI scope. Once the shunt passes the VVJ, the Foley balloon is inflated with air (up to 100 cc) and then it is gently pulled back until it is firmly seated cranial to the VVJ. The endoscope is then introduced into the working channel of the shunt. Even though visualization of the vagina may be improved with the use of the shunt, there is a reduced ability to manipulate the endoscope since it is restrained in a working channel. There is also an increased risk of perforating the vaginal wall in case of a sudden movement by the bitch, but these limitations are overcome with practice. Also, the shunt prevents observation of ves - tibular abnormalities since the endoscope is inside the shunt until it exits cranially to the VVJ. The use of the shunt depends on veterinarian preference and its use is considered optional and to be decided case by case. For diagnostic vaginoscopy, the cystourethroscope seems to be better due to the size of the working channel and a larger image. Therefore, the cystourethroscope is recom- mended for the diagnosis of vaginal masses, bleeding, for - eign bodies, and for uterine lavage in case of treatment of pyometra. For TCI, uterine biopsy, uterine cytology, and cultures, the thin TCI scope is easier to manipulate. In our group, all procedures are done with the TCI scope. 7.3 Cleaning and Sterilization of Equipment Immediately after usage, the endoscope is rinsed with demineralized water. Once thoroughly rinsed, the endoscope is submerged in an enzymatic solution, for example, Alkazyme®, a combined cleaner, and pre- disinfection agent for metal surgical devices, for 20 minutes. After this soaking period, the instruments are again rinsed thoroughly with demineralized water. The endoscope is then dried with pressurized air. High-level disinfection with a glutaraldehyde solution (Cidex®, New Brunswick, NJ) for 20 minutes has been suggested by Lopate 2012. Independent of the solution used, three important procedures are followed: (i) the endoscope is rinsed immediately after its use to avoid secretions drying inside the channels, (ii) the cleaning solution is rinsed very well with water since the majority of solutions are harmful to the vagina and are also deleterious to semen, and (iii) the endoscope is dried with pressurized air soon after cleaning to avoid mold growth inside the working channel. For TCI, the best catheters are single use. In case of reutilization, cleaning is performed the same as for the Figure 7.4 TELE PACK™-Karl Storz SE & Co. KG. Any solution used should be followed by thorough rinsing with water to remove any residue. The catheters are single packed and then sterilized with ethylene oxide gas. Before use, the recycled catheters are inspected. Other instruments such as biopsy forceps, cytology brushes, and TCI shunts are cleaned to remove all biologi- cal debris and meticulous rinsing is done to eliminate any chemical residue. The sterilization technique is selected based on the characteristics of the material used in each instrument (plastic or metal). 7.4 Procedures in the Bitch 7.4.1 Transcervical Insemination (TCI) Use of endoscopy to perform artificial insemination in the bitch has increased exponentially in the last few years. Recommendations for using TCI are normally related to the quality and viability of the semen, since this technique can potentially improve fertility. Therefore frozen/thawed and poor quality or low-count semen are directly introduced into the uterus. Also, insemination done at the very end of estrus may benefit from TCI by overcoming cervical closure (Verstegen et al. 2001). Options that are available to achieve intrauterine insemination include an open surgical or laparoscopic approach, use of a Norwegian catheter, or with endoscopic TCI. Surgical artificial insemination has all the risks and complications related to abdominal surgery and general anesthesia plus the constraint of not being repeatable in the same estrous period. The Norwegian catheter is a blind technique that attempts to place an intrauterine cannula by palpation without visualization for positioning. TCI with endoscopic guidance has the advantage of the visualization of the whole procedure including the passage of the catheter through the cervix. Being able to see the procedure is highly appreciated by the owner during the insemination, it increases the probability of successful insemination, and it allows visualization of potential problems during the procedure. In recent years, demonstration of similar pregnancy rates with frozen–thawed semen using TCI in comparison to the surgical approach had a positive impact on the use of TCI. TCI is also a less invasive technique than surgery and is easily repeatable during the same estrous cycle. TCI has been shown to have a 20% better pregnancy rate than surgical insemination with frozen–thawed semen (Mason and Rous 2014). Today, endoscopic TCI is considered the gold standard for frozen–thawed semen insemination. There is no special preparation needed to perform TCI. The bitch needs to be comfortable. Sitting is to be avoided after artificial insemination. In rare cases, a full bladder or rectum can make identification and/or catheterization of the cervix more difficult. Therefore, encouraging the bitch to urinate and defecate before starting the TCI can help with the procedure and also makes the bitch less inclined to sit afterwards. Fasting is not necessary and enemas are not needed. The bitch is placed in a standing position on a hydraulic table. The use of a hydraulic table is highly recommended for the comfort of the veterinarian and to better position the bitch depending on her size. Sometimes, giant breeds such as Mastiff or Great Dane are extremely apprehensive when placed on a table and in these cases it is better to do the TCI with the dog on the floor. Tables are available with a wide belt that can be placed around the abdomen to stabilize the animal and avoid sitting during vaginoscopy. However, in most cases, the owner or an assistant can easily keep the bitch in position without any constraining device. Since bitches are in estrus when TCI is performed, the procedure is well tolerated due to standing behavior during natural breeding and sedation is rarely necessary. Overall, based on the bitches’ reactions, signs of discomfort during the TCI seem to be related to introduction of the endoscope, air insufflation around the urethral opening, passage of the endoscope into the paracervical area, and catheterization of the cervical opening. The slight pressure necessary to pass the narrower zone around the paracervical area appears to cause discomfort (Lindsay 1983; Lopate 2012; Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). Primiparous bitches sometimes are agi- tated at the beginning of the procedure due to insufflation of the vagina. In these cases, it is best to stop the procedure and let the bitch walk for a few minutes. Normally, at the second attempt the animal is calmer. Slightly warming the part of the endoscope that will touch the bitch first by gen- tle friction with a gauze is done to avoid an adverse reaction that occurs in some bitches when the endoscope is first introduced into the vagina. Contact of the endoscope or air insufflation at the urethral opening can cause discomfort and is avoided by proper positioning of the endoscope and by reducing the amount of insufflation air. Good tolerance has been observed with the use of the rigid TCI scope (Lopate 2012) but mild discomfort has been demonstrated using a flexible endoscope (Hayashi et al. 2013). 7.4.1.1 Introduction of the Endoscope and Catheterization of the Cervix Introduction of the rigid endoscope should consider the anatomy of the bitch’s vagina in a vertical direction to follow the steep angle of the vulva of 40–80° and then

7 .4 ­eocedqees in the Bitch 367 rotated to a horizontal approach around the caudal margin of the pelvic floor. All movements are gentle to reduce dis - comfort. To avoid touching the clitoral fossa and the ure - thral papilla (the urethral tubercle), the introduction of a finger ventral to the endoscope pressing slightly to a verti- cal direction may be helpful (Figure 7.6). The introduction of the endoscope into the urethral meatus is the most com- mon mistake (Figure 7.7) and its catheterization will incite discomfort in the female. The urethra is smooth and highly vascularized. In cases of catheterization of the urethra, the endoscope is withdrawn and redirected more dorsally into the vagina. The mucosal folds in the vagina are easily rec- ognized (Figure 7.8) and can protrude into the lumen, reducing visibility. Air insufflation may help to create a bet - ter image. Once the ischiatic arch is passed, endoscope position is more horizontal. The endoscope is advanced under visual control until the prominent DMF is identified (Figure 7.9). Ultimately, the endoscope will follow the direction of the DMF until the cervical tubercle is observed. The paracervical area (Figure 7.10) adjacent to the DMF is narrower requiring extra pressure to advance the endo - scope, especially in small breeds and maiden bitches. Pressure during this portion of the procedure is firm, but gentle, and some bitches will show signs of discomfort. The vaginal lumen will be slightly enlarged around the cervix. The goal is to visualize the external cervical os and align this opening with the endoscope. Identification of the cer - vical os during endoscopy requires some degree of practice and might take a few minutes. Observation of bloody discharge or air bubbles at the cervical tubercle is a good indication of the location of the os (Figure 7.11). If the vag - inal fornix is reached, the scope is gently withdrawn 1–2 cm to locate the cervix. Figure 7.6 Introduction of the TCI scope in an angled direction. The catheter is introduced far enough into the cervical canal to deposit the semen in the uterine body (Wilson 2001; Makloski 2012). The catheter should pass through the canal without resistance. The twisting motion helps the progression and reduces the chances of the catheter being trapped by the cervical or endometrial folds (Wilson 2001; Lopate 2012; Makloski 2012). If there is some resistance, the catheter is gently redirected. Once the catheterization is completed, it is recommended to stop insufflation. Passage of the catheter can be challenging when the cervix is angled to the side, downward or upward. In these cases, it is possible to manipulate the cervix with the end of the rigid endoscope or with the catheter to improve cervical position (Wilson 2003; Lopate 2012). Gentle compression on the ventral part of the abdominal wall close to the cervical area can also be used to change the position of the cervix and facilitate catheterization. In some bitches, especially breeds with pendulous abdominal walls such as English Bulldogs, estrous fluid and/or urine can accumulate in the cranial vagina obscur - ing the view of the cervix (Figure 7.13). Sometimes, it is possible to lift the cervix with the endoscope and pass the catheter. In other cases, the endoscope is removed and the fluid carefully aspirated using a urinary catheter attached to a 5- to 10-ml syringe. In cases of foul smell, sterile saline is used to flush the vagina. Small bitches (<5.0 kg) are more challenging to catheter - ize since the paracervical area is narrower. However, with the TCI scope, this task can be easily overcome. It is very important to adequately restrain the female, since with the 43 cm TCI scope any movement has more impact because a large part of the endoscope is outside the vagina. In some cases, the use of a smaller catheter (4 Fr) may be necessary due to the smaller os and cervical canal. 7.4.1.2 Insemination Once the catheter is passed into the cervical canal, the sty - let is removed, and a syringe with the semen and an adapter are connected to the catheter. In general, the insemination volume varies with the size of the bitch and parity (primi- parous or multiparous). Ideal volume has been determined to be around 1.0 ml for toy breeds up to 3.0 ml for giant breeds (Macedo et al. 2012). The time of injection of the semen may influence the capacity of the uterus and there - fore the insemination volume. In case of a larger volume, a slow injection of semen, up to 15–20 minutes (Mason and Rous 2014; Mason 2017) will allow the uterus to expand, increasing its capacity. Back flow of some semen out of the cervix may be observed (Figure 7.14). In any case, the num- ber of progressively motile spermatozoa (PMS), at least 150 million for each insemination dose, seems to be a more limiting factor than a higher volume, for frozen–thawed semen to achieve pregnancy rates of 76% (Mason 2017). Catheterization of the cervix is a challenging procedure. The efficiency and time required to perform this task depend on multiple interconnected factors: position of the cervical os, experience of the specialist, resistance to passage of the catheter, the levels of progesterone affecting Figure 7.13 Endoscopic view of fluid in the cervical area in the bitch. Figure 7.14 Endoscopic view of cervix catheterization (a) and semen back flow (b) in the bitch.

7 Vaginal Endoscopy in the Bitch 370 cervical tone, and parity of the bitch with old maiden bitches being more challenging. Practice will help to overcome some of these difficulties, but even for experts, there are a few bitches that will test their abilities. Different levels of difficulty catheterizing the cervix, unrelated to the levels of progesterone, have been described in 20% (6/30) of Labrador bitches due to the location and increased mobility of the cervical tubercle (Macedo et al. 2012). Approximately 20% of endoscopic TCIs will be more challenging, requiring manipulation of the cervix with the endoscope and catheter or cervical transposition with abdominal pressure required to achieve success. Due to these multiple factors it is not so easy to predict the needed time to perform endoscopic TCI. With a flexible endoscope, catheterization was done on average in 7.5 minutes (Hayashi et al. 2013) and for the rigid endoscope on aver - age less than 10 minutes has been reported for experienced practitioners. Time may be a concern only when using fro - zen–thawed semen due to low sperm longevity. Catheterization of the cervix prior to thawing the semen may be helpful but if this is done, it is important to con- sider that the bitch will have to be kept immobile to avoid dislodging the catheter for at least an additional five min- utes to thaw the semen. After insemination, technique such as lifting the hind legs or tilting the table to have the caudal end of the bitch at a higher level to help transportation of the semen has been advocated. Even though these procedures may be helpful, one that seems to be essential is the manual stimu- lation of the clitoris, vestibular area, and dorsal wall of the vagina to increase uterine contractions and semen trans - portation (England et al. 2012). 7.4.2 Observation of the Vaginal Changes Throughout the Estrous Cycle Changes in appearance of the vaginal mucosa are influenced by the hormonal status of the bitch. Both the color and texture of the mucosa reflect progress from anestrus through proestrus to estrus and can be easily monitored with vaginoscopy. As proestrus begins, the changes noted initially are due to the rise in estrogen, followed later by the rise in progesterone. Therefore, vaginoscopy will provide important information such as normal progression of each phase (Lindsay 1983) since it will allow observation of the changes in shape, color, and secretions of the vagina. Aspects of the vaginal folds can provide extra information to estimate the time of ovulation (Hotston-Moore and England 2008; Mason and Rous 2014) and optimal insemination time (Jeffcoate and Lindsay 1989; Goodman 2001). Physiological changes of the vaginal mucosa during proestrus and estrus can be indicative of the most fertile days for mating or insemination of fresh, chilled, or frozen semen. The first day of maximal crenulation, where the shrinking and angulation of the vaginal folds are greatest (Lindsay and Concannon 1986) and progesterone concentration is greater than 10 ng/ml, has been used as the first day for insemination using frozen–thawed semen (Mason and Rous 2014; Mason 2017). Although, a Sigmoidoscope (32020 Fibreoptic Sigmoidoscope; WelchAllyn, Skanea-teles, NY, USA) is more commonly used for this procedure, the ureteroscope can be used as well. 7.4.2.1 Proestrus Rising levels of estrogen during proestrus cause edema of the vaginal mucosa. Vaginoscopy reveals a light pink mucosa, smooth on the surface with rounded folds. In the majority of bitches, a bloody discharge is presented during late proestrus and this is when the edema is more evident (Figure 7.15) and the mucosa becomes paler. If bloody vagi - nal secretions hamper the view, a gentle touch of the endo - scope against the vaginal wall may help to clean the lens. 7.4.2.2 Estrus During estrus, there is a shift in concentration of hor - mones, levels of progesterone rise, and estrogen falls. The mucosa becomes wrinkled, shrunken, and pale. Crenulation of the mucosa will progress during estrus with greatest intensity of shrinkage between three and eight days. The day of maximal crenulation is a reference day. The collapsed vaginal folds are angulated with sharp edges (Figure 7.16). Figure 7.15 Endoscopic view of the vagina during proestrus in the bitch.

7 .4 ­eocedqees in the Bitch 371 7.4.2.3 Diestrus and Anestrus In these two phases of the estrous cycle, vaginoscopic examination shows similarities. The mucosa is pink and smooth with less prominent folds (Figure 7.17). During anestrus, only the DMF is well identified (Figure 7.18). The vaginal wall is very thin during these phases and endos - copy is done with extra caution to avoid trauma. Direct contact of the endoscope on the wall can produce petechiae. A thick mucous secretion may be visible in some bitches during diestrus. 7.4.3 Diagnostic Vaginoscopy Vaginoscopy is recommended as part of a routine exam for all breeding bitches. The first report using endoscopes to visualize the post-uterine reproductive tract was done by Lindsay (1983). Visualization of the vagina by endoscopy is the best technique to explore the post-uterine genital tract (Fontbonne 2010; Lévy 2016). Vaginal length and progres - sive narrowing limit examination by speculum and digital palpation to the caudal vagina. Vaginoscopy will help in the diagnosis of disorders associated with abnormal vulvo- vaginal discharge, excessive vulvar licking and excoriation, perivulvar dermatitis, dysuria, urinary incontinence, for - eign bodies, breeding problems (Watts et al. 1998), and may also provide important information in cases of infertility. If vaginoscopy is performed during proestrus or estrus, seda- tion is usually not necessary. For procedures during dies - trus and anestrus, when the vaginal wall is thin and therefore more sensitive and the bitch is less likely to stand quietly, sedation is considered depending on the behavior (willingness) of the animal. Common substances used for sedation are aceproma- zine, butorphanol, dexmedetomidine, or xylazine. The best sedation is the one the clinician is comfortable with but is also light enough to allow the animal to stay in a standing position. The goal of sedation is to take the edge off with- out reducing reflexes since a pain reaction may be helpful Figure 7.16 Endoscopic view of the vagina during estrus in the bitch. 7 Vaginal Endoscopy in the Bitch 372 to better guide manipulation of the endoscope while allow - ing the animal to be ambulant. In cases with a history of chronic foul-smelling vaginal discharge, indicating severe vaginitis, where the inflammation will provoke intense discomfort, general anesthesia is recommended. Vaginoscopy as a diagnostic procedure has been done under general anesthesia in dorsal recumbency (Lulich 2006). The level of discomfort of the bitch is associated with the instrumentation used and the clinical reason for the procedure. Lesions close to the VVJ can be missed if close attention is not given at the time of introduction of the endoscope. To improve the chances of diagnosing vagi- nal abnormalities, a careful observation of the images is done during both introduction and withdrawal of the endoscope. 7.4.3.1 Anomalies Related to the Paramesonephric Ducts During sexual development, the paramesonephric ducts fuse to form the uterine body, cervix, and cranial third of the vagina. The other parts of the vagina derive from fusion of the paramesonephric ducts with the proliferation of the urogenital sinus called the vaginal plate (Mcgeady et al. 2006). On the site where the vagina fuses to the urogenital sinus, the VVJ, a thin membrane may be present known as the hymen (Kyles et al. 1996). The hymen normally disappears around puberty or during the first natural breeding. The urogenital sinus also forms the vestibule and the urethra (Noden and de Lahunta 1985). An impartial fusion or failure of fusion of the caudal paramesonephric ducts and the urogenital sinus will lead to vaginal abnormalities (Colaço et al. 2012) observed endoscopically as a segmental stenosis, a vestibulo-vaginal constriction, a vaginal septum (Figure 7.19) or band (Figure 7.20), and an imperforate hymen. Clinical signs are associated with the severity of the problem. Pain during mating, intolerance to breeding, and dystocia are com- monly described. Other signs are cystitis, dysuria, urinary incontinence, and recurrent vaginitis or urinary tract infec- tions. In cases of complete obstruction (imperforate hymen), it is possible to have an accumulation of fluid in the vagina and the uterus. Correction of the problem can be achieved by manual removal of the hymen or thin band (Figure 7.20) or by resection of a thicker band or vaginal septum using the endoscope (Figure 7.21) (Arlt et al. 2012) or an open surgical approach. Except for the imperforate hymen, all other pathologies are not a problem when per - forming endoscopic TCI. Treatment is recommended to allow the bitch to have a natural parturition. Other cases related to abnormalities in the paramesonephric ducts can present as a double vagina with or without a double cervix. Both of these abnormalities are rare. Diagnosis of developmental abnormalities is done with X-ray contrast, ultrasonography, CT, and vaginoscopy. Endoscopy allows determination of the extent of the sep - tum and also provides the option for its possible resection. Diagnosis is sometimes made during routine endoscopic TCI. Asymptomatic nonbreeding bitches may never be diagnosed (Arlt et al. 2012). Figure 7.19 Endoscopic view of a vaginal septum (dorso- ventral septum) that prevents natural breeding and whelping. 7 .4 ­eocedqees in the Bitch 373 7.4.3.2 Vaginitis, Vaginal Mass, and Foreign Body Vaginitis can be triggered by any serious disturbance in the vaginal flora such as conformation of the perineal area, uri- nary tract infection, and presence of foreign bodies. Chronic vaginitis is the most common vaginal disorder (Soderberg 1986). The primary problems commonly reported are: urinary tract infections (26–60% of cases), vaginal anatomical anomalies (20–36% of cases), and sys - temic disease (15% of cases) (Johnson 1991; Parker 1998). Inspection of the vagina using an endoscope helps to local- ize the origin of the inflammation or foreign body, allowing collection of samples in specific and in the most critical areas (Figure 7.22). The presence of lymphoid follicles (1–3 mm), a nonspecific indicator of long-term inflamma- tion (Figure 7.23) in the vestibular and vaginal mucosa may indicate chronic inflammation of the genital tract. Vaginal masses are not common in the bitch and are nor - mally observed in older animals (Soderberg 1986; Silva et al. 2014). In cases of neoplasia, they are most commonly benign (Manohaiudom and Johnston 1991). Clinical signs are variable, but typically the complaint is related to exces - sive licking of an area or protruding tissue in the perineal region. During endoscopy, it is important to diagnose the origin, the shape, the size, and if the urethral papilla is compromised. Since the space to maneuver may be limited by the presence of a large vaginal mass, endoscopy is done with extreme care (Figure 7.24). Biopsy is not frequently done since removal of the mass is the treatment of choice. Removal of pedunculated masses (Figure 7.25) can be done using endoscopy (Silva et al. 2014). Vaginal lacerations and foreign bodies, such as fragments of bones from a macer - ated fetus, can also be explored using endoscopy (McCabe and Steffey 2004; Snead et al. 2010). 7.4.4 Other Uterine Procedures Transcervical endoscopic procedures, hysteroscopy, are used for uterine biopsy, sampling for bacteriology and Figure 7.21 Endoscopic view of the resection of a vaginal septum in the bitch by Arlt et al. Collection of uterine sam- ples for cytology and culture has been done in standing bitches with or without sedation (Watts and Wright 1995; Watts et al. 1996, 1998; Fontaine et al. 2009) and under general anesthesia (Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). 7.4.4.1 Hysteroscopy Hysteroscopy is not a routine examination and indications are limited to specific cases. It has been performed using the rigid uretero-renoscope (63002LA; 9.5 Fr, 43 cm length, Karl Storz SE & Co. KG) with air insufflation to distend the cervix allowing passage of the endoscope into the uterus in bitches under sedation (Fontaine et al. 2010). Once the technique of endoscopic TCI is mastered, performing hyst - eroscopy with the TCI scope (Figure 7.26) is relatively easy since the principles to perform both tasks are the same. Passing an insemination catheter through the cervical canal can be used as a guide for passage of the endoscope. After catheterization of the cervix, insufflation is continu- ous to allow the passage of the endoscope through the cer - vix and for visualization of the endometrium. Maiden bitches, small breeds, and bitches with an awkward posi- tion of the cervical os increase the challenge of endoscope passage. General anesthesia has been advocated for hyster - oscopy, regardless of the stage of the cycle, due to the increased risk of perforation of the uterus with any sudden movement of the bitch (Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). Good restraint of the bitch is very important since the uter - ine wall is more fragile and space is reduced increasing the risk of trauma. Sedation and general anesthesia are always considered to reduce the risks of perforation depending on the time of the cycle when hysteroscopy is performed and the character of the bitch. The best time to perform this procedure is not easy to determine. There are advantages to performing hysteroscopy in late proestrus or estrus. Passage of the endoscope is easier, bitches tolerate the procedure better due to standing behavior for breeding, and the uter - ine wall is thicker reducing the risk of laceration. The pres - ence of erythrocyte diapedesis may decrease visualization but this is mainly during proestrus (Kustritz 2006). During diestrus, observation of the endometrium may be more representative since the uterus is physiologically ready to Figure 7.24 Endoscopic view of vaginal mass in the bitch. Passage of the endoscope through the cervix may be more difficult at this stage due to the high levels of progesterone and increased tone of the cervix. Another consideration is that when under the influence of progesterone, the uterus will be more susceptible to infec- tions (endometritis and pyometra). In the period of anes - trus, the risks of developing endometritis or pyometra are reduced since the uterus is not under influence of proges - terone. During anestrus the uterine wall is thinner; there - fore, any sudden movement may increase the risk of laceration of the uterine or vaginal walls. It is recom- mended that any bitch being examined during anestrus be anesthetized to reduce the risk of perforation (Lopate 2012). Treatment with aglepristone or prostaglandin is recom- mended after endoscopy during diestrus to reduce the risk of infection as it will arrest the effects of progesterone. The use of prophylactic antibiotics has been advocated, regard- less of the phase of the estrous cycle, when the procedure is performed (Gerber and Nothling 2001). Other considerations for hysteroscopy: i) Visualization of the entire extension of each horn may not be possible in all bitches due to the sinuosity and length of the uterus. Position of the intestinal tract and the bladder will also affect the extent of the uterus that can be examined. ii) Insufflation may cause overdistension of the uterus and a pain reaction in the bitch. With ambulatory bitches, the procedure is stopped if discomfort leads to excessive movement of the bitch that could increase the risk of laceration. iii) Uterine discharge such as blood or pus can obliterate the field of view. Infusing sterile saline may be helpful to clear the endoscope and re-establish the view. Good visualization of the endometrial wall is imperative during the procedure for safety reasons and to observe possible focal lesions. iv) The use of a cystourethroscope will only allow passage into the cervix during the postpartum period up to day 17–23 (Watts and Wright 1995; Watts et al. 1997). Characterization of the endometrium using a different approach by uterine endoscopy after ventral celiotomy has been done in German Shepherd bitches. The endometrium was described as homogenous and pink in normal bitches. Helical folds of the endometrium were observed during diestrus. Irritation of the endometrium due to endoscopy resulted in the development of petechial lesions (Gerber and Nothling 2001). 7.4.4.2 Endometrial Biopsy The use of endometrial biopsy is controversial in the bitch. Infertile females are good candidates for the procedure since causes of infertility such as cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH) and inflammation can potentially be diagnosed by uterine biopsy. The presence of free fluid in the uterus is a contraindication for performing the biopsy; therefore, uterine ultrasound is done in all bitches prior to this procedure. Instrumentation for endometrial biopsy is similar to endoscopic TCI using the TCI scope, but instead of the catheter, biopsy forceps (5 Fr) are passed through the cervical canal and endometrial biopsy samples are col- lected (Günzel-Apel et al. 2001; Christensen et al. 2012). It is very important to keep the biopsy forceps closed during the transcervical passage. Once inside the uterus, the jaw is opened and the forceps is pressed gently against the uterine wall. The jaw is then closed and the sample is taken with a quick turning and pulling movement of the forceps. Normally, it is possible to feel when the tissue is cut. The forceps is removed from the uterus, pulled back into the ureteroscope, and then withdrawn from the vagina. The sample is handled by washing the jaw with sterile saline or using a small needle to remove the sample from the biopsy forceps. For better chances of diagnosis at least three to four biopsies are taken and for each one the procedure is repeated as described. It has been suggested to apply gentle pressure through the abdominal wall to ensure endometrial tissue is seated inside the jaws of the biopsy forceps (Günzel-Apel et al. 2001) or to use transabdominal ultrasonography to guide biopsy of a specific uterine horn (Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). Due to the very small size of the sample (1–2 mm or less), handling is done with extreme caution to avoid damaging the sample which could make the diagnosis inconclusive. Biopsies are submitted in formalin to be processed for interpretation. For uterine biopsy, the bitch can be awake, sedated, or under general anesthesia. The decision is based on behavior of the female, experience of the specialist, and duration and complexity of the procedure (use of ultrasound). The rationale is to guarantee the safety of the bitch during all procedures. Stages of the estrous cycle with endocrine activity result - ing in increased glandular function will provide the most information and stages of endometrial repair (mid–late anestrus) are avoided (Lopate 2012). The best diagnostic time is diestrus but this is also the time of increased risk for pyometra. All bitches sampled during diestrus receive treatment to counteract the influence of progesterone after the procedure (aglepristone or prostaglandin). As an alternative, biopsies are taken during proestrus, estrus, or very early anestrus when the glandular epithelium might still show the influence of progesterone but progesterone is close to baseline. It has been recommended that bitches undergoing this procedure during proestrus or estrus not

7 Vaginal Endoscopy in the Bitch 376 be bred on that cycle due to the risk of sperm peritonitis at the time of breeding in case of uterine perforation during biopsy (Lopate 2012). Prophylactic antibiotics have been advocated due to the possibility of local endometritis resulting from the biopsy developing into pyometra regardless of the stage of the cycle (Lopate 2012; Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). In our group, transcervical biopsy (TCB) are performed at the end of diestrus followed by treatment with aglepristone. Genital ultrasound is performed weekly until levels of progesterone are less than 2.0 ng/ml and no fluid is observed in the uterus. Rarely, the bitches are treated with antibiotics. Complications including uterine perforation, hematomuco metra, and pyometra have been described (Günzel-Apel et al. 2001; Christensen et al. 2012; Lopate 2012). Based on research results, Günzel-Apel et al. (2001) concluded that due to the severity of complications, TCB collection should not be recommended as a routine tech- nique in bitches. For Christensen et al. (2012), the luteal phase altogether is avoided when performing uterine biopsy. The size of endometrial samples harvested by transcervi- cal endoscopy is also a limitation of the technique (Günzel- Apel et al. 2001). With three endoscopic uterine biopsies, similar interpretation was obtained when compared with full-thickness uterine samples (Christensen et al. 2012). Histomorphometric evaluation of the uterus has been pos - sible by TCB (Ramos et al. 2016). TCB is normally per - formed blindly, obtaining a small specimen that routinely contains a small amount of superficial endometrium, and is prone to contain significant crush artifact. These factors limit the ability of pathologists to render as accurate an interpretation as is possible with a full-thickness wedge biopsy (Schlafer 2012a, b). 7.4.4.3 Uterine Cytology and Culture Another technique used to assess the health of the uterus is endometrial cytology and culture with samples collected with endoscopy. Although this technique can be performed during all phases of the estrous cycle (Watts et al. 1997, 1998; Fontaine et al. 2009), samples taken during proestrus and estrus allow treatment if it is necessary prior to insemination during the same cycle. Samples collected at the end of diestrus may provide a better understanding of the cause of pregnancy failure. There are two techniques to obtain material for cytology, by small-volume uterine lavage or with a cytology brush. The TCI scope is introduced into the vagina until the cervical os is identified. For the first technique, a catheter is passed through the cervix and a small volume of sterile saline (depending on the size of the bitch) is instilled into the uterus and retrieved by applying negative pressure using a syringe. Since the uterine wall may collapse around the catheter, gentle back and forth movement will help to collect fluid. If the amount of fluid is inadequate, the procedure is repeated using the same volume that was used in the first attempt. Once fluid is collected in the syringe, an aliquot is used for culture and the rest centrifuged to form a pellet that is placed on the slide for cytology. In the second technique, the catheter is replaced with a cytology brush that is passed through the cervical canal into the uterus. The brush is extended and gently moved against the uterine wall to collect the sample, and before withdrawing from the uterus, the cytology brush is retracted inside the sheath. The cytology brush is then removed from the sheath and rolled over a slide to disperse the cells for examination. For uterine cultures two cytology brushes are used, the first one for culture and the second for cytology. A limitation of both techniques is that the sample may not be representative of the whole uterus. Disadvantages of the cytology brush are an increased risk of endometritis due to entering the uterus twice (Watts and Wright 1995; Watts et al. 1997) and, due to flexibility of the cytology brush, passage through the cervix may not be achieved. The use of a small cytology brush (Olympus single-use mini cytology brushes) seems to reduce the risk of endometritis (Lopate 2012). Sampling during diestrus increases the incidence of endometritis (Watts and Wright 1995; Watts et al. 1997, 1998) and pyometra (Fontaine et al. 2009). Interpretation of the cytology is sometimes difficult; however, the presence of degenerated endometrial cells, isolated endometrial cells, foamy cytoplasm, and rare neutrophils indicates CEH (Groppetti et al. 2010). During all phases of the estrous cycle, the most common polymorphonuclears are leukocytes but during anestrus, the presence of lymphocytes and macrophages prevails (Watts et al. 1998; Groppetti et al. 2010). Endometritis is identified by observation of increased numbers of neutrophils and intracellular bacteria (Groppetti et al. 2010), by leucocyte score (Watts et al. 1998) and heavy growth of one or two bacteria (Fontaine et al. 2009). Other clinical signs such as infertility, fetal resorption, abortion, cervicitis, and vaginitis are used as supplementary information to support endometrial cytology. With uterine cultures, the microflora of the uterus during proestrus and estrus is similar to the vaginal flora. Bacteria were rarely observed during anestrus and diestrus (Watts et al. 1997). 7.4.4.4 Uterine Lavage A more recent use of the endoscopic TC procedure in the bitch is the local treatment of pyometra. The purulent fluid presented in the uterus is emptied with the aid of a cathe -

7 .4 ­eocedqees in the Bitch 377 ter. Either instrument, the cystourethroscope or the TCI scope is used; however, due to the dense mucoid character - istic of secretions, the use of a larger catheter will facilitate the task. Therefore, the cystourethroscope may be a better choice bearing in mind the limitations of its length and diameter as this instrument may be too short for some large breeds and too thick to pass into the paracervical area of others. Extra caution is taken during the whole procedure, as the vaginal wall is thinner and more prone to laceration during diestrus and anestrus. Due to the bacterial characteristic of pyometra, any lesion in the vagina can potentially lead to peritonitis or abscess. The procedure is to evacuate the contents of the uterus. First, the uterine fluid is withdrawn with the aid of a syringe attached to the catheter and then the uterus is lavaged with saline or lactated Ringer’s solution. In most cases, the fluid will drain out of the cervix. Caution is taken to avoid overfilling the uterus. Ultrasound of the uterus is done to assist in determining the amount of fluid to instill and to withdraw based on distention of the uterus. Lavage is discontinued when the fluid is less purulent and the uterus has been well evacuated. In a recent publication, five bitches were treated with transcervical endoscopic catheterization and uterine lavage while simultaneously under medical systemic treatment for pyometra (Greer et al. 2014). The use of local antibiotics is controversial and no controlled studies have been done to verify its efficacy. Since a large number of pyometras are caused by Escherichia coli , uterine lavage normally improves the clinical signs most likely due to the reduction of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) to which the bitch is exposed. All depressed or febrile bitches or those whose vaginal discharge is not notable are good candidates for this technique. 7.4.4.5 Other Usages The use of vaginoscopy during the postpartum period and with dystocia is helpful in selected cases. A limitation during postpartum is the presence of secretions (lochia) which impair visualization. Irrigation with sterile saline is necessary to help visualization in these cases. Normal invo - lution (Figure 7.27) can be observed as well as abnormal secretions during the postpartum period. Vaginoscopy has been used by our group in rare cases of dystocia when the fetus was dead to attempt vaginal delivery and avoid C-section (Figure 7.28). 7.4.5 Complications and Limitations If vaginal endoscopy is done as described, complications are rare. During estrus, perforation of the vagina is very unlikely due to the thickness of the wall under the influence of estrogen. During examination in diestrus and anestrus, extra caution is taken since the wall is thinner. To avoid any trauma, movements of the endoscope are gentle and a vis - ual field is maintained at all times during the procedure. Abrupt movements of the bitch are avoided and particular attention is given to any attempt of the bitch to sit, in which case the endoscope is removed. It is very important to avoid the urethral papilla and introduction of the endoscope in the urethra or bladder. 7 Vaginal Endoscopy in the Bitch 378 consequences can occur due to inadvertent introduction of the ureteroscope into the urethra (Figure 7.29) and bladder during the procedure. This error has been a motive for law suits in the veterinary field. Complications such as endo - metritis, vaginitis, and vaginal tears described by Watts and Wright (1995) are less frequent nowadays with better adap - tation of endoscopic instruments to veterinary medicine. The paracervical region (Figure 7.30) is the most common location of tears (Wilson 2003), especially in anestrous bitches. Normally, the bitch will recover uneventfully and surgical correction is not necessary (Romagnoli and Lopate 2014). Sudden acute pain reflexes are extremely rare, but are worth mentioning. In our group, during the last year and performing endoscopic TCI on more than 1000 bitches, only 4 bitches showed pain behavior after the procedure. The signs of pain vary from mild discomfort (crying and some abdominal discomfort) to acute abdominal pain in three of these cases. The TCI procedure was uneventful with cervical catheterization considered easy. In all bitches, abdominal ultrasound was performed to determine the ori- gin of the pain. No free fluid or air was observed in the abdominal cavity. A full clinical examination also did not reveal the cause of the acute pain. Differential diagnosis pointed to pain due to a musculoskeletal problem. Two bitches showed signs similar to prostaglandin-induced colic in mares; however, this hypothesis could not be proven. All bitches became pregnant despite showing signs of pain. The definitive cause of this acute pain needs to be established. Overall, TC procedures are safe. The best way to prevent and observe any problem is to be attentive to visualization of the vagina during the introduction and also during the withdrawal of the endoscope. 7.4.6 Tips and General Comments Slightly bending the tip of the catheter upward may be helpful to catheterize the cervix in bitches with a more angled position (more dorsal) since the catheter will be directed upward instead of being straight out of the sheath. Another possibility suggested by Romagnoli and Lopate (2014) is to cut 7–10 cm off the end of an 8 Fr catheter and then pass a smaller 5 Fr catheter that has been bent upward through this larger catheter. The rigidity of the 8 Fr cathe - ter and the upward angle of the smaller catheter will allow catheterization of the cervix in some bitches. This method has not been tested by our group. When the catheter is stuck in the cervical canal and can- not be pushed forward, injection of a small amount of fluid (semen or extender) can be helpful due to the lubricating effect and by causing slight distention of the canal allowing the catheter to progress. The downside of this technique is that to inject fluid, the stylet of the catheter needs to be removed making the catheter soft and more easily bendable. If the TCI shunt is used, lubrication of the working chan- nel is considered. Friction between the scope and the metal ring may lead to displacement of the ring and sudden loss of air from the vagina producing a noise that could poten- tially frighten the bitch. For the TCI scope, a simple gentle tap against the vaginal mucosa can improve the view. 7.5 Conclusion The learning curve for endoscopic transcervical (ETC) pro - cedures in the bitch may be steep, but this challenge is overcome with patience and practice. Although the invest - ment in endoscopic instrumentation might be considered substantial, it is soon returned (Davidson 2016). Multiple uses of endoscopy in different areas of veterinary medicine make it very appealing. The rigid endoscope (TCI scope) is specific for reproductive and urinary tract endoscopy, but the tower (camera and light) and insufflation can be used for many other procedures. The routine use of the endoscopic TCI makes surgical AI ethically debatable as it is a more invasive technique to obtain similar pregnancy rate results. Other indications like uterine lavage for cytology, bacteriology, and treatment of pyometra are still under exploration but have a wide range of possibilities. Applications for uterine biopsy and hysteroscopy need further study to prove general usage. Even though diestrus may be the best period for endo - scopic procedures to diagnose problems such as CEH and endometritis, the increased risk of pyometra should not be ignored. Treatments to reduce the influence of progester - one (aglepristone or prostaglandins) are imperative when procedures are performed during this phase of the cycle. An alternative is to perform endoscopic procedures in early anestrus when the samples will still be representative of possible pathology but progesterone levels are negligible. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 8.1 Introduction Laparoscopy is endoscopy of the abdomen or peritoneal cavity. This area of diagnostic endoscopy and minimally invasive surgery has seen major changes over the last 10 years and has become one of the most commonly employed endoscopic techniques in small animal practice. Examination of the abdomen with laparoscopy requires that the abdomen be distended with gas to create a visual space or field. Laparoscopes are rigid telescopes with com- monly used diameters of 3.0, 5.0, and 10.0 mm, most are zero degree angle of view or in a straight line with the axis of the telescope, and lengths from 14 cm for the 3.0 mm tel- escope to 30 cm for the standard length of two larger tele - scopes with special telescopes up to 42 cm length (Figure 2.26). Laparoscopy can be performed with a single- port allowing passage of an operating telescope with an instrument channel (Figures 2.32 and 8.1), a single incision portal that allows passage of a telescope and multiple oper - ating instruments (Figure 8.2), two portals using a telescope portal and a single operating instrument (Figure 8.3), and with a telescope portal plus multiple portals for operating instruments (Figure 8.4). As with most of the endoscopic techniques used in small animal practice, laparoscopy was initially used as a diagnos - tic procedure and has progressed to include treatment of an ever-increasing number of surgical diseases. Abdominal exploration with laparoscopy can be as complete as with an open surgical exploration when using multiple portals and a tilt table that allows the patient’s position to be changed to move abdominal organs for examination of underlying tis - sues (Figure 8.5). Gravity is the best retractor for minimally invasive surgery and a powered tilt table is essential for per - forming complex laparoscopic surgical procedures. Magnification and lighting provided by laparoscopes improve our diagnostic capabilities over open surgery. A wide, and rapidly expanding, list of diagnostics (Table 8.1) and surgical procedures (Tables 8.2 and 8.3) are performed with this mini- mally invasive technique. Laparoscopy is preferred over open surgery whenever pos - sible. The decision to open the abdomen or to use a mini- mally invasive approach is based on the needs of individual cases, skill of the surgeon, and instrumentation that is avail- able. There are too many variables to allow anyone to state which approach to take with any individual patient in any particular practice setting. The question “Can this procedure be done with minimally invasive technique”needs to be asked when approaching every abdominal surgery. If this question is asked with every case, there will be a significant increase in the number of minimally invasive abdominal surgeries performed. On the other hand, if MIS is only con- sidered for procedures that have been proven to be success - ful with laparoscopy, the number of MIS abdominal procedures performed will be far fewer. The decision for many cases is easy and the preferred approach is taken. With cases where it is not known if the procedure can be com- pleted with MIS, it is easy to place a telescope, evaluate the options with minimal time invested, and make a decision. If this approach is taken, a significant number of procedures will be completed successfully with MIS. For those that are not amenable to MIS, conversion to an open procedure is quick and easy. Conversion is not a failure but a learning experience and a normal step in increasing the number of MIS procedures performed. The minimally invasive nature of laparoscopy decreases operative and postoperative pain, in many cases decreases hospitalization time, speeds up recovery, reduces post - operative incision complications, and is faster than an open surgical procedure.
