8 Laparoscopy 386 considered as a preferred alternative. Unless there are preop - erative findings dictating that an open surgery is required, laparoscopy is the procedure of choice and is the standard of care. With laparoscopy we are able to examine and biopsy almost all abdominal organs, tissues, or masses. If we are unable to achieve an adequate exploration with laparoscopy, conversion to an open surgery is indicated. This is not a fail- ure of laparoscopy but is a normal progression when using the best available techniques for maximum benefit to the patient. Laparoscopy will not completely replace open abdominal exploratory but when successful provides a mini- mally invasive alternative avoiding unnecessary trauma and pain. If no conversions to open surgery are being performed, then laparoscopy is not being done often enough. Biopsies obtained with laparoscopy are superior to most biopsies taken with less invasive percutaneous techniques (Wang et al. 2004). One of the most common diagnostic indications for laparoscopy is obtaining liver biopsies (Petre et al. 2012). Other commonly biopsied organs include the pancreas (Webb and Trott 2008), kidneys (Grauer et al. 1983; Lees et al. 2011; Vaden 2005), spleen (Ballegeer et al. 2007), full-thickness gastrointestinal (Evans et al. 2006; Gieger 2011; Mitterman et al. 2016), lymph nodes, and peri- toneal surfaces. Biopsies are also taken from masses arising in any of these organs or from masses not obviously attached to an organ. Staging of intra-abdominal malignancies is a common indication for laparoscopy (Balsa and Culp 2019; Liptak 2009) and biopsies of multiple sites are performed quickly and safely. Magnification produced by the laparo - scope and video system allows identification of small sub- macroscopic lesions that cannot be seen with open exploration or with imaging techniques. Magnification is particularly helpful in seeing peritoneal nodules indicative of mesothelioma or metastatic disease. Hollow abdominal organs such as the stomach, intestines, and bladder are biopsied using laparoscopic-assisted techniques. The organ to be biopsied, most commonly the stomach and intestines, has a small portion of its wall exteriorized and open surgical technique is used to obtain full-thickness biopsies. 8.2.2 Indications for Operative Laparoscopy One of the major changes in application of endoscopic techniques in small animal practice over the last 10 years is the increased use of minimally invasive abdominal surgery (Table 8.2). This is due to both an increased number of practices performing common procedures such as ovariec- tomy and the increased variety of procedures performed. More and more practices are performing laparoscopic ovariectomies with increased frequency. This is a procedure that belongs in general practice as opposed to many of the more complex surgeries that require a specialty practice. There is typically a single procedure that drives new technology into common use such as laparoscopic cholecys - tectomy in people. Laparoscopic ovariectomy is this proce - dure in small animal practice. It has been an interesting finding that many practices rarely perform traditional open ovariectomy or ovariohysterectomy due to the competition of low-cost spay clinics and because many shelters spay and neuter animals before adoption. When laparoscopic ova- riectomies are added to a practice, this changes, and in a short period of time the practice is performing “Lap Spays” every day or sometimes more than one a day. The rational for this change is that clients are unable to understand the cost difference between a “cheap spay” and an “expensive spay” but they can understand the cost difference between a traditional open spay and a laparoscopic spay. And most clients are willing, sometimes excited, to pay significantly more for this improved surgery for their pets. Since we as a profession started spaying dogs and cats over 100 years ago, we have improved the procedure with better preanesthetic evaluation, better anesthetic agents, better monitoring, better supportive care, better suture materials, better aseptic technique, and better postoperative pain man- agement but we are still using the same barbaric tissue han- dling technique where we rip the ovarian pedicles out by the roots. Laparoscopic ovariectomy is the last piece of the puz- zle and completes the overall picture for improved technique to provide a truly modern surgical procedure. Minimally invasive abdominal surgery has many advan- tages over conventional open laparotomy. Smaller incision sites allow faster patient recovery with less risk of incision dehiscence, shorter hospitalization times, less tissue trauma, less intraoperative and postoperative pain, decreased morbidity, and decreased postoperative infec- tions. Because there is less pain, there is less need for pain medication and lower doses are used for shorter periods of time. Shorter patient activity restriction times are required and there is faster return to full function. The advantages of minimally invasive surgery extend beyond those related to the effects of incision size. The most common and obvi- ous example of reduced intra-abdominal tissue trauma with laparoscopy compared with traditional open surgery is, as was previously discussed, related to ovariectomy or ovariohysterectomy. With traditional open ovariohysterec- tomy, the ovarian pedicles are stretched and torn to achieve access for ligations performed at the level of the skin inci- sion. This causes excessive tissue trauma (Figure 8.6), bleeding (Figure 8.7), and increased risk of significant hemorrhage. With laparoscopic ovariectomy, the ovaries are elevated above the surrounding tissues without tearing the tissue and transection is performed at the ovarian pedicles with no need to tear tissue leaving a thin line of fused tissue (Figure 8.8).

8.2 ­IndicadiIns ior ca coinsiiap 387 Pathophysiology associated with surgery has been proven to be reduced with minimally invasive technique when compared with traditional open surgical procedures (Culp et al. 2009; Davidson et al. 2004; Devitt et al. 2005). Stress-mediated markers have been studied and have proven a reduction in all measurable indicators for pain and stress (Case et al. 2011; Gauthier et al. 2015; Hancock et al. 2005). Minimally invasive surgical techniques currently being performed in small animal practice are rapidly increasing (Table 8.2). In addition to ovariectomy and ovariohysterec- tomy, common general practice procedures include cryp - torchid surgery, cholecystectomy, partial pancreatectomy, and removal of relatively small tumors. More complex pro - cedures requiring greater skills and instrumentation that probably belong in a specialty practice include adrenalec- tomy, nephrectomy, splenectomy, lymph node removal, portosystemic shunt occlusion, artificial urethral sphincter implantation, cisterna chyli ablation, relatively large tumor removal, gastric volvulus correction, intra-abdominal gas - tropexy, and hernia repair. There are few abdominal proce - dures that have traditionally been performed with open surgery that are not amenable to minimally invasive sur - gery. As our skills increase, instrumentation improves, and we continue to push the limits of what we try, more and more abdominal surgeries will be performed with mini- mally invasive technique. Laparoscopic-assisted procedures that are performed in small animal practice are also increasing in variety and number (Table 8.3). Laparoscopic-assisted procedures use the advantages of laparoscopy combined with advantages of open surgery to expand our application of minimally invasive surgery and can substantially shorten surgery times. Laparoscopy is used to identify the organ or tissue requiring surgery which is then grasped with a laparo - scopic instrument and elevated to the abdominal wall. The operative portal is enlarged as needed to allow a portion of the involved organ to be exteriorized. Traditional open sur - gical technique is then used to perform the needed surgery with no requirement for advanced skills or instrumenta- tion. This approach allows us to perform many procedures that would not be possible today with strictly minimally invasive technique. Laparoscopic-assisted cystoscopy is a great example and allows us to perform almost all bladder surgery in all sizes of male and female dogs and cats with minimally invasive technique. The effectiveness of this technique has made traditional open cystotomy an obso - lete procedure. Laparoscopic-assisted prophylactic gastropexy is another commonly performed MIS procedure that uses the advan- tages of both laparoscopy and open surgical techniques. Laparoscopic-assisted surgery in small ani- mal practice can be applied to any procedure involving tis - sue that is mobile enough to be elevated to the abdominal wall and exteriorized. 8.3 Instrumentation for Small Animal Laparoscopy A video system tower is required for laparoscopy as described in Chapter 2. Specific additions to the tower that are required to perform laparoscopy include an insufflator (Figure 8.9) and a radio-frequency vessel sealing device (Figure 2.14). The insufflator fills the abdominal cavity with CO 2 and auto - matically maintains a set distension pressure throughout the laparoscopy procedure. Abdominal insufflation is required to create a visual space in which to examine and perform procedures within the abdominal cavity. Vessel sealing devices eliminate the need to ligate blood vessels dramati - cally facilitating minimally invasive surgical procedures. 8.3.1 Insufflator A major difference of laparoscopy compared to other endo - scopic techniques is that insufflation of the abdomen is required to provide a visual field. This insufflation is differ - ent than that used for gastrointestinal endoscopy as air cannot be used for laparoscopy, leakage of gas is prevented, and insufflation pressure is controlled to a specific range. Carbon dioxide gas is used for insufflation of the abdomen to minimize the risk of air embolism and because it is not combustible. This requires containers of compressed car - bon dioxide, high-pressure tubing, a piece of equipment called an insufflator (Figure 8.9), and low-pressure insufflation tubing (Table 8.4). The Veress needle is a 14 gauge (2.1 mm) 10 cm long needle with a hollow spring-loaded blunt stylet with side ports at its tip. When advancing the needle through the resistance of the abdominal wall, the blunt stylet is forced back into the outer needle exposing its sharp point. When the peritoneal cavity is entered, decreased resistance allows the blunt stylet to extend creating a blunt instrument and greatly reducing the potential for organ damage. Insufflation is initiated and when abdominal distension is achieved, tel - escope and operative portals are placed. The second tech - nique for initiating abdominal insufflation, the Hassan technique, places the first portal trocar prior to abdominal insufflation by making a small abdominal wall incision through the linea alba, elevating the abdominal wall with traction sutures, and placing the cannula using a blunt obturator followed by insufflation. A third technique uses a Ternamian EndoTIP cannula (Figure 2.39) with the tele - scope in the cannula at the time of initial insertion (Anderson and Fransson 2019). A depth of insertion attachment is placed on the telescope to control the position of the tele - scope in the cannula allowing visualization of abdominal wall tissue as the cannula is screwed into the peritoneal cav - ity. Penetration of tissue is observed during the insertion process until fat or abdominal organ tissue is seen indicating entry into the peritoneal cavity and insufflation is initiated. A high-pressure CO 2 tank is connected to the insufflator with high-pressure tubing. Small E tanks of CO 2 mounted on the tower are used or CO 2 is piped into the operating room from larger remote H tanks. Both sources work and each has advantages and disadvantages. The small tanks are easier and less expensive to install as they do not require modification of the facility but are more expensive per liter of CO 2 used. The larger H tanks provide CO 2 at a lower cost per liter but require installation of high-pressure piping to a remote location where the large tanks are stored. Both systems require a second tank as a backup so that laparo - scopic procedures are not terminated or converted due to an empty tank. A primary CO 2 source using a large remote H tank with a small E tank on the tower as a backup is an option. If old piping for nitrous oxide or another obsolete unused gas is present in the facility, the connectors can be changed to convert the system to CO 2 . An insufflator is required to reduce gas pressure from the CO 2 source to the controlled pressure and flow rate of gas delivered to the patient. A high flow rate is delivered until the abdomen is insufflated to the pressure set on the insuf - flator. When the set pressure is reached, gas flow is reduced and then varies to maintain the desired intra-abdominal pressure. Current modern insufflators have adjustable CO 2 flow rates and adjustable insufflation pressure. Older units have a preset pressure of 15 cm H 2 O and do not allow adjust - ment. Pressure adjustment is important for longer more complex procedures where insufflation times are prolonged and pressure reduction after portal placement is indicated. Flow rate is adjusted based on patient size with higher flows for larger patients to speedup initial abdominal insufflation and maintain insufflation more effectively. In large dogs, a flow rate of 4.0 l/min is commonly used. In small dogs and cats, a flow rate of 1.0 l/min is more appropriate. Insufflators measure and display flow rate in liters per minute, pressure in centimeters of water, and the number of liters of CO 2 that have been used. Insufflators used today are very reliable and rarely fail but any piece of equipment can malfunction, so it is very important to monitor patient function and abdomi - nal distension for any indication of a problem. Recent com - munication from a veterinarian with extensive laparoscopy experience reported death of a patient due to over insuffla - tion from a malfunctioning insufflator. Low-pressure insufflation tubing is used to connect the insufflator to the patient. This tubing is provided presterilized and is intended for single use (Figure 8.11). A filter is present at the insufflator end of the tube to remove possible bacteria or other contaminants. The patient end of the tubing has a Luer connector to provide secure connection to the needle or can - nula that provides access to the peritoneal cavity. Although this tubing is intended for single use, it is frequently resterilized and repeatedly reused. Resterilization is not recommended and is left to the discretion of the individual practice. 8.3.2 Laparoscopes Telescopes used for laparoscopy in small animal practice are most commonly zero degree telescopes with a field of view that is straight ahead in line with the long axis of the telescope. Various diameters are available ranging from 10.0 to 3.0 mm and lengths ranging from 14 to 30 cm (Figure 2.26 Figure 8.11 Disposable low-pressure insufflation tubing with a filter for connecting the insufflator unit to the patient. Ten-millimeter telescopes are occa- sionally used in very large dogs but are not required as 5-mm laparoscopes are adequate for all small animal patients. The primary need for the larger telescope is image capture where additional light is required for the best-qual- ity images. The smaller telescope, 3.0 mm, is advantageous for smaller dogs and for cats. The primary advantage of this telescope is that it is shorter, 14 cm, than the typical 5.0 and 10 mm laparoscopes making manipulation in small abdom- inal cavities easier. The smaller diameter is helpful but the 5 mm telescope has been used in dogs as small as 1.0 kg and the 10 mm laparoscope has been used in cats. Single puncture or operating telescopes for laparoscopy have a large straight working or operating channel that allows procedures to be performed with a single-port. Currently available operating laparoscopes are 10 mm diameter, 0°, with 23 cm or 25 cm working lengths, and an operating channel that will accommodate 5 mm instru- ments (Figure 2.32 and Table 8.6). These telescopes allow simple diagnostic and operative procedures to be per - formed through a single abdominal puncture or portal. This approach has the advantage of a single abdominal incision and decreased skill level is required for the begin- ner to perform basic procedures. Their disadvantage is that only one instrument can be placed into the abdomen and there is no ability to triangulate the operative instrument greatly decreasing depth perception. Additional telescope options that are suitable to use for laparoscopy in small animals include the 2.7 mm MPRT, a 4.0 mm arthroscope, smaller telescopes adapted from other specialties, and 30° versions of the previously listed 0° lapa- roscopes (Figure 2.26 and Table 8.7). The MPRT is com- monly used for laparoscopy in smaller patients. Because this telescope has many uses, it is more likely to be available in small animal practices than a small scope limited to laparos - copy. Its 18 cm length also makes this ideal for small patients. The primary disadvantage of this telescope is that it has a 30° viewing angle. This angle has advantages in many applica- tions where the direction of telescope placement is limited by surrounding structures, but this is not the case when per - forming laparoscopy. This angulation makes orientation of the image more difficult but with experience, this angled alignment becomes less and less important. It can be chal- lenging for the beginning endoscopist. Ideally a small zero degree telescope is recommended for laparoscopy but if the 2.7 MPRT is available in the practice, its use is better than not performing laparoscopy. A 4.0 mm diameter 0° arthro - scope with an 18 cm length also works very well for laparos - copy in smaller patients providing more light than the 2.7 mm or 3.0 mm laparoscopes. Thirty-degree versions of the 10, 5, and 3 mm laparoscopes are available but are not recommended for laparoscopy due to the reasons listed for the 2.7 mm MPRT. A new telescope, the ENDOCAMELEON (Figure 2.28), is available as a laparoscope with an adjustable angle of view from 0° to 120°, a diameter of 10 mm, and lengths of 32 cm or 42 cm. An ENDOCAMELEON arthroscope is also available with an adjustable angle of view from 15° to 90°, a diameter of 4 mm, and a length of 18 cm. 8.3.3 T rocar-Cannulas (Figures 2.38–2.40) (T able 8.8) Access to the abdomen for laparoscopy is provided with specially designed trocar-cannulas. These cannulas are designed to allow easy penetration of the abdominal wall and create an airtight seal to prevent leakage of insufflation gas. Trocar-cannulas are available in sizes from 2.5 to 13.5 mm diameter and 4–11.5 cm in length. The most com- mon sizes used are 3.5, 6, and 11 mm. Shorter versions of the various diameters are recommended. Cannula size used is dictated by the telescope and instrument sizes being used for the procedure. Telescope cannulas and operating can- nulas are the same design but are simply used for different functions. Their use is interchangeable, and this is easily done by moving the telescope from one cannula to another. In addition to multiple sizes, there are multiple trocar- cannula designs and they are available in reusable or single- use disposable options. Reusable cannulas are more expensive than disposable units, but they can be reused many times and if cared for properly will last for years and hundreds of procedures. All laparoscopy cannulas have an internal valve system that prevents leakage of insufflation gas when a telescope or instrument is not in the cannula. A gasket is present at the outside end of cannulas to create an airtight seal and prevent loss of insufflation gas when there is a telescope or instrument in the cannula. Three basic valve designs are available with different advantages and disad- vantages, but all the systems work well. Most reusable can- nula-trocars come with both sharp trocars (Figure 2.38a) and blunt trocars (Figure 2.38b) for use in penetrating the abdominal wall. Sharp trocars are used to create or cut a new portal when the abdomen is insufflated ( Video 8.3). Blunt obturators are used when creating a portal using the Hassan technique or when replacing a cannula that has been removed from an already established portal ( Video 8.4). Disposable trocar-cannulas have an integral cutting blade that is spring loaded similar to the mechanism in a Veress needle. The blade is exposed by abdominal wall resistance and retracted after penetration into the peritoneal cavity. An additional cannula type is called a Ternamian EndoTIP cannula (Figure 2.39) that has a threaded exter - nal shaft surface. This cannula is designed to be used with- out a sharp trocar or blunt obturator. The tip of the cannula allows it to be screwed through the abdominal wall after insufflation ( Video 8.5). They can also be used for initial portal placement prior to insufflation by observing abdom- inal wall penetration with the telescope in the cannula dur - ing the placement procedure. A telescope depth control clamp is used during this procedure to help hold the tele - scope at the correct depth. One of the major advantages of EndoTIP cannulas is that they are threaded over their entire length which helps stabilize them in the abdominal wall decreasing inadvertent displacement of the cannula. Their disadvantage is that tissue can be picked up by the leading edge of the thread at the end of the cannula and this interferes with telescope passage if the telescope lens contacts the tissue dirtying the image. EndoTIP cannulas are preferred by some surgeons and in some applications but are not the preferred instrument for all uses. Three different types of valves are supplied with the can- nulas including multifunctional valves (Figure 2.39), auto - matic valves (Figure 2.38a), and silicone leaflet valves (Figure 2.40). Multifunctional valves have a lever to open the valve and a spring to close the valve (Figure 2.39). The telescope is placed into the cannula gasket and the valve is opened with the lever to prevent contact of the tel- escope lens with the valve surface. Contact of the telescope lens with the valve scratches the lens and over time will decrease image clarity. Another problem when the tele - scope lens contacts with the valve surface is that when per - forming complex procedures with bleeding, the valve surface can get dirty with blood. If the telescope is removed for lens cleaning during the procedure, when it is replaced into a cannula with a bloody valve surface, the telescope lens will get dirty when it contacts the valve requiring repeated removal for cleaning. With a multifunctional valve, the valve is opened with the lever and there is no need for contact of the telescope lens with the valve sur - face. Automatic valves do not have a lever and can only be opened with pressure from an instrument or telescope (Figure 2.38a). These work well for instruments but as pre - viously discussed, do not work well for telescopes. Silicone leaflet valves are made of flexible silicone rubber with four valve leaflets and allow passage of instruments or tele - scopes without a metal valve mechanism (Figure 2.40). The number of cannulas needed depends on the procedure being performed and the technique being used. A single puncture technique places one cannula and uses an operat - ing telescope with an instrument channel. All other tech- niques place a telescope cannula and one or more operative cannulas. The telescope cannula used is determined by the telescope size. If a 5 mm telescope and 5 mm instruments are being exclusively used for the procedure, then all can- nulas are 6 mm. If there is a need for larger instruments at any phase of the procedure, then 11 mm or 13.5 mm can- nulas are placed where needed. Trocar-cannulas come in multiple lengths but for small animal practice the shortest available length is preferred. A reducer is available that cre - ates an airtight seal with 5 mm instruments passed through 11 mm cannulas. Diagnostic or surgical procedures are per - formed with single-port, two-port, three-port, or more. This is all dependent on the procedure being performed and the preference of the operator. If a procedure is rou- tinely performed with a telescope cannula and two opera- tive portals but a specific case requires additional access, then additional cannulas are added as needed. If a larger cannula is needed the smaller one is removed, and a larger cannula placed. 8.3.4 Operative Instruments An extensive array of diagnostic laparoscopy instrumen- tation and operative instrumentation for minimally inva- sive surgery is available in multiple sizes and reusable or disposable options. Catalogs of laparoscopic instrumentation are thicker and heavier than those for traditional open surgery. The variety of instruments available is over - whelming. Fortunately, the number of instruments needed for diagnostic procedures and for basic operative procedures currently performed in small animal practice is reasonable. The most common instrument size is 5 mm diameter (Figure 2.43) and is effective for the vast major - ity of our patients with 3 mm diameter instruments for the smallest patients and there is an occasional need for a 10 mm instrument. The 5 mm diameter instruments are composed of three parts, the working insert with the instrument jaws, an outer insulated metal sheath, and a handle (Figures 2.43, 8.12 and Table 8.9). They are disassembled for cleaning. The inserts, sheaths, and handles are interchangeable within the two available lengths of 36 and 43 cm. The shorter length is most commonly used for small animal procedures, but the longer instruments are needed for use with the operating laparo - scopes. Handles are available without a locking ratchet or with one of two types of ratchets, the hemostat type or a swing-away ratchet. For biopsy forceps and scissors, a han- dle without a ratchet is recommended. For strictly diagnostic procedures such as liver biopsies, a 5 mm manipulation probe and a 5 mm biopsy forceps are all that is needed (Figure 8.13 and Table 8.10). Two types of biopsy forceps are common. One has a clam shell or appos - ing cup configuration with or without a tissue spike. This instrument is ideal for liver biopsies. The presence or absence of a spike in the center of the biopsy cups has advantages and disadvantages but both harvest similar quantities of tissue that are well suited to achieve an accu- rate diagnosis. The other type of biopsy forceps is the punch or cutting forceps where one jaw fits inside the other. This type of biopsy forceps is preferred for tougher tissue such as the pancreas. A 3.0 mm diameter apposing cup biopsy forceps without teeth is also available for use in very small patients. Operative instruments for minimally invasive surgery commonly used in small animals include (Figure 8.14 and Table 8.11) curved scissors for cutting tissue, hook scissors for cutting tough tissue and sutures, curved dissecting for - ceps, atraumatic grasping forceps with or without a fenes - tration, right-angle dissecting forceps, a suction-irrigation cannula, a fan retractor, and an injection cannula. The irri- gation cannula is a long tube that can be placed through a laparoscopy cannula with a valve mechanism that allows fluid inflow for irrigation and fluid outflow for suction. This instrument is needed if there is significant bleeding following biopsy or if there is fluid or exudate in the perito - neal cavity. An injection cannula is used for injections and can also be used for aspiration of tissue for cytology or

A 10 mm diameter fan retractor is also available in 36 mm length. A limited selection of 3 mm diameter instruments with 20 cm length is also available for use in very small patients (Table 8.13). The handles of these instruments are the same as for the 5 mm set and are interchangeable among instruments. This instrument is inserted through the abdominal wall around an 11 mm portal cannula and is opened to retract the abdominal wall tissue allowing removal of tissue too large to fit through the original opening. For this to occur, an optical or visual and working space must be created. This is achieved by distending the abdomen with carbon dioxide gas instilled into the peritoneal cavity. This procedure is called insufflation. To initiate insufflation, one of three techniques is used. One uses a Veress needle (Figure 8.10) placed through the abdominal wall of the undistended abdomen to access the peritoneal cavity (Figure 8.20). A Veress needle is a spe - cially designed large bore needle with a spring-loaded blunt obturator (Figure 8.10). When the needle is pushed against the resistance of the abdominal wall, the obturator is forced back into the needle lumen exposing the sharp needle tip allowing penetration of the abdominal wall (Figure 8.10). When the abdominal wall has been pene - trated placing the tip of the needle in the peritoneal space, decreased resistance allows the blunt obturator to protrude converting the sharp needle to a blunt cannula (Figure 8.10). An insufflator (Figure 8.9) is attached to the Veress needle with sterile flexible tubing (Figure 8.11) and the abdomen Figure 8.19 Curved CLICKline instruments for use with SILS ports. Once insufflation pressure has reached 15 cm of water, the telescope trocar- cannula is inserted through the abdominal wall (Figure 8.21). The Veress needle is placed either at the site for initial trocar-cannula placement or at a separate site depending on surgeon’s preference. If the Veress needle is placed at the initial portal placement site, it is removed prior to trocar-cannula insertion. If the Veress needle is placed at another location, it can be left in place until the initial portal is established, it can be removed prior to tro - car-cannula placement, or it can be left in place and used for maintenance of insufflation. The Veress needle technique works well and is relatively safe. However, if the needle is placed over a solid organ such as the spleen or liver, the obturator will not deploy properly leaving the sharp tip of the needle exposed and organ damage occurs. Hollow viscus penetration is also possible with this technique. If not recognized prior to ini- tiation of gas flow, the carbon dioxide will infuse the solid organ or hollow viscus and potentially the blood vessels. Carbon dioxide is used because it is absorbed rapidly from the vascular system reducing the risk of detrimental or fatal embolism. A safety step with the Veress needle technique is to per - form the “hanging drop” test after needle placement. To perform this test, the stopcock on the Veress needle is closed (Figure 8.22) and a drop of saline is placed in the hub of the needle (Figure 8.23). The stopcock is opened Figure 8.22 The Veress needle is inserted until the tip of the needle is in the peritoneal space with the stop cock in the closed position. Figure 8.23 The “hanging drop” test for proper Veress needle position in the peritoneal space is performed by placing a drop of saline in the hub of the Veress needle with the stopcock valve closed.

8.4 Laparoscopy Technii ue 401 and if the tip of the needle is properly positioned in the peritoneal space, the saline drop will disappear into the needle (Figure 8.24). If the tip of the needle is in a solid organ, or if it is still within the abdominal wall, the saline drop will not move but will remain visible in the hub of the needle (Figure 8.25). This test is not effective when a hol- low viscus has been penetrated. Another commonly used technique for abdominal access to initiate insufflation places a trocar-cannula into the empty abdomen prior to insufflation and then the abdomen is distended. This is called the Hassan tech - nique and is widely used in human laparoscopy to mini - mize the risk for organ damage that can occur with the Veress needle technique. To perform the Hassan tech - nique, a mini-laparotomy incision is made in the linea alba at the umbilicus or slightly caudal to the umbilicus. The length of the incision is an appropriate size for the telescope trocar-cannula that will be used. A skin and subcutaneous incision is made that is slightly larger than the trocar-cannula that will be placed. This incision is deepened to expose the linea alba. In thin dogs and cats, nothing further needs to be done prior to incising the linea alba but with fat patients, removing fat will facilitate locating the linea alba. This is done by elevating fat in the incision and amputating the elevated fat with scissors. Once the linea alba is adequately exposed, an incision is made through the linea alba that is long enough to allow passage of the size trocar-cannula that will be used but will also provide an airtight seal around the cannula. The incision is carefully deepened until the linea alba is pen - etrated. Penetration is determined by visualization of fat in the incision, a change in color of tissue is noted, or the deep edges of the incision start to separate. When the linea alba has been penetrated, a suture is placed in one side of the incision including the full thickness of the abdominal wall. The suture is placed as would be done for abdominal wall closure using the size and type of suture that would be appropriate for abdominal closure in a patient of the same weight. Both ends of this suture are grasped by an assistant and traction applied to elevate that side of the linea alba incision. A suture bite is then placed through the second side of the incision and the loose suture between the bites is not tightened but is kept as a free loop (Figure 8.26). The assistant now grasps both arms of the suture on the second side of the linea alba inci- sion. Traction on the suture on both sides of the incision is used to elevate the linea alba away from the underlying tis - sue. The telescope trocar-cannula with a blunt obturator is placed through the mini-laparotomy incision, the obtura- tor is removed, insufflation tubing is connected to the Luer connector on the cannula, and insufflation is initiated. 8 Laparoscopy 402 This technique is safer than the Veress needle technique but is not totally free of risk. Too long an incision will allow leakage of carbon dioxide which at a minimum will waste gas but can also interfere with maintaining adequate insufflation. The suture used for trac - tion is left in place during the procedure. When the procedure is completed, the cannula is removed, traction is applied to both free ends of the suture, the loop is pulled tight, and the suture tied to close the portal. This single suture will effec - tively close 6 mm cannula incisions but may need to be converted to a cruciate suture for 11 mm cannula incisions. A third technique uses a Ternamian EndoTIP cannula (Figure 2.39) with the telescope in the cannula at the time of initial insertion (Anderson and Fransson 2019). A depth of insertion attachment is placed on the telescope to con- trol the position of the telescope in the cannula allowing visualization of abdominal wall tissue as the cannula is screwed into the peritoneal cavity. Penetration of tissue is observed during the insertion process until fat or abdomi- nal organ tissue is seen indicating entry into the peritoneal cavity and insufflation is initiated. All three techniques take about the same amount of time to produce full insufflation. Placement of a trocar-cannula for the Hassan technique takes more time than Veress nee - dle placement but CO 2 flow rate is greater through a large telescope cannula than can be achieved through the smaller Veress needle. Gas flow through 6 mm or 11 mm diameter laparoscopy cannula is only limited by flow rate setting of the insufflator being used. Flow rate of gas through the smaller Veress needle at the 15 cm water pres - sure setting on the insufflator typically does not exceed about one liter per minute. The Veress needle is placed quickly and then there is a waiting period while the abdo - men slowly fills with gas. Hassan trocar-cannula place - ment and Ternamian EndoTIP techniques are time consuming but the abdomen insufflates very quickly. The total times from start to full insufflation are very similar. We in veterinary medicine live in a charmed world. Penetration of the spleen with the Veress needle or even with a laparoscopy trocar-cannula has little consequence in dogs or cats. Bleeding will occur with injury to the spleen, but it will consistently stop without intervention. In over 35 years of performing laparoscopy in practice and teaching laparoscopy in courses and practices, the spleen has been damaged multiple times but intervention has never been required. This was true even when an 11 mm diameter trocar-cannula was passed completely through the spleen. In human medicine, even minor damage to the spleen with a Veress needle requires splenectomy with resultant legal intervention. The lack of consequence in our patients does not mean that we do not do everything we can to avoid splenic trauma or that we ignore bleeding when it does occur. What it does mean is that it is not necessary to panic and convert. The most significant disad- vantage of splenic injury is that bleeding interferes with the visual field increasing difficulty of the procedure. It is also always very important to confirm that bleeding is not excessive, and that active bleeding has stopped before exit - ing the abdomen at the end of the procedure. If either of these problems are confirmed, intervention is indicated either by applying a hemostatic agent to the injury or by conversion to suture the injury or perform splenectomy. With advanced skills, the laceration can be sutured with intracorporeal technique if needed. Another insufflation error occurs when the Veress nee - dle or Hassan trocar-cannula does not fully penetrate the abdominal wall. This is a common mistake for beginners becoming less common with experience. When a needle or cannula is properly placed and insufflation is initiated, the flow rate will quickly increase to the insufflator setting or the Veress needle limiting flow and the pressure will be low (Figure 8.27). If the needle or cannula is not properly placed, the pressure will immediately go up to, or close to, the insufflator pressure setting of 15 cm of water and flow will be low or zero (Figure 8.28). If this incorrect pressure- flow pattern is seen, insufflation is discontinued and trou- bleshooting is initiated to determine the cause of flow occlusion. The first step in trouble shooting is to make sure the stopcock valve on the needle or cannula is in the open position. If this pressure flow error occurs and the stopcock valve is open, insufflation is discontinued, the needle or cannula is repositioned, and insufflation is initiated again. Proper Veress needle or trocar-cannula placement is also monitored by observation and percussion of the abdomen during insufflation. There should be evenly distributed dis - tension of the abdomen visually and symmetrical tympani on percussion. Asymmetry detected by either technique indicates a problem and insufflation discontinued until the problem is determined and corrected. The first trocar-cannula placed with either the Hassan technique or the Veress needle technique is the telescope cannula. Operating cannulas are then placed sequentially based on the procedure being performed and using visual guidance with the telescope to determine optimum portal location. The telescope cannula size is based on the size of the telescope that will be used. If 5 mm instruments are being used exclusively for the procedure, then one or more 6 mm diameter operative cannulas are placed. If there is a need for larger instruments at any phase of the procedure, then 11 mm diameter cannulas are place where needed. A reducer is available that creates an airtight seal for 5 mm instruments passed through 11 mm cannulas and for 3 mm instruments passed through 6 mm cannulas. Diagnostic or surgical procedures are performed with single-port, two- port, and three- or more operative ports. This is dependent on the procedure being performed and the preference of the operator. Portal locations are relatively standard for many common surgical procedures and their specific locations will be dis - cussed with each surgical procedure. The basic principles of portal location are discussed in terms of a baseball diamond with the telescope at home plate, the lesion or area of operation at second base, and operative portals placed at first and third bases. Portal placement is also discussed in terms of “triangulation” where the telescope portal and two opera - tive portals form a triangle with the telescope at the apex of the triangle and the operative portals at the ends of the base of the triangle. The distance between the portals and angles of instruments relative to the telescope and lesion varies widely based on patient size and the procedure being per - formed. Important factors in determining portal sites relate to positioning portals to provide optimum function without instruments interfering with the telescope or each other. The condition where instrument portals are too close to each other or to the telescope is termed “sword fighting” and greatly increases the difficulty of operative procedures. An ideal angle for instrument intersection at the operative site is 45° with an acceptable range of 30° to 60°. At angles less than 30°, the incidence of sword fighting increases and at angles approaching 90°, instrument interaction is less pro - ductive. Angles greater than 90° with instruments pointed back toward the telescope greatly increases the difficulty of eye–hand coordination and instrument movement. Another critical factor in operative room setup and por - tal placement is to arrange the telescope portal, patient, and monitor so that the telescope is pointed directly at the monitor (Figure 8.29). This alignment greatly facilitates eye–hand coordination especially for the beginner but also for the experienced surgeon when performing complex procedures. For many procedures, even those as simple as ovariectomies, having two monitors in the operating room can make the logistics of minimally invasive surgery far easier. Once the abdomen is insufflated and the telescope is in place, operative portal site position is selected. Initial site location is determined by transillumination of the abdomi- nal wall with the telescope light (Figure 8.30). Portal posi- tion is fine-tuned by observation with the telescope while applying finger pressure to depress the abdominal wall at the portal site and visualize abdominal wall displacement (Figure 8.31). This point of finger pressure is moved until the optimum portal site is determined. It is difficult to achieve optimum portal placement by simply looking at the abdominal wall from the outside. This technique takes very little time and reduces frustration caused by improp - erly located portals. Once a portal site is selected, a skin incision is made that is large enough to allow passage of the trocar-cannula size that will be used for this operative portal. Trocar-cannulas with a sharp trocar are designed to be pushed through the abdominal fascia, muscles, and peritoneum but this takes considerable force (Video 8.4) for larger, 11 mm diameter, sizes and is difficult for beginners. To ease this step, an appropriately sized stab incision is made completely through the abdominal wall with a scalpel blade (Figure 8.32). The size blade used depends on the size cannula that will be placed. Unfortunately, a #10 blade makes an incision that is slightly too big to provide an airtight seal with 6 mm trocar- cannulas and a smaller size needs to be used, either a #15 or #11 blade. A #10 blade works well for placing 11 mm trocar- cannulas. This incision also makes placing EndoTIP cannu - las much easier. With smooth cannulas, using either a sharp trocar or a blunt obturator, the selected insert is placed into the cannula and the outside end of the trocar-cannula unit is grasped with the trocar in the center of the palm of the hand and the digits parallel to the cannula shaft (Figure 8.33). This position holds the movable trocar in the cannula with its tip protruding and occludes the hollow center of the trocar. This hand position prevents the tip of the trocar from slid- ing back into the cannula, prevents loss of insufflation gas during placement, and allows controlled pressure to be applied to the trocar-cannula. The tip of the cannula is placed into the incision perpendicular to the abdominal wall and while observing with the telescope, the trocar is positioned so that the tip is visible through the peritoneal incision (Figure 8.34). Pressure is then applied to push the cannula into the abdomen using oscillating rotation and gradually increasing pressure until the cannula is fully through the abdominal wall (Figure 8.35). The ends of smooth cannulas are beveled, and it is impor - tant to continue the insertion process without changing hand position until the short side of the bevel is completely through the peritoneum (Figure 8.35). The trocar is then removed quickly to prevent loss of insufflation gas and the portal is ready for use (Figure 8.36). Placement of EndoTIP cannulas is done differently than smooth cannulas as they do not have a removable trocar and these cannulas are screwed through the abdominal wall. A stab incision is made in the same manner as for placement of smooth trocar-cannulas and with the same incision-cannula size considerations. Having a skin inci- sion that is larger than the cannula and larger than the abdominal wall incision is important to prevent wrapping the skin around the cannula during its rotation for inser - tion. The cannula is grasped with similar hand position as is used for smooth cannula placement but for different rea- sons. There is no trocar to hold in place and there is not a gas leakage problem, but application of continuous Figure 8.33 Proper hand position for holding a laparoscopy trocar-cannula for insertion through the abdominal wall. This position keeps the trocar properly seated in the cannula when pressure is placed against the abdominal wall and also occludes the hollow trocar to prevent loss of insufflation gas. 8 Laparoscopy 406 pressure is required while the cannula is rotated. If inward pressure is released with hand repositioning during inser - tion, the cannula loses its position and does not smoothly penetrate the abdominal wall. Continuous pressure must be applied during rotation for the cannula to be inserted properly. The leading edge of the tip of the EndoTIP can- nula is observed with the telescope while it rotates through the abdominal wall and when the peritoneum is approached, this leading edge is positioned into the perito - neal incision (Figure 8.37) (Video 8.5). Rotation is contin- ued until the cannula tip is completely through the abdominal wall and an adequate cannula length is visible within the abdomen (Figure 8.38). Once the telescope and all operative cannulas are placed, the procedure is started. If patient rotation or tilting is needed, it is done at this time after all cannulas are in posi - tion. Instruments selected for the procedure are passed through the cannulas one at a time. Each instrument is observed with the telescope as it enters the abdomen and followed visually until it is in position at the operative site. This is very important. Blind passage of instruments is extremely dangerous and significant or fatal organ damage can occur. Always observe the instrument tip from the time it appears in the tip of the cannula until it is in position where it will be used for the procedure. This is a difficult step to follow because the interest is at the operative site and passing an additional instrument without observing its tip is easy to forget. For many procedures the first instrument is used to grasp tissue and this process is completed prior to inserting a second instrument. The grasper is then held sta - ble by an assistant and placement of the next instrument is observed. Backing the telescope away from the operative site giving a panoramic view of the abdomen will allow place - ment of a second instrument without losing sight of the tip of the first instrument. When both instruments are inserted, the telescope is advanced to the operative site to enhance and focus the visual field. The closer the telescope is to the operative field the greater the magnification, the better the lighting, and depth of field orientation is improved. A critical factor making minimally invasive surgery eas - ier, or more difficult, is camera orientation to keep the image upright on the monitor. Cameras have an orientation indicator that is used to keep the camera in the upright posi - tion. Most have control buttons on the camera head and the buttons are on the top of the camera so if the buttons are kept on top, the image will be upright. It is very easy to lose this orientation thereby rotating the image on the monitor. The further the image is from upright, the more difficult eye–hand coordination becomes and the more difficult sur - gical procedures are. When an assistant is positioning the camera, it is very important that they focus on this position - ing. For the beginning minimally invasive surgeon or when there is a new camera operator, it is very helpful to have an additional observer watching camera position. This observer does not have to be scrubbed in with the surgical team but can be a circulating nurse or anesthetist. An insufflation pressure of 15 cm of water is used for initi - ating laparoscopy as trocar-cannula placement is facilitated with a tightly distended abdominal wall. Once all portals are placed, pressure can be reduced to a range of 10 cm of water to decrease the effects of insufflation on cardiopulmonary function. For short procedures in young healthy patients, this may not be necessary but for long procedures and espe - cially in compromised patients, this pressure reduction is indicated. At no time are pressures greater than 15 cm of water used for insufflation. Currently available insufflators have adjustable pressure settings that allow easily changed pressure settings. 8.4 Laparoscopy Techniiue 407 but as with any equipment they can fail, so attention is given to monitoring abdominal distension and cardiopulmonary function. Carbon dioxide is the standard gas used for abdom- inal insufflation. CO 2 is an inert gas that will not combust or explode. This property is critical for use in the presence of radio-frequency devices and also for general operative room safety. The other important property of carbon dioxide is that it is rapidly absorbed from the blood stream greatly reducing the risk of gaseous embolism in the presence of a pressurized abdomen. Gas embolism can also be produced by solid organ penetration with a needle or cannula causing direct infusion of gas into the organ with subsequent vascu- lar insufflation. Carbon dioxide does interact with the body forming carbolic acid when in contact with the peritoneal surface or when absorbed through the peritoneal surface. The resulting acid is irritating to the peritoneal surface caus - ing inflammation and pain. Acid formed in the tissues also pushes the body toward acidosis. These effects of CO 2 on the body are typically mild but must be taken into consideration especially in the compromised patient. Nitrous oxide is another gas used for abdominal insuffla- tion that was very popular in the beginning of laparoscopic applications. Nitrous oxide was a popular anesthetic gas used for its analgesic properties as an adjunct to other injectable and inhalation anesthetics. With the introduc- tion of anesthetics with improved analgesia and anesthetic properties, its use has disappeared. One of the advantages of nitrous oxide for abdominal insufflation was that it was already available in many small animal practices. Initial applications in small animal practice did not use an insuf- flator but ran the nitrous oxide through the flow meter of an anesthesia machine. This was a very primitive tech- nique but was adequate for most of the simple short diag - nostic procedures performed at the time. Liver biopsies are a good example of when this protocol was used. A Veress needle was placed, the abdomen insufflated with nitrous oxide until the abdomen was adequately distended based on observation and abdominal wall palpation, nitrous oxide flow was stopped, portals were placed, insufflation was added if needed, and biopsies taken. The extent of abdominal distension was observed and was the focus of interest whenever nitrous oxide flow was turned on. Nitrous oxide flow was discontinued whenever the focus was elsewhere as during portal placement or biopsy collec- tion. This seat of the pants approach was discontinued and is no longer recommended. The other issue with nitrous oxide is that if mixed with methane, it becomes an explo - sive mixture. Large bowel perforation is rare but with com- mon use of radio-frequency devices in minimally invasive surgery, nitrous oxide use presents too great a risk. When laparoscopic procedures are completed, the abdo - men is examined for any residual bleeding or depending on the procedure for any other concerns. When this has been completed, instrumentation is removed, insufflation is discontinued, and one or more cannula valves are removed to allow complete decompression of the abdomen. The more CO 2 that is removed the less possible postoperative discomfort there is for the patient. Cannulas are removed one at a time especially if portals are placed off the midline. Tissue plane shifting at the portal sites is least immediately after cannula removal. If all cannulas are removed at once, closure of the last portal may be more difficult than needed. This is not as important for portals on the midline. The preplaced traction suture at the telescope portal, if the Hassan technique was used, is used for closure of this inci- sion by applying traction to both ends of the suture to pull the free loop into the deep side of the incision. The suture is tied, and this achieves closure of the linea alba for 6 mm diameter or smaller cannulas. For 11 mm or larger cannulas, an addi- tional suture may be needed or the initial suture is converted into a cruciate suture. The linea alba or muscular layer of portals off the midline are closed with a single suture or mul- tiple simple interrupted sutures, a cruciate suture, or other suture patterns as needed based on portal size. Subcutaneous and dermal layers are closed with a single suture or multiple sutures as indicated. Skin sutures are only placed if needed when appropriate closure is not achieved with buried sutures. 8.4.2 Laparoscopic-Assisted T echnique Laparoscopic-assisted surgery combines the benefits of mini- mally invasive surgery and traditional open surgery. Laparoscopy is used to identify the involved organ or tissue, grasp the structure, and elevate it to the abdominal wall. The operative portal is then enlarged to allow exteriorization of the surgery site. Insufflation is discontinued during this phase of the procedure and restarted at a later time if indi- cated. Standard open surgery is then used to perform proce - dures on the exteriorized tissue. Exteriorization may involve removing all of the involved structure from the abdomen or a small area of the wall of a hollow viscus. This approach com- bines the benefits of minimally invasive technique with those of traditional open surgery skills. Procedures that are techni- cally difficult, time consuming, and instrumentation inten- sive to perform totally with minimally invasive surgery are made easier, faster, and possible with traditional open surgery instruments that are already available in the practice. 8.4.3 Anesthesia for Laparoscopy There is a saying that “minimally invasive surgery has max - imum anesthetic consequences.” This is true. Abdominal insufflation interferes with ventilation and venous return causing a long list of cardiopulmonary changes (Table 8.20)

8 Laparoscopy 408 that are all bad (Baratz and Karis 1969; Beazley et al. 2011; Bufalari et al. 1997; Ciofolo et al. 1990; Duke et al. 1996; Gross et al. 1993; Ivankovich et al. 1975; Mama and de Rezende 2015; Shih et al. 2015). Patient’s position especially at an angle with the head down exacerbates these changes. The “Rule of 15” applied to minimally invasive surgery dic - tates that the body is never placed at more than a 15° head down position and abdominal insufflation pressure is never allowed to exceed 15 cm of water pressure. When this rule is followed and with appropriate patient monitoring and sup - portive treatment, minimally invasive abdominal surgery is a safe effective technique. Anesthesia protocols for laparoscopic surgery are the same as for open abdominal surgery and are based more on the patient than the procedure. All phases of patient man- agement from admission to discharge are focused on patient needs rather than whether an abdominal proce - dure will be performed with an open abdominal incision or minimally invasive technique. A patient properly prepared for open surgery will, with few exceptions, tolerate abdom- inal insufflation for minimally invasive surgery. The need of intermittent positive pressure ventilation may be an exception to this statement because of the adverse effects of insufflation on the patient’s ability to maintain itself with spontaneous ventilation. Short procedures in healthy patients may be performed without assisted ventilation but if there is any doubt about the patient’s ability to safely tol- erate abdominal insufflation, then intermittent positive pressure ventilation is indicated. If the thought occurs questioning the need for a ventilator, then use a ventilator. Pain is less with minimally invasive surgery and there - fore less pain medication may be needed. “May” is the operative message and again patient management takes precedence over the procedure being performed. 8.5 Normal Laparoscopic Anatomy A wide spectrum of structures and organs are visible with laparoscopy and all look the same as they do with an open abdomen except for magnification and limited or no distor - tion due to the surgical approach. Gravity is the most com- mon and most effective method for retraction of tissues causing normal shifting of structures as would occur with positioning of an awake animal (Video 8.6). 8.5.1 The Abdominal Wall, Diaphragm, and Falciform Ligament The abdominal wall is visible wherever the telescope is pointed. The ovary is not usually seen directly as it is enclosed in the mesosalpinx which is identified to locate the ovary. The suspensory ligament, proper ligament, and cranial end of the uterine horn are also used to locate the ovary. On the left side, the ovary is positioned in close prox - imity to the caudal pole of the left kidney (Figure 8.105) whereas on the right side, it is found isolated in the right lumbar gutter in a position more lateral or craniolateral to the right kidney (Figure 8.106). With estrus, vascular sup - ply to the ovary becomes more prominent and easier to identify (Figure 8.107). Older dogs develop more fat around the ovary also facilitating identification (Figure 8.108). If there is any doubt about the possibility of any other abdominal pathology, then a full exploration is performed. Use of a powered tilting operating table greatly facilitates abdominal exploration. 8.6.1 Abdominal Wall Abnormalities Few abdominal wall abnormalities are diagnosed with lap - aroscopy but when present are easily seen. Trauma to the abdominal wall in acute injuries is visible as bruising or hemorrhage (Figure 8.124) and as chronic incidental find- ings (Figures 8.125 and 8.126) or as adhesions to the abdominal wall (Figure 8.127). Iatrogenic abdominal wall injuries are also seen from needles passed through the abdominal wall (Figure 8.128), adhesions to previous sur - gical incisions (Figure 8.129), and scar tissue from previous laparoscopy portals (Figure 8.130). Adhesions of abdomi- nal organs to the abdominal wall are uncommon but do occur (Figure 8.131) and separation of these adhesions leaves a lesion on the abdominal wall (Figure 8.132). Additional adhesions in this patient were seen attached to the ventral midline from a recent open surgical exploration (Figure 8.133). Extensive adhesions may interfere with laparoscopy or make laparoscopy impossible or contraindi- cated. Adhesions like the ones seen in Figures 8.127, 8.129, 8.131, and 8.133 are divided with blunt dissection when adhesions are recent (Figures 8.131 and 8.132), with sharp dissection (Figure 8.134), sharp dissection with monopolar cautery or bipolar cautery, or with a vessel sealing device (Figure 8.135). The most significant inguinal ring abnormalities are inguinal hernias (Figure 8.136). 8.6 Laparoscopic AAbominal AAnormalities 437 Fibrosis or cirrhosis of the liver develops with chronic pro - gressive liver diseases. Non-bridging fibrosis is seen early in chronic liver disease and has been mentioned in the descrip - tion of Figure 8.166. Fibrosis becomes significant when it becomes bridging and with sufficient quantity to interfere with liver structure and function. Fibrosis on the surface of the liver (Figure 8.173) may be related to hepatic disease or to other peritoneal processes. Focal areas of fibrous tissue are visible in diseased livers that may or may not be related to the liver disease and may or may not be indicative of sig - nificant liver disease (Figures 8.174 and 8.175). In human medicine, there are four defined stages of liver fibrosis based on hepatitis C termed the META VIR score: stage 0: no fibrosis; stage 1: mild fibrosis without walls of scarring; stage 2: mild-to-moderate fibrosis with walls of scarring; stage 3: bridging fibrosis or scarring that has spread to different parts of the liver but no cirrhosis; and stage 4: severe scarring or cirrhosis (De Groote et al. 1968). In this staging, cirrhosis is not a diagnosis until there is severe bridging fibrosis. Cirrhosis has been divided into compensated and non-compensated or liver failure. Some of these cases have been diagnosed with preoperative imaging, such as gall stones, and others are not diagnosed until after lapa - roscopic cholecystectomy or when transabdominal chole - cystoscopy and choledochoscopy are performed. Laparoscopic examination of adrenal masses is primarily to assess resectability with minimally invasive surgery, if an open surgical approach is indicated, or if resection is not indicated with either technique. Occasionally laparoscopy is employed for adrenal gland biopsy, but this indication is uncommon, and adrenalec- tomy is typically performed when adrenal masses or adre - nal enlargement is documented with preoperative imaging. Tumor type is not as important a factor as is tumor size, location, or vascular invasion. Resectability of adrenal glands and adrenal masses is determined by size, location, and the presence or absence of vascular invasion. Minimally invasive resection is preferred for small adrenal masses, up to about 2 cm in diameter, that do not have vascular inva- sion. The maximum resectable size of adrenal masses is changing as we have more experience. Resectability of adrenal masses is also greatly dependent on the minimally invasive surgery skills of the operator. Both adrenal glands are easily visible with laparoscopy either with the patient in lateral recumbency using a lateral telescope portal or from dorsal recumbency using an umbili - cal telescope portal and sufficient obliquity to expose the adrenal glands. Diseased adrenal glands are typically more easily seen than normal adrenal glands (Figures 8.117– 8.119) that can be obscured by fat. Occasional adrenal atro - phy or hypoplasia are present making the adrenal glands more difficult to see but the majority of adrenal pathology causes enlargement by hyperplasia (Figures 8.262 and 8.263) or neoplasia (Figures 8.264 and 8.265). Laparoscopic adre - nalectomy is successfully performed in many cases with smaller noninvasive lesions (Figures 8.262, 8.263, and 8.265) with larger masses (Figure 8.266) and invasive tumors (Figure 8.264) requiring conversion to an open surgery. 8.6.12 Bladder and Ureteral Abnormalities Abnormalities of the bladder visible from its outside surface are presented in this section and those visible from the inside with transurethral cystoscopy or laparoscopic-assisted cys - toscopy are presented in Chapter 6. CT is another potential diagnostic modality for documenting the presence of an ovarian remnant but again cannot definitively rule out this diagnosis. Laparoscopy is the best way to diagnose or rule out ovarian remnants and also allows removal of the ovarian tissue at the same procedure. Examination of the ovarian pedicle sites is conducted with the same setup, patient position, and portal placement as for performing a laparoscopic ovariectomy using a two or pref - erably three-port technique. Right-side ovarian remnants are far more common than left-side lesions. Both ovarian pedicle sites are examined and with magnification produced by the telescope video camera system, small amounts of ovarian tissue that would be missed with open surgery are easily found (Figure 8.294). The small size of this ovarian remnant would make it easy to miss with an open surgical approach. Exploration for ovarian remnants with open sur - gery requires a full-length ventral midline abdominal inci - sion from xiphoid to pubis. Any incision shorter than that is a recipe for failure unless laparoscopy is used. Is it neoplasia? If it is neo - plasia, what kind of cancer is present? If it is not neoplasia, what is the diagnosis? Is it operable with minimally invasive technique? If it is not operable with MIS, is it operable with open surgery? Is it inoperable? Laparoscopy is the ideal approach when the answers are not available with a less invasive technique. This is especially true in older medically compromised patients. Finding inoperable cancer with an open surgical exploration is excessively traumatic, unneces - sarily painful with greater morbidity, and longer recovery than when a minimally invasive approach is used. Any time an open exploratory lap - arotomy is being planned, a minimally invasive approach also needs to be considered. With experience, laparoscopic exploration is as thorough as an open surgical approach. The only way one becomes experienced is to perform cases with minimally invasive technique. It is agreed that some cases will obviously not be candidates for a minimally inva - sive procedure and the procedure will be started as an open surgery. In other patients, a minimally invasive approach will obviously be the procedure of choice and will be per - formed successfully without conversion. In other cases, it cannot be determined prior to surgery which approach is indicated. If there is any suggestion that the procedure can be performed with laparoscopy, then that is the procedure of choice. Some of these cases will be completed with the minimally invasive approach and others will need conver - sion to an open surgery. When laparoscopy is elected, it may become apparent immediately that the procedure can be performed with MIS or conversion is indicated because the procedure exceeds the surgeon’s current skill level for MIS or completion with MIS is not possible. The only way one’s skill level will advance is to perform MIS whenever the chance occurs. This approach will greatly increase the num - ber of minimally invasive abdominal surgeries that are per - formed, and each case will increase the surgeon’s skill level. There are a large number of cases that have been performed by the author where the chance of completing the proce - dure with minimally invasive technique was unknown prior to surgery. The option of a minimally invasive approach was discussed with the client with the under - standing that if the procedure could not be completed with MIS that conversion to an open surgery would be done. And that the cost would be the same no matter how the case was completed. Clients eagerly accepted this approach. 8.7 .2 Liver Biopsy One of the most common laparoscopic diagnostic procedures is obtaining liver biopsies (Eulenberg and Lidbury 2018; Lidbury 2017; Poldervaart et al. 2009; Rothuizen and Twedt 2009; Wang et al. 2004). This is a relatively simple procedure that can be easily performed by anyone who has the skills to establish an insufflated abdomen. Laparoscopic liver biopsies are also a very quick procedure that obtains suf - ficient sample quality and quantity to establish an accurate diagnosis in a very high percentage of cases (Wang et al. 2004). Sample size is also adequate for establishing quantitative copper levels (Poldervaart et al. 2009). Laparoscopy allows visual inspection of the liver providing accurate selection of biopsy sites to include representative pathology. Exploration of the remainder of the abdomen is also included when indi - cated to rule out any other pathology. Laparoscopic liver biopsies are a very safe procedure with few problems or com - plications. Laparoscopy is superior to other techniques for obtaining liver biopsies (Wang et al. 2004). The most significant deterrent to laparoscopic liver biop - sies is the fear of bleeding from biopsy sites. This is an unnecessary fear because LIVER BIOPSIES DO NOT BLEED. In over 35 years of performing laparoscopy and obtaining hundreds of liver biopsies, a significant bleeding episode has not occurred. Biopsy of liver tumors is differ - ent, and the only exception was a biopsy taken from a large neoplastic liver tumor. All biopsies of liver tissue have had minimal blood loss with insufficient bleeding to require any intervention. This is even true in patients with coagu- lopathies. Remembering that the image of the biopsy site is magnified with the telescope and camera system blood loss appears more significant than it is ranging from minimal (Figure 8.327), to minor (Figure 8.328), and moderate but not significant (Figures 8.329 and 8.330). Biopsy of liver tumors rarely produce significant bleeding although more bleeding is typically seen (Figure 8.325) than from biopsy of non-neoplastic liver lesions and bleeding typically stops spontaneously from these liver tumor biopsy sites (Figure 8.326). Biopsy of liver tumors can rarely cause Figure 8.327 A laparoscopic liver biopsy site performed with a 5 mm diameter opposing cup biopsy forceps showing a minimal amount of bleeding. This was as small but otherwise normal- appearing liver with the biopsy revealing microvascular dysplasia.

8 Laparoscopy 470 sufficient bleeding to require intervention. It would be difficult to collect a measurable amount of blood from most liver biopsy sites. Laparoscopy is the procedure of choice for obtaining liver biopsies in patients with advanced liver disease and with coagulopathies. Ascites, hypoproteinemia, and coagu- lopathies secondary to liver disease or from unrelated pathology compromise the ability of patients to undergo open abdominal surgery making the minimally invasive nature of laparoscopy advantageous. Less blood loss will occur from all steps of a laparoscopic procedure than from the skin incision for an open surgical procedure. An added advantage of laparoscopy is that any bleeding that does occur from the liver biopsy sites can be monitored until all bleeding has stopped. If for some reason bleeding does not stop, appropriate measures are taken using laparoscopic techniques for hemostasis. Dorsal recumbency is most commonly used for obtain- ing liver biopsies. This position allows examination of all liver lobes, the gall bladder, and extrahepatic bile ducts. There is also more flexibility for exploration of the remain- ing abdomen using the ventral approach. The monitor is placed at the head of the patient with the surgeon and assistant standing on opposite sides of the patient (Figure 8.331). An umbilical or subumbilical telescope por - tal is placed with either the Hasson or Veress needle tech- nique. When the abdomen is insufflated, the liver is examined and a quick 360° tour of the abdomen is per - formed. If no other pathology is found, a site is selected for an operative portal and a second cannula is placed. Operative portal sites are usually in the cranial abdomen over the liver on the midline or paramedian on either side (Figure 8.331). The site is selected based on the findings in the individual patient, operator preference, or operating room arrangement. The position of the monitors in the operating room at the facility where the author has per - formed many of these procedures makes a left cranial para- median operative portal work better than other sites. This portal site is consistently used effectively with access to all liver lobes and without the need to place an additional por - tal in any case. If another portal site is preferable for any reason, then the preferred site is used. If other procedures are to be performed at the same time as the liver biopsies, the portals used for the other procedures are used for the liver biopsies. A multiport technique as just described is the preferred procedure for obtaining liver biopsies with laparoscopy as there is more flexibility for exploration and liver manipula- tion using triangulation of the operative instrument. A single-port technique using an operating laparoscope is also used with the advantage of only having to place one portal at the umbilicus. This does not mean that the biopsy sites are ignored after biopsy collection has been completed. All biopsy sites are examined after the samples have been collected. When the biopsy procedure has been completed, any additional examination of the remaining abdomen is conducted. After this examination all biopsy sites are examined again. It is uncommon that any bleeding is continuing at this time. If there is any active bleeding, it will be seen at this time. If all bleeding has stopped, instrumentation is removed, the abdomen is decompressed, cannulas are removed, and portals are closed. If there is ongoing bleeding that has not stopped in a rea - sonable amount of time or does not appear to be stopping on its own, there are several options to speedup hemostasis. Pressure on the bleeding biopsy site with the palpation probe is effective similar to pressure in any other situation with bleeding. Electrocautery can be applied using any MIS instru - ment with a cautery connection. Hemostatic agents can be applied to the bleeding biopsy site and are available as sponges, powders, and gels. This tissue is commonly seen in the abdomen but may not be present after the forceps are removed from the portal cannula. In some procedures, a significant quantity of tis - sue will be found in the cannula when it is disassembled and is included in the samples that are submitted. Operating room setup, patient positioning, draping, and portal placement are the same as for the liver biopsy procedure (Figure 8.331). Under visual guidance, this is an easy, effective, and safe procedure. A 20 gauge spinal needle of sufficient length is used for this procedure and is placed directly through the abdominal wall without a portal or cannula (Figure 8.338). Samples are also obtained using an injection cannula or needle. This injection needle has a 5 mm shaft diameter and is 36 cm long with a Luer-lock connection on the out - side end and a 22, 20, or 16 gauge hypodermic needle on the tip end. The lumen throughout its length matches the inside of the needle gauge. This instrument is passed through a 5 mm portal cannula and can be used to aspirate fluid from the gall bladder or bile ducts. Cholecystocentesis is most commonly performed for diagnostic procedures but emptying the gall bladder with this technique may be indi- cated in some cases (Figure 8.339). 8.7 .4 Pancreatic Biopsy Laparoscopic biopsy of the pancreas is a proven technique with minimal postoperative morbidity (Webb and Trott 2008). Pancreatic manipulation causing pancreatitis has been a major concern with open surgery, but this does not appear to be true with laparoscopy (Twedt 1999). Pancreatitis secondary to laparoscopic biopsies did not occur in a study in normal dogs (Harmoinen et al. 2002). The possible reason for decreased morbidity following lap - aroscopic pancreatic biopsy may be decreased tissue manipulation by taking biopsies with biopsy forceps with- out tissue manipulation or suture closure of the biopsy sites and may not be related directly to the minimally inva- sive approach. Open surgical biopsy of the pancreas, whether with the blunt dissection technique or the suture fracture technique requires significant tissue manipula- tion, and this is more likely the cause of postoperative pan- creatitis. Pancreatic biopsies are indicated with suspected acute or chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic hypoplasia, pan- creatic atrophy, and pancreatic neoplasia. When indicated at the time of laparoscopy for diagnosis of acute pancreati- tis, a jejunostomy feeding tube is placed to aid in patient management. Patient positioning for pancreatic biopsies has tradition- ally been with the patient in left lateral recumbency using right lateral portals (Figure 8.340). This gives excellent access to the right lobe of the pancreas, the duodenum, the extrahepatic biliary system, and the right liver lobes.
