8 Laparoscopy 484 8.7 .8 Biopsy T echniques for Additional Organs and Tissues Any organ or tissue visible with laparoscopy can be biopsied using laparoscopic or laparoscopic-assisted technique. Enlarged prostates due to inflammation, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and cancerous prostatic masses are accessible for biopsy using laparoscopy. Small prostatic lesions may be difficult to visualize except in very thin patients. Even with significant prostatic enlargement, visualization may be dif - ficult in obese patients and dissection of fat away from the prostate may be indicated. The patient placed in dorsal recumbency and the patient’s caudal end elevated provides the best access to the prostate. An umbilical telescope portal with a caudal paramedian operative portal, on either side, are used. Opposing cup or punch-type biopsy forceps are adequate for prostatic biopsies and 14 gauge “core-type” biopsy needles are also used. If a biopsy needle is used, it is passed directly through the abdominal wall and not through a laparoscopy portal cannula. Adrenal gland and adrenal mass biopsies are performed with laparoscopy when indicated, although adrenalectomy is more commonly performed rather than biopsy. Adrenal biopsies commonly bleed and procedures to ensure hemo - stasis are required. Apposing cup or thru cut punch biopsy forceps are used for adrenal biopsies. Enlarged lymph nodes are easily seen and biopsied with laparoscopy but normal lymph nodes may be difficult to visualize especially in fatter patients. Abdominal masses originating from any organ or tissue are amenable to minimally invasive biopsy with the risk of hemorrhage related to the character of individual lesions. Aspiration of unexplained abdominal effusion is facili- tated with laparoscopy for diagnostic sample collection. Marked ascites may allow portal placement without insufflation and ascitic fluid may be crystal clear allowing laparoscopic examination through the fluid. Abdominal fluid clouds very quickly with biopsy of any organ or tissue. Aspiration of opaque fluid is facilitated with laparoscopic direction enabling examination of the abdomen. Peritoneal pathology is associated with undiagnosed abdominal fluid and peritoneal biopsies are easily performed with laparos - copy to frequently establish a diagnosis. 8.7 .9 Cancer Staging Laparoscopy is an effective technique for staging primary or metastatic cancers involving the abdominal cavity (Balsa and Culp 2019). Diagnosing, prognosing, and planning for cancer treatment are important applications of laparos - copy in small animal practice. The older and the more debilitated the patient the greater the advantages of lapa- roscopy. When owners need answers in the old debilitated cancer patient with abdominal involvement, there is no better approach than laparoscopy especially when the find- ings indicate a terminal situation. A minimally invasive approach provides minimal operative pain, minimal post - operative pain with reduced need for pain management, minimal operative time, minimal postoperative hospitali- zation, and minimal postoperative recovery at home. In a terminal patient with limited life expectancy, this approach decreases treatment days and increases the number of happy days at home. Preparation for exploratory laparoscopy for cancer stag - ing is extremely varied and case dependent. A defined protocol that is specifically tailored to each patient cannot be stated here as a generality. Dorsal recumbency on a table with full side-to-side and end-to-end tilt capabilities plus adequate clipping and draping for conversion to a full-length abdominal incision is suggested to allow maxi - mum flexibility once the procedure is started. An umbili - cal telescope portal is recommended as a starting point with operative portal number and location based on ini - tial exploration. The telescope is moved to one of the operative portal sites if indicated. The more preoperative diagnostic information available the easier the planning for laparoscopy. The range of procedures needed to adequately stage can- cer involving the abdomen with laparoscopy is also extremely varied and case dependent. Experience with cancer staging has ranged from a five-minute peak finding extensive carcinomatosis with an immediate exit, to thor - ough abdominal exploration with dissection to expose a hidden lymph node or lesion, or laparoscopy followed by conversion for excision surgery that is not possible with minimally invasive technique. 8.8 Minimally Invasive AAbominal Surgery 485 8.8 Minimally Invasive Abdominal Surgery Minimally invasive abdominal surgery in small animal practice is currently one of the most rapidly expanding fields in our profession. Initially, this area of practice was limited to specialty practices and academic institutions, but this has changed with addition of laparoscopic ovariec- tomy to the armamentarium of general practice. Many minimally invasive surgeries are still performed and devel- oped primarily in specialty facilities from both the private practice and public institution sectors. However, laparo - scopic ovariectomies and when indicated, laparoscopic ovariohysterectomies belong in general practice. They do not belong in specialty practice. This does not mean that they cannot be performed in specialty practices but as a routine procedure in a young normal patient, the expertise of a specialist is not needed and the added cost to the client is not warranted. The list of minimally invasive abdominal surgeries cur - rently being performed and the practices where these sur - geries are done has expanded dramatically in the last decade from occasional procedures in widely scattered facilities to everyday everywhere. 8.8.1 Laparoscopic Ovariectomy Since we started doing “spays” over 100 years ago, we have developed better anesthetics, we practice better asepsis, we have better suture materials, we perform better preanes - thetic patient evaluation, we have better monitoring proce - dures during anesthesia, we provide better supportive treatment during anesthesia, and we provide better postop - erative pain management, BUT we are still using the same barbaric tissue handling technique that James Harriot used in rural England in the 1930s. The attachment of the ovar - ian pedicle is damaged extensively with the old traumatic technique where we rip the ovarian pedicle out by the roots (Figure 8.6) and there is significant bleeding (Figure 8.7). Laparoscopic ovariectomy, or ovariohysterectomy if you insist, moves the tissue-handling technique of these surger - ies into the modern era of medicine in line with the other aspects of this surgery. No tissue is torn, and the ovarian pedicle is transected atraumatically using a vessel sealing device causing minimal tissue damage and leaving a thin line of fused tissue with no bleeding (Figure 8.8). This is the last piece of the puzzle and we now have a truly modern surgical procedure that fits with how we as a profession practice today. Multiple studies have documented that there is less pain with laparoscopic ovariectomy and ovariohyster - ectomy than there is with the same surgery performed with traditional open technique (Devitt et al. 2005; Gauthier et al. 2015; Hancock et al. 2005; Höglund et al. 2011; Lee and Kim 2014). Decreased pain associated with laparoscopic ovariec- tomy is not due to decreased abdominal wall incision size as many argue. The statement that I can do a spay with a really small incision that is not much larger than the tele - scope portal and is definitely smaller than the total incision length for the three-port technique is not addressing where the most pain is generated. Incision pain is minimal com- pared to the pain caused by tearing the ovarian pedicles out by the roots. Elimination of tissue tearing with laparo - scopic technique is where pain is decreased. One of the sig - nificant complications of traditional ovariohysterectomies especially in large dogs is hemorrhage. This is virtually eliminated with laparoscopy. Incision dehiscence is another complication with traditional ovariohysterectomy, and this is also eliminated with laparoscopy as the inci- sions are too small for dehiscence. Laparoscopic ovariectomies are easiest to perform in medium-size thin juvenile dogs and selection of these patients is recommended for learning this procedure. Once the techniques for laparoscopic ovariectomy are mastered, all size, shape, age, breed, body condition score, and repro - ductive history of dogs and cats can be sterilized laparo - scopically. There is no longer the need to fear spaying old fat dogs or dogs in heat. The author’s experience has included a size range of dogs from 1 to 100 kg, from 4 months to 14 years, body condition scores from 2 to 5 out of 5, nulliparous to multiparous, during estrus or anestrus, and a 30 day pregnant bitch. There is no patient limit for this procedure. The current standard of care is to remove the ovaries and leave the uterus in place. This technique is supported by good science (Bender 2012; De Tora and McCarthy 2011; Dunn 2012; Graves 2012; Mcanulty et al. 2012; Okkens et al. 1997; Van Goethem et al. 2006) and, except in the pres - ence of uterine disease, there is no science that supports the need to remove the uterus. Some countries in Europe have been removing the ovaries only for as long as we in the United States have been removing the uterus with the ova- ries (De Tora and McCarthy 2011; Okkens et al. 1997; Van Goethem et al. 2006). This procedure selection is based on tradition and not on science. When a discussion is started about ovariectomies vs ovariohysterectomies, the first argu- ment questions the occurrence of uterine stump pyometra as a reason for removing the uterus. This argument is not valid because uterine stump pyometra is an ovarian remnant problem, not a uterine remnant problem. The other com- mon argument is about the possible incidence of uterine tumors. I personally have seen 2 uterine tumors in 50 years. One was in a very old intact Chihuahua and the other was in

8 Laparoscopy 486 the cervix of an ovariohysterectomized female cat. Both were benign tumors. The reported incidence of uterine neo - plasia in dogs and cats is 0.03% (Brodey 1967). If we compare this incidence with the increased risk of removing the uterus, it is safer for the patient to leave the uterus in place. We have not answered the question about the amount of uterine pathology that dictates a need for ovariohysterec- tomy. This question needs an answer derived from good science. Until the time that this question is answered, the recommendation is to error on the conservative side with removal of the uterus when there is any pathology present. Age, the number of heat cycles, or the number of litters produced are not factors determining the need for removal of the uterus. An ovariectomy was performed in a 12-year- old retired breeding bitch with no adverse consequences. Multiple techniques have been used for laparoscopic ova- riectomies and ovariohysterectomies in dogs and cats. Single-port (Binder et al. 2018; Case et al. 2011; Dupré et al. 2009), two-port (Arntz 2019; Case et al. 2011; Dupré et al. 2009; Proença 2015; Gonzalez-Gasch and Monnet 2015) with the TT ovariectomy hook, two-port with suture or suture needle retraction of the ovary, two-port with the Mouret falciform retractor (the toad stabber), three-port techniques (Bakhtiari et al. 2012; Case et al. 2011; Mayhew and Brown 2007; Tapia-Araya et al. 2015), use of a SILS port (Corriveau et al. 2017; Gonzalez-Gasch and Monnet 2015; Lopez et al. 2017; Manassero et al. 2012; Runge and Mayhew 2013; Runge et al. 2012; Tapia-Araya et al. 2015), laparoscopic-assisted techniques (Corriveau et al. 2017; Gower and Mayhew 2008), and NOTES (Arntz 2019; Bakhtiari et al. 2012; Freeman et al. 2009; Linhares et al. 2019) procedures. Each of these approaches has its own set of advantages and disadvantages but all work and the one used is selected based on many factors including personal preference and if ovariectomy or ovariohysterec- tomy are being performed. Personal experience has been with single-port, two-port with TT hook, two-port with Mouret needle retractor, and three-port techniques initially for ovariohysterectomy and then changing to use this tech- nique for ovariectomies. Initially, ovariohysterectomies were performed using ligatures with extracorporeal knot techniques and with a three-port procedure. This was effec- tive but time consuming. The advent of vessel sealing devices has greatly improved this procedure reducing sur - gery time and risks. The single-port technique has the advantages of only needing one abdominal wall perforation and that instru- ments are directed in a fixed position through the telescope making alignment of instruments easier for the beginner; however, this technique has the disadvantage of not allow - ing triangulation and thus restricting tissue manipulation capabilities. Multiport techniques have the disadvantages of requiring more than one abdominal wall perforation and positioning instruments is more difficult for the begin- ner as the instruments are freely mobile in the abdomen. Advantages of multiport techniques are that triangulation of operative instruments is possible allowing improved vis - ibility and far greater tissue manipulation capabilities. The number of portals used is a matter of personal preference because they all work. Personally I prefer the three-port technique. This is, in my hands, faster than using less por - tals and provides much more flexibility in manipulating tissues. Single-port, two-port, and three-port techniques will be described. All three of these techniques place the patient in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table with a single movable monitor or ideally with two monitors placed at the ends (Figure 8.365) or sides of the patient (Figure 8.366). 8.8.1.1 Single-Port T echnique This technique requires an operating laparoscope and longer instruments than would be used for two-port or three-port technique. A single 11 mm portal is placed at or immediately caudal to the umbilicus (Figure 8.367) using the Hassan or Veress needle technique. The abdomen is insufflated to 15 cm H 2 O with CO 2 . The patient is obliqued to one side with the surgeon and assistant standing on the ventral side to remove the ovary on the contralateral side of the patient. This places the ovary to be removed on the upper side with the abdominal organs sliding ventrally out of the way. The ovary is identified visually (Figure 8.368) and the suspensory ligament or utero-ovarian (proper) ligament is grasped with Babcock forceps passed through the operating channel of the operating laparoscope (Figure 8.369). The ovary is elevated above the surrounding tissues and placed against the abdominal wall in an acces - sible location without excessive tension on the ovarian pedicle (Figure 8.370). A TT ovariectomy hook or suture is passed through the abdominal wall at the site where the ovary is placed, and this is used to fix the ovary to the abdominal wall (Figure 8.371). This hook placement site is on the lateral abdominal wall ventral to the lumbar mus - cles (Figure 8.372). The exact location for hook placement is determined by palpating the abdominal wall while visu- alizing where the wall is depressed with the telescope. The position of palpation is adjusted until it is at the site of the elevated ovary. This dorsal hook placement is the most sig - nificant disadvantage of the TT ovariectomy technique as it requires a great deal more shaving than for the other tech- niques that place portals on the ventral midline. When laparoscopic ovariectomies were first performed with the original two-port technique, the TT hook was used. This caused much complaining from nurses, owners, and veterinarians because of the amount of clipping required.

8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 487 The hook is placed on the lateral abdominal wall a signifi - cant distance away from the midline and requires clipping at least half of the circumference of the body. The techni - cians complained about how much clipping this took and the time involved. The doctors complained about how long the clipping took. The clients complained about how much of their precious pet was clipped. And everyone worried about the extra anesthesia time required. The TT ovariec - tomy hook technique is still used but there are other options. These disadvantages created pressure for a better tech- nique. The Mouret needle retractor was found to provide this better option. The Mouret retractor is a 30 cm long 2 mm diameter needle with a sharp trocar insert and a blunt obturator insert designed to retract the falciform liga- ment during laparoscopy. The advantage of this technique is that the retractor is placed on the midline eliminating the excessively wide clip needed for the TT hook technique. Use of the Mouret needle will be described here with the single-port technique but it can also be used with the two- port technique. The ovary is identified, grasped, and elevated to the abdominal wall with the same technique as for the TT ova - riectomy procedure. When the ovary is elevated and posi - tioned against the abdominal wall, a small stab skin incision is made in the ventral midline halfway between the umbili - cus and the pubis (Figure 8.373). The Mouret needle retrac - tor is inserted into the abdomen, passed across to the ovary under visual guidance, and the needle is passed through the mesovarium into the abdominal wall to fix the ovary in position (Figure 8.374) (Video 8.15). The Babcock forceps are removed leaving the ovary in place (Figure 8.375) and a vessel sealing instrument is inserted. The transected pedicle is checked for any bleeding (Figure 8.380). 8 Laparoscopy 492 8.8.1.2 T wo-Port T echniques There are three options for the two-port technique. One uses the TT ovariectomy hook, one uses the Mouret needle retractor, and one uses an intra-abdominal hanger. As usual, each has advantages and disadvantages. Use of the hook and Mouret needle retractor was presented in Section 8.8.1.1 and are employed in the exact same manner for two-port procedures (Video 8.15). The two-port technique requires a standard 5 mm or 10 mm 0° laparoscope with a cannula appropriate for the telescope used, one 6 mm or 11 mm operating cannula, and a TT hook or a Mouret retractor. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency in a side-to-side tilt table. An umbilical telescope portal is placed (Figure 8.385) using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. The operative portal is placed on the midline approximately halfway between the umbilicus and the xiphoid (Figure 8.385). Except in very small patients, an 11 mm cannula is used as the ovarian package will typically be too big to remove through a 6 mm cannula and the larger cannula size facili- tates extraction. An 11 mm cannula also allows use of a 10 mm LigaSure handpiece, if this is the vessel sealing device used, as the 10 mm handpieces are far more robust lasting for many more uses than the 5 mm instruments. A 5 mm reducer is used on the 11 mm cannula so that 5 mm Babcock forceps can be used. The patient is tilted to one side and the ovary identified (Figure 8.386). The suspen- sory ligament or the utero-ovarian ligament is grasped with the Babcock forceps (Figure 8.387), the ovary is elevated away from the adjacent tissue (Figure 8.388), and placed against the abdominal wall (Figure 8.389) (Videos 8.16 and 8.17). When using the TT hook, the hook is passed through the abdominal wall and the ovary is fixed in place as was done for the single-port technique (Figure 8.371). When using the Mouret needle retractor technique, a small stab incision is made on the ventral midline halfway between the umbilicus and the pubis (Figure 8.385). The retractor with the sharp trocar insert is passed through this incision into the linea alba, across the insufflated perito - neal cavity under direct visualization, and through the ovarian pedicle into the abdominal wall (Figure 8.390) (Video 8.15). This fixes the ovary to the abdominal wall. The Babcock forceps is removed leaving the ovary sus - pended with the Mouret needle (Figure 8.391). A vessel sealing device is passed through the operating portal and the ovarian pedicle is transected with a vessel sealing device (Figures 8.392 and 8.393) (Videos 8.18–8.21). With transection completed, the vessel sealing device is replaced with Babcock forceps and the ovarian package is grasped for removal (Figure 8.394) through the operative portal. The Mouret retractor or TT hook is removed from the abdomen. The ovary is pulled up to the cannula (Figure 8.395) or completely into the cannula if possible. The ovarian removal procedure is repeated on the second side and portal closure is as previously described. 8.8.2 Laparoscopic Ovariohysterectomy There is no current science that shows that a healthy uterus needs to be removed if the ovaries are removed (Bender 2012; De Tora and McCarthy 2011; Dunn 2012; Graves 2012; Mcanulty et al. 2012; Okkens et al. 1997; Van Goethem et al. 2006). The fear that uterine pathology will develop if the uterus is not removed when the ovaries are removed is ungrounded. Uterine neoplasia is exceedingly rare in both intact and in neutered female dogs and cats (Brodey 1967). In 50 years of practice as a general practi - tioner and as a surgeon, two cases of uterine neoplasia have been diagnosed, one in an intact female dog and one in a spayed female cat. Both tumors were benign. The most common argument against leaving the uterus in at the time of surgical sterilization of bitches is the chance for uterine stump pyometra. Uterine stump pyometra is an ovarian remnant problem, not a uterine remnant problem. Ovariectomy, whether performed with traditional tech - nique or laparoscopically is faster, safer, and less painful than ovariohysterectomy. The original laparoscopic ovari - ohysterectomy technique in small animals was a research procedure to determine the feasibility of the procedure but Endo GIA staplers were used for the ovarian pedicles and this is cost prohibitive for use in practice. A technique using extracorporeal knots for ligatures was initially used as a cost-effective technique in private practice. This tech - nique is no longer used but worked well prior to the intro - duction of vessel sealing devices. The technique put into common application in private small animal general prac - tice was a laparoscopic-assisted technique. The ovarian pedicles were visualized and transected with minimally invasive technique using ligatures prepared with extracor - poreal knots and the uterus was pulled out of the abdo - men through a caudal midline incision, ligated, and transected. This is an effective technique and is still in use. Surgery times using this technique in cats and dogs was compared with operative times for traditional ovariohys - terectomies. There was very little difference in operative times with laparoscopy requiring six additional minutes in dogs and three additional minutes in cats when compared to traditional surgery (unpublished data). When the same surgeon progressed to ovariectomies, the laparoscopic procedures were faster than traditional surgery in both cats and dogs (unpublished data). The time differences are not sufficient to use as a decision factor in determining which procedure to perform but the data eliminate the argument that laparoscopy takes too much time to use in private practice. Positioning for laparoscopic ovariohyster - ectomies is the same as for laparoscopic ovariectomies in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table with side-to-side and end-to-end positioning capabilities (Figures 8.365 and 8.366). Clipping and draping are also the same as for laparoscopic ovariectomies and a telescope portal is placed at the umbilicus or slightly caudal to the umbilicus using the Hassan technique. Cranial and caudal midline opera - tive portals are used with the cranial portal halfway between the umbilicus and the xiphoid and with the cau - dal portal halfway between the umbilicus and the pubis (Figure 8.385). A 15° head down position improves access to the caudal abdomen for transection of the mesome - trium and uterine body. If one technique is not working in a particular patient, then the other tech - nique is used. When dissection has proceeded as far cau - dally as possible, two options are available. The uterine horn is dropped, and the patient is tilted to the other side with a repeat of the procedure and with transection of the uterine body after dissection is complete on both sides. The other option is to transect the freed uterine horn (Figure 8.414) and remove that ovary and uterine horn prior to proceeding with dissection and removal of the sec - ond side. This step eliminates the bulk of the freed uterine horn from interfering with visualization for dissection of the second uterine horn. In some large dogs, the distance from the cranial opera- tive portal to the uterine body and cervix may be greater than the length of the grasping forceps. When this occurs, the telescope is transferred to the cranial operative portal and the grasping forceps are moved to the umbilical tele - scope portal. If dissection of the first side was completed to the cervix, then when the second side dissection has reached the same level, the uterine body is transected at the cranial surface of the cervix, through the cervix, or immediately caudal to the cervix. In young juvenile dogs, the uterine body and vessels are sealed and divided together using one or more bites as needed to complete the transec- tion (Figure 8.415). In large, older, and multiparous dogs, the vessels are sealed and divided separately from the uter - ine body (Figure 8.416). When transecting the cervix (Figure 8.417) or a substantial uterine body, the vessel seal- ing device may have a tendency to slip off of the thick tis - sue requiring replacement and reactivation of the device. This may need to be repeated several times to complete transection. When the dissected uterine horns with their ovaries are removed individually or when both horns and both ovaries are dissected as one procedure and removed together, the free caudal cut end of uterine horn or the uterine body is grasped (Figure 8.418). The Babcock for - ceps are retracted to the operative portal cannula for removal by extracting the uterus or uterine horn first fol- lowed by the ovary or ovaries. When removing the uterine horns individually, the ovary is typically extracted with lit - tle or no difficulty. Removing both uterine horns and ova- ries as one piece may be more difficult because of the bulk of the tissue. An alternative is to grasp the utero-ovarian ligament of one ovary and extracting that ovary first. Once the first ovary has been exteriorized, the remainder of that uterine horn is pulled through the portal site, followed by the uterine body, the second side uterine horn, and the sec- ond side ovary as one long strand. Once the first ovary has been extracted, the remainder comes easily. Recurrent estrus cycles after sterilization is an obvious indication that ovarian tissue has been left in place but silent cases occur that are presented for other reasons or detected with ultrasound or other imaging. An example of a silent case is an eight-year-old female Chocolate Labrador Retriever that was spayed at a young age then presented with vaginal hyperplasia at eight years of age. There was no history of detectable estrus cycles reported by the owner. Laparoscopy found a right- side ovarian remnant. Another case presented with uterine horn pyometra following a “hysterectomy” performed to train medical students and an attempted ovariectomy at the same facility. Ovarian remnants are most commonly seen on the right side (Ball et al. 2010) but left-side lesions and bilateral lesions have also been seen. The technique for laparoscopic ovarian remnant removal is the same as for laparoscopic ovariectomy using any num - ber of portals (Brückner 2016; Krauss and Krauss 2015; Naiman et al. 2014; Phipps et al. 2016; Van Nimwegen et al. 2018). Most ovarian remnants are easily seen caudal to the kidney at the normal location for the ovaries (Figures 8.297–8.300). Magnification with the telescope, perfect lighting, with gravity retraction of adjacent tissues and organs eliminates the issues with an open surgical approach. Once the ovarian remnant is identified (Figure 8.298), tissue is grasped with Babcock forceps adja - cent to the ovarian remnant tissue and the remnant is ele - vated (Figure 8.419) to allow dissection to free the ovarian tissue. A vessel sealing device is used for the dissection (Figure 8.420) to minimize bleeding and surgery time. When transection is completed, the transection site is checked for any bleeding as is done for ovariectomies (Figure 8.421), the ovarian remnant is maintained in the grasp of the Babcock forceps (Figure 8.422), and the resected tissue is retracted to the end of the operative cannula for extraction as is done with the ovarian package (Figure 8.423). Most ovarian rem - nants are unilateral on the right side but both sides are Figure 8.417 Transection through the cervix of the patient seen in Figure 8.416. When cutting a thick solid tissue structure such as this the vessel sealing device has a tendency to slip off the tissue. Repositioning and repeating the procedure may be required to complete the transection. The ability to clearly locate and identify intra-abdominal testicles greatly reduces the potential for complications such as inadvertent prostatec- tomy when attempting cryptorchid castration (Flesher et al. 2016; Powers et al. 2010; Puttick and Sereda 2012; Schulz et al. 1996; Vititoe and Pack 2013). Blind probing typically encountered with traditional open cryptorchid castrations is eliminated when laparoscopy is performed. Examination of the internal inguinal rings is not only pos - sible with laparoscopy but is too easy to describe and immediately determines without any doubt where the incriminating testicle is located. If the Vas Deferens and the testicular vessels are seen coursing through the inter - nal inguinal ring (Figures 8.56 and 8.57), this confirms 100%, for sure, that the testicle has escaped from the abdo - men. There is no doubt, no question, and no possibility for error. There is no need to pursue looking for the testicle in the abdomen because it is not there. The testicle is either in the inguinal canal, in the subcutaneous tissue between the inguinal ring and the scrotum or has already been removed. However, if the Vas Deferens and testicular vessels are not seen entering the internal inguinal ring (Figure 8.137), the testicle is still in the abdomen. There is no doubt, no ques - tion, and no possibility for error. The testicle is still in the abdomen, has already been removed from the abdomen, or never developed. Typically, the gubernaculum testicle is visible as an indistinct pale structure entering the inguinal ring (Figure 8.137). Locating the intra-abdominal testicle is also very easy. The gubernaculum is grasped with forceps, traction is applied, and the testicle will appear from under the loops of bowel as an obvious testicle (Figure 8.303). There is no difficulty with identifying the testicle as a testi- cle and there is no difficulty differentiating the testicle from the prostate. To perform a laparoscopic cryptorchid castration, the dog is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table that can place the patient in a head down position and the monitor is placed at the foot of the patient (Figure 8.426). The ductus deferens is visualized (Figures 8.56–8.58), isolated, and a 2 cm segment is removed using scissors and monopo - lar electrocautery, a vessel sealing device, Endoclips, or ligatures for resection (Silva et al. 1993; Wildt et al. 1981). The resected segment is removed, and the procedure is repeated on the second side. 8.8.6 Prophylactic Gastropexy Prophylactic gastropexy was not performed as a standalone procedure prior to introduction of minimally invasive sur - gery and was only done in combination with corrective surgery for gastric dilatation with volvulus (Allen and Paul 2014). Laparoscopic gastropexy was first performed as a totally intra-abdominal procedure using Endo GIA sta- pling devices for attachment of the gastric wall to the abdominal wall (Hardie et al. 1996). This technique worked well with excellent gastropexy strength and appropriate operative times but was cost prohibitive and did not become an established technique in practice. Development of a laparoscopic-assisted procedure for gastropexy produced clinical acceptance and widespread application (Rawlings et al. 2001). This approach is easy to learn and perform with acceptable surgery times, is economically reasonable, and produces consistent results with excellent gastropexy strength (Loy Son et al. 2016; Rawlings et al. 2002a), a low incidence of complications (Dujowich et al. 2010; Loy Son et al. 2016), and less postoperative pain when compared to open gastropexy (Allen and Paul 2014; Haraguchi et al. 2017). The initial technique was a multiport tech- nique (Rawlings et al. 2001) but single-port access systems have also been used successfully (Stiles et al. 2016). Laparoscopy has also allowed reduction of gastric volvulus in selected cases when performing laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy (Dujowich et al. 2010; Rawlings et al. 2002a; Runge and Mayhew 2013; Van Heerden et al. 2018). Studies determined that gastric function was not impaired by lapa- roscopic-assisted gastropexy (Balsa et al. 2017; Coleman et al. 2019; Gazzola et al. 2017). Progression of surgical skills, instrumentation, and suture materials has pushed this technique to a totally intra-abdom - inal laparoscopic technique using intracorporeal suturing with various techniques and suture materials (Coleman and Monnet 2017; Coleman et al. 2016; Mathon et al. 2009; Mayhew 2009; Spah et al. 2013; Takacs et al. 2017). Mechanical testing of intracorporeally sutured gastropexies have demonstrated load to failure values similar to laparo - scopic-assisted techniques (Mathon et al. 2009) and tradi - tional open incisional gastropexy (Imhoff et al. 2015). Both of the laparoscopic-assisted technique and the intra- abdominal laparoscopic technique with intracorporeal suturing are currently used in practice with equal efficacy (Mayhew 2009). Each approach has advantages and disad - vantages involving technical aspects related to performing the procedure, but both achieve the same excellent results. Operating times are similar for surgeons experienced with each technique and healed gastropexy strengths are essen - tially the same. The laparoscopic-assisted technique is eas - ier to learn and uses less specialized instrumentation but creates a larger abdominal wall incision. The purely laparo - scopic technique requires additional instrumentation, intracorporeal suturing skills making it more difficult to learn, and requires special sutures. The technique selected is based on personal preference, skill level, and instrumen - tation available. Both are acceptable techniques. Laparoscopic ovariectomy and laparoscopic-assisted or total intra-abdominal gastropexy are commonly combined and performed as a single surgery using both single-port (Gandini and Giusto 2016; Runge and Mayhew 2013) and multiport techniques (Rivier et al. 2011). 8.8.6.1 Laparoscopic-Assisted Gastropexy Laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy is performed with the patient in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table that allows side- to-side positioning. The monitor is placed at the head of the patient or obliquely to the right of this position (Figure 8.441). At this point, alignment of the grasping forceps is maintained and not allowed to rotate or the gastropexy is rotated creating a kink in the gastric outflow tract. The grasped gastric wall is elevated to contact the portal cannula, but the end of the cannula is kept away from the abdominal wall (Figures 8.453 and 8.454). A #10 scalpel blade is passed through the abdominal wall with the back side of the scalpel blade in contact with the portal cannula and the sharp side in line with the desired angle of the enlarged portal (Figure 8.455). At this point, insufflation is lost and the insufflator is turned off. Decompression of the abdomen at this point is desired because it reduces the dis - tance from the pyloric antrum wall to the abdominal wall facilitating elevation of the gastropexy site on the gastric wall to the exterior of the abdomen. As soon as any of the gastric wall is visible from the outside through the enlarged portal, a cruciate stay suture of #0 or #1 monofilament material is placed on the proximal or distal side of the grasping forceps (Figure 8.456). Either side is acceptable. The important point of this step is to get a stay suture in the gastric wall before the forceps slips off of the stomach. Loss of gastric wall grip is a common occurrence and compli- cates the procedure requiring reinsufflation and regrasping the gastric wall. Once a stay suture is in place, this problem is eliminated. The first stay suture is placed with a cruciate pattern using #0 or #1 monofilament suture material. After place - ment of the first stay suture, a larger portion of the gastric wall at the gastropexy site is exteriorized, a second stay suture is placed using the same cruciate pattern and suture material on the opposite side of the grasping forceps to sta- bilize the gastric wall for the exterior portion of the surgery (Figure 8.457). Once stay sutures are in place, the grasping forceps are removed. The stay sutures are placed far enough apart to allow the gastropexy to be performed between the sutures. If initial stay suture placement is not adequate, the stay sutures are moved. This is done by walking suture bites to the desired location. When the stay sutures are in place, they are tied with a loose loop of suture under the knot and are grasped with hemostatic forceps. Alignment of the pyloric antrum and placement at the midpoint between the greater and lesser curvatures are confirmed. Additional extension of the abdominal wall incision is done at this point if indicated. The laparoscopy portion of the gastropexy is performed with the surgeon on the left side of the patient. The exterior portion of the surgery can also be done from this position but reaching across the patient may be awkward. Moving to the right side of the patient to perform this portion of the procedure may be more comfortable. This is a personal preference choice. If the lumen of the pyloric antrum is entered, this layer is closed with a standard gastric mucosal closure pattern and the surgery site thoroughly irrigated to minimize contamination and reduce the risk of suture fistula formation. The margins of the inci - sion are dissected to create an adequate free margin of the seromuscular layer to provide solid suture purchase. A con - tinuous suture pattern using #0 or #2-0 monofilament slowly absorbable suture is used to suture the margin of the gastric incision to the margin of the transversus abdominis muscle incision taking care to include the peritoneum in the suture line (Figure 8.458). The suture is started at the midpoint of the cranial side of the incision with purchase in both the seromuscular layer of the gastric wall and the transversus abdominis muscle and this first suture bite is tied to fix the suture in place. The free suture end of this knot is left long to tie to when the suture pattern is com - pleted. Suture bites are taken on one side of this suture to the medial end of incision and at the end of the incision, the suture is locked on itself to hold the tissues in apposition. The suture line is continued laterally on the second or cau - dal side of the incision to the lateral end where a second locking suture is placed. The continuous suture line is com - pleted on the first or cranial side to the site of the initial knot where it is tied to the free suture end of the initial knot. The direction of suture passage from gastric incision to abdominal wall incision or from abdominal wall incision to gastric wall incision is selected based on personal prefer - ence of the surgeon, position of the surgeon relative to the gastropexy site, the direction that works best for the indi - vidual case, and for the direction that works best on the cra - nial and caudal sides of the incision. One direction of passage may be used on the cranial side of the incision and the other direction of passage used on the other side of the incision. It is important to visualize the parietal peritoneal surface and include this in each suture bite. Visualizing and accessing the transverse abdominis muscle and peritoneum may be difficult due to retraction of the muscle and can be aided by placement of towel clamps, other grasping forceps, or stay sutures in the muscle (Figure 8.458). When the gas - tropexy suture is completed, the abdomen is reinsufflated, the telescope placed into the abdomen, and the gastropexy site is inspected to ensure appropriate gastric alignment and adequate tissue apposition (Figure 8.459). It is very impor - tant that there is proper gastric alignment at the gastropexy site. Loss of orientation of gastric alignment is very easy and it is important during grasping of the gastric wall, elevation to the abdominal wall, during portal enlargement, and stay suture placement to maintain accurate orientation. Rotation of the grasping forceps must be prevented once the gastric wall has been grasped. This is done by noting the direction of the handle relative to the gastropexy incision and holding the handle and shaft of the forceps together as one unit. Remember that the shaft of the forceps rotates independent from the handle. Stay suture place - ment is also important to prevent inappropriate gastric position. The stay sutures are placed midway between Figure 8.456 The enlarged gastropexy portal from the outside with a small portion of the gastric wall exposed in the grip of Babcock/Duval forceps and with the first stay suture being placed. 8 Laparoscopy 512 the greater and lesser curvatures of the pyloric antrum. It may be necessary to allow the stomach to drop away from the abdominal wall a short distance to provide ade - quate exposure for conformation of accurate stay suture placement. Once stay sutures are placed, it is important not to confuse which suture is which and get them reversed in the abdominal wall incision. Maintaining proper gastric alignment, preventing slip - ping of the grasping forceps with loss of elevation of the stomach, and finding the appropriate tissue layers during suturing are the most difficult portions of the procedure. All of these issues become less with experience. All will occur during the learning phase of this technique. All can be corrected or overcome. Maintaining proper alignment is done by careful attention to forceps’ position on the gastric wall, observing position of the exterior portion of the for - ceps and holding it so that its inside and outside positions remain unchanged. If knowledge of forceps rotational position is lost, the gastropexy portal is occluded with a wet gauze sponge and the abdomen reinsufflated to allow visu- alization of gastric position with the telescope. When the grasping forceps slips off of the gastric wall, the abdomen is reinsufflated and the gastric wall regrasped or if the portal site has already been enlarged, the gastric wall may be vis - ible through the portal to regrasp the proper location. Identifying the proper tissue layers for suturing is much easier with a larger incision and when learning, a longer abdominal wall incision is used. With experience, a shorter incision is used but if tissue plane identification is difficult in any individual case, the abdominal wall incision is extended to provide adequate visualization. Following completion of the gastropexy layer, the abdo - men is reinsufflated, and visual inspection of the gastropexy site is done to ensure proper alignment and serosal apposi - tion (Figure 8.459). The abdomen is decompressed, and the remaining tissues are closed in layers with standard surgical technique. Careful separation of tissue layers is important to minimize skin puckering when the dog is recovered and in a standing position. This is not detrimental to the patient and will resolve with time but can be concerning to the client. Confirmation of healing of the gastropexy site using ultrasound was recommended when the procedure was first introduced (Rawlings et al. 2002a). This step would still be recommended for the beginner but with the extremely high success rate without documented breakdown of the gastropexy site, this may not be needed with surgeons expe - rienced with the procedure. An alternative procedure is to place stainless steel skin staples in the ends of the gastric wall seromuscular incision and in the ends of the abdomi - nal wall incision. If confirmation of gastropexy integrity is indicated, radiographs will show the position of the staples close together if intact and separated if the gastropexy has broken down. There is little indication for laparoscopic examination of healed gastropexy sites but laparoscopy per - formed for other indications in dogs with previously per - formed laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy is an ideal opportunity to assess their appearance (Figure 8.460). 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 513 8.8.6.2 Laparoscopic Gastropexy Laparoscopic gastropexy with intra-abdominal suturing is performed with the patient in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table and with slight left oblique positioning. When com- bined with laparoscopic ovariectomy, clipping, prepara- tion, and draping are done to accommodate both procedures and to allow conversion with a full-length ventral abdomi- nal midline incision. An initial telescope portal is placed at the umbilicus using the Hassan technique and the abdo - men is insufflated. Two additional midline portals are placed with one halfway between the umbilicus and the xiphoid and the other halfway between the umbilicus and the pubis. A recent modification of portal placement for this procedure moves the cranial operative portal to a left paramedian position in line with the transverse abdominis muscle incision to facilitate suturing. All trocar-cannulas can be 6 mm or if indicated, one or more 11 mm trocar-can- nulas with reducers are used. Most gastropexies are done in large breed dogs and the advantages of 11 mm diameter cannulas were discussed in Section 8.8.1. These are the same portal sites for laparoscopic ovariectomy which is commonly performed in association with gastropexy. The ovariectomy is performed prior to performing the gastropexy to avoid interference of the gastropexy with ovarian manipulation. After completion of the second ova- riectomy, the patient is returned to dorsal recumbency or to a slight left oblique position. The telescope is moved to the caudal operative portal and operative instruments are posi- tioned in the cranial two-portals. The position of the gastropexy incision on the abdominal wall is parallel and 2–4 cm caudal to the right costal arch and lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle. An incision is made in the peritoneum and deep fascia of the transverse abdominis muscle for a 3–4 cm length. This incision is made with monopolar radio-frequency electrocautery using an “L” or “J” shaped electrode, Metzenbaum scissors to make a full-thickness transversus abdominis incision using monop - olar cautery as needed, or with a vessel sealing device used to make a full-thickness transversus abdominis incision. A seromuscular gastric wall incision is made at the same location as for the laparoscopic-assisted technique at the midpoint of the ventral wall of the pyloric antrum proceeding distally 3–4 cm from a point approximately 8–12 cm from the pylorus. This incision is made with Metzenbaum scissors or with a vessel sealing device using a 5 mm handpiece. An ini - tial temporary stay suture is placed at the lateral end of the transversus abdominis incision by passing a #0 monofila - ment suture through the abdominal wall, grasping the suture needle, pulling part of the suture into the abdomen but leav - ing the free end outside the abdomen, taking a bite with the suture in the wall of the pyloric antrum at the aboral end of the seromuscular incision, and passing the needle back out through the abdominal wall. Traction is applied to both ends of this suture to elevate the gastric wall to the abdominal wall and the suture is tied loosely outside the abdomen. This suture can be placed prior to making the abdominal wall and gastric seromuscular incisions or after they have been made. Another technique places stay sutures at both ends of the abdominal wall and gastric seromuscular incisions. Suturing of the gastropexy site is done with barbed suture, standard suture and intracorporeal knots, or with an EndoStitch device. All techniques work but barbed sutures eliminate the task of intracorporeal knot tying and reduce operative times. Intracorporeal suturing requires forehand and backhand needle passage with one direction through the transversus abdominis muscle and the other through the free gastric seromuscular layer. The direction selected for the incision sides is by personal preference. Standard or barbed sutures are passed through the abdominal wall adja - cent to the lateral end of the abdominal wall incision. The needle is passed through the abdominal wall, grasped with endoscopic needle holders, and pulled into the abdomen. EndoStitch sutures are loaded into the EndoStitch device and passed through the cranial most operative portal. With barbed suture, initial bites are taken in the cranial margin of the transverse abdominis incision at its lateral end and in the cranial margin of the aboral end of the gastric wall seromuscular incision. The needle is then passed through the loop at the tail end of the suture. A continuous suture line is then placed in the cranial margins of the incisions to the medial/oral end of the gastropexy pulling each suture bite tight as it is placed. At the end of the incision, the suture is locked on itself with an interlocking suture placement. A continuous suture line is placed in the caudal margin of the incisions back to the lateral/aboral end pulling each bite tight as it is placed. One or two bites of the locking suture are placed beyond the lateral/aboral end of the gastropexy site. The temporary stay suture or sutures are removed. Use of monofilament suture requires intracorporeal knot tying that is technically challenging but can be mastered with practice. The suture is passed into the abdomen and initial bites are taken as described for barbed sutures, but Figure 8.460 A healed laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy site seen during laparoscopy for assisted removal of a bladder mass.

8 Laparoscopy 514 instead of passing the needle through the loop of the barbed suture, a knot is tied to secure the starting end of the suture. The suturing procedure is the same as with barbed suture except there is more slippage between suture bites and keeping the individual suture loops tight between bites is more problematic. An interlocking suture pattern corrects this problem even if every suture bite is not interlocked. At the medial end of the suture line, a locking suture pass is used and is more important than with the barbed suture. The return arm of the suture line in the caudal margins of the incisions does not have the problem of keeping the suture passes tight. When the lateral/aboral end of the suture line is reached, the suture is tied and added to the original knot. This technique is slightly more time consum- ing than barbed sutures but most of the time is involved with placing the sutures and not with knot tying. Monofilament suture can also be used with extracorporeal knot tying. This technique was the original procedure used for laparoscopic ovariohysterectomies prior to effective ves - sel sealing devices. Knots are tied outside of the abdominal cavity and positioned at the suture line with a knot pusher. An 11 mm trocar-cannula is used and the suture needle needs to be of a size and shape to allow passage through the cannula. The suture is initially passed into the abdominal cavity through the abdominal wall as has been previously described. Suture passes are made through the abdominal wall and gastric wall at the lateral/aboral end of the incisions and both suture ends are pulled out through the same opera- tive cannula. Alternatively, the suture needle is passed into the abdomen through the operative cannula leaving the tail end of the suture outside the abdomen, suture passes are taken through the abdominal wall and gastric wall at the lat - eral/aboral end of the incisions, and the needle is pulled out through the cannula so that both ends of the suture are out - side the abdomen. One of several knots are tied outside the abdomen and slid into position with a knot pusher. Continuous suture lines are placed as previously described. Securing the finished end of the suture line to the origin of the suture line requires one intracorporeal knot. The EndoStitch technique requires a special suturing instrument and special sutures. The sutures have a short straight needle with two sharp ends and suture attached to the center of the needle. This needle is loaded into the EndoStitch device with one side of the needle locked into one side of the instrument jaw. The needle is transferred from one side of the jaw to the other by closing the jaws and switching the position of a toggle that releases the nee - dle from the first jaw and locks it to the second side jaw. This manipulation allows placement of sutures through one or more layers of tissue in a continuous pattern. Intracorporeal knots are tied with this device. Barbed suture with an end loop is also available for the EndoStitch. Considerable practice is required to become proficient with this technique, but it can speedup suture line placement. One other disadvantage is that the needles are short, and it does not work well with tissues that are too thick. 8.8.7 Laparoscopic-Assisted Gastrotomy This technique is indicated only when the needed proce - dure cannot be performed with flexible gastroscopy (Haider et al. 2009; McCarthy 2004). Any time a foreign body, polyp, or other lesion cannot be managed with an intralu- minal approach using a flexible gastroscope, laparoscopic- assisted gastrotomy is preformed eliminating the need for an open laparotomy. Any foreign body that can be removed with open surgery can be removed with laparoscopic- assisted gastrotomy. Operating room setup, patient position, clipping, prepara- tion, and draping are done the same as for laparoscopic- assisted gastropexy (Figure 8.441). An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdo - men is insufflated. A right paramedian operative portal is placed in the same location and with the same procedure as for gastropexy (Figure 8.442). An alternative portal is placed on the midline directly over the body of the stomach. The skin, subcutaneous, and superficial muscle layers are incised with the same technique as for laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy, but the incision length is adjusted to the length needed for removal of the foreign body. The stomach is vis - ualized, and the ventral gastric wall is grasped equidistant from the greater and lesser curvatures as is done for laparo - scopic-assisted gastropexy, but the pickup point is at the junction of the pyloric antrum and gastric body. Five or ten millimeter Babcock forceps are used depending on the size of the patient. The gastric wall is elevated to the cannula but kept away from the abdominal wall, the portal is enlarged by passing a #10 scalpel blade through the remaining abdominal wall layers with the back of the scalpel blade against the cannula (Figure 8.455), a portion of the gastric wall is exteriorized, and stay sutures are placed with the same technique as for gastropexy. Maintaining gastric align- ment is important but is not as critical as it is with gas - tropexy. The stay sutures are placed far enough apart to allow a gastric incision that is long enough for removal of the foreign body or other procedure required. The most sig - nificant difference with this procedure when compared to laparoscopic-assisted gastropexy is that the gastric wall inci- sion is full thickness allowing access to the gastric lumen. A telescope cannula is placed into the stomach and the stom- ach is insufflated with CO 2 . Leakage of CO 2 occurs but suf- ficient opening of the gastric lumen still occurs. Any gastric contents or fluid are removed with suction and irrigation as needed. The gastric lumen is examined by placing the tele - scope into the cannula used for insufflation. Minimally invasive surgery forceps are used to grab foreign bodies for removal or if needed, open surgical instruments are used (Figures 8.461 and 8.462). The gastric lumen is re-examined

8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 515 after removal of the identified foreign body or bodies to confirm that all foreign material has been removed (Figure 8.463). This technique was used for removal of 8 (EIGHT) snow man chew toys from the stomach of a Saint Bernard (Figures 8.464–8.466). Confirming that all foreign bodies have been removed is critical to success of foreign body removal with whatever technique is used. Confirming removal of all gastric foreign bodies with this technique is superior to traditional open surgery. This technique has been used most commonly for removal of foreign bodies that cannot be removed with gastroscopy, but it is also applicable to other gastric lesions. Closure of the gastrot - omy is with standard open surgical technique, the stomach is returned to the abdomen and the abdominal wall incision is closed with standard technique. If a gastropexy is performed at the same surgery, it is per - formed at a site separate from the gastrotomy and is performed with the same technique as for laparoscopic- assisted gastropexy. 8 Laparoscopy 516 8.8.8 Laparoscopic Pyloroplasty Laparoscopic pyloric surgery to relieve gastric outflow obstruction is a relatively common procedure in people with multiple variations (Gonzalez et al. 2019; Grišin et al. 2017; Hedberg et al. 2019; Jiang et al. 2017; Landreneau et al. 2019; Moggia et al. 2016; Shada et al. 2016) but has only been reported in the dog as a research study (Holak et al. 2016). A modified hybrid pyloromyotomy technique is readily performed with laparoscopy. This technique is a combina- tion of the Fredet-Ramstedt pyloromyotomy and the Heineke-Mikulicz pyloroplasty where the longitudinal myotomy is performed leaving the pyloric mucosa intact as with the Fredet-Ramstedt procedure and then closing the seromuscular incision transversely as with the Heineke- Mikulicz procedure. This eliminates the potential for gas - trointestinal leakage, allows primary intention healing, and decreases the potential for adhesions. The patient is positioned in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table with the monitor in a right cranial oblique position. The surgeon stands on the left side of the patient and the assistant stands on the right side of the patient. An umbili- cal telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. Two paramedian operative portals are placed in the cranial abdomen with one on each side of the midline. The right-side operative portal is used to grasp the caudal aspect of the gastric side of the pylorus for stabilization. Metzenbaum scissors are placed in the left cranial operative portal and a pyloromyotomy is performed. Sutures are then placed to close the pyloromyotomy trans - versely. A single interrupted suture is placed to oppose the proximal and distal ends of the pyloromyotomy incision. This suture is tightened and tied using an extracorporeal knot or an intracorporeal knot depending on the skill level of the surgeon. A single suture is adequate in many cases but an additional suture on each side of this initial suture improves myotomy closure. 8.8.9 Laparoscopic-Assisted Enterotomy and Intestinal Resection with Anastomosis Intestinal foreign bodies and isolated intestinal masses are identified, exteriorized, and removed using laparoscopic (Omotosho et al. 2011; Sonoda et al. 2007) or laparoscopic- assisted technique (Case and Ellison 2013). Unless deter - mined with preoperative imaging or for other indications, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table capable of end-to-end and side-to-side tilting. The surgeon stands on one side of the patient with the assistant on the other side and monitors are placed at each end of the patient. An umbilical telescope portal is placed with the Hassan technique and the abdomen insufflated. The abdo - men is examined with operative portal placement deter - mined for each individual case. If the site of intestinal pathology is obvious, the intestine is grasped immediately cranial or caudal to the involved segment in normal tissue (Figure 8.467) and is elevated to the abdominal wall, the portal is enlarged, and the intestinal segment is exterior - ized as previously described. If the site of intestinal pathol- ogy is not obvious, the bowel is run until the lesion or lesions are identified. The required surgery is performed outside of the abdomen with standard open surgical tech- nique (Figure 8.468). When enterotomy closure or anasto - mosis is completed, the exteriorized segment is returned to the abdomen. If the bowel is not run prior to the assisted Figure 8.466 Examination of the gastric lumen was repeated to remove all eight of the snow man chew toys, this being the last one. If examination reveals that open surgery is indicated, conver - sion to open surgery is conducted. 8.8.10 Laparoscopic-Assisted Cecectomy Indications for cecectomy are not common but when needed, this procedure is performed effectively with lapa- roscopic-assisted technique. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table and the abdomen is clipped, pre - pared, and draped as for laparoscopic-assisted enterotomy. The surgeon stands on one side of the patient, the assistant stands on the other side, and a monitor is placed at each end of the table. An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insuf- flated. Initial exploration is conducted to confirm that the lesion involves the cecum and operative portals are placed that will allow the cecum to be elevated to the abdominal wall (Figure 8.469). The cecum is grasped with Babcock forceps and elevated to the operative cannula (Figure 8.470), the portal is enlarged, the cecum is exteriorized (Figure 8.471) with resection and closure using standard open surgical technique (Figure 8.472). The resection site is irrigated with saline to reduce contamination and is returned to the abdomen. If it cannot be determined that the cecum is involved on initial exploration, operative por - tals are placed to allow exploration with running the bowel. 8.8.11 Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was the procedure that drove minimally invasive human surgery into common use. Cholecystectomy, open or laparoscopic, in small ani- mal practice is generally ignored as a treatment option. 8 Laparoscopy 518 Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is an easy surgical proce - dure in dogs with high success rate and low morbidity and mortality (Gamal et al. 1999, 2001; Hotokezaka et al. 1996; Kanai et al. 2018; Lovell et al. 2019; Mayhew and Brown 2009; Mayhew et al. 2008; Scott et al. 2016; Szabó et al. 2005, 2007). This surgery is drastically underutilized in small animal practice. There is a viable argument for performing cholecystectomy whenever a laparoscopic liver biopsy is performed. Agreed this is an aggressive approach but is a push to move away from only performing cholecys - tectomy in compromised patients with mucoceles and a mortality rate of 30% or greater (Aguirre et al. 2007; Amsellem 2006; Jaffey et al. 2008; Malek et al. 2013; Pike et al. 2004 Smalle et al. 2015 Worley et al. 2004). Studies are needed to determine the indications for early cholecystec- tomy, mortality, morbidity, and long-term medical effects. A case in point suggesting the need for these studies is a patient with a full-page long problem list of medical abnor - malities that was presented for laparoscopic liver biopsy. Preoperative ultrasound indicated mild gall bladder sludge. Liver biopsies were taken and on examination with the laparoscope, the gall bladder appeared mildly abnormal. A cholecystectomy was performed. Recovery from laparos - copy was rapid and uneventful. Over the next few months, ALL of this dog’s medical problems resolved. Agreed this is just one case and proves nothing but does raise questions about the benefits of early cholecystectomy. At the other end of the spectrum of gall bladder and bil- iary tract disease there is a point when laparoscopic chole - cystectomy is deferred to open surgery either as the primary approach or as a conversion from laparoscopy. Conditions for determining selection of open surgery over laparoscopy have not been established. Mucoceles in compromised patients, ruptured gall bladders, bile leakage from an unde - termined location, and extrahepatic bile duct obstruction are currently conditions where open surgery may be indicated. Severity of the disease process will impact the decision-making process and as our skill development pro - gresses, we will be able to move some or all of these condi- tions into the MIS column. When in doubt, scope first. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency at the caudal end of a tilt table with the monitor at the head of the patient or obliquely to the right of the head of the patient (Figure 8.473). The abdomen is clipped, prepared, and draped to allow exposure of the entire ventral abdomen, wide enough to provide an aseptic field for left and right paramedian portals, and to allow for conversion with a full- length ventral midline abdominal incision. An initial umbilical telescope portal is placed with the Hassan tech- nique and the abdomen is insufflated (Figure 8.474). Two or three operative portals are placed, a right paramedian portal at the lateral margin of the rectus slightly cranial to the level of the umbilicus, a second right paramedian por - tal that is further cranially and further laterally, and a left paramedian portal that approximately mirrors the right cranial operative portal (Figure 8.475). All operative portal sites are adjusted for individual patient anatomy, using guidance with the telescope from the initial umbili- cal portal, to focus triangulation on the location of the gall bladder. Gall bladder dissection is done in either a top down or bot - tom up technique. For either technique, partial or complete emptying of the gall bladder facilitates dissection. This is pos - sible with liquid bile but is not possible with solidified bile or mucoceles. Cholecystocentesis is performed with a spinal needle, Menghini needle, Veress needle, Mouret needle retractor, or any needle of sufficient length to reach the gall bladder and sufficient diameter for bile aspiration (Figure 8.338). If the gall bladder is turgid, the needle is inserted directly into the gall bladder without stabilization (Figure 8.338) or if needed, the gall bladder is stabilized by grasping with Babcock or other atraumatic grasping forceps (Figure 8.476). Complete emptying of the gall bladder is ideal and is done if possible (Figure 8.339) but is not essential. Removing sufficient material to facilitate easy grasping of the gall bladder wall is the goal (Figure 8.477). For the top down, ventral to dorsal, dissection technique the gall bladder is grasped at or near its apex with atraumatic grasping forceps from the right caudal paramedian portal and retracted cau - dally (Figure 8.478). When there is significant gall bladder wall compromise due to disease, the grasping forceps are used with great care, a retractor is used to position the gall bladder, or the procedure is converted to open surgery. A fan or other type retractor is placed in the left or right cranial paramedian operative portal depending on which position provides the best retraction of the adjacent liver lobes (Figure 8.479). Curved Metzenbaum scissors are placed through a remaining unused operative portal that aligns the instrument with the visceral attachment of the gall bladder at the intersection of gall bladder and liver parenchyma. Additional sharp transection of the visceral peritoneal attach - ment is done as blunt dissection separates more gall bladder from the liver. Care is taken to establish the correct plane for dissection of the gall bladder from the hepatic fossa. Entering and staying in the optimum tissue plane during dissection (Figure 8.481) results in a smooth clean liver surface, mini - mal liver trauma, and minimal bleeding. Entering and main - taining this ideal plane during dissection is not always possible and many cholecystectomies are accomplished through liver tissue for all or part of the dissection. This leaves an exposed rough liver surface (Figure 8.482) that does not appear to be detrimental to the patient. Dissection through liver tissue requires more hemostasis accomplished with monopolar radio frequency, bipolar radio frequency, a vessel sealing device, or hemostatic powder. Dissecting elec - trodes combined with suction and irrigation work well for this dissection. Dissection is continued until the cystic bile duct is encountered and isolated to the common bile duct. There are multiple options for occlusion of the cystic bile duct including Endoclips, pretied loop ligatures, ligatures placed using extracorporeal knots, and ligatures placed with Figure 8.476 Grasping a flaccid gall bladder wall for stabilization to allow cholecystocentesis. Figure 8.477 Following cystocentesis of the gall bladder in Figure 8.476 with removal of sufficient material to provide a flaccid gall bladder to facilitate grasping the wall. The ragged liver margin on the left side of the image is from liver biopsies. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 521 intracorporeal knots. All are used and none are documented to be better than any others. Endoclips are the easiest and fastest method of cystic duct occlusion and are commonly used (Figure 8.483). Multiple clips are applied with at least two clips on the bile duct to be left in the patient and one clip on the side to be removed (Figure 8.484). If the Endoclips are too small and do not reach completely across the bile duct (Figure 8.485) with the clip ends visible beyond the far side of the bile duct, additional clips are added placed in the opposite direction to ensure adequate bile duct occlusion. With the top down dissection, pretied loop ligatures are used for bile duct occlusion (Figure 8.486). These are passed through the opera - tive portal used for dissection, the grasping forceps on the apex of the gall bladder are released, this grasper is passed through the pretied loop, the gall bladder is regrasped, the loop is passed over the gall bladder and cystic duct to the desired position, and the loop is tightened to ligate the cystic duct (Figure 8.487). Ligatures and clips are used indepen - dently or clips and ligatures are used in combination to ensure an adequately secured cystic duct (Figure 8.487). Ligatures placed using knots tied with extracorporeal and intracorporeal technique are also used but increase operative time and have no advantages over pretied loops. Pretied loops are not inexpensive but typically cost less than three Endoclips. Once ligatures or clips are applied, the cystic duct is cut to free the gall bladder for removal. 8 Laparoscopy 522 Bottom up, dorsal to ventral, dissection is also used for cholecystectomy. For this technique the cystic duct is iden - tified, isolated, and occluded prior to dissection of the gall bladder from the hepatic fossa. The same portal arrange - ment is used, and the fan retractor is used to retract the gall bladder cranially for visualization and access to the cystic duct and artery. Right-angled forceps, curved dissec - tors, and curved Metzenbaum scissors are used to dissect and isolate the cystic duct and artery prior to cystic duct occlusion and division. The same considerations are given to cystic duct occlusion techniques for this technique as for the top down technique except that pretied loop liga - tures cannot be used. With practice, extracorporeal knots are fast, easy, and secure. Intracorporeal knots require more skill development but with practice, can be an acceptable alternative. An advantage of ligatures over clips for this technique is that the suture ends of the liga - ture on the gall bladder side of the transection are used for retraction of the gall bladder during dissection of the gall bladder from the hepatic fossa. When this is done, it is recommended to place a clip or a second ligature distal to the traction suture so that if this suture is displaced during the procedure the cystic duct is still occluded. Dissection of the gall bladder from the hepatic fossa is performed in the same way as with the top down tech - nique but in reverse. Vessel sealing devices are ubiquitous in minimally inva- sive surgery and have greatly extended the range of surger - ies that can be performed, reduced operative times, and improved results but they are not recommended for bile duct occlusion. A permanent seal is not produced when these devices are used on the bile duct and failure of the seal is common. So do not use a vessel sealing device for bile duct occlusion. After the gall bladder is completely free, it is removed from the abdomen. If the cholecystocentesis was effectively performed prior to gall bladder dissection, removal may be possible through an 11 mm cannula or through the portal incision using the traction suture on the cystic duct or with a grasping instrument on the cystic duct. If this is not pos - sible, a specimen retrieval bag is used to partially expose the gall bladder at a portal site for bile aspiration to reduce its size to facilitate removal. The cystic duct can also be pulled through a portal sufficiently to provide access to aspirate bile and allow gall bladder removal. A retrieval bag is recommended for extraction of severely diseased gall bladders, but many can be removed without this expense. Prior to exiting the abdomen, inspection of the surgery site is conducted for any bleeding, bile leakage, or spilled bile. Bleeding from the liver surface at the resection site typically stops spontaneously (Figure 8.488). Residual bleeding is addressed with radio frequency, a vessel sealing device, or hemostatic powder. Any bile residue is removed with irrigation and suction. 8.8.12 Laparoscopic Partial Pancreatectomy Laparoscopic resection of the caudal extremity of the right lobe of the pancreas and the left extremity of the left lobe of the pancreas are possible (McClaran et al. 2017; Naitoh et al. 2002). 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 523 The caudal extremity of the right lobe is readily accessi- ble and easy to resect anywhere caudal to its separation from the duodenum. The patient is placed in dorsal recum- bency on a tilt table or in left lateral recumbency. Dorsal recumbency with a tilt table is preferred as it provides increased access for exploration of the entire abdomen and initial portal placement for insufflation is easier with less trauma. The surgeon is positioned on the left side of the patient with the monitor across the patient on the right side (Figure 8.489). An umbilical telescope portal is placed with the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated (Figure 8.490). The table is tilted to the left to expose the organs on the right side. Tilting is continued until there is an adequate view of the pancreas. Depending on the find- ings on initial exploration and personal preference, two right paramedian operative portals are placed with the patient in the tilted position (Figure 8.491) or the patient is returned to dorsal recumbency, two midline operative por - tals are appropriately placed cranial and caudal to the tel- escope portal (Figure 8.492), and the table is tilted to expose the pancreas. The lesion is identified and the extent of pancreas to be resected is determined (Figure 8.493). The mesentery attached to the caudal extremity of the right lobe of the pancreas is elevated and incised to isolate the area to be resected (Figure 8.494). The pancreas is only grasped where the tissue will be removed with the resec- tion to minimize postoperative pancreatitis. In thin dogs with minimal mesenteric fat, this can be done with Metzenbaum scissors and monopolar radio frequency or in dogs with significant fat, a vessel sealing device is used. When adequate pancreas has been isolated, the pancreas is transected using a vessel sealing device or a pretied loop ligature is placed around the pancreas (Figure 8.495) and after tightening the suture (Figure 8.496), the pancreas is cut distal to the suture with scissors (Figure 8.497). The resected portion of pancreas (Figure 8.498) is placed in a tissue retrieval bag (Figure 8.499) and extracted from the abdomen (Figure 8.500). The left lobe of the pancreas is much more difficult to access laparoscopically because of its location under the stomach, colon, and spleen. Small cysts may resolve spontane - ously, others resolve with ultrasound-guided aspiration, and only those causing clinical signs that do not resolve with nonsurgical intervention or those that continue to enlarge require surgery (Brückner 2019). A minimally invasive approach is indicated for local resection of cysts, partial pancreatectomy, or to determine if an open surgical approach is indicated.
