8 Laparoscopy 526 Operative room setup and patient positioning are the same as for partial pancreatectomy (Figure 8.489). An umbilical telescope portal is established using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated (Figure 8.490). Initial exploration is conducted, and operative portal site selection is determined based on lesion location but typi- cally is similar to those sites used for partial pancreatec- tomy of the caudal portion of the right lobe (Figures 8.491 and 8.492). Lesions on the left side require incision of the omentum for exposure and lesions externally appear simi- lar to insulinomas (Figure 8.501). Once identified, the lesion is aspirated (Figure 8.502) to confirm its cystic nature, to obtain diagnostic samples, and to remove its con- tents to reduce potential abdominal contamination (Figure 8.503). The grasping forceps are moved to the cyst wall (Figure 8.504), the cyst is opened with Metzenbaum scissors (Figure 8.505), and resection of the cyst-free wall is continued with scissors or a vessel sealing device as indi- cated (Figure 8.506), until the cyst-free wall is completely excised (Figure 8.507). The removed tissue is extracted from the abdomen and the surgery site is lavaged to mini- mize contamination with cyst contents (Figure 8.508). 8.8.14 Laparoscopic Nephrectomy Both kidneys are amenable to laparoscopic removal and this approach is preferred over open surgery when appro - priate minimally invasive surgery skills and instrumenta- tion are available. The patient is positioned in either lateral recumbency with the kidney to be removed on the upper - most side or in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table. For the lateral recumbent position, the surgeon and assistant stand on the ventral side of the patient with the monitor on the dorsal side of the patient (Figure 8.345). The entire lateral abdominal wall is clipped, prepared, and draped for the procedure to allow placement of three- or four-portals and for conversion to open surgery through a vertical incision in the lateral abdominal wall. Laterally recumbent patients are insufflated with the Veress needle technique and the initial telescope portal is placed after insufflation at the level of the umbilicus and the ventrodorsal level of the junction of ventral and middle thirds of the abdominal wall (Figure 8.509). 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 527 kidney to be removed and the monitor is placed on the same side as the kidney to be removed similar to the arrangement for partial pancreatectomy (Figure 8.489) so that when the table is tilted, the surgery team is placed on the ventral side of the patient and the monitor is on the dorsal side. The abdomen is clipped, prepared, and draped asymmetrically with the side of the kidney to be removed exposed dorsally to the level of the lumbar muscles and ventrally to provide access for a full-length ventral abdominal incision should conversion be necessary. For dorsally recumbent patients, a telescope portal is placed at the umbilicus with the Hassan technique and the abdo - men is insufflated (Figure 8.490). The table is tilted and operative portals are placed at the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis muscle or approximately one third of the distance from the ventral midline to the ventral mar - gin of the lumbar muscles with a cranial portal immedi - ately caudal to the last rib and a caudal portal adjacent to the hind leg (Figure 8.491). An additional portal, if needed, is placed at the dorsal extent of the lateral abdom - inal wall (Figure 8.509). Placement of operative portals use these described land - marks but the best location for each portal is confirmed by palpation and observation of abdominal wall indentation. A 0° telescope is most commonly used but a 30° telescope allows better visualization in some cases, especially for the dorsal recumbent obliqued technique. Six and eleven mil - limeter diameter cannulas are used depending on tele - scope and instrument size but a combination of the two sizes is common. 8 Laparoscopy 528 Gravity is used to move the organs to expose the kidneys. On the right side, the duodenum and liver interfere with kidney exposure and dissection. For the left kidney, the spleen and colon are the interfering organs. A power tilt table greatly facilitates patient positioning. After explora- tion of the accessible abdominal structures, kidney dissec- tion is initiated by freeing the kidney from its attachment to the abdominal wall with incision of the dorsal perito - neum at the junction of the abdominal wall and kidney with sharp dissection using scissors and monopolar elec- trocautery as needed or with a vessel sealing device depend- ing on vascularity of the tissue. This incision is extended cranially and caudally as the kidney is reflected away from the abdominal wall. Transection of the hepatorenal ligament is performed on the right side and this avascular structure is cut with Metzenbaum scissors. In normal kid- neys, there is little vascularity and minimal attachment of the dorsal aspect of the kidney to the retroperitoneal tissue. Perirenal vascularity and the strength of kidney attach- ment changes with pathology and can be substantial. The hilar structures are exposed, and the artery, vein, and ure - ter are isolated with sharp and blunt dissection as indi- cated. There is significant variability of anatomy involving the renal artery and vein requiring careful dissection to identify these variants. A vessel sealing device is used for vascular occlusion and transection except in giant breeds where the vessels are greater than 7 mm in diameter. A sin- gle activation of a computer-controlled vessel sealing device in one position on the vessel produces the desired vessel wall fusion for maximum seal strength and is a more secure vessel occlusion than can be achieved with liga- tures. Vascular clips are inadequate for safe occlusion of the renal artery. Multiple activations of the vessel sealing device at one site or side-by-side activations may actually weaken the seal. After the artery and vein have been sealed and divided, cranial traction is applied to the ureter and periureteral dissection is extended caudally to the ureter - ovesicular junction. Ligatures or Endoclips are applied to the ureter with two clips or ligatures on the ureteral seg - ment left in the patient and the most distant occlusion as close to the bladder wall as possible. A clip or ligature is also placed on the ureter proximal to the transection site or the end of the ureter is grasped transversely with dissecting forceps and the ureter is used for traction to manipulate the freed kidney. The kidney is placed in a specimen retrieval bag or extracted directly through an enlarged portal. A specimen retrieval bag is recommended for contami- nated or neoplastic kidneys. Examination of the surgery site is done to ensure complete hemostasis prior to exiting the abdomen. These techniques with the lateral or ventral obliqued positions approach the kidney through the peritoneal space or transperitoneal. A retroperitoneal technique is employed in human surgery and equals the transperitoneal approach in advantages over open surgery. Both minimally invasive approaches are superior to open surgery. 8.8.15 Laparoscopic Adrenalectomy Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the procedure of choice over open surgery for appropriately selected adrenal lesions (Ko et al. 2018; Mayhew et al. 2014; Naan et al. 2013; Peláez et al. 2008; Pitt et al. 2016) and in many ways is easier to perform than open adrenalectomy for the experienced Figure 8.508 Thorough lavage of the surgery site is done after excision of the cyst-free wall and extraction of the excised tissue from the abdomen. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 529 minimally invasive surgeon. Case selection is critical to success of this surgery and preoperative imaging with contrast CT and ultrasonography or both are needed to define the size and location of lesions with particular atten - tion to vascular invasion. Lesions up to 4 cm diameter in the cranial pole without vascular invasion are the best cases for laparoscopic removal. Larger lesions have been successfully resected with laparoscopy but are more challenging. Right adrenalectomy is stated to be more challenging than left side lesions but there is typically less fat around the right adrenal gland making some aspects of dissection easier. Caudal pole masses may be more difficult to remove due to close proximity to the renal veins. A thorough knowledge of adrenal anatomy especially of the surrounding blood ves - sels is required before approaching adrenalectomy laparo - scopically. Addition of vessel sealing devices has greatly advanced surgical technique for both open and minimally invasive adrenalectomy. Early laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed with Liga clips and was far more difficult and time consuming than after vessel sealing devices were available. Preparation for conversion to an open surgery is more important with laparoscopic adrenalectomies than with many other minimally invasive surgeries. Repositioning of the patient for conversion may or may not be possible as uncontrolled hemorrhage is the most critical indication for conversion to open surgery. Patients positioned in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table that is angled to one side for lapa - roscopic access to one of the adrenal glands are easily repo - sitioned into dorsal recumbency, allowing a ventral midline laparotomy to be performed. Laparoscopic approaches to the adrenal glands using lateral or sternal recumbent posi - tions are common and a vertical flank incision immediately caudal to the last rib may be required. Preparation and draping for conversion using this approach is strongly recommended. Lateral recumbency is commonly used for unilateral adrenalectomies with the involved gland on the upper - most side. Sophisticated preoperative imaging is required to accurately determine the location of adrenal pathology. With the patient in lateral recumbency, the surgical team stands on the ventral side of the patient with the monitor directly across the table on the dorsal side (Figure 8.510). 8 Laparoscopy 530 A power tilt table is an asset if rotation beyond lateral is needed to move organs out of the way. Clipping, prepara - tion, and draping are done to allow access to the entire lateral abdominal wall. The area of abdominal wall expo - sure required for laparoscopic portal placement is greater than that needed for the open surgical approach with a vertical flank incision. Lateral recumbency is not recom - mended for resection of bilateral adrenal lesions as the time required for repositioning the patient makes anesthe - sia time excessive, increasing patient risk. If the lateral approach is used for bilateral lesions, it is suggested that the two procedures be staged with sufficient time for recovery between the two surgeries. Sternal recumbency is an alternative position for laparo - scopic adrenalectomy and is preferred when bilateral resec- tion is indicated or if examination of both adrenal glands is indicated prior to determining the side to be removed. Clipping for this approach is from dorsal to ventral midline for unilateral adrenalectomy and for bilateral surgery a full circumferential clip is performed. After positioning on the operating table, preparation and draping of one or both sides are done at the beginning of the procedure to allow rapid transition to the second side for bilateral procedures. A power tilt table is an asset when using this position both for the laparoscopic approach but more importantly if con- version is indicated a tilted sternal position improves visual access. Sternal positioning also requires that the pelvis and sternum support the patient’s weight allowing the abdo - men to expand more easily with insufflation. Both lateral and sternal techniques use a Veress needle to initiate abdominal insufflation. Portals for lateral recumbency place the telescope lateral to the umbilicus at the junction of the ventral and middle thirds of the abdominal wall with operative portals placed caudal to the last rib, cranial to the hind leg at the junction of the ventral and dorsal halves of the abdominal wall, and dor - sal to the caudal portal at the dorsal extent of the lateral abdominal wall (Figure 8.511). Availability of both 0 and 30° laparoscopes provides optimum visibility for adrenal - ectomies and switching between the two may be indicated for stages of the surgery for both lateral and sternal posi - tions. Portals for sternal recumbency are placed more dor - sally with the camera portal below the lumbar muscles, cranial to the kidney on the left side, and at the level of the kidney on the right side (Figure 8.512). Operative por - tals for sternal recumbency are placed slightly ventral to the telescope portal with the cranial portal immediately caudal to the last rib and the caudal portal approximately halfway between the telescope portal and the hind leg (Figure 8.512). Variation of portal placement is deter - mined by abdominal wall palpation and observation of abdominal wall indentation. Telescope, cannula, and instrument size are dependent on patient size with limitations based on available instru - mentation. Larger portals may be required for vessel sealing devices, Endoclip applicators, and for adrenal extraction. Both blunt and sharp dissections are used for adrenalecto - mies and an appropriate selection of minimally invasive surgical instruments is required. Atraumatic grasping for - ceps are essential, but many adrenal lesions are friable and there is a lack of substantial periadrenal tissue to allow adrenal manipulation with grasping forceps. Blunt instru - ments and “peanuts” providing manipulation by pushing rather than pulling may be more effective. Dissecting fur - ther away from the adrenal gland leaving more attached tis - sue to use as handles for grasping facilitates adrenal manipulation. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 531 important vascular structures more difficult. An additional important instrument for adrenalectomies is an irrigation and suction cannula as lavage is used to improve visual access to the dissection site. On the left side, the spleen and kidney interfere with visualization, manipulation, and dis - section of the adrenal gland. The spleen is best moved with gravity by adjustment of the tilt angle of the table, but a fan retractor is used if indicated. The kidney is retracted cau - dally if needed from the additional caudo-dorsal operative portal using a fan, hook, or “J” retractor. On the right side, the liver and kidney obscure visualization and access to the adrenal gland. This is especially true with liver enlarge - ment. The first step in improving access is to transect the hepatorenal ligament that is seen extending from the liver to the right kidney as an avascular band of translucent tis - sue (Figure 8.513). This is cut with scissors as hemostasis is not generally needed (Figure 8.513). Transection of this structure allows caudal retraction of the kidney and greatly improves access to the right adrenal gland. Dissection technique for the adrenal glands varies depending on the extent of increased vascular supply, den- sity of periadrenal tissue reaction, and the size and charac- ter of adrenal tumors. Adrenal tissue and adrenal tumors are friable and are easily fractured. Careful sharp dissec- tion is used wherever possible (Figure 8.514) with use of monopolar or bipolar electrocautery. Blunt dissection is employed primarily when using a vessel sealing device where vascular supply is sufficient to require this level of hemostasis. A 5 mm handpiece with a narrow tip is used to gently isolate tissue for sealing and division. The phrenicoabdominal vein is readily visible crossing the ventral surface of the adrenal gland (Figure 8.117). This vessel is dissected free of surrounding tissue lateral to the adrenal gland and is occluded with two Endoclips (Figure 8.515) and transected between the clips with scis - sors (Figure 8.516) with sufficient vessel remaining to use as a handle for manipulation of the adrenal gland. The phrenicoabdominal can also be sealed and transected with the vessel sealing device. The adrenal mass is sepa - rated from the vena cava with sharp dissection (Figure 8.517) taking advantage of magnification pro - duced by the video system. The phrenicoabdominal arte - rial trunk originates from the aorta and crosses the dorsal surface of the adrenal gland supplying its cranial pole. This vessel is divided, sealed, and taken with the adrenal gland or separated from the adrenal gland with control of bleeding from branches supplying the adrenal gland (Figure 8.518). Dissection of the dorsal surface of the cau - dal pole is done with sharp dissection using the phrenico - abdominal vein as a grasping site to elevate the adrenal gland and provide visibility and access (Figure 8.519). Caudal pole tumors require care due to their close prox - imity to the renal veins and arteries. Adrenalectomy is completed by isolation of the origin of the phrenicoab - dominal vein (Figure 8.520), application of Endoclips for occlusion (Figure 8.521), and transection of the vessel peripheral to the Endoclips with Metzenbaum scissors (Figure 8.522) leaving all the clips on the patient side of the cut (Figure 8.523). The vessel at this location is also occluded and divided with a vessel sealing device. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 533 8.8.16 Laparoscopic Portosystemic Shunt Occlusion Congenital single extrahepatic shunts are amenable to mini - mally invasive surgical correction (Miller 2011). Intrahepatic shunts and acquired portosystemic shunts are not correcta - ble laparoscopically or have not yet been approached with this technique. This is not a procedure for the beginning endoscopic surgeon. Open surgical techniques for single extrahepatic shunts have used techniques that gradually occlude the shunt including Ameroid constrictors or cello - phane placed around the shunt. Ameroid constrictors slowly occlude the shunt by expansion of the constrictor material due to absorption of body fluids and stimulation of fibrous tissue reaction. Cellophane bands cause a fibrous tissue reaction to occlude the shunt. Simple ligation of shunts is no longer recommended due to the risk of portal hypertension seen with acute occlusion of the shunt. Cellophane is the preferred material for laparoscopic shunt occlusion, but the material is not a medical-grade product and even though it has worked without reported complications secondary to the material itself it is time to have an actual medical device. An alternative is to redesign an Ameroid constrictor-type device that can be implanted with minimally invasive technique. Preoperative imaging to accurately define the shunt is essential to effective minimally invasive shunt occlusion. This is critical both to determine if the shunt is of a type amenable to a laparoscopic approach and to define its loca- tion for operative planning. Ultrasound has been used extensively to diagnose portosystemic shunts and to define their configuration. Contrast CT studies and C arm fluoros - copy are currently recommended with 3D reconstruction used to provide more information. Operating room setup places the monitor at the head of the patient and the surgical team caudal to the patient (Figure 8.524). The entire ventral abdomen is clipped, pre - pared, and draped to provide exposure for multiple widely spaced portals and for conversion to a full-length ventral midline abdominal incision. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a powered tilting operating table with end- to-end and side-to-side tilting capabilities. An umbilical tel - escope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. Operating portal placement location is dependent on shunt location with left, right, or bilateral portal options. Initially, two paramedian operative portals are placed at the level of the telescope portal and lateral to the rectus abdominis muscles (Figure 8.525). These portals are used for exploration of the abdomen to confirm shunt location as well as to define its size and configuration. Using the tilt table, the abdomen is explored in dorsal recumbency with the table flat and with the head elevated, with the table variably tilted to left lateral recumbency, and with the table variably tilted to right lateral recumbency. The stomach interferes with visualization and access to the areas of inter - est and retraction is necessary using fan retractors, intra- abdominal tissue hangers, or multiple stay sutures placed through the abdominal wall and into the gastric wall. Stay sutures are the simplest, easiest, and most effective tech - nique for gastric retraction. Two sutures are typically suffi - cient, but more can be used as needed. A completely empty stomach is essential. If there is any residual food, fluid, or gas, a stomach tube is placed with suction applied. After the shunt has been located and its configuration defined, additional portals are placed on the left or right sides as indicated (Figure 8.526). Location of the portals is determined by abdominal palpation with observation of abdominal wall indentation with the telescope. An addi- tional paramedian portal is placed on the side of the shunt craniolateral to the initial operative portal on that side. Optimum portal placement for triangulation facilitates dis - section and band placement. With two active operative portals on one side of the abdomen, improved triangula- tion may be achieved by moving the telescope to the initial operative portal on that side and placing an operative instrument into the original telescope portal (Figure 8.527). Tissue around the shunt is typically translucent and avascular. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 535 using sharp dissection with Metzenbaum scissors. Blunt dissection using curved or right-angle dissectors is also effective. A smooth monofilament suture attached to the cellophane band is passed around the shunt vessel and the cellophane is pulled into position around the shunt. Tension is applied to sutures on both ends of the cello - phane and Endoclips are applied to fix the two arms of the cellophane around the shunt. Extracorporeal or intracor - poreal knots are also used to oppose and secure the ends of the cellophane. Occlusion or even partial attenuation of the shunt with the cellophane at the time of surgery is avoided. Prior to exiting the abdomen, careful inspection for a dry surgery site is done. Exploration of the remainder of the abdomen is also indicated to look for any sign of shunt occlusion causing interference with blood flow to the intes - tines. Postoperative problems and complications seen fol- lowing laparoscopic portosystemic shunt attenuation are more likely to be the same as for an open surgical proce - dure rather than due to the minimally invasive approach. Conversion to open surgery is elected if the shunt cannot be adequately identified with minimally invasive tech- nique, access to the shunt cannot be achieved, placement of cellophane is not possible, cellophane placement is not acceptable, the shunt is inadvertently occluded with the cellophane band and cannot be removed or modified safely, or if there is hemorrhage that obscures dissection or risks compromising the patient. 8.8.17 Laparoscopic Splenectomy Minimally invasive splenectomy is indicated for primary splenic pathology and for small splenic masses (Collard et al. 2010; Khalaj et al. 2012; Mayhew et al. 2018; Petroianu et al. 2004; Shaver et al. 2015; Wright et al. 2016). Splenomegaly and large splenic masses are currently indications for an open surgical approach. A specific division for minimally invasive vs an open approach has not been defined. Operating room arrangement is with the surgeon and assistant on the right side of the patient, the monitor on the left side of the patient, and the patient in dorsal recumbency (Figure 8.528). Dorsal recumbency is used with clipping, preparation, and draping being the same as for an open splenectomy allowing for a full-length ventral abdominal midline incision. A powered table allowing side-to-side and end-to-end tilting is helpful for this procedure. An initial telescope portal is placed at the umbilicus using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. Exploration of the abdomen is done to determine if minimally invasive splenectomy is feasible or if conversion is indicated. One or more operative portals may need to be placed to answer this question. 8 Laparoscopy 536 the same pattern as for two-port ovariectomy using the Mouret needle or for three-port ovariectomy with a cranial portal midway between the umbilicus and xiphoid and a caudal portal midway between the umbilicus and the pubis (Figure 8.385). Multiple other portal sites have been reported (Collard et al. 2010; Khalaj et al. 2012), use of a SILS port has been recommended (Khalaj et al. 2012; Mayhew et al. 2018), as has laparoscopic-assisted technique with a wound retractor (Wright et al. 2016). Manipulation of the spleen to expose the hilus is required to perform a laparoscopic splenectomy. This is done using the side of a blunt probe, a fan retractor, or the side of any minimally invasive dissector or grasper. A vessel sealing device is absolutely essential for this procedure and will seal all splenic arteries and veins in all patients except the largest giant dogs. Other techniques for hemostasis are too cumbersome, time consuming, expensive, and provide less secure vascular occlusion. Using a vessel sealing device has also become standard procedure for open splenectomy greatly reducing operative times and intraoperative or post - operative bleeding episodes. The vascular seal produced with the LigaSure or other vessel sealing devices is more secure than any other technique. The spleen is manipulated to expose the hilus and the vessel sealing device is placed on any accessible portion of the hilus to initiate transection. There is no need to start at one end or to transect continuously from one end to the other. Starting in the middle of the hilus and working either or both directions works well by attacking the most accessible tissues as the procedure progresses. When the splenic hilus has been totally transected, a specimen retrieval bag is introduced for extraction to minimize the chance for seeding of neoplastic disease. A wound retrac- tor/protector can also be used after the hilus has been tran- sected and insufflation is no longer needed. Abdominal inspection for any residual bleeding is done prior to exiting the abdomen. 8.8.18 Laparoscopic Herniorrhaphy Inguinal hernias are ideally suited to minimally invasive repair as they are typically small with easily reducible Surgeon Assistant Anesthesia Machine Video Cart Sterile Table Setup Figure 8.528 Operating room and patient position for laparoscopic splenectomy. Symptomatic inguinal hernias contain - ing strangulated compromised, necrotic, or septic tissue are managed better with open surgery. Acute traumatic hernias are also approached with open surgery as insuf - flation extends into the subcutaneous tissue resulting in insufflation of the entire patient. A two-stage approach to perineal hernia repair has been reported using laparos - copy for cystopexy and colopexy combined with a tradi - tional open surgical approach for closure of the hernia ring (Brissot et al. 2004; Gilley et al. 2003). Selected dia - phragmatic hernias are repairable with a minimally inva - sive approach (Monnet and Fransson 2015) but insufflation pressures below 5 cm water must be used to avoid excessive lung compression. Inguinal hernias are approached with the patient in dor - sal recumbency on a tilt table with the monitor at the foot of the patient, and with the surgeon and assistant on oppo - site sides of the table. This is the same arrangement as for laparoscopic cryptorchid castration (Figure 8.426). The patient is clipped, prepared, and draped to allow placement of multiple portals and to allow conversion for direct expo - sure of the hernia with a full-length ventral abdominal midline incision if indicated. An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen insufflated. Patient is tilted to a head down position and this causes the abdominal organs to slide cranially out of the surgery site. Exploration confirms operability of the hernia with minimally invasive technique and two para- median instrument portals are placed lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle at the level of the umbilicus (Figure 8.525) The inguinal ring or rings are examined (Figures 8.56–8.60) to identify the hernia or hernias (Figure 8.136). Hernia contents are reduced using atrau- matic grasping forceps for traction. The hernia ring is closed using intracorporeal suturing technique to place a purse string suture around the hernia, interrupted sutures, cruciate sutures, or a continuous suture pattern is used depending on the size and configuration of the hernia. Hernia repair staples and surgical mesh products are avail- able from the human field but their use in small animals has not been reported. 8.8.19 Laparoscopic Urethral Occluder Implantation Hydraulic urethral occluders are one of the options for management of urinary incontinence. They were origi- nally designed for open surgical implantation, but laparo - scopic insertion has been evaluated in cadavers (Luckring et al. 2016) and has been performed by the author. The occluders were modified to allow minimally invasive inser - tion by turning the attachment of the occluder actuating tubing 90° so that it comes off the end of the occluder cuff rather off the side to allow it to be passed through an 11 mm laparoscopy cannula. To perform this procedure, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table. The surgeon stands on one side of the table with the assistant on the other side of the table and the monitor is placed at the foot of the table. This is the same arrangement as for cryptorchid castration (Figure 8.426). The patient is clipped, prepared, and draped to allow access to the ventral abdomen for portal placement and for conversion to a full-length ventral abdominal inci - sion if indicated. An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the patient is tilted into a head down position. Bilateral paramedian operative portals are placed approximately halfway from the umbilicus to the pubis and an additional paramedian operative portal is placed on either side cranial to the umbilicus (Figure 8.529). This additional operative portal is used to apply cranial trac - tion to the bladder that facilitates dissection around the ure - thra (Figure 8.530). One of the caudal operative portal cannulas is an 11 mm diameter cannula to allow passage of the occluder cuff. The median ligament of the bladder and its extension caudally ventral to the urethra is cut with a ves - sel sealing device (Figure 8.531) or with Metzenbaum scis - sors using monopolar electrocautery as needed. Sharp dissection is used to cut holes in the translucent avascular lateral ligaments of the bladder where they extend caudally along the urethra and the reflections of peritoneum in the vesicogenital pouch and pubovesical pouch (Figure 8.532). Dissection is continued to establish circumferential access around the urethra for approximately 2 cm caudal to the ure - ters. It is important that this window is placed far enough caudally to avoid the ureters where they enter the bladder. This entrapment interferes with easy access to the bladder. Once the site of portal placement has been established, a skin incision is made the length needed for the procedure to be performed. This incision needs to be long enough for removal of the largest stone or mass in the bladder. 8.8 Minimal ly Invasive AAbominal Surgery 545 The direct percutaneous approach to the bladder is not a laparoscopic-assisted technique but approaches the blad- der directly through the abdominal wall. A version of this procedure, prepubic percutaneous cystoscopy (PPC), was the first approach used for endoscopic access to the bladder in small animal practice (McCarthy and McDermaid 1986). For this original technique, the bladder was distended and a trocar-cannula passed directly through the abdominal wall and through the adjacent bladder wall into the bladder lumen (Figures 6.67–6.71). This technique has the advan- tages of only requiring one telescope system, it is quick and easy, and it works very well for bladder examination. The disadvantages are that additional portals are needed to per - form operative procedures and maintaining multiple por - tals is very difficult. This approach has been replaced with the laparoscopic-assisted technique. A modification of this PPC technique uses a threaded EndoTIP cannula large enough to pass both the telescope and instruments through a single cannula (Runge et al. 2011). The threads on the cannula also help stabilize the bladder on the cannula. Another modification of this percutaneous technique uses a distended bladder with bladder location determined by palpation. A small abdomi- nal wall incision is made to expose a small portion of the bladder wall and a stay suture is placed in the bladder wall or the bladder is grasped with an atraumatic instrument. The bladder is emptied, a small portion of the bladder wall is exteriorized, stay sutures are placed, and a small cystot - omy incision is made. The telescope is then placed in the bladder. From this point, the procedure is the same as for the laparoscopic-assisted technique. Procedures performed in the bladder are presented with cystoscopy in Chapter 6. 8.8.21 Laparoscopic-Assisted Cystopexy Cystopexy is an uncommonly indicated surgery but when needed, is performed effectively with laparoscopic-assisted technique or potentially totally within the abdomen using intracorporeal suturing (Brissot et al. 2004; Gilley et al. 2003). Indications for cystopexy include recurrent bladder herniation after perineal hernia repair and for pel- vic bladders in incontinent female dogs. The concept of this surgery follows the same concept as laparoscopic- assisted gastropexy as laparoscopy is used to visualize and position the bladder with open surgical technique being used to suture the bladder wall to the abdominal wall. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table and the ventral abdomen is clipped, prepared, and draped to provide access to the caudal abdomen for portal place - ment and for conversion to a full-length ventral midline abdominal incision. The surgeon stands on one side of the patient with an assistant on the other side and the monitor is placed at the foot of the patient (Figure 8.426). An umbil- ical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. The patient is tilted into a head down position. The bladder is visualized and a right cranial paramedian operative portal is placed, and a second caudal paramedian operative portal is placed for the cys - topexy based on bladder size and position (Figure 8.561). A 5 mm Babcock forceps is used to grasp the apex of the bladder from the cranial operative portal and traction is applied to the bladder to move it into the desired position. A second operative portal is placed for the cystopexy with its location based on bladder size and position and using abdominal palpation to produce abdominal wall indenta- tion to select the exact location (Figure 8.562). The bladder wall is grasped with Babcock or other atraumatic forceps at Figure 8.561 Portals for laparoscopic-assisted cystopexy. An umbilical telescope portal is placed, and the abdomen insufflated. An initial cranial paramedian operative portal is placed on either side for applying traction to the bladder. A second operative portal is placed based on the site selected for the cystopexy on the same side as the first operative portal. (Source: Illustration by Cindy Cox.) Figure 8.562 Cranial traction is applied to the apex of the bladder from the cranial paramedian portal and a second operative portal is placed with its location selected based on bladder size and location.

A portion of the bladder wall is exteriorized and the cys - topexy procedure is performed with the same steps and technique as for gastropexy. Stay sutures are placed at each end of the desired cystopexy site, a cranio-caudal seromus - cular incision is made between the sutures, a continuous suture of monofilament slowly absorbed suture is placed starting at the center of the medial side of the incision to oppose the bladder incision margin to the abdominal wall incision margin, and is continued circumferentially to its point of origin (Figure 8.564). When healed, this technique produces solid fixation of the bladder to the abdominal wall (Figure 8.565). 8.8.22 Laparoscopic-Assisted Intestinal Feeding T ube Placement Duodenostomy and jejunostomy feeding tubes are placed using laparoscopic-assisted technique to locate the site for tube placement and exteriorizing the desired level of intes - tine through the abdominal wall to insert the tube exter - nally (Rawlings et al. 2002b). The selected bowel segment is identified, the proximal part of the jejunum for jejunos - tomy placement or distal duodenum for duodenostomy tube placement and is exteriorized using technique similar to that used for intestinal biopsy (Figures 8.353–8.358). The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table with the entire ventral abdomen clipped, prepared, and draped for aseptic surgery to allow widely spaced portal placement and to be prepared for conversion to open sur - gery with a full-length ventral midline abdominal incision. The surgical team stands on the right side of the patient with the monitor on the left side of the patient (Figures 8.353 and 8.354). An umbilical telescope portal is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. Two instrument portals are placed so that two grasping forceps can be used to “run” the bowel for exploration and to iden - tify the desired segment of the bowel. One portal is placed cranially on the right side at the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis muscle at the site for tube exit from the abdomen and the other to allow triangulation for bowel manipulation either in a similar position on the left side or on the right side caudal to the telescope portal lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle. An 11 mm trocar-cannula is placed for the right cranial operative portal to facilitate exteriorization of the bowel and two 5 mm atraumatic grasping forceps are used to manipulate the intestines. The location of the bowel for tube placement is grasped on its antimesenteric border, the intestine is pulled up the right cranial paramedian can - nula, and the portal incision is extended using a scalpel blade. With the intestine in contact with the cannula, the intestine, grasp - ing forceps, and cannula are pulled through the abdominal wall simultaneously. Orientation of the intestine is observed so that the feeding tube is placed in the aboral direction. This is easier with the duodenum than the jejunum. A short loop of intestine is exteriorized and stay sutures are placed in the intestinal wall to prevent loss of the intes - tine into the abdominal cavity. A purse-string suture is placed in the antimesenteric border of the intestine. A #11 scalpel blade is used to puncture the intestine at the center of the purse-string suture and a feeding tube is placed into the bowel lumen. The purse string suture is tightened and tied. The exteriorized intestine is returned to the abdominal cav - ity and the stay sutures are used to fix the intestine to the abdominal wall. The abdominal wall portal incision is closed around the tube so that the tube exits through the incision. If the feeding tube is placed when performed in conjunc- tion with other laparoscopic procedures, the feeding tube is done last. This sequence is done because the presence of the intestine attached to the abdominal wall interferes with instrument and organ manipulation, the pneumoperito - neum is lost during this procedure, and entering the intes - tine also contaminates the surgical field. 8.8.23 Laparoscopic-Assisted Gastrostomy Feeding T ube Placement Gastrostomy feeding tubes are placed using gastroscopy whenever possible but if laparoscopy is performed for other reasons, the tube is inserted as part of this surgery (Rawlings et al. 2002b). This procedure is similar to laparo - scopic-assisted gastropexy except an area of the gastric body is exteriorized through the left abdominal wall. The patient is placed in dorsal recumbency on a tilt table with an asymmetrical ventral abdominal preparation extending further dorsally on the left side than on the right. An umbilical telescope port is placed using the Hassan technique and the abdomen is insufflated. A single 11 mm diameter left cranial paramedian operative trocar-cannula is placed caudal to the last rib at the level within its distal third. Five or ten millimeter atraumatic grasping forceps, depending on patient size, are used to grasp the body of the stomach at the selected site for placement of the feeding tube. The stomach wall at this site is exteriorized with the same technique as for gastropexy and for intestinal feeding tube placement. Stay sutures and a purse-string suture are placed in the wall of the stomach. The gastric wall is punc- tured with a #11 scalpel blade in the middle of the purse- string suture and a Foley or Pezzer catheter is introduced into the stomach. If a Foley catheter is used, the balloon is inflated. The purse-string suture is tightened and tied. The stay sutures are used to fix the stomach wall to the body wall. As with intestinal feeding tubes and gastropexy, the gastrostomy feeding tube is the last laparoscopic procedure performed. 8.8.24 Additional Minimally Invasive Abdominal Surgical Procedures The previous edition of this book listed adrenalectomy, ovarian remnant removal, correction of hiatal hernias, pancreatic tumor removal, and nephrectomy as other surgical procedures possible to perform using laparos - copy. These are all being performed today. Surgical lapa- roscopy in small animal practice is limited only by our imagination and instrumentation available to perform additional procedures. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 9.1 Introduction The minimally invasive technique of thoracoscopy allows diagnostic exploratory examination and therapeutic operative procedures to be performed in the chest through 3–10 mm diameter portals without the requirement for a painful and traumatic open thoracotomy. Visualization of intrathoracic structures and pathology is far superior to open surgery because of high intensity light transmission giving excellent illumination, magnification produced by the telescopes and video system, and ability to place the telescope into surgically inaccessible areas. Submacroscopic lesions that elude us with open surgical exploration are easily visualized with thoracoscopy. Organs and tissues deep within the chest are no longer operated in the proverbial hole because the visual field and instruments are moved into the area of the operative site. Structures too small to see are easily magnified and made obvious, which allows accurate lesion identification, sample collection, dissection, hemostasis, and preservation of important structures. Operative stress to the patient is reduced by eliminating the tissue trauma of a thoracotomy and by decreased operative time. Old dogs with pericardial effusion is an excellent example because they are typically active like nothing was done to them within a few hours after minimally invasive pericardial window surgery rather than slowly recovering from a painful sternotomy. Postoperative pain management is greatly facilitated by eliminating the “operative” portion of the equation. Samples for histopathology, culture, and cytology are easily and quickly obtained with thoracoscopy, which started primarily as a diagnostic technique but has evolved into an accepted operative approach for treatment of many conditions in small animal medicine. Surgical procedures currently being performed include pericardial window, subtotal pericardiectomy, partial and total lung lobectomy, foreign body removal, mediastinal mass removal, lymph node removal, thoracic duct occlusion, PDA closure, per - sistent right aortic arch transection, and atrial appendage tumor removal. Laparoscopy and thoracoscopy are very similar in technique, instrumentation requirements, and basic indications but thoracoscopy is easier to perform than laparoscopy, and it is more effective for examining the chest than open thoracotomy. 9.2 Indications Thoracoscopy is indicated whenever more information is needed for diagnosis of intrathoracic pathology than can be obtained with less invasive techniques and when open surgical invasion of the chest is indicated. Specific indications for diagnostic thoracoscopy include pulmonary, mediastinal or hilar masses, primary pulmonary disease, spontaneous pneumothorax, pericardial effusions, pleural effusions including chylothorax, foreign body identification and location, cancer staging, and for assessment of chest trauma (Table 9.1). Minimally invasive thoracic surgery is indicated whenever open thoracic surgery is being considered, and it encompasses most of the commonly performed thoracic surgeries in small animal practice (Table 9.2). Indications for thoracoscopy and minimally invasive thoracic surgery are truly only limited by our operative skill level, instrumentation that we have available, and willingness to expand our ideas and imagination. Management of pleural effusion is greatly facilitated by thoracoscopy and is one of the most common indications for thoracoscopy in human medicine (Jany and Welte 2019; Kastelik 2013; Pereira et al. 2017; Wan et al. 2019; Wang Timothy C. McCarthy Veterinary Minimally Invasive Surgery Training (VetMIST), Beaverton, OR, USA 9 Thoracoscopy

9 Thoracoscopy 554 et al. 2015). Cases with intractable pleural effusion of undetermined origin are definitively diagnosed more easily with thoracoscopy than with any other technique. Pleural pathology is visually assessed using magnification of the telescope and video system, allowing lesions to be accu- rately identified. Truly representative biopsies are taken under direct visualization greatly increasing diagnostic yield and diagnostic accuracy. Submacroscopic inflamma- tory nodules, early metastatic lesions, and mesotheliomas are identified much earlier with thoracoscopy before they have progressed to a size where they can be seen with open surgery. Lung lobe torsion is easily identified with thora- coscopy to confirm the diagnosis and lung lobectomy is performed with minimally invasive technique or with an open thoracotomy. Thoracic duct pathology is evaluated in cases of chylothorax and thoracic duct occlusion is achieved using minimally invasive surgical techniques. The magnifi- cation provided by the telescope greatly enhances visualization of the thoracic duct, allowing the extent and location of thoracic duct pathology to be assessed, the potential for surgical success evaluated, and clips applied for a potentially more successful occlusion. Pericardial effusions are accurately and effectively drained under thoracoscopic guidance and samples col- lected for fluid analysis, cytology, and cultures. Permanent drainage is established by creating a pericardial window on the cranial aspect of the heart using minimally invasive surgical technique (Video 9.1). Instrumentation and tech- nical skills required to perform a pericardial window are only slightly more than those required for diagnostic thora- coscopy and sample collection. It is possible to create a pericardial window with minimally invasive technique in patients using standard open surgical instruments such as Alice forceps and Metzenbaum scissors, and this was per - formed by the author in a situation where a laparoscope was available but MIS instrumentation was not. Spontaneous pneumothorax management is greatly facilitated using thoracoscopy to establish the exact site of air leakage and to determine the extent of pulmonary involvement. Emphysematous degeneration of the lung is evaluated and determined if the lesions are localized and resectable (Video 9.2) or diffuse and inoperable involving multiple lung lobes. An unnecessary thoracotomy is avoided in cases of diffuse emphysematous pulmonary dis - ease when surgical resection is not beneficial. Spontaneous pneumothorax caused by migrating foreign bodies that have penetrated into the pleural space have been located and removed, and air leakage is controlled without an open surgery (Video 9.3). Accurately locating the site of air leak - age and the site of lesions with thoracoscopy allows accu- rate decisions on surgical intervention such as the determination if resection can be completed with mini- mally invasive technique, or if required more effective planning of an open surgical approach. The most difficult aspect of managing spontaneous pneumothorax is deter - mining the side of the air leakage. Because of this, median sternotomy has been the recommended approach for oper - ation of spontaneous pneumothorax cases because it pro - vides exposure of both hemithoraces. If the side of the lesion is definitively determined with thoracoscopy and if a minimally invasive resection is not possible, an easier less painful lateral thoracotomy is performed decreasing oper - ating time, decreasing morbidity, and facilitating complete lobectomy if indicated. An unnecessary thoracotomy is avoided in cases of diffuse emphysematous pulmonary dis - ease when surgical resection is not beneficial. 9.3 Thoracoscopy Instrumentation 555 does not solve the problem, a “blood patch” is employed. Blood patch treatment of various forms of pneumothorax in humans is an effective treatment (Andreetti et al. 2007; Blanco et al. 1996; Cagirici et al. 1998; Dugan et al. 2017; Dumire et al. 1992; Evman et al. 2016; Lang–Lazdunski and Coonar 2004; Zhang et al. 2019) but results are less effective in our patients (Oppenheimer et al. 2014). One considera- tion for this difference is that human patients with pneumo - thorax are placed on continuous underwater seal drainage with suction, whereas in veterinary patients, intermittent hand suction with a syringe is common practice. Intermittent suction, whether with a syringe or with chest suction sys - tems, is inadequate to achieve the same result. Lung biopsies are not commonly performed but are indi- cated for assessment of primary pulmonary disease, pulmo - nary nodules or masses, and areas of undefined pulmonary density. Lung biopsies taken with thoracoscopy have tradi- tionally been performed using loop ligatures (Adamiak et al. 2008; Faunt et al. 1998a), linear staplers (Marvel and Monnet 2013), or assisted techniques with standard open surgical closure. A 10 mm diameter LigaSure vessel sealing device was shown to be safe and effective for taking small peripheral biopsies (Mayhew et al. 2012) but not for resec- tion of larger segments of lung lobes. A much easier, faster, and less expensive but safe technique has been tested (Ben– Isaac and Simmons 1975) in a series of human clinical cases (Boutin et al. 1982) and has been employed in dogs and cats by the author. This technique uses 5 mm diameter cup biopsy forceps and the same procedure as for obtaining liver biopsies. Air leakage and bleeding from biopsy sites using this technique are too insignificant to be measured. Sample size using this technique is sufficient for evaluation of dif- fuse pulmonary disease with adequate tissue to preserve pulmonary architecture greatly increasing diagnostic yield. Small focal lesions are also selectively biopsied to identify neoplastic or inflammatory disease. Thoracoscopy is particularly useful for diagnosing and planning surgical intervention or medical management of thoracic neoplasia (Balsa and Culp 2019). Examination, biopsy, tumor staging, and determining surgical resectabil- ity are achieved accurately by determining location, local invasion, lymph node involvement, and differentiating solitary verses disseminated disease. Visually directed biopsies ensure representative histopathology greatly increasing diagnostic sensitivity. Using thoracoscopy to determine if a neoplastic process is surgically resectable without performing a thoracotomy avoids subjecting the patient to an unnecessary major surgery. Application of minimally invasive surgical techniques allows removal of many mediastinal masses and removal of many pulmonary masses by partial or total lung lobectomy. If the lesions are not amenable to minimally invasive surgical removal or if the extent or location of the lesions is technically beyond the skill level of the surgeon, then an open surgical inter - vention is more accurately planned. Patent ductus arteriosus occlusion or division (Borenstein et al. 2004) and persistent right aortic arch division have been successfully performed with minimally invasive tech- nique (Macphail et al. 2001; Townsend et al. 2016; Nucci et al. 2018). Thoracoscopy has been used in emergency management of chest trauma cases with hemothorax, pneumothorax, or extensive pulmonary contusions. The need for surgical intervention to control bleeding, air leakage, or for resec- tion of devitalized pulmonary tissue is determined. In some cases, the problem has been definitively resolved with minimally invasive technique or it is determined that conservative management will be effective. When open surgery is indicated, the surgical approach that will provide the best access to the lesions is selected, facilitating the operative procedure. These indications are by no means a complete list and are expanding as application of thoracoscopy in small ani- mal practice evolves. Diagnostic thoracoscopy in lieu of an open exploratory thoracotomy is as strong an indication and as much of an application of minimally invasive tech- nique as is major thoracic minimally invasive surgical pro - cedure. Procedures such as video-assisted thoracoscopy for intervertebral disk fenestration have been evaluated for application in dogs (Remedios et al. 1995). Further incor - poration of diagnostic thoracoscopy and minimally inva- sive thoracic surgery into veterinary medicine will continue to expand the indications for thoracoscopy. 9.3 Thoracoscopy Instrumentation Instrumentation needed for thoracoscopy is essentially the same as that used for laparoscopy with a few important exceptions. Thoracoscopy in small animal practice is performed with the same hand instruments, vessel sealing devices, EndoGIA staplers, and endoclips that are used for laparoscopy. Additional required equipment for thoracoscopy are an anesthetic ventilator and a chest tube with an active underwater seal system for postoperative pleural drainage. Additional optional instruments include an abdominal insufflator, thoracic portal trocar–cannulas that are shorter without a valve or gasket, and telescopes with a 30° viewing angle. 9.3.1 T elescopes Almost any rigid telescope usable for laparoscopy is suita- ble for thoracoscopy (Figures 2.26, 2.28, and 2.30) but 30°

The most common telescopes used for thora- coscopy in small animals are a 10 mm diameter 30° laparo - scope, a 5 mm diameter 30° laparoscope, a 3.0 mm diameter 0° laparoscope, and the 2.7 mm diameter 30° MPRT (Figure 2.30). Additional telescopes that work well for thoracoscopy are the 10 mm diameter ENDOCAMELEON (Figure 2.28), 30° 4.0 mm diameter cystoscope, a 30° 4.0 mm diameter arthroscope, and a 4.0 mm diameter ENODOCAMELEON. An important feature to consider when selecting a tel- escope for thoracoscopy is the 30° visual angle or angle of view (Figure 2.27). Most laparoscopes are 0° tele - scopes that look straight ahead with the axis of the vis - ual field centered on the axis of the telescope. This provides the truest image with the least image distortion and the least operator disorientation. This factor is very important for a beginner endoscopist performing opera- tive procedures. Thirty-degree telescopes facilitate thoracoscopy because the ribs of the rigid chest wall interfere with positioning the telescope. Additional advantages of this angled view are that structures can be visualized, even when they are out of the axis of the tel- escope, and the field of view is greatly enlarged by rotat - ing the telescope to project the 30° angle in all directions around the axis of the telescope. Thirty-degrees of angle produces little distortion or disorientation and the endoscopist has the sensation of looking straight ahead. Visual angles above 30° cause greater disorientation and are typically not needed or recommended for thoracos - copy. Introduction of the ENDOCAMELEON with its variable viewing angle may change this recommenda- tion. Both 0° and 30° telescopes are used for thoracos - copy with interchanging between the two during the same procedure. A 5 mm diameter, 30° angle of view, and 30 cm long laparoscope is the most common telescope used for thoracoscopy, which works in almost all of our small animal patients (Table 9.3). For cats and small dogs, the 2.7 mm diameter 30° MPRT is commonly used (Table 9.3) with the 3.0 mm 0° laparoscope or a 4.0 mm 30° arthroscope being alternatives (Table 9.3). A 10 mm diameter 30° laparoscope is an option for large to giant dogs (Table 9.3). There is no defined size separation for application of each of these telescopes and the 5 mm tel- escope can be used through almost the full range of small animal patients. Limitations of these telescopes are present at both ends of the size spectrum. Smaller telescopes transmit less light and are less effective in large patients. The 2.7 mm MPRT (18 cm), the 3.0 mm laparoscope (14 cm), and the 4.0 mm arthroscope (18 cm) are shorter than the standard 30 cm long 5 mm and 10 mm telescopes making their use in very small patients easier. The smaller shorter telescopes limit access to some areas of the thorax in larger dogs but this can be partially overcome by careful attention to tele - scope portal placement. Physical size of the 10 mm tel- escope is a problem with the narrow intercostal space in cats and small dogs. The 5 mm diameter telescope has the widest range of patient application for small animal thoracoscopy and will function adequately for the larg - est dogs to cats and small dogs. Telescopes commonly used for thoracoscopy do not have operative or biopsy channels although the 10 mm operating laparoscope has been used for diagnostic proce - dures. Additional chest wall portals are typically created for operative procedures, for sample collection, or for manipulation. Operating laparoscopes with a biopsy chan- nel are available as 10 mm 0° telescopes and are usable for thoracoscopy but have limitations so they are not com- monly used.

9.3 Thoracoscopy Instrumentation 557 9.3.2 Cannulas Cannulas specific for thoracoscopy are available as reusa- ble (Figure 9.1 and Table 9.4) and disposable (Figure 9.2 and Table 9.5) versions. Cannulas specific for thoracoscopy are different than those used for laparoscopy. The simplest form of thoracoscopy uses a semi-open pneumothorax technique without insufflation where an airtight seal is not required, and the cannulas do not have to have a valve or gasket allowing air to move freely through the cannulas. Distances from the chest wall to the organs are frequently less in the thorax than in the abdomen so thoracoscopy cannulas are shorter than laparoscopy cannulas. Some thoracoscopy cannulas are flexible allowing conformation to the adjacent ribs. Laparoscopy cannulas (Figures 2.38, 2.39, 2.40, and Table 8.8) are commonly used in small animal practice for thoracoscopy with their valve assembly and gasket removed to provide an open cannula for the semi-open pneumotho - rax technique. For thoracoscopy, shorter versions of lapa- roscopy trocar–cannulas are selected as longer laparoscopy cannulas are cumbersome to use for thoracoscopy because of their length when placed through the lateral chest wall. Standard length laparoscopy cannulas work well for the paraxiphoid portal. Insufflation is occasionally employed for thoracoscopy, and with this technique, laparoscopy cannulas are used with their valve and gaskets assemblies attached. A cannula is required for telescope portals, especially at the paraxiphoid site, but cannulas at lateral operative portals are optional when the semi-open pneumothorax technique is used. Operative portals on the lateral chest wall are established and maintained effectively without a can - nula by performing a mini thoracotomy and passing instru - ments directly through these small incisions. A cannula is used for the telescope portal for thoracoscopy to allow the telescope to be passed into the pleural space without getting the lens dirty by contact with chest wall tissue. This cannula also allows the initial pneumothorax to form. Sharp and blunt trocars supplied with laparoscopy cannulas are used for thoracoscopy cannula placement. A blunt obturator is recommended for initial entry into the thorax to reduce the risk of damaging thoracic viscera at the time of cannula placement before a pneumothorax has been created. Once the pneumothorax is established and a camera is placed to allow visualization of the thoracic wall, sharp trocars are used for additional portal placement. Thoracoscopy cannu - las do not have significant advantages over laparoscopy cannulas for the paraxiphoid telescope portal. Since an airtight seal is not needed for many thoracos - copy procedures, direct passage of instrumentation through a mini-thoracotomy incision without a cannula is as effective, and in many times, less cumbersome than using a cannula. If insufflation is needed for a procedure, operative cannulas are placed. 9 Thoracoscopy 558 9.3.3 Operative and Sample Collection Instruments Laparoscopic sample collection and operative instruments are applicable to thoracoscopy. A basic instrumentation set for thoracoscopy is the same as for laparoscopy and includes biopsy forceps, grasping forceps, dissecting forceps, right angle forceps, scissors, a palpation probe, and a fluid aspira - tion or combination aspiration–irrigation cannula. This set of instruments will allow a wide variety of samples to be collected and operative procedures to be performed. Solid tissues and lung biopsies are obtained for histopathology and impression cytology. Liquid samples are harvested for fluid analysis, cytology, and for bacterial or fungal cultures. The above instruments and Tru-cut biopsy needles are also used effectively for obtaining biopsy samples. Additional instrumentation required for more advanced minimally invasive thoracic surgery includes pre-tied suture loops, clip applicators, tissue retractors, tissue retrieval bags, linear EndoGIA staplers, lasers, monopolar and bipolar rad - iofrequency electrocautery, computerized radiofrequency vessel sealing devices, and harmonic scissors. As the level of knowledge and experience increases, and skill develops, the procedures available will expand and instrumentation needs will also increase. Fortunately, the list of instruments avail - able for minimally invasive surgery is endless. Almost every instrument available for open surgery has been developed for minimally invasive application. Standard surgical instruments can also be used for some thoracoscopy diagnostic and operative procedures. An air - tight seal at the portal sites is not required for most thora- coscopy, distance to many lesions is relatively short, and mini-thoracotomy operative portals can be used to provide access with Metzenbaum scissors, hemostats, thumb forceps, sutures, and standard surgical suction tips for tissue manipu - lation, sample collection, and some operative procedures. Specialized endotracheal tubes and endobronchial block - ers specifically designed for one lung ventilation are used when this technique is needed to perform certain thoraco - scopic surgical procedures such as lung lobectomy (Pascoe and Mayhew 2015). Standard veterinary endotracheal tubes can be used and placed “too deep” for standard intubation but deep enough to achieve selective main stem bronchial intubation on one side. Endobronchial blockers are also used in combination with standard endotracheal tubes to selectively occlude specific areas of the lungs. These techniques are difficult to employ requir - ing an anesthesiologist experienced with one lung ventila- tion. Low pressure pleural insufflation has been used effectively in people, horses, and pigs to achieve the same result as one lung ventilation and is easily employed with- out special instrumentation or skills (Bohaychuk-Preuss et al. 2017; Caso et al. 2018; El-Dawlatly et al. 2003; Okamura et al. 2016; Peden and Prys-Roberts 1993; Wong et al. 1995). In dogs, intrapleural pressures of 2–5 cm water are tolerated (Daly et al. 2002; Polis et al. 2002). Clinical application of pleural insufflation by the author in dogs and cats as confirmed that it is effective in collapsing lungs to create sufficient space to perform surgical procedures typically requiring one lung ventilation. The advantages of this technique are that it is simple and easy to perform, pressures can be adjusted to the level tolerated by the patient, and pressures can be quickly varied depending on the needs of the patient and surgeon. A surgical table that tilts in multiple directions greatly facilitates both diagnostic thoracoscopy and minimally invasive thoracic surgery (Figures 2.20–2.25). Gravity is the best retractor for minimally invasive surgery and using a table that tilts in all four directions is a huge asset. A table with an electrically powered tilt system that is controlled with a joystick and accessible from the sterile field is avail- able for small animal application (Figures 2.23–2.25). This table allows for easy repositioning of the patient during procedures, which takes advantage of gravity for tissue and organ retraction. Equipment for postoperative management of the pleural space is needed when performing thoracoscopy. Chest tubes and underwater seal suction devices for thoracos - copy are the same as for open surgical procedures. Pleural space management following thoracoscopy is no less important than with open surgery. 9.4 Thoracoscopy General T echnique 9.4.1 Patient Preparation Preparation of patients for thoracoscopy is essentially the same as for a standard open thoracotomy. Anesthetic considerations are also similar to those for an open thoracotomy when performing diagnostic thoracoscopy and simpler minimally invasive thoracic operative procedures. A cuffed endotracheal tube, intermittent positive pressure breathing, adequate monitoring, and supportive treatment are employed. With more sophisticated and complex operative procedures, using one lung ventilation or pleural insufflation may be required. The area of the chest wall that is shaved, prepared, and draped for aseptic surgery is as large or larger for thoracoscopy than the area that would be used for an open thoracotomy. A sufficiently wide area of the chest wall is prepared to allow placement of the camera portal, two or more triangulated operative portals, and a chest drain tube. Preparation is also designed to allow conversion to an open thoracotomy without the need for re-draping. This is strongly recommended so that, if the diagnostic evaluation determines that an open thoracotomy is indicated or if emergency conversion is required during a minimally inva- sive surgical procedure, the transfer is accomplished quickly, effectively, and aseptically. Preparation for conver - sion is done by ensuring that an adequate area is shaved, prepared, and draped for a thoracotomy incision, and sur - gical instrumentation is readily available. Although rarely needed, even the simplest diagnostic procedure can require conversion. Patient positioning is selected based on the location of the lesion or lesions or the area of the thorax to be examined and on the specific surgical procedure to be performed. Dorsal recumbency, ventral recumbency or lateral recumbency are employed. Dorsal recumbency with a paraxiphoid telescope portal is effective for evaluation and operation of ventral tho - racic structures including the pericardium, cranial mediasti- num, and bilateral examination of all but the most dorsal portions of the lungs and pleural surfaces. Lateral recum- bency with a lateral camera portal allows more complete examination of the dorsal thoracic structures and hilar areas on the side selected but is limited to unilateral access. Total lung lobectomy is more easily performed with the patient in lateral recumbency, but minimally invasive lung lobectomy has been performed with the patient in dorsal recumbency. Multiple positioning techniques are effective and are con- sistently employed with position and technique based on the needs of the individual patient rather than on superiority of one technique over the other. 9.4.2 T echnique Anesthesia and Pneumothorax Anesthetic requirements for thoracoscopy are similar to those for open thoracotomy. Intermittent positive pressure breathing using a mechanical ventilator is required for minimally invasive thoracic surgery just as it is required for open thoracic surgery. Ventilator requirements and

9 Thoracoscopy 560 technique of operation are the same for the simple semi- open pneumothorax technique and pleural space insufflation as both are for open thoracic surgery. With one lung ventilation, ventilator tidal volume is decreased and the rate is increased because functional lung volume is decreased when one of the lungs is excluded from the ventilator circuit. This technique with decreased tidal volume and increased rate is also used with semi-open pneumothorax bilateral lung ventilation to improve visual access. Preanesthetic medications, induction drugs, and maintenance anesthetics are the same as are used for open thoracotomy. Local anesthetic blocks at the portal sites are also recommended. An open gas-filled optical space must be established to allow for thoracoscopy to be performed. This optical cavity is required to provide a working space for the telescope and operative instruments so that the end of the telescope can be kept away from tissues allowing visualization. A semi- open pneumothorax is created for thoracoscopy and mini- mally invasive thoracic surgery by allowing air into the pleural space so that lungs collapse away from the rigid chest wall that is supported by the ribs ( Videos 9.1, 9.2, and 9.3). This follows the same basic principle as for laparoscopy and is also the main difference between laparoscopy and thoracoscopy. An open gas filled space is required for both techniques to provide a cavity for placement of the telescope and operative instruments. Without this open space, the end of the telescope is in contact with tissue all the time and nothing is visible. In contrast to laparoscopy, where the per - itoneal cavity is insufflated with CO 2 to distend the abdo - men and hold the abdominal wall up away from the viscera for thoracoscopy, a pneumothorax is created by allowing air into the pleural space so the lungs collapse away from the rigid chest wall that is supported by the ribs. With abdomi- nal insufflation, an airtight abdominal cavity must be main- tained and all portals must use tightly fitting cannulas with valves and gaskets that seal around the telescope or instru- ments to prevent gas leakage. Positive pressure insufflation is not commonly employed for thoracoscopy, and when not using insufflation, an airtight seal at the portal sites is not needed or desired. Three different techniques are used for creating and maintaining a pneumothorax: a simple semi-open pneu- mothorax with standard endotracheal intubation, pleural space insufflation, and one lung ventilation with selective intubation. Each technique has advantages, disadvantages, and specific indications. Standard intubation with intermittent positive pressure breathing and a “semi-open” pneumothorax is the simplest of the techniques. It works well for diagnostic procedures and for simpler minimally invasive surgical procedures (Faunt et al. 1998b; McCarthy 1999). Two different methods are used to establish a pneumothorax for thora- coscopy. One approach uses the Veress needle to penetrate the chest wall so that air is allowed into the pleural space to establish a pneumothorax. The telescope cannula is intro - duced using a sharp trocar after the pneumothorax has been established. The second technique uses blunt dissec- tion and a blunt obturator to place the telescope cannula through the chest wall prior to establishing a pneumotho - rax. Air is then allowed to enter the pleural space through the telescope cannula. Pneumothorax is established much faster with this technique because air is entering through a 5 or 10 mm cannula rather than through a smaller Veress needle. This second technique is superior and has almost completely replaced the first technique because it is faster, easier, and carries less risk of trauma to the thoracic vis - cera. Placement of a paraxiphoid telescope trocar–cannula is particularly effective using this technique. The semi-open pneumothorax technique does not work well when the anesthesia system provides PEEP , which maintains a low level of increased intrabronchial pressure during the expiratory phase of the breathing cycle and pre - vents the lungs from collapsing interfering with formation of a pneumothorax. This effect in some systems makes thoracoscopy impossible. The newer ventilator design with the bellows on top of the system inherently produces PEEP simply with the weight of the bellows. Since this is almost all that is available currently, this presents a problem for performing thoracoscopy using the semi-open pneumotho - rax approach. One lung ventilation is commonly used in human thora- coscopy (Bernasconi and Piccioni 2017; Mehrotra and Jain 2019; Meleiro et al. 2018; Senturk et al. 2015) and becomes necessary with more complex surgical procedures but is not necessary for most diagnostic thoracoscopy or many of the simpler minimally invasive thoracic surgical procedures performed in dogs and cats. One lung ventila- tion uses selective bronchial intubation with special double lumen endotracheal tubes or with endobronchial blockade and complete collapse of the lung on the side of the invaded hemithorax (Floriano et al. 2017; Mehrotra and Jain 2019; Park et al. 2018; Pascoe and Mayhew 2015). This approach has the distinct advantages of improved visualization due to reduced lung volume and reduced tissue movement with ventilator excursions. These advantages greatly facili- tate performing complex surgical procedures. One lung ventilation also has its own set of problems and complica- tions (Floriano et al. 2017; Park et al. 2018; Steffey 2015; White et al. 2018). The most important being greatly increased complexity and difficulty of the anesthetic com- ponent of thoracoscopy. Selective intubation is a difficult time-consuming procedure that requires bronchoscopy to accurately place the double lumen endotracheal tube or

9.4 Thoracoscopy eneral Technii ue 561 endobronchial blocker. An anesthesiologist adept at one lung ventilation is required to initiate and maintain one lung ventilation. As the level of sophistication of operative thoracoscopy procedures in dogs and cats increases, one lung ventilation will become necessary and will become part of the standard protocol for thoracoscopy. Pleural insufflation is an additional technique for estab - lishing an optical space in the thorax that is much easier, faster, and more flexible than one lung ventilation (Bohaychuk-Preuss et al. 2017; Caso et al. 2018; El-Dawlatly et al. 2003; Okamura et al. 2016; Peden and Prys-Roberts 1993; Wong et al. 1995). Adequate lung col - lapse is achieved in most cases without insufflation (Figure 9.3). Cases with noncompliant lungs that do not collapse well with a semi-open pneumothorax (Figure 9.4) alone benefit from insufflation (Figure 9.5) even for the simplest diagnostic and operative procedures. When using a ventilator with PEEP , pleural insufflation is fre - quently needed to achieve adequate lung collapse and working space. Studies have been performed showing that thoracic insufflation with CO 2 to pressures up to 5 cm water has minimal deleterious effects on cardiopulmo - nary function (Daly et al. 2002; Polis et al. 2002). This establishes that it is safe to use insufflation when neces - sary, and clinical experience has supported the results of this research. Fortunately, insufflation is not required for evaluation of the thorax and for sample collection in most cases. Pleural insufflation increases the complexity of the procedure by requiring an insufflator, CO 2 , and maintain - ing airtight portals. Insufflation also increases the risks of thoracoscopy with the potential for over inflation, tension pneumothorax, and severe cardiopulmonary compromise (Daly et al. 2002; Polis et al. 2002). Even with these nega - tive considerations, pleural insufflation is a very positive addition to our armamentarium. Advantages of pleural insufflation are that it is done without an anesthesiologist experienced in one lung ventilation, it can be added to any thoracoscopy procedure during surgery, and it can be instituted and discontinued intermittently if needed. If pleural insufflation is initiated and the patient becomes compromised, pleural pressure is released instantly to allow stabilization of the patient. This most commonly occurs over a period of time after insufflation is started and is not typically an immediate effect. In this scenario, surgery proceeds with insufflation as long as it is tolerated by the patient. The pressure is released to allow the patient to stabilize, reestablish insufflation, and proceed with surgery, repeating this cycle until surgery is com - plete. The level of insufflation can also be adjusted, for example, if 5 cm water is too much, a lower pressure is used. Frequently, when 5 cm water is too much, 3 cm water will work well.
