9 Thoracoscopy 562 9.4.3 T elescope Portal Placement Portals for access to the thoracic cavity include lateral intercostal, transdiaphragmatic or paraxiphoid, and cranial or thoracic inlet (Faunt et al. 1998b; Garcia et al. 1998; Potter and Hendrickson 1999; Walton 1999, 2001; Zaal et al. 1997). The first two techniques have equal indica- tions, advantages, benefits, and drawbacks with the approach selected based on the needs of each individual case, not on the superiority of one technique over the other. The cranial portal is a translation from the human surgical technique of mediastinoscopy and has limited, if any appli- cation, in small animal thoracoscopy. 9.4.3.1 Paraxiphoid T elescope Portal (Figure 9.6) For this portal, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency or in a dorsal oblique position with the patient’s sternum tipped toward the surgeon. The patient is draped to include an area from the thoracic inlet to the cranial one third of the abdomen and the ventral three quarters of the lateral thoracic walls. This provides exposure for the telescope portal adjacent to the xiphoid cartilage, lateral intercostal operative portals, and chest drain placement, and allows conversion to an open sternal splitting thoracotomy if that becomes necessary. The telescope portal site is located by palpation of the notch between the xiphoid cartilage and the costal arch. A short 2–3 cm skin incision is made either to the right or left of the xiphoid process between the costal arch and the xiphoid. An access tract is created into the pleural space using a large hemostat and blunt dissection directed cranially, dorsally, and slightly laterally from the skin incision. The telescope cannula is inserted through this tract using a blunt obturator rather than a sharp tro - car. If a disposable laparoscopy cannula and trocar with a spring-loaded trocar guard are used, the guard mecha - nism is fired prior to insertion by pushing the tip of the assembly against a towel or gauze sponges. This locks the guard over the sharp end of the trocar and effectively converts it into a blunt obturator. Once in the chest, the obturator is removed, and the cannula valve is held open or the valve assembly is completely removed to facilitate air leakage to establish the pneumothorax. With this technique, the risk of organ damage is minimized, and an adequate pneumothorax will be present by the time the telescope is inserted. When the telescope is inserted, it will be in one hemith - orax and is separated from the contralateral hemithorax by the ventral mediastinum. The ventral mediastinum typically appears as a curtain like structure hanging from the sternum (Figure 9.7). The normal ventral mediasti - num is an incomplete thin translucent membrane with vascular structures surrounded by fat. The membrane may appear complete or may have scattered visible fenes - trations. Occasionally, the mediastinum is complete, so rather than hanging on the midline, it is compressed against the chest wall contralateral to the side with the pneumothorax and placement of the telescope portal. When the chest is entered and there is no visible ventral mediastinum hanging from the sternum, examination of the chest walls will reveal that one side has an overlying branching pattern of blood vessels and scattered fat. This is the mediastinum overlying the chest wall (Figure 9.8) and the mediastinum is also seen overlying lung tissue (Figure 9.9). To access the contralateral hemithorax, the mediastinum is penetrated through a visible fenestration (Figure 9.10), or if there are no visible fenestrations, one is created using scissors (Figure 9.11) or a vessel sealing device (Figure 9.12). The same procedure is employed with scissors using monopolar electrocautery or a vessel Figure 9.6 Paraxiphoid telescope portal with the patient in dorsal recumbency and the telescope portal placed in the xiphoid notch on the right side and directed into the right hemithorax.

The mediastinum is cut off of the sternum to facilitate bilateral visualization, and for instrument access, when performing minimally inva - sive operative procedures. For the normal mediastinum, this is performed with scissors to cut avascular translu - cent areas (Figure 9.14) and using monopolar electrocau - tery as needed for blood vessels to achieve hemostasis (Figure 9.15). When there is increased blood supply (Figure 9.16), a vessel sealing device is used cutting crani - ally from a natural fenestration or from initial mediasti - nal penetration (Figure 9.17). Cutting is continued as far into the cranial mediastinum as needed (Figure 9.18) and then caudally (Figure 9.19), if indicated to provide an adequate visual field (Figure 9.20). When there is a com - plete mediastinum and unilateral pneumothorax, diag - nostic procedures and short operative procedures can occasionally be performed without penetrating the medi - astinum or cutting it off the sternum. In these cases, the mediastinum stays out of the way (Figures 9.8 and 9.9) for a period of time but slowly moves away from the chest wall due to migration of air through the tissue from the pneumothorax into the contralateral hemithorax. If the procedure has not been completed by the time this hap - pens, the mediastinum is cut off of the sternum. Another important issue when taking the mediastinum off of the sternum is achieving adequate hemostasis. The blood ves - sels in the mediastinum are rarely large enough that con - tinued bleeding is an issue for the patient. However, even a small amount of continued bleeding interferes with visualization by blood dripping onto the telescope and obscuring a clear visual field. 9.4.3.2 Lateral T elescope Portal Placement A site for the telescope portals is selected that is not directly over the lesion to be examined or the area of interest for operative procedures in the chest but is close enough to allow access for visualization. Operative portals are then placed so that biopsy or other sample collection instrumen- tation is placed directly over the lesion. For minimally invasive surgery procedures, operative portals can be placed based on the principles of triangulation. Multiple lateral chest wall telescope portal sites have been described in the literature (Cantwell et al. 2000; Dupre 2015; Isalow et al. 2000; Malone et al. 2001; Mayhew and Culp 2015; Monnet 2015; Radlinsky et al. 2002; Remedios and Fergusun 1996; Walton 2001; Zaal et al. 1997). Using one of these published sites may or may not fit the specific case or procedure. For many procedures, the portals are well- defined, but for some, more effective portal site selection is done case-by-case. 9 Thoracoscopy 566 Lateral chest wall telescope portal placement is also per - formed with the Veress needle and sharp trocar technique: a small skin incision is made at the site selected for tele - scope placement that is of adequate size for the telescope to be used. The Veress needle is inserted through the chest wall into the pleural space and air is allowed to enter the pleural space until the lungs are sufficiently collapsed for trocar and cannula placement. A large pneumothorax is not required but sufficient lung collapse is needed to allow placement of the endoscope cannula with its sharp trocar without damaging the lungs or other thoracic viscera. The Veress needle is removed when an adequate pneumotho - rax has been created. The telescope cannula and trocar assembly are inserted through the chest wall, through the same incision. Placement of the cannula trocar assembly must be done carefully and without excessive depth of pen- etration to prevent damage to the thoracic viscera. A two- hand technique is used with one hand on the chest wall around the cannula and the other hand on the end of the cannula assembly. The two hands are placed so that they are separated by the desired depth of penetration. The can- nula is forced through the chest wall with the upper hand using a back and forth rotational movement until the chest wall is penetrated. If too much force is applied and the tro - car suddenly penetrates the chest wall, it is stopped when the upper hand hits the lower hand and the chance of intrathoracic damage is minimized. Once the cannula is in the pleural space, the trocar is removed and replaced with the telescope. The extent of pneumothorax is evaluated and adjusted as needed to provide adequate space for examination. Additional air is allowed to enter the pleural space to increase the pneumothorax as needed after place - ment of the telescope cannula. 9.4.4 Operative Portal Placement Techniques for establishing operative portals are the same for all patient positions. Technique does vary depending on whether free instrument passage or operative portal cannulas are used and the type of cannula employed. Sites for operative portal placement are selected to allow access to lesions for tissue manipulation, sample collection, and operative procedures. The easiest and most effective method for selecting operative portal sites is to palpate the chest wall with visualization through the telescope to locate the portal site by intercostal muscle indentation produced by palpation. Palpation is repeated in different areas until the appropriate portal site is determined. For biopsy of tissues or masses that do not need to be manipu- lated, the portal is placed directly over the site to be biop - sied. When manipulation of tissues is required for examination, sample collection, or minimally invasive surgical procedures, portal sites are selected based on the principles of endoscopic instrument triangulation (Potter and Hendrickson 1999). To apply this concept, all portals are on the same side of the lesion or area to be operated. The portals are placed far enough apart so that the instru- ments do not interfere with each other. Portals are placed where the area to be examined can be reached by the instruments being used, and the visual field of the tele - scope and the operative instruments converge on the lesion or area of interest. Operative ports can be established with or without a cannula. If cannulas are used, they are placed with a sharp trocar or with blunt dissection and a blunt obtura- tor. With all three techniques, the deep surface of the chest wall is observed with the telescope, while the portal is being established to avoid trauma to thoracic viscera (Figures 9.21–9.26). For cannula insertion with a sharp trocar, a short skin incision is made at the portal site and the cannula trocar assembly is inserted with similar tech- nique to that used for sharp trocar telescope portal place - ment except trocar penetration is observed with the telescope (Figure 9.21). Blunt cannula placement is per - formed by making a short skin incision bluntly dissect - ing through the chest wall with a hemostat (Figure 9.22) or cutting completely through the chest wall with a scal- pel (Figure 9.23), and passing the cannula-blunt obtura- tor assembly through the hole in the chest wall (Figure 9.24) or placing a threaded EndoTIP cannula (Figures 9.25 and 9.26). To create an operative portal without a cannula, a short skin incision is made, and the fascia, muscles, and pleura are bluntly dissected (Figure 9.22) or sharply incised (Figure 9.23) to establish a mini-thoracotomy into the chest cavity. Instruments are passed through this tissue tract without placing a cannula. When the patient is placed in dorsal recum- bency, lateral chest wall portals are placed as far ventrally as possible at or near the lateral margin of the transver - sus thoracis muscle (Figures 9.22, 9.23, 9.25, and 9.26). Placing these portals further ventrally through the trans - versus thoracis muscle increases the risk of damage to the internal thoracic artery that is hidden by this muscle as it runs caudally adjacent to the sternum. 9.4.5 Portal Closure and Pleural Space Management When examination, sample collection, or minimally inva- sive operative procedures have been completed, instru- mentation is removed, portals are closed, and the lungs are re-expanded. An airtight seal at all portal sites is critical to

9 Thoracoscopy 568 prevent postoperative pneumothorax. The technique for pleural space management depends on the extent of tho - racic disease present and the type and complexity of the surgical procedure performed. A chest drain is placed in all patients. For patients where a paraxiphoid telescope portal is placed, the easiest technique for chest tube placement passes the chest tube through the telescope cannula (Video 9.4). When this technique is used, the pleural drain tube is placed through the telescope cannula (Figure 9.27) well into the chest using visualization of the tube through one of the operative portals to confirm appropriate tube position (Figure 9.28), the telescope can - nula is removed over the end of the chest tube leaving the tube in place (Figure 9.29), the tissues of the portal are closed in multiple layers around the chest tube, and the chest tube is anchored to the skin. The maximum size chest tube that can be used with an 11 mm telescope can - nula is 24 Fr because the flare at the outside end of tubes larger than this will not fit through the telescope cannula. This technique is used in cases where there will be mini - mal expected fluid production from the disease process and when there is minimal risk of postoperative bleeding or air leakage. The paraxiphoid telescope portal is best suited for this technique and chest tubes placed at this site are left in place for up to 24 hours following mini - mally invasive surgery. Cases with significant thoracic disease where there is high risk of pleural fluid accumulation because of the disease process and when there is increased risk of bleeding or air leakage secondary to more complex surgical procedures have a standard lateral chest drain tube placed as would be done for an open thoracotomy (Figure 9.30). For this approach the chest tube is not placed through a portal site because it is difficult to achieve an airtight seal around the tube. Standard sub - cutaneous tunnel chest tube placement technique is employed. Continuous underwater seal suction is employed dur - ing portal closure and recovery from anesthesia. After recovery, continuous or intermittent underwater seal drainage with suction is employed depending on the requirements of the individual case. With all these tech - niques, postoperative chest radiographs are recom - mended during recovery prior discontinuing the initial phase of continuous suction and again prior to chest tube removal. Even with simple cases, chest tubes are typically left in place overnight or until the patient is prepared for release from the hospital. 9.5 Thoracoscopy: ormal Thoracic Anatomy 569 Portal cannulas are removed, and the chest wall holes are closed with interrupted sutures in layers to produce an airtight seal. Six-millimeter cannula portals are closed with superficial muscle fascia, subcutaneous and skin layers. Eleven-millimeter cannula or larger portals and portals where cannulas are not used are closed with deep fascia, superficial muscle fascia, subcutaneous, and skin layers. Intermittent positive pressure breathing is continued until the lungs are fully re-expanded and the patient is sta - ble. Transition is made to promote spontaneous breathing. Patient monitoring is continued until the patient has recovered from anesthesia and has stabilized. Thoracoscopy is a minimally invasive technique with far less trauma, less anesthesia, and takes less time than open surgery, but the chest has still been invaded, the lungs col - lapsed, and cardiopulmonary compromise has occurred. Adequate patient monitoring and supportive treatment are essential to realizing the benefits of thoracoscopy over thoracotomy. 9.4.6 Postoperative Recovery Postoperative recovery is much faster with minimally invasive thoracic surgery than with an open thoracot - omy. Patients are typically fully recovered, pain free, and active within a few hours after the procedure. The need for pain management, the amount of drug required, and the duration of treatment is substantially less than with conventional open surgery. Postoperative hospitalization time after minimally invasive surgery is dictated more by the disease process and by anesthetic recovery than by the minimally invasive surgical proce - dure itself. Some patients are released from the hospi - tal on the day of the procedure and most are released on the day after surgery with very few requiring more hospitalization. 9.5 Thoracoscopy: Normal Thoracic Anatomy Visualization of intrathoracic structures with thoracoscopy is far superior to open thoracotomy because of the excel- lent lighting, magnification produced by the telescope video system, and ability to place the telescope into areas of the chest inaccessible with open surgery. Lateral recum- bency and lateral endoscope placement allows visualiza- tion of the structures of the entered hemithorax but not the contralateral hemithorax. The ventral paraxiphoid portal allows bilateral examination of the chest but is limited to ventral structures. Chest wall structures are visualized and the internal surfaces of the ribs, muscles, blood vessels, and nerves are clearly defined (Figure 9.31). The sympathetic trunk is visible running from cranial to caudal at the dorsal end of the ribs (Figure 9.32). The thoracic duct is visible on the right side in the caudal thorax ventral to the aorta and dorsal to the sympathetic trunk as a sin - gle vessel (Figure 9.33) or as a branching structure (Figure 9.34). Other smaller lymphatic vessels are occa - sionally seen when they are dilated secondary to pleu - ral insufflation (Figure 9.35). The normal diaphragm seen during thoracoscopy with the semi-open pneumo - thorax technique extends into the thorax as a convex muscular dome (Figure 9.36) with a central opaque to translucent central tendon of the diaphragm as a con - tinuation of the muscular dome (Figure 9.37) that meets the chest wall peripherally at an acute angle (Figure 9.38). In the ventral thorax, the enlarged costo - chondral junctions are visible with the transversus tho - racis muscle covering the ventral end of the costal cartilages, the ventral end of the intercostal muscles, and the internal thoracic artery and vein (Figure 9.39). The lateral margin of the transversus thoracis muscle is an important landmark for portal placement to avoid the internal thoracic artery and vein. The azygos vein is seen in the dorsal aspect of the right hemithorax run - ning dorsal and lateral to the aorta (Figures 9.5 and 9.40) with the right intercostal veins draining into the azygos vein rather than the vena cava. The thoracic aorta is visible bilaterally from its penetration through the diaphragm (Figure 9.35) running cranially in the dorsal thorax (Figure 9.41) to the hilus (Figure 9.5). Figure 9.30 Chest tube placement is done with standard open surgical technique when lateral recumbent patient position is used and when chest drains are expected to be in place longer than 24 hours. Appropriate intrathoracic chest tube placement is confirmed visually with the telescope.

9.6 Thoracic athology 573 9.6.1 Pleural and Pericardial Fluid In cases with significant pleural or pericardial fluid present sufficient to compromise cardiopulmonary function under anesthesia, every effort is made to evacuate the fluid prior to anesthetic induction. If it is not possible to remove all the pleural fluid prior to performing thoracoscopy, then as soon as the telescope portal is placed into the thorax, an aspiration tube is passed through the endoscope cannula or through an operative portal, suction is applied, and the remainder of the fluid removed (Figure 9.54) (Video 9.5). If there is sufficient residual pericardial fluid, a Veress needle is placed into the pericardium with endoscopic visual guid- ance to evacuate the fluid (Figure 9.55). Samples of the pleural or pericardial fluid are collected if needed, for fluid analysis, cytology, and for bacterial and fungal cultures. 9.6 Thoracic athology 575 Preoperative thoracentesis or pericardiocentesis produce iat - rogenic lesions in the chest wall (Figure 9.56), lung (Figure 9.57), and pericardium (Figure 9.58) that are typically insignifi- cant but potentially cause bleeding, air leakage, or benefi- cial drainage from the pericardium into the pleural space. 9.6.2 Chest Wall Abnormalities Abnormalities of the chest wall are more commonly sec - ondary to lesions within the thorax than they are primary pathology arising in the chest wall. These reactive lesions are both focal (Figure 9.33), generalized (Figures 9.5, 9.13, and 9.35) or there may be no changes in the chest wall (Figures 9.42 and 9.46). A few chest wall lesions originate in the chest wall as primary pathology, but these are rela - tively uncommon. Primary rib tumors occur both in the rib (Figure 9.59) and in the costal cartilages (Figure 9.60). Migrating foreign bodies penetrate into the chest causing primary chest wall lesions (Figure 9.61). Reactive chest wall lesions are also seen secondary to foreign bodies migrating from the airways into the pleural space (Figure 9.62) and to foreign bodies still within the lung causing pneumonia with secondary chest wall reaction (Figures 9.5 and 9.35). Pyogranulomatous pleuritis is also seen that is suspicious of foreign body reaction but no for - eign material is found (Figure 9.63). Inflammatory pulmo - nary disease frequently causes adhesions to the chest wall (Figure 9.63) that when extensive (Figure 9.64) interfere with minimally invasive procedures requiring division of adhesions or conversion in some cases. Pleural disease also affects the chest wall when the parietal pleura is involved. An example of this is chylothorax with pleural inflammation and fibrosis obscuring visualization of ana - tomic structures (Figure 9.65). This is of particular impor - tance in finding the thoracic duct for occlusion (Figure 9.66). Mesothelioma is another significant exam - ple of pleural disease effecting the chest wall with lesions varying from a few submacroscopic clear to white nodules (Figure 9.67), extensive white nodules scattered over all pleural surfaces (Figure 9.68), or occasionally larger masses (Figure 9.69). 9 Thoracoscopy 580 9.6.4 Mediastinal Abnormalities As with the chest wall and diaphragm, many mediastinal abnormalities are due to primary pleural disease or pleural reaction to other pathology. 9 Thoracoscopy 584 9.6.6.1 Neoplasia Diagnosing intrathoracic neoplasia, staging disease, and determining resectability are major applications of thora- coscopy (Balsa and Culp 2019; Gandhi and Naunheim 1996; Lobe and Schropp 1994; Reed 1994; Schropp 1994; Steffey 2015). A wide variety of neoplastic processes are found with thoracoscopy involving the lungs, and as described in previous sections of this chapter, other tho - racic tissues and organs. Primary and metastatic pulmo - nary neoplasia lesions are visible when they reach the surface of the lungs, even submacroscopic lesions. Primary lung tumors are more commonly solitary and typically are larger than metastatic lesions but include all sizes of masses in all lung lobes with widely varied appearance (Figures 9.93, 9.94, 9.95, 9.96, and 9.97). Smaller superficial primary pulmonary masses are seen directly (Figure 9.98), many small deep pulmonary masses are identified by over - lying pulmonary changes (Figure 9.99), and other small deep masses are located by manipulation with a palpation probe revealing changes in lung tissue pliability. Metastatic lung lesions are typically small and multiple with variation in appearance equal to or greater than pri - mary lung lesions. Secondary lung tumors vary from flat small red dots on the surface of any lung lobes (Figures 9.100, 9.101, and 9.102) to small slightly raised nodules (Figure 9.103), small polypoid masses (Figure 9.104), larger variably colored solid masses (Figure 9.105), and massive infiltration of all lung lobes with an uncountable number of variable sized lesions (Figure 9.106). The primary limitation in visualizing and collecting biopsies of lung tumors is when intrapulmonary masses are small, deep, and cannot be detected with minimally invasive technique. Metastatic disease typically goes to the lungs from other locations in the body but primary lung neoplasia metastases most commonly to the hilar lymph nodes (Figure 9.107). Primary pulmonary tumors rarely seed to the pleura. Pleural masses were seen in a patient with what was thought to be a primary a lung tumor but this was determined to be a mesothelioma using immuno - histochemistry to establish a diagnosis (Figures 9.70, 9.71, 9.72, 9.73, and 9.74). In this case, it is not known which occurred first, the pleural lesions or the pulmonary mass. 9.6 Thoracic athology 585 9.6.6.2 Pneumothorax Trauma is the most common cause of pneumothorax in human medicine and in small animal veterinary medicine but most of these cases resolve without medical or surgical intervention. Some trauma patients with extensive or persis - tent air leakage require treatment using active pleural evacu - ation with continuous underwater seal drainage and suction or with surgical intervention. Cases requiring surgical inter - vention are best evaluated with thoracoscopy and managed with minimally invasive technique without subjecting an already traumatized patient to the additional trauma of an open thoracotomy (Lodhia et al. 2019; Schermer et al. 1999). 9.6.6.3 Spontaneous Pneumothorax Pneumothorax due to anything other than trauma is by default called spontaneous pneumothorax with a long list of etiologies. One etiology for spontaneous pneumothorax is secondary to foreign body migration into the pleural space with effective evaluation and management with thoracoscopy (Gandhi and Naunheim 1996; Gibson et al. 2019; McCarthy 2004; Shamir et al. 2016). 9.6 Thoracic athology 587 management resolving most cases without a requirement for open or minimally invasive surgery (Mooney et al. 2012). The most difficult part of managing spontane - ous pneumothorax cases in dogs is locating the site of the air leakage with noninvasive procedures including CT (Reetz et al. 2013) prior to surgical intervention. The site of active air leakage can be found, the cause defined effec - tively with minimal trauma using thoracoscopy, and in most cases, the area of the involved lung is also resectable with thoracoscopy. Cases that do not respond to conserva - tive treatment with chest tubes using continuous or inter - mittent underwater seal drainage with suction are managed with thoracoscopy for removal of the leaking bulla (Case et al. 2015), and those that cannot be corrected with minimally invasive technique require open surgical intervention. A series of 22 consecutive pneumothorax cases from 1998 to 2006 were managed by the author using thoracoscopy. Of these cases, one was secondary to trauma, and when thoracoscopy was performed, there was no active leakage and no further leakage occurred. Four pneumothorax cases with a foreign body etiology were also included and removal of the foreign bodies using thoracoscopy resolved air leakage with no lung resection. This leaves 17 cases of spontaneous pneumothorax in this series. Ten patients were resolved with thoracoscopy leav - ing seven patients without resolution. Euthanasia was per - formed in two of these patients without further intervention. Thoracotomy was performed in five cases at the same anesthesia as thoracoscopy with localization and resection of a leaking lesion in only two patients and no lesions were found in three patients all with continued air leakage. Euthanasia was performed in two of these patients without further treatment. In one case, no abnormalities, bullae, or a leakage site was found with CT, bronchoscopy, multiple thoracoscopies, multiple thora - cotomies, and a postmortem examination including removal of the lungs with inflation while submerged. This series of cases is not large enough to determine exact data but demonstrates that thoracoscopy is an effective approach to diagnosis and management of spontaneous pneumothorax. Only two patients in this series that were not resolved with thoracoscopy were successfully man - aged when an open thoracotomy was performed. Even though the total success rate for managing spontaneous pneumothorax is not great, conversion to open thoracot - omy did not substantially increase the success rate. 9 Thoracoscopy 588 Pulmonary degeneration with bulla formation and air leakage can occur at a solitary site or at multiple sites in multiple lung lobes. With solitary sites, surgical removal will control the current air leakage and substantially reduce or eliminate the incidence of recurrence. When multiple sites are found in multiple lung lobes, open surgi- cal intervention may control the current episode of air leakage but may not have a significant effect on the inci- dence of future episodes of pneumothorax. Open surgical intervention is of questionable value in these cases. Bullae appear as variable sized air filled (Figures 9.108– 9.112) or collapsed (Figures 9.108 and 9.113) structures protruding from the margins (Figures 9.109, 9.112, and 9.113) or surfaces of any part of any lung lobe (Figures 9.108, 9.110, and 9.111). Although bullae can occur in any part of any lung lobe, personal experience indicates the cranial lung lobes are more commonly involved. The ruptured leaking bulla may or may not be air filled and determining the exact location of air leakage is critical. Occasionally, a hole will be seen in a distended bulla (Figure 9.114) but this is uncommon. When the actual leak is not easily detected, the area is flooded with saline and observed for air bubbles escaping during the inspiratory phase of the ventilator (Figure 9.115). Another technique runs a continuous flow of saline across the lesion during the ventilator cycle (Figures 9.111 and 9.112). When air leakage is seen, the area of leakage and surround- ing abnormal lung is resected. If no air leakage is found, the area of the visible bullae and surrounding abnormal lung is still removed. The blood patch technique is an alternative if thoracos - copy is not available, thoracoscopy fails to find the source of the leak, correction with thoracoscopy is not effective, or clients decline invasive intervention (Andreetti et al. 2007; Blanco et al. 1996; Cagirici et al. 1998; Dugan et al. 2017; Dumire et al. 1992; Evman et al. 2016; Lang–Lazdunski and Coonar 2004; Oppenheimer et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2019). 9 Thoracoscopy 590 Diagnostic sensitivity for diffuse pulmonary disease is greatly increased when thoracoscopy is employed for obtaining large lung biopsies (Boutin et al. 1982; Faunt et al. 1998a; Gandhi and Naunheim 1996; Reed 1994; Vachon and Fischer 1998). Thoracoscopy surpasses nee - dle aspiration, brush cytology, and transbronchial biopsy (Boutin et al. 1982). An adequate portion of the lung is obtained with thoracoscopy to allow histopathologic eval - uation of parenchymal disease and pulmonary architec - ture (Boutin et al. 1982; Gandhi and Naunheim 1996; Reed 1994). Minimally invasive biopsies of pulmonary tissue are obtained with opposing cup or clam shell biopsy forceps, Tru-cut biopsy needles, and partial lung lobec - tomy apical resections with pre-tied loop ligatures or endoscopic staplers (Boutin et al. 1982; Campbell et al. 1995; Gandhi and Naunheim 1996; Garcia et al. 1998; Lobe and Schropp 1994; Potter and Hendrickson 1999; Walton 1999). Minimally invasive partial or complete lung lobectomy is also performed for managing intracta - ble pulmonary disease with tissue samples and submitted for histopathology. 9.6 Thoracic athology 591 When partial or complete lung lobectomy is not indicated for therapeutic purposes, the biopsy forceps technique is the easiest, simplest, cheapest, and safest technique for obtaining biopsies of lung tissue. Every time I present this technique everyone insists that the biopsy sites will leak air but they do not. In 12 normal dogs and an equal number of clinical cases, no air leakage has been detected. None! An attempt was made to measure the leak time in the initial group of normal dogs with a stopwatch but I was not quick enough to measure the time because there was no detectable air leakage as observed with magnification from the telescope and video system. None! No detectable air leakage was seen in any of the clinical cases. None! I admit that I have not biopsied every type of lung pathology in every species, but multiple biopsies have been taken in both cats and dogs without any detectable air leakage. Chest tubes were placed in all clinical cases at the time of lung biopsy and intermittent episodes of continuous underwater seal drainage with suction were applied over a minimum of eight hours after lung biopsy was completed. No air leakage was detected in any patient. None! If you do not believe me, and no one does, try this technique in the next case you have that needs lung biopsies, and if you observe air leakage after biopsies have been taken, apply a loop ligature or linear stapler to control the air leak. 9.6.6.5 Lung Lobe T orsion Lung lobe torsion is an uncommon condition and can be spontaneous or associated with or secondary to pleural effusion. Pleural effusion also occurs secondary to lung lobe torsion so the affect or effect of pleural fluid may be difficult to determine. Identification of lung lobe torsion is easily performed with thoracoscopy as the involved lung is dark purple to black and its shape is distorted (Figure 9.122). In some patients, it is possible to see the twisted hilus to confirm that the lobe is torsed and minimally invasive lung lobectomy is also possible. 9.6 Thoracic athology 593 part of the procedure. These samples are used as indicated based on the findings with thoracoscopy. Pleural biopsies are taken with particular attention to areas of abnormal tissue. The most common etiology of pleural effusion includes neo - plastic and non-neoplastic pleural disease that was presented previously with the discussion of pleural pathology. Additional etiologies of significant pleural effusion include chylothorax, pseudochylothorax, congestive heart failure, hypoproteinemia secondary to liver or other disease, lung lobe torsion, and other diseases that typically produce only small quantities of fluid. Pleural lesions are evaluated and selectively biopsied to establish a diagnosis and rule out neoplasia or other pleural dis - eases. Diagnostic accuracy of thoracoscopy for pleural effusion secondary to neoplasia approaches 100% (Kovak et al. 2002). Thoracoscopy is not the first step in diagnosis or man- agement of pleural effusions and an appropriate medical work up will diagnose or rule out many of the systemic or focal diseases that cause pleural effusions. Thoracoscopy is indicated for pleural effusions not diagnosed with less invasive techniques or when thoracoscopy is indicated for treatment of intrathoracic disease related to pleural effu- sion. It is important to recognize that reactive mesothelial cells or lack of mesothelial cells in pleural fluid does not rule our mesothelioma. Mesothelioma is far more common than popular belief because it has been difficult to diag - nose without thoracoscopy. Typically, mesothelioma lesions are too small to see without the magnification of the telescope video system, which helps visualize small nodules on any or all pleural surfaces (Figures 9.67, 9.68, 9.72, 9.73, 9.123, and 9.124). Larger mesothelioma lesions are occasionally found on pleural surfaces (Figures 9.69, 9.70, and 9.71) and as pulmonary masses (Figure 9.74) but are rare compared to the small nodular presentation. 9.6.8 Chylothorax Chylous effusions are a sufficiently different entity from other pleural effusions that they are discussed separately. Pleural fluid in chylothorax cases seen with thoracoscopy has the same skim milk appearance as seen with thoracen- tesis and open surgery (Figures 9.125 and 9.126) Extensive discussions on chylothorax are available in many publica- tions and presentations and will not be presented here. Only material learned from thoracoscopy and directly related to thoracoscopy will be included (McCarthy 2003). There are many possible etiologies of chylothorax, and some are easy to identify such as cranial mediastinal masses, but most have no identifiable etiology. An early case in a nine-year-old neutered male Domestic Shorthair cat examined with thoracoscopy and thoracic duct abla - tion was attempted in June of 2000. This case was an important learning experience at many levels and steps throughout its management. When first presented, medi - cal management was initiated with a low-fat diet (Hills dry Rd), Rutin, and furosemide. This resulted in clearing of the pleural fluid and a reduction in its volume. Then it was determined that the cat was not eating any of the low-fat food. A different low-fat food was selected that the cat would eat resulting in an increase in fluid volume and a return to chylous appearance. Thoracoscopy was per - formed with the cat in right lateral recumbency using left lateral portals. Examination revealed moderate pleural thickening (Figure 9.125) and an accumulation of sub - pleural chyle in the cranial mediastinum (Figure 9.126). A pericardial window was created and pleural nodule biopsies were taken with minimally invasive technique to establish a diagnosis of mesothelioma and to manage the effects of the pericardial effusion. 9.6 Thoracic athology 595 appetite, and no indication of medical deterioration. The cat was then presented in an agonal state. Immediate chest taps were attempted but no fluid could be obtained with multiple efforts. The patient was intubated, ventilation was initiated, and an emergency thoracotomy was per - formed. Chylous fluid squirted out of the chest with initial entry into the pleural space. The patient’s condition improved with decompression of the “tension chylotho - rax” . Exploration of the thorax revealed moderate pleural thickening with constrictive pleuritis affecting multiple lung lobes. The pericardium appeared thickened suffi - ciently to obscure visibility of the heart and seemed to be interfering with cardiac function. A pericardiectomy was performed. With initial incision into the pericardium, the heart ballooned out of the incision dramatically increasing in size (McCarthy 2003). Resection of the pericardium was completed, a chest drain was placed, the thorax was lav - aged with saline, and the thorax was closed. Since this was done as an emergency procedure, it was not done as an aseptic procedure. So, if the cat survived, I will have added pyothorax to its chylothorax or, at best, converted its chy - lothorax into a pyothorax. In two days, the pleural fluid was clear, and by three days, had ceased to form. This patient recovered completely with no further chylothorax, no pyothorax, and radiographs taken at four months showed that the lungs were fully expanded with no indica - tion of residual constrictive pleuritis. Long-term follow-up to five years determined that there was no recurrence of chylothorax or occurrence of any other thoracic pathology. Five more cats with chylothorax were seen over a period of one year. Pericardiectomy was performed as the initial treatment on all these patients with complete resolution of chylothorax in all cases. Thoracoscopy was performed as a diagnostic procedure in all these patients but the proce - dure was converted to an open surgery to perform the pericardiectomy. Findings with thoracoscopy in this group of six cats did not fit the consensus of our understanding of chylothorax. The duration of chylothorax prior to thoracoscopy did not correlate with the severity of pleural disease with recent onset cases having had only one thoracentesis with marked pleural thickening (Figure 9.131) with significant constric- tive pleuritis (Figure 9.132) and chronic cases after long- term medical management with multiple chest taps did not have severe pleural disease (Figures 9.125–9.127). Another unsuspected finding is that the amount of pleural thicken- ing and constriction is not uniform throughout the thorax and can be widely varied (Figures 9.133 and 9.134). Direct observation of the pericardium with thoracoscopy and pericardioscopy and collection of biopsies for histopathology and cultures are essential for establishing a diagnosis (Cagle et al. 2014; Dunning et al. 1998). Analysis of pericardial fluid has little diagnostic value (Cagle et al. 2014; Dunning et al. 1998). Various heart-based neo - plastic masses have been the most common cause of pericar - dial effusion in the author’s experience while primary inflammatory disease has been rare. The large distended pericardial sac is examined and defined effectively with thoracoscopy (Figure 9.20). The normal pericardium may be clearly visible (Figures 9.46 and 9.48) but is commonly cov - ered partially or completely with normal fat (Figures 9.20 and 9.49) or visibility may be partially or completely obscured by pleural reactions (Figures 9.79 and 9.133). With effusion caused by heart base lesions, the pericardium may look nor - mal without observable pericardial fluid or may appear as a large fluid filled sack (Figures 9.20 and 9.137). Occasionally, pericardial masses are identified through the intact pericar - dium (Figures 9.138 and 9.139). If there was inadequate evacuation of pericardial effusion prior to thoracoscopy, the pericardium is tapped or catheterized and drained under direct visualization (Figure 9.55). A pericardial window is then created on the anterior surface of the heart by removal of a 2–3 cm 2 patch of pericardium. A pericardial window allows continued drainage of pericardial effusion preventing recurrent cardiac tamponade and can be a definitive treat - ment for pericarditis or a highly effective palliative manage - ment for neoplasia within the pericardium. The operative procedure to create a pericardial window requires only slightly more than diagnostic instrumentation and tech - nique. The removed portion of pericardium is available for diagnostic biopsy and culture. 9.6 Thoracic athology 599 Primary pericardial disease is also a cause for pericardial effusion. In the author’s experience, primary pericardial infectious disease has been rare but this is not consistent with the findings of others (Aronson and Gregory 1995; Casamian–Sorrosal et al. 2008). Bacterial (Aronson and Gregory 1995; Fraga Veloso et al. 2014; Peterson et al. 2003; Stafford Johnson et al. 2003), fungal (Casamian–Sorrosal et al. 2008; Heinritz et al. 2005; Ribas et al. 2015), granula- tion tissue without a determined cause (Parra et al. 2009), various vector borne diseases (Tabar et al. 2018), and viral (Zini et al. 2009) etiologies have been found with infectious pericardial disease. The appearance of the pericardium in the few cases that the author has seen have been similar to changes secondary to heart base masses (Figure 9.146). Primary neoplasia of the pericardium causing pericardial effusion is seen, mostly as mesothelioma, with scattered individual nodules (Figure 9.147) or as a solid covering of coalesced lesions (Figure 9.148). Reactive mesothelial cells listed with previous figures may be pre-neoplastic disease or early mesothelioma, and some of these cases present in 12–18 months with diagnosable mesothelioma. Migration of mesothelial cells to mediastinal lymph nodes in dogs with idiopathic pericardial effusion suggests that some of these cases may be a “pre-diagnosable” stage of mesothe - lioma (Peters et al. 2003). The difficulty in diagnosing mes - othelioma in patients with apparent idiopathic pericardia effusion is also reported in a retrospective look at 17 cases with 1 of the 2 diagnoses (Stepien et al. 2000). With the extension of thoracoscopy into the pericar - dium, pericardioscopy is used for visualization and biopsy of pericardial lesions (Carvajal et al. 2019), including removal of heart base tumors (Crumbaker et al. 2010; Ployart et al. 2013), and it has also been used for removal of cardiac foreign bodies (McCarthy 2004). Observation of pericardial lesions is associated with a significantly shorter survival time compared to normal appearing pericardial and epicardial surfaces (Carvajal et al. 2019). The reasons for this difference were not determined in this pub - lication. The decision on an open or MIS approach involves a thorough discussion with the client about the advantages and disadvantages of both approaches. A great number of the author’s patients have been presented specifically for a minimally invasive approach with clients declining open surgery. If open surgery was the only option, the clients would elect to manage the patient with repeated pericar - diocentesis rather than surgery. 9.7 Diagnostic Thoracoscopy Procedures The first and most important diagnostic procedure using thoracoscopy is visual examination of the chest to identify abnormalities. This step is simple and intuitive but provides the basis of all other diagnostic procedures. Complete examination of the thoracic cavity is not possible with thoracoscopy but is faster, easier, less traumatic, and with significantly less recovery time when compared with open thoracotomy. When compared with open exploration of the chest with a lateral thoracotomy incision, both approaches are approximately equal in area of the chest that can be examined. Both are limited to the hemithorax entered with the open technique allowing greater manipulation of tis - sues but poor access to the cranial and caudal extent of the thorax. The limitations are reversed with thoracoscopy allowing better visual access to the cranial and caudal extent of the chest with less ability to manipulate tissues. Starting every chest exploration with thoracoscopy is rec - ommended with conversion to an open technique only if the minimally invasive approach is inadequate. 9.7.1 Pleural, Hilar Lymph Node, Mediastinal, Pericardial, and Chest Wall Mass Biopsy Any area of the pleura visible with the telescope is accessi- ble for biopsy using minimally invasive technique. Nodules on the pleural surface are biopsied with standard opposing cup or clam shell MIS forceps (Figure 9.156) by grasping the tissue and retracting the forceps. Mesothelioma most commonly appears as small white nodules but larger masses with varying appearances also are seen and biop - sies taken with the same technique (Figure 9.157). The same technique also applies to any area of abnormal tissue on or in the pleura (Figure 9.158). Primary lung tumors rarely metastasize to the pleura, but when this does occur, they are readily accessible for biopsy (Figure 9.159). Mediastinal mass biopsies are performed in the same man- ner as for biopsy of other structures and lesions. The most common position for mediastinal biopsies is dorsal recum- bency using a paraxiphoid telescope portal. Most mediasti- nal masses are visible with this approach and commonly are examined for minimally invasive excision with biopsies taken only when they are inoperable (Figure 9.160). This same approach is taken for primary chest wall masses (Figure 9.161). Hilar lymph node biopsies are taken in association with lung lobectomy when indicated and with hilar lymphadenopathy, not associated with lung lesions (Figure 9.162). Sternal lymph node biopsies are also taken when enlarged or even if they appear normal when meso - thelioma is suspected (Peters et al. 2003). Needle aspirate samples are also obtained with laparoscopic guidance. Pericardial biopsies are typically taken when a pericardial window is created with submission of the resected window tissue or when a subtotal pericardiectomy is performed. When partial or complete lung l obectomy is not indicated for therapeutic purposes the biopsy forceps technique is the easiest, simplest, least expensive, safest, and best technique for obtaining biop - sies of lung tissue. Every time I present this technique everyone insists that the biopsy sites will leak air, but they do not . In 12 normal dogs and an equal number of clinical cases where this technique was performed, no air leakage has been detected. None! An attempt was made to measure the leak time in the initial group of normal dogs with a stopwatch, but I was not quick enough to measure the time because there was no detectable air leakage as observed with magnification from the tele - scope and video system. None! No detectable air leakage was seen in any of the clinical cases. None! I admit that I have not biopsied every type of lung pathology in every species, but multiple biopsies have been taken in both cats and dogs without any detectable air leakage. Chest tubes were placed in all clinical cases at the time of lung biopsy and intermittent or continuous underwater seal drainage with suction was applied over a minimum of 8 hours, and typically 12 hours, after lung biopsy was completed. No air leakage was detected in any patient. If you do not believe me, and no one does , try this tech - nique in the next case you have that needs lung biopsies and if you observe air leakage after biopsies have been taken, apply a loop ligature or linear stapler to control the air leak. Taking lung biopsies with opposing cup or clam shell biopsy forceps uses exactly the same procedure as for tak - ing liver biopsies. The lung lobe is selected for biopsy or partial lung lobectomy as a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure (Figure 9.167). 9 Thoracoscopy 606 Small peripheral lung biopsies have been taken success - fully and safely with a LigaSure vessels sealing device, but air leakage occurs with more substantial biopsies (Marvel and Monnet 2013; Mayhew et al. 2012). The biopsy forceps technique for lung biopsy is the easi- est, fastest, least expensive, safest, best procedure for obtaining lung biopsies, and obtains sufficient tissue for diagnostic procedures. This technique is inadequate for therapeutic resections. The loop ligature technique is inex - pensive, obtains adequate tissue for diagnostic and for lim- ited therapeutic purposes, but is cumbersome and time consuming to apply. The EndoGIA stapler technique is the most expensive of the three techniques due to the cost of stapler cartridges but this technique removes sufficient tis - sue for diagnostic procedures and for therapeutic resec- tions, and is relatively easy to use and apply, and provides a safe airtight seal of the resection line. 9.8 Thoracic Operative Procedures 9.8.1 Pericardial Window Creation of a window in the pericardium establishes per - manent drainage for patients with pericardial effusion (Video 9.1) (Aronsohn and Carpenter 1999; Carvajal et al. 2019; Case et al. 2013; Crumbaker et al. 2010; Dupre 2015; Dupre et al. 2001; Jackson et al. 1999; Kerstetter et al. 1997; Stafford Johnson et al. 2004; Michelotti et al. 2019). This technique is performed effec- tively with minimally invasive technique that greatly reduce operative trauma, operative time, and postoperative pain (Walsh et al. 1999). Indications for permanent peri- cardial drainage include neoplastic effusions, hemorrhage from neoplastic masses, inflammatory disease, and i diopathic effusions. This procedure prevents future car - diac tamponade episodes by allowing continual drainage of pericardial fluid into the pleural space. Results with this procedure are excellent with long-term resolution in cases with idiopathic or inflammatory disease and dramatically improve quality of remaining life in cases with neoplasia. To perform a pericardial window, the patient is placed in dorsal recumbency with a monitor at the head of the table or angled on the left side of the patient near the head of the table (Figures 9.172 and 9.173). A paraxiphoid telescope portal is established (Figures 9.174 and 9.175). There are two options for placing operative portals. The first places both portals on the right side (Figure 9.174), the authors preference, and the second places one portal on the right side and one on the left side (Figure 9.175). Each has advan - tages and disadvantages with the choice between the two related mostly to surgeon’s preference. The first option places one operative portal in the right fifth to seventh inter - costal space and the second operative portal in the right ninth or tenth intercostal space (Figure 9.174). The surgeon and assistant both stand on the right side of the patient for this technique. Oblique positioning of the patient slightly to the left (10–15°) facilitates visualization and manipulation when both portals are placed on the right side. The second option places portals in the left and right ninth to tenth intercostal spaces (Figure 9.175). The surgeon stands on the right side of the patient with the assistant at the foot of the patient or across the patient from the surgeon. All portals are placed ventral to the costochondral junction in the area of the lateral margin of the transverse thoracic muscles (Figures 9.21, 9.22, 9.23, 9.25, and 9.26). A lateral intercostal approach can also be used as an alter - native with the patient placed in left lateral recumbency with the monitor across the table from the surgeon (Figure 9.176). This approach allows better visualization of the right atrial appendage and aortic root for evaluation of tumor masses. The telescope portal is placed in the ventral third of the sixth or seventh intercostal spaces and two instrument portals are placed, one at the midpoint of the fourth intercostal space and the other at the midpoint of the eighth intercostal space (Figure 9.177). With this technique, the pericardial window is created on the right side of the heart. The phrenic nerve is identified prior to incising the pericardium. With all portals in place when using the dorsally recum- bent position, the first step of the procedure is to cut the ventral mediastinum off of the sternum to get it out of the visual and operative field. Scissors with electrosurgical assistance to control bleeding (Figures 9.14 and 9.15) is adequate in most patients, or a vessel sealing device is used in patients with enlarged blood vessels or when there is significant pleural reaction (Figures 9.12, 9.16–9.19). 9.8 Thoracic Operative roceeures 607 vessels interferes with the procedure by allowing blood to drip onto the telescope lens obscuring visualization. It is recommended to explore the cranial mediastinum for lymph node enlargement and to biopsy any suspicious lymph nodes. Biopsy of cranial mediastinal lymph nodes may establish a diagnosis of mesothelioma that may not be diagnosed with biopsies of the pleura or pericardium. A site is selected for the pericardial window on the cranial surface of the heart. When the pneumothorax is established with the patient in dorsal recumbency, the apex of the heart falls dorsally presenting the cranial surface of the heart to the surgeon (Figure 9.20) rather than the apex that would be seen without the pneumothorax present. Babcock forceps or aggressive grasping forceps with teeth are used to pick up a fold of pericardium (Figure 9.178). The grasping forceps are passed through the cranial operative portal. This creates a greater angle, more than 90°, from the telescope than desired but the primary function of this instrument is to hold and stabilize the pericardium and little manipulation of these forceps are needed. In some patients, there is sufficient fat or loose pleural tissue that it is difficult to get an adequate grip of the actual pericardium (Figures 9.179 and 9.180), and it is not possible to determine if the pericardium is elevated with the forceps (Figure 9.181), and in other cases, it is obvious that the pericardium is elevated but it cannot be determined if the forceps include the pericardium (Figure 9.182). When the pericardium cannot be adequately grasped due to overly - ing tissue, this tissue is dissected away to provide exposure of the pericardium (Figures 9.180 and 9.183). When the peri - cardium is adequately elevated away from the heart, Metzenbaum scissors are used to cut into the elevated fold of tissue for initial penetration into the pericardium (Figure 9.184). Once initial pericardial penetration has been achieved, the scissors are used to continue cutting the peri - cardium (Figure 9.185) making sure that there is safe separa - tion of the pericardium from the heart. Pericardial transection is continued while maintaining traction to ele - vate the pericardium away from the heart (Figure 9.186). This technique minimizes the potential for cardiac damage. This process is continued until a patch of pericardium has been resected that is approximately 2 × 2 cm (Figure 9.187). The previous figures have illustrated creation of the pericardial window with scissors because these patients had thin avascular pericardial tissue or tissue that was mildly thickened with limited vascularity. Thickened pericardial tissue may require more robust scis - sors (Figure 9.191), and for pericardial disease with signifi - cant vascularity, a vessel sealing device is used with either a 5 mm diameter (Figure 9.192) or 10 mm diameter (Figure 9.193) vessel sealing device. Any excess pericardial fluid, which has not been previously evacuated, that interferes with visualization is removed with suction (V ideo 9.8). This was a significant problem in early cases with inadequate preoperative pericardial evacuation but has not been an issue since then due to improved preop - erative pericardial evacuation. The pericardial incision is extended to remove a patch of pericardium taking care not to damage the phrenic nerves, heart, lungs or great vessels. There is no scientific data to define how much pericardium to remove. The portion removed needs to be large enough to prevent closure of the defect by the healing process and small enough to preclude herniation of the heart through the win - dow. A 1 in 2 patch has been considered to be an acceptable size. The removed patch is extracted from the chest through one of the operative portal cannulas (Figure 9.194) or a portal incision without a cannula (Figure 9.195) and is inspected for size and to define pathology. A specimen retrieval pouch is used to remove tissue whenever there is concern for tumor seeding at the portal site. Samples are submitted for histopa - thology and for cultures. The internal surface of the pericardium and a variable area of the heart can be examined through the window including masses on the heart base (Videos 9.9, 9.10, and 9.11), on the aorta, and on the internal surface of the pericardium (Video 9.12), and the rare intrapericardial for - eign body (Video 9.13), as was illustrated in the Section 9.6. 9.8 Thoracic Operative roceeures 609 Any residual pericardial and pleural fluid is removed with suction and these cavities are irrigated with saline. A standard lateral wall chest drain tube is placed with rou - tine open surgical technique away from all of the portal sites. Placement of the tube through the chest wall and position of the tube within the chest is controlled with endoscopic guidance. An alternative technique that is acceptable when pleural evacuation will be needed for 24 hours or less, places the tube through the paraxiphoid telescope portal. The telescope is removed, leaving the cannula in place while a chest tube is passed through the cannula, and the cannula is removed over the chest tube (Figures 9.27–9.30). Deep, subcutaneous, and skin clo - sure is performed to achieve an airtight seal around the tube. This technique is only acceptable at the paraxiphoid site and for tubes that will be in place for less than 24 hours. This technique is not acceptable for lateral chest wall portals and for long-term chest tubes because it is difficult to achieve an airtight seal, and there is an increased risk for air leakage around the chest tube. After chest tube placement, operative portal cannulas are removed and the portals are closed in layers to achieve an airtight closure. 9.8.2 Right Atrial Mass Resection Resection of small peripheral right auricular masses using minimally invasive technique has been performed (Crumbaker et al. 2010; Ployart et al. 2013). The auricular appendage, including the tumor, is positioned in the jaws of the stapler, the sta - pler is activated, and the resected tumor is extracted from the chest using a tissue retrieval bag. If tumors are too large (>2 cm) or are too close to the base of the auri - cle and MIS resection is not possible, conversion to open surgery is considered. Discussion with the client prior to surgery concerning possible conversion is man - datory as some clients will elect to proceed with open surgery, but some will not. Many of the clients pre - sented to the author for pericardial effusion due to heart base masses specifically request minimally invasive sur - gery and decline open surgery for any reason. A specific example is a client who had been having monthly peri - cardiocentesis performed for recurrent pericardial effu - sion for over a year because he did not want his old dog to go through an open chest surgery. When he found out that a minimally invasive approach was available, he was excitedly ready for the procedure. Thus this is a very personal decision that is up to the client. 9 Thoracoscopy 616 chest for cases where the side of the pathology cannot be determined such as with spontaneous pneumothorax and some apical masses in the cranial lung lobes, when they cannot be differentiated from cranial mediastinal masses (Figure 9.121). If the side of involvement is determined preoperatively with radiographs, CT, or other diagnostic techniques, lateral recumbency pro - vides greater unilateral access and is the preferred posi - tion. The telescope and initial operative portals are inserted using appropriate triangulation to access the involved pathology. For small peripheral lesions and for lung biopsies, a loop ligature technique can be used (Figure 9.167). The tip of the lobe to be removed is posi - tioned through a pretied loop ligature (Endo-loop), the loop is tightened, the ligated portion of the lung is tran - sected, and the resected portion of the lung is removed (Figure 9.168). This technique is relatively fast, moder - ately difficult, and saves the significant expense of an endoscopic stapler. Larger or more central lesions require an endoscopic GIA stapling device for occlusion and transection of the portion of the lobe to be removed (Figures 9.169, 9.201–9.204, and 9.206). When perform - ing partial lung lobectomy with an endoscopic stapler, the telescope and initial operative portals are placed, the lung lobe lesion is defined and retracted or elevated as needed, an additional portal is placed to provide optimal alignment for application of the stapler, and the stapler is placed through this portal (Figures 9.170, 9.201, 9.202, and 9.205). Because of the cost of endoscopic staple car - tridges, the longest staple cartridges (65 mm) are used whenever possible to minimize the chance of needing to fire two cartridges. Following transection of the lung lobe, the excised portion is removed from the chest by enlarging one of the portals to allow passage of the tis - sue or an endoscopic tissue retrieval pouch (Endo- pouch) is used to facilitate tissue removal. The transected lung margin is observed for air leakage or bleeding before exiting the chest with the telescope (Figure 9.207). A chest drain is placed with endoscopic guidance at an appropriate site away from all lateral portals or through the paraxiphoid cannula, operative and telescope can - nulas are removed, and the portals are closed to create an airtight seal. 9.8 Thoracic Operative roceeures 617 9.8.5 Lung Lobectomy Indications for removal of whole lung lobes are essentially the same as for partial lung lobectomy, except for lung biopsy, but are considered for lesions that are larger or more centrally placed. The decision for total or partial lobectomy is made on a case-by-case basis, and no hard rules determine, which pro - cedure is indicated. Case selection criteria for complete lung lobectomy with minimally invasive technique for neoplastic lesions have been established (Bleakley et al. 2015; Garcia et al. 1998; Monnet 2015; Potter and Hendrickson 1999; Zaal et al. 1997) but this information is not available for non-neoplastic diseases. Small to medium-sized neoplastic masses, up to 5–7 cm in diameter that are away from the hilus of the lung, are candidates for removal with minimally inva - sive surgical technique. Large tumors and neoplastic masses that are too close to the hilus impair visualization of the struc - tures of the hilus of the lung and make manipulation for dissec - tion and stapler placement difficult. When the size and location of lung tumors prevents a preoperative decision for a minimally invasive versus an open surgery, then starting with thoracos - copy is indicated, and conversion is performed if it is deter - mined that the procedure cannot be completed endoscopically. Non-neoplastic lesions, including inflammatory and degenera - tive diseases, are also candidates for total lung lobectomy, with similar selection criteria as for neoplastic lesions. Lateral recumbency with intercostal portal placement is the preferred technique for total lung lobectomy although dorsal recumbency with a paraxiphoid telescope portal has been used effectively for the removal of cranial lung lobes. Operating room setup is done to place the surgeon across the patient from the monitor so that the telescope is pointed as close as possible directly at the monitor. For cranial lung lobectomy, this places the monitor cranial to the patient or angled to be dorsal to this cranial position with the surgeon standing at the foot of the table and an assistant standing ventral to the patient (Figure 9.208). For caudal lung lobec- tomy, the monitor is placed at the foot of the patient with the surgeon standing cranioventral to the patient and the assistant standing craniodorsal to the patient (Figure 9.209). If a tilt table is used total lobectomy of cranial or caudal lung lobes is facilitated with a slight tilting of the patient with the sternum placed below the spine. Cranial lung lobectomy using dorsal recumbency uses the same operat - ing setup as performing a pericardial window in dorsal recumbency (Figures 9.172 and 9.173). 9 Thoracoscopy 618 Portal placement also varies depending on the lung lobe to be removed and the shape of the thorax in the individual patient. A portal pattern similar to the intercostal approach for creating a pericardial window in lateral recumbency has been used with an additional portal added for place - ment of the stapling device after the chest has been explored (Figure 9.177). Options for portal placement use the center of the third or fourth intercostal space for the telescope portal with caudal lung lobectomy and the center of the tenth intercostal space for cranial lung lobectomy. Operative portals are placed dorsally in the same intercos - tal space as the telescope, ventrally in the space cranial to the telescope portal, and after exploration, an additional operative portal is placed for the stapler aligned for best access to the hilus (Figures 9.210 and 9.211). Cranial lung lobectomy has also been performed using the same portals as for creating a pericardial window when the patient is in dorsal recumbency (Figures 9.174 and 9.175). For the tech- nique with both portals placed on the same side of the patient, the caudal operative portal is typically used for the stapler with or without an additional operative portal for lung lobe positioning. One lung ventilation is recommended to increase the amount of space available in the thoracic cavity for the visual field and to manipulate instruments and the lung lobe. The difficulty of one lung ventilation requires an experienced anesthesiologist to properly place the endotra- cheal tube and selectively intubate or block the correct main stem bronchus to ventilate only one lung. An alterna- tive that is much easier to accomplish and maintain is pleu- ral insufflation. To perform this technique, cannulas with valves and gaskets are used at all portal sites. An insufflator is set to 3–5 cm of water pressure and is connected to an insufflation port on one of the cannulas. Insufflation is ini- tiated when more visual space is needed, and the amount of insufflation pressure is adjusted to maintain cardiopul- monary function, while achieving the desired visual space. The other advantage of this technique is that insufflation is started and stopped quickly depending on the needs of the patient balanced with the needs of the surgeon. 9.8 Thoracic Operative roceeures 619 For caudal lung lobes the dorsal pulmonary ligament (Figure 9.212) is divided with Metzenbaum scissors (Figure 9.213) or a vessel sealing device (Figure 9.214) to free the lung lobe to allow manipulation for place - ment of the endoscopic stapling device. Individual structures of the hilus are not isolated for minimally invasive lung lobectomy and are separated from sur - rounding structures only enough to place the stapling device. A 45–65 mm long stapling cartridge with 3.5 mm staples is placed across the hilus of the lobe to be removed through its additional portal that is placed ventrally and cranially at a location to allow the sta - pler to be placed perpendicular to the bronchus and blood vessels (Figure 9.215). The stapling cartridge long enough to include the entire hilus to be stapled is recommended and failure to do this requires the use of a second expensive stapler cartridge (Figure 9.216). Endoscopic GIA staplers consistently achieve com - plete hemostasis and occlusion of the airways but it is still wise to observe the margins of the resection at the time that the stapler is removed (Figure 9.207). The resected lung lobe is removed from the chest through a small intercostal thoracotomy. An endoscopic tissue retrieval pouch facilitates the removal of the lung lobe and decreases the potential of seeding neoplastic cells or infection to the chest wall (Figure 9.217). Total lobectomy of the cranial lung lobes can be done in either lateral or dorsal recumbency. With a well-defined location of pathology to one side and confirmation that the lesion is in pulmonary tissue, the lateral approach is used with caudally placed portals (Figure 9.210). A case where a right cranial total lung lobectomy with the patient in lateral recumbency was presented and described with diagnostic procedures (Figures 9.169–9.171). One lung ventilation or pleural insufflation is employed as available and as needed. The hilus of the involved lung lobe is manipulated into the open jaws of the stapling device, the jaws are closed, and the stapling and cutting function is activated. It is indicated when the location of the pathology cannot be determined accurately before surgery. This most commonly occurs when cranial mediastinal masses cannot be differentiated from cranial lung lobe masses. Operative portal placement is the same as for the creation of a peri- cardial window with the operative portals on the same side (Figure 9.174). Two operative portals have been sufficient in most cases with the caudal portal used for the stapling device, but an additional portal is placed if indicated. A mass in the cranial thorax of a nine-year-old neutered male Bernese Mountain Dog was preoperatively diagnosed as a cranial mediastinal mass. The patient was positioned in dorsal recumbency, and thoracoscopy was performed. Discovery of the mass in the right cranial lung lobe (Figure 9.121) required a revision in the approach. Retraction to elevate the lung lobe was done to expose the hilus (Figure 9.218), a stapling device was employed, and the lung lobe resected (Figure 9.219). This approach was also used in a dog with spontaneous pneumothorax when the air leakage was found to originate from a bulla on the dorsal surface or the left cranial lung lobe (Figures 9.110 and 9.115). The left cranial lung lobe was resected from this approach using an EndoGIA stapling device (Figure 9.220) and achieving total resection of the cranial portion of the lung lobe (Figure 9.221). Examination for enlarged hilar lymph nodes is done after lung lobectomy (Figure 9.107) and biopsies are taken if indicated (Figure 9.162) or the lymph nodes are removed with minimally invasive technique. Magnification produced by the telescope and video system greatly enhances visualization of the thoracic ducts (Figures 9.33, 9.34, and 9.127) and instrumentation designed for minimally invasive surgery facilitates the manipulation of structures deep in the chest. Occlusion is achieved with vascular clips specifically designed for minimally invasive surgery (Endoclips) or with a vessel sealing device. Clips work well in large dogs but tend to fall off the thoracic duct in cats. If thoracic duct occlusion is planned to be combined with subtotal pericardiectomy, the patient is placed on a tilt table with the capability to achieve an angle of 45° to both sides. Intercostal portals are placed on the right lateral chest wall with the patient in left lateral recumbency for dogs and in the left chest wall with the patient in right lat - eral recumbency for cats. The surgeon and assistant stand ventral to the patient with one monitor placed on the dor - sal side of the patient, and a second monitor is placed cra- nial to the patient (Figure 9.222). The telescope portal is placed in the seventh intercostal space at the dorsoventral midpoint of the intercostal space, and operative portals are placed midway between the telescope portal and the dorsal end of the ribs in the sixth and ninth intercostal spaces (Figure 9.223). Preoperative contrast CT studies of the tho - racic duct are recommended (Birch et al. 2014; Chun et al. 2009; Esterline et al. 2005; Johnson et al. 2009; Millward et al. 2011; Singh et al. 2011; Steffey and Mayhew 2018) and injection of a popliteal lymph node or the cisterna chyli with methylene blue or fluorescent dyes have also been used to improve visualization of the thoracic duct and duct branches (Radlinsky et al. 2002; Steffey and Mayhew 2018). Pleuritis and pleural thickening associated with chy - lothorax obscures visualization of the thoracic duct in both dogs (Figure 9.224) and cats (Figure 9.225). Postoperative dietary management is the same as for open surgical PRAA correction. 9.8.9 Mediastinal Mass Removal Removal of cranial mediastinal masses has become one of the more common applications of minimally invasive thoracic surgery in the authors experience. Selected neo - plastic and inflammatory masses are removed effectively with minimally invasive technique and masses that are inoperable with minimally invasive technique are evalu - ated for open surgical resectability or are biopsied and staged for appropriate non-surgical treatment. Operating room setup, patient position, and portal placement is defined by the location of the mass. The majority of medi - astinal masses are in the cranial mediastinum and are visualized most effectively using the same operating room setup as for creating a pericardial window (Figures 9.172 and 9.173) with the patient in dorsal recumbency using a paraxiphoid telescope portal and with operative portals placed on one side of the patient or bilaterally (Figures 9.174 and 9.175). Intercostal space selection for the operative portals depends on the location and size of the cranial mediastinal mass. Portals are placed as far ventrally in the appropriate intercostal spaces as possible without damaging the internal thoracic artery. Cranial mediastinal masses can also be visualized and removed through a lateral intercostal approach with the patient in lateral recumbency. A wide variety of cranial mediastinal masses have been removed with minimally invasive technique. Size, vascu- larity, or tumor type has not affected resectability. For the last 20 years, thoracoscopy has been the primary first-line approach to cranial mediastinal masses, with few conver - sions to open surgery. A comparison of minimally invasive surgery for cranial mediastinal mass removal to the mor - bidity of a sternal splitting open approach makes thoracos - copy the procedure of choice. Masses are dissected with sharp and blunt dissection, as indicated using a vessel seal- ing device almost exclusively for hemostasis. The addition of vessel sealing instrumentation is a major factor in mak - ing these surgeries possible. All of the cranial mediastinal masses shown with the section on thoracic pathology (Figures 9.80–9.88) were removed with minimally invasive technique. The first of these masses removed was the larg - est (Figure 9.87) and was the first surgery performed by the author using a LigaSure vessel sealing device. The mass was highly vascular but was loosely attached to the sur - rounding tissues making dissection with the vessel sealing device fast, easy, and bloodless (Figure 9.235) requiring less than 15 minutes to complete, and the mass was removed through a small intercostal incision (Figure 9.236). Removal of this mass with an open sternal splitting approach and without the vessel sealing device would have been long and bloody. Additional cranial mediastinal masses removed with minimally invasive technique have included an ectopic thyroid carcinoma (Figures 9.85, 9.237, and 9.238) and a lymphocyte rich thymoma (Figures 9.83, 9.239, and 9.240). Large highly vascular masses are more challenging than smaller masses, but minimally invasive resection is an individual case decision not based on size, vascularity, or tumor type. An unu- sual foreign body case presented for pericardial effusion and a porcupine quill was found protruding from the heart (Figure 9.248) and was removed with MIS after the crea- tion of a pericardial window (Video 9.13). 9.9 Contraindications for Thoracoscopy The primary contraindication for performing thoracoscopy or minimally invasive thoracic surgery is an inadequate level of minimally invasive surgical skills. There are few true con - traindications for performing thoracoscopy in small animal practice. Many of the contraindications discussed in human and veterinary medicine for minimally invasive thoracic surgery and for diagnostic thoracoscopy are relative con - traindications. They can arguably be presented as indica - tions for these procedures. Multiple pleural adhesions that prevent the creation of an adequate visual cavity or that substantially increase the risks of establishing an adequate visual cavity are one of the true contraindications for min - imally invasive thoracic surgery. Fortunately, the inci - dence of adhesions that are extensive enough to present a problem is very low in our patients.
