9 Thoracoscopy 630 9.10 Complications of Thoracoscopy Experience with complications from the human field is well documented (Metintas et al. 2013; Nour Moursi Ahmed et al. 2016; Pio et al. 2017). Insufficient data is available to effectively define the complications of veterinary thoracos - copy and minimally invasive thoracic surgery. Severe or life threatening complications associated with the creation of a pneumothorax that is possible include laceration of the lung (Figure 9.249), heart, or major vessels with the Veress needle or with trocar placement, perforation of the esopha - gus or trachea with a trocar, over insufflation causing cardi - orespiratory compromise, and injury to the thoracic wall or diaphragm. Other than the lung laceration these are possi - ble complications that have not been encountered in the author’s experience. Additional potential pneumothorax related complications that are not life-threatening but can compromise the patient and interfere with completion of the procedure include: hypercapnia, hypotension, thoracic wall vascular injury, and subcutaneous emphysema. Potential non-insufflation related complications include electrosurgical injuries, hemorrhage, portal air leakage, seeding of tumors at portal sites, nerve injuries, disorienta - tion or inability to recognize anatomic structures, and lack of technical expertise. Displacement of one lung ventila - tion, endotracheal tubes and endobronchial blockers are more common complications. Insufflation is not typically employed for minimally invasive thoracic surgery but when used carries the same potential for complications that exists for abdominal insuf- flation. Thoracic wall penetration related complications, including vascular and organ damage, are the same as for laparoscopy. All of these complications are concerns for veterinary thoracoscopy and minimally invasive thoracic surgery. Techniques used in human surgery to avoid these problems need to be employed to minimize any complications and eliminate defining animal complications by adverse expe - rience. Conversion to open surgery when the procedure cannot be completed with minimally invasive technique is not considered a complication for the beginning minimally invasive surgeon. It is simply part of the learning curve. Conversion for excessive blood loss during removal of a cranial mediastinal mass was required in one patient undergoing surgery using minimally invasive technique. With proper care, attention to detail, and adequate train- ing, the incidence of significant complications with mini- mally invasive thoracic procedures is very low. 9.11 Conclusions Diagnostic thoracoscopy and minimally invasive thoracic surgery are safe, effective, and easy to perform techniques with significant applications for obtaining important diag - nostic information and performing thoracic surgery with minimal trauma. There is much more to be learned about indications, advantages, disadvantages, problems, complica - tions, and contraindications. The incidence of complications associated with thoracoscopy is very low. Significant postop - erative hemorrhage or air leakage has not occurred. A recent experience by the author with an open intercos - tal thoracotomy emphasized the advantages and benefits of thoracoscopy. When compared to thoracoscopy, an open thoracotomy is a barbaric procedure, with excessive tissue trauma, extended procedure time, and poor chest visuali- zation. Postoperative pain is excessive, and recovery is pro - longed. Thoracoscopy is a superior procedure with dramatically reduced operative trauma, reduced operative time, significantly reduced postoperative pain, and infi- nitely better visualization. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 637 Ear disease is one of the most common problems seen in Veterinary Practice. Otoscopy provides for the visualiza- tion of the ear canals, tympanic membrane (TM), and mid- dle ear and is considered a mandatory part of the diagnostic workup and management of all ear disease. Recognition of the value that video otoscopy brings to the diagnosis and management of otitis continues to grow. When compared to the 3–6 × magnification provided by conventional, hand- held otoscopes, video otoscopes provide 15 × – 50 × magni- fication. This results in an enhanced ability to visualize both normal structures and pathologic changes within the ear, especially in the area of the TM and middle ear. Through this technology, pet owners are able to visualize their dog’s or cat’s ear disease in the examination room. Direct visualization by the client improves compliance with prescribed therapies and, on re-examination, offers positive reinforcement for therapeutic efforts. Because of superior visualization capabilities, video otoscopy also allows for the enhanced performance of many procedures within the ear, including ear canal and middle ear clean- ing, mass removals, biopsies, foreign body removal, intral- esional injections, and myringotomy. In all the above situations, video monitor images can be captured as digital photographs, or as video movies. These may be added to the patient’s medical record. They can also be given to the client as documentation of the disease process and proce - dures performed. 10.1 Normal Anatomy of the Ear as Seen Through the Video Otoscope Figure 10.1 provides a general overview of the important anatomic structures of the normal canine ear utilizing an ear model. On the lateral edge of the entrance to the verti- cal ear canal, there is a “notch” called the intertragic incisure. It is present in both the dog and the cat. The tip of the video otoscope cone is placed in the “notch” to start the otoscopic examination. The notch area is not particularly sensitive and provides stability for the cone as it is then advanced further into the vertical ear canal (Figure 10.2). A prominent fold of the canal wall called the luminal fold separates the vertical from the horizontal ear canal (Figure 10.3). Its prominence varies between breeds and between individuals within breeds. It variably obstructs the view into the horizontal canal and may preclude passage of the otoscope cone into the horizontal canal. It is a sensitive structure. Contact with the luminal fold may result in a painful response on the part of the patient and may reduce the possibility of performing a successful otoscopic examination. Pulling the pinna up and out, away from the base of the skull, flattens this prominence. When the patient is in lateral recumbency, the pinna is pulled vertically to minimize the fold. The luminal fold is less prominent in the cat but still warrants minimization utilizing the techniques outlined above for the dog. In brachycephalic breeds in general, including the Mastiff and St. Bernard, the horizontal canal tends to significantly narrow just in front of the TM (Figure 10.4). This is a degree of canal stenosis that is normal for these breeds. The lining of the ear canal is essentially modified skin that contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands in the more superficial dermis, ceruminous glands (modified apocrine glands) in the deeper dermis, nerves, and blood vessels. In normal dogs, blood vessels are often seen within the walls of the canals with video otoscopy (Figure 10.5). One of the earliest signs of canal wall thickening due to inflammation is an inability to visualize these vessels. This structure has the potential to dilate or “bulge” into the horizontal canal with relatively minor increases in air pressure within the middle ear (Figure 10.8). It is likely a part of the pressure-equalizing system across the tympanum of the dog. Finding a dilated pars flaccida during examination of the ear is considered a normal variant in the dog (not pathologic). Some degree of dilatation is often induced with intubation and general anesthesia. At times the “nondilated” pars flaccida is not very prominent at all (difficult to visualize well) (Figure 10.9). In the presence of otitis media, the pars flac- cida may become thickened (myringitis), and filled with inflammatory debris. Inflammatory debris accumulation may cause the pars flaccida to widely dilate, completely occluding the horizontal canal. The pars flaccida is sepa- rated from the larger pars tensa by the malleolar fold (Figure 10.7). This is a narrow linear thickening of the tym- panum that spans the tympanum. Most of what is seen of the TM through the otoscope is the large pars tensa. This is a tense structure that generally does not dilate with pres - sure changes within the middle ear and seldomly bulges with the accumulation of exudates/debris within the mid- dle ear. The manubrium (handle) of the malleus is situated within the fibrous layer of the pars tensa, extending down from the malleolar fold. It is white in color and curved, such that the opening of the curve is pointed cranially (Figures 10.7–10.9). A thin vascular supply can be seen along the margins of the handle. Striations may be seen extending from the handle of the malleus to the periphery of the tympanum. Tension on the manubrium gives the pars tensa a mildly concave outer contour. Both the normal pars tensa and pars flaccida are rice paper in color. The pars tensa of the dog is variably translucent, with the tympa- num often becoming less translucent with age. Translucency often allows the otoscopist to see the bulla septum, located within the middle ear. The bulla septum is a bony ridge extending out from the medial wall of the middle ear. It is seen through the TM as a whitish line whose light color is highlighted by the contrast between this and the adjacent dark-colored area that is the opening to the tympanic bulla (Figures 10.7 and 10.8). The opening to the tympanic bulla is caudoventral to caudal (varies among individuals). Starting at the malleolar fold, the TM is oriented at about a 30–40° angle from perpendicular, with the more dorsal aspects of the pars tensa being closer to the otoscopist (Figure 10.1). The TM of the cat (Figure 10.10) also consists of a pars tensa and parsa flaccida, but the pars flaccida does not undergo “normal” dilatation as seen in the dog (Figure 10.9). The pars flaccida tends to only dilate in the presence of otitis media, wherein the dilatation is both due to pars flaccida thickening (myringitis) and debris accumu- lation. The manubrium of the malleus is only slightly curved at its end, with the open end of the curve again ori- ented cranially. The TM is rice paper in color, but is not as translucent as it can be in the dog. The middle ear of the dog, starting from dorsal to ventral, is made up of the epitympanic recess, the tympanic cavity, and the tympanic bulla (Figure 10.1). The epitympanic recess houses the three small middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes). The vestibular (oval) window is a “hole” in the bone of the dorsal medial wall of the middle ear (in the epitympanic recess). It is covered by epithelium. The stapes attaches to this. The inner ear is deep to the vestibu - lar window (primarily semicircular canals). The tympanic cavity is the area just inside the TM (between the epitym - panic recess and the tympanic bulla below). The dorsome - dial surface of this cavity is primarily made up of the barrel-shaped cochlear promontory (Figures 10.11 and 10.12). The cochlea (responsible for hearing) sits behind this structure. The promontory is situated opposite to the dorsal half of the TM. At the caudal end of the promontory is the cochlear (round) window, which is another “hole” in the bone of the medial wall of the middle ear that leads to the inner ear (cochlea). It is covered with epithelium. It is dorsal and caudal in the middle ear (Figures 10.11 and 10.12). The sympathetic nerve courses horizontally across the cochlear promontory. The facial and parasympa - thetic nerves pass through a bony channel in the most dor - sal aspect of the middle ear. About midway through the middle ear, there is a small area of this bony channel that is devoid of bone, exposing these nerves to the middle ear. It is important to note that all of these potentially “sensitive” structures are dorsal in the middle ear, prompting the rec - ommendation to orient all operative procedures (myringot - omy, middle ear cleaning, etc.) to the more ventral aspects of the TM/middle ear where there are no significant blood Pars flaccida Manubrium (handle) of the malleus Parstensa Figure 10.10 Normal tympanic membrane of the cat.

The opening of the auditory tube (Eustachian tube) lies in the rostro-medial part of the tym - panic cavity and opens into the nasopharynx, serving to equalize pressure on either side of the TM (Figure 10.11). The tympanic bulla is the largest of the three cavities of the middle ear. It is separated dorsally from the tympanic cavity by a bony ridge called the bulla septum. The bulla septum is most prominent over the medial and anterior aspects of the bulla (Figures 10.11 and 10.12). The septum varies in width among dogs. It has variable numbers of projections (none to many) called “bony spicules” along its margin. These pro - jections may end in sizeable (1 mm), round bony forma - tions. Catheters passed into the middle ear frequently “hang up” on the bulla septum, precluding their advancement into the more ventral tympanic bulla. If the TM is perforated in the dog, conical video oto - scopes may allow for the visualization of the bulla septum with its spicules and the medial bony wall of the middle ear. The dorsal nerves, ossicles, round and oval windows, and the opening to the auditory tube cannot be seen. It is not possible to visualize into the depths of the tympanic bulla. In the dog, a longer, narrower telescope with a 30° angled tip may facilitate visualization into the tympanic bulla. The middle ear of the cat is similar to that of the dog, but for the presence of a bony plate that extends from the lat - eral wall of the middle ear to the medial wall of the middle ear, effectively almost totally dividing the upper tympanic cavity/epitympanic recess (termed the dorsolateral cham- ber in the cat) from the larger tympanic bulla (termed the ventromedial chamber in the cat) (Figures 10.13 and 10.14). Communication between the upper and lower chambers is limited to a small opening at the caudomedial aspect of the bony plate. The sympathetic nerves come through the anterior aspect of the “slit” and arborize over the medial wall and cochlear prominence of the middle ear (Figure 10.14). Sympathetic nerves are therefore found more ventrally on the medial wall of the middle ear of the cat than in the dog and are therefore more exposed to trauma from manipulation in the dorsal half of the middle ear. With TM perforation, it is possible to see the medial bony wall of the middle ear, but the sympathetic nerves, ossicles, round and oval windows, and opening into the auditory tube usually cannot be seen. In both the dog and the cat, the tympanic cavity and auditory canal are covered by a mucous membrane type of respiratory epithelium, which is a pseudostratified, ciliated, columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. This lining produces secretions that are moved to and passed down the auditory tube as the normal “flushing” mechanism of the middle ear. If the auditory tube is not patent (obstructed or not capable of opening), there is a resultant accumulation of secretions (watery to mucoid) within the middle ear. 10.2 Pathophysiology of the Ear as Seen Through the Video Otoscope With chronic inflammation of the ear canals, the canal walls tend to thicken and the canal lumen tends to narrow. Ceruminous gland dilatation and hyperplasia may be seen as a cobble - stone appearance on the surface of the canals (Figure 10.15). Markedly dilated ceruminous glands may take on a bluish color which is the color imparted by the secretions accumu - lated within the glands. Marked thickening of the canal walls often results in folding of the walls to potentially com - pletely occlude the canal lumen. Some breeds (e.g. Spaniel breeds) are prone to developing canal wall fibroproliferative nodules that may also contribute to occlusion of the canals (Figure 10.16). It is uncommon to see the ear canals of cats develop these degrees of canal wall thickening with even severe, chronic otitis externa. We do not expect to see fibro - proliferative nodules nor ossification of the auricular carti - lages with chronic otitis externa in the cat. The most common pathologic change associated with the TM of the dog and the cat is a tendency for the TM to become thicker and more opaque in response to debris that has been sitting on the surface of the TM for protracted periods of time. These tympana are usually more whitish or grayish in color. In the dog, this debris may “push” the tympanum into the tympanic cavity to various degrees. This is less likely to occur in the cat, wherein debris accu- mulation that pushes the tympanum is more likely to cause TM perforation. Pathologic changes of the TM associated with the presence of otitis media include thickening, becoming opaque and whitish, potentially with neovascu- larization and discoloration (darker color, brownish, etc.) (Figures 10.17–10.19). These are manifestations of TM inflammation, termed myringitis. In the dog, otitis media may result in the pars flaccida becoming not only thick - ened, but also very dilated with inflammatory debris. The dilatation may expand to occupy the entire horizontal canal. In the cat, it is also possible to see the pars flaccida dilate in the presence of otitis media. The dilatation is often related to severe edema of the pars flaccida, with less related to the accumulation of inflammatory debris from the otitis media. Contemporary emphasis is being placed on the development of more compact, more mobile, less expensive units that can be used on a routine basis in the examination room. However, products that are less expensive often sacri - fice quality of picture, size of visual field, depth of visualiza - tion, and capabilities of doing manipulative procedures through the scope. Karl Storz Veterinary Endoscopy, America (Goleta, CA), manufactures a variety of video otoscope systems that are popular and representative of this technology. The Veterinary Otoendoscope (Karl Storz Veterinary Endoscopy, America, Goleta, CA) features an 8.5 cm long conical telescope with a 5 mm diameter tip (Figure 10.20). This telescope has a 2 mm (5 Fr) working channel, which exits the tip of the probe at the 12 o’clock position. The tel- escope has a 0° lens angle with a field of vision of 100–120°. The working channel of the Storz Otoendoscope allows passage of 5-Fr or smaller catheters for irrigation and suc- tion, biopsy forceps, grasping forceps, ear curettes, brushes, polypectomy snares, myringotomy needles, and diode laser fibers. The Storz Otoendoscope also has a double-port adapter, which is attached to the working channel and allows for simultaneous passage of fluid and either suction or instrumentation (Figure 10.21). A miniature, handheld color video camera is attached to the eyepiece of the tele - scope. It has a digitally controlled wheel that allows for focusing. The light source cord is attached to the base of the video otoscope (Figure 10.20). It is possible to rotate the otoscope cone at its attachment to the mini camera, to change the orientation of the 12 o’clock exit point of the working channel (Figure 10.20). This facilitates directing instruments passed through the working channel to vari- ous areas of the ear canal. Both one- and three-chip cam- eras are available. One-chip cameras are most commonly employed for units that are primarily used for video otos - copy. Three-chip cameras are much more expensive but provide improved clarity. Three-chip cameras are used with units that consist of a high-definition monitor and xenon light source which provides more natural white light and colors. Alternatives include an open-ended 5 Fr tomcat catheter (5.5″) or 5.5″ 16 gauge Teflon intravenous catheter (Milacath No. 1611; Mila International Inc.). Curettes are used to loosen debris from the walls of the canals, to facilitate flushing or grasping. The major advantage associated with units such as this is exceptionally effective, potentially continuous flushing capabilities. The degrees of positive pressure associated with flushing and negative pressure associated with suc- tioning are controllable on the instrument. Because the on/ off buttons for both flushing and suctioning can be held in one hand, this is a procedure that can be performed by the otoscopist alone (Figure 10.27). 10.5 Video Otoscopy as a Diagnostic Aid – “In Examination Room” Use An otoscopic examination is considered a mandatory part of the evaluation of any dog or cat with an ear problem. Because otitis is very frequently associated with underlying dermatologic diseases (i.e. allergic dermatitis), every indi- vidual with a dermatologic problem should also receive an otoscopic examination, looking for the presence of subclin- ical otitis. Video otoscopy provides the ideal technology to perform this examination. It is usually very difficult to point out changes seen on the monitor during the examina- tion. Pictures are generally taken and then demonstrated to the client. It is ideal to have pictures of representative nor - mal canine and feline ear canals and tympanae in the examination room that can be shared with the client such that they may better appreciate the pathologic changes in their pet’s ears. Pet owner recognition of pathologic changes within the ear enhances compliance with medica- tion regimes and/or the need for advanced diagnostics or treatments including radiographs, CAT scan, tissue biopsies, and deep ear cleaning. The visualization of changes within the ears, as seen on follow-up evaluation is greatly facilitated by being able to refer back to original pic- tures. Visualization of the ears at follow-up examination allows for owner appreciation for the benefits associated with prescribed treatments. For less than desired responses to therapy, owners are often stimulated to “do even better” with “at home” treatments. Owner visualization at follow- up examinations also allows for a greater understanding and acceptance of the need for further diagnostics and treatments such as “deep ear” cleanings if significant debris is persisting in ears. Successful use of the video otoscope in the examination room is largely dictated by operator expertise. For the neo - phyte, the hand–eye coordination required can prove frus - trating. Expertise can only be developed through routine performance of the procedure. It is important that video otoscopic examination be done before taking samples for cytologic examination with cot - ton tipped swabs. If cytology is done first, debris may be driven further down into the ear canal, obscuring struc- tures within the deeper ear canal. Proper animal restraint is important for this examination. It may be possible for a client to provide this restraint with appropriate instruction. However, if there is any indication that this will not be adequate, the restraint is best performed by a trained technician. This facilitates a quick procedure with less discomfort for the patient. While most canine examinations are best done on an examination table, the lack of a need to have the operator eye close to the scope, as required of conventional otoscopy, readily allows for examination of larger dogs on the floor. For the dog, it is best to have the person doing the restraining direct the muzzle slightly downward into the thoracic inlet by holding the hand over the bridge of the nose. This prevents the patient from throwing the head upward, which is often the dog’s natural response to discourage the examination. The otoscopist grasps the pinna and pulls it up and out, away from the skull (Figure 10.2), to minimize the Figure 10.27 Flushing and suctioning device (Storz Vetpump 2); allows control of irrigation (flushing) positive pressures and suction negative pressures. Both can be controlled in one hand.

10 Video Otoscopy 650 prominence of the luminal fold (Figure 10.3). The tip of the video otoscope is placed in the intertragic incisure as the starting place for the examination (Figure 10.2). The cone is generally at about a 45° angle at the start of the examination. Once in the canal, advancement is facilitated by visualization on the monitor. When the otoscope tip is about one halfway into the vertical canal, the video otoscope cone is rotated downward to a more horizontal position. This will facilitate visualization and advancement into the deeper aspects of the canal. Whenever possible, a thorough examination concludes with visualization of the TM. Consideration is given to taking at least four pictures of the ear canal for recording purposes: (i) at the entrance to the vertical canal; (ii) just outside the luminal fold, so that the luminal fold is seen over the more dorsal aspect of the picture; (iii) just inside the luminal fold; (iv) halfway down the horizontal canal – deep enough to clearly evaluate the TM. For a patient that is not very co-operative, pictures are taken very quickly, even without thorough visualization on the monitor. The captured pictures are then examined more thoroughly after the examination has been completed to assess for adequacy. For cats, restraint is usually minimal, consisting of an individual holding the shoulders and back of the cat to keep it from moving. The operator pulls the pinna up and out with significant force, which may have an immobilizing effect on the cat, and the scope is advanced. During video otoscopic examination, the degree of inflammation, nature of debris, color of debris, degree of proliferation (narrowing of canals), proliferative changes, masses, and the nature and integrity of the TM are assessed. If the patient has a normal ear, it can be used to demonstrate the significant changes in the pathologic ear. It is preferable to begin the video otoscopic examination with the more normal of the two years. This reduces the tendency to carry bacteria or yeast from one ear to the other. The outside of the cone is wiped down with 70% alcohol after the examination of a given ear to also reduce the tendency to transfer infectious agents. In light of the high incidence of bacterial and Malassezia infections associated with otitis, the routine cleaning of the video otoscope between examinations or procedures is mandatory. For routine cleaning between examinations, wiping down the outer aspect of the cone and flushing/ passing a cleaning brush through the working channel, using a 70% isopropyl alcohol solution, is very effective in negating transmission of infection via contamination. It is mandatory that this be done routinely. Some awake dogs and cats simply do not accept the use of the video otoscope, regardless of the otoscopist’s experience and adequacy of restraint. In addition, the pain associated with severe inflammation may also preclude successful visualization. Sedation may mitigate these problems. Large amounts of debris within the ears or severe stenotic changes within the canals may also be impediments to examination. The inability to get a clear picture due to lens fogging and debris accumulation on the otoscope cone tip is a very common problem and potential source of frustration during video otoscope examinations. A commercial antifogging solution (e.g. Karl Storz “Ultra Stop” anti-fog solution or Dexide™ Fred™ Anti-Fog solution from Coviden) can be used for this purpose. However, the author more routinely uses 70% isopropyl alcohol-soaked cotton balls to clean the cone tip if the picture is unclear. Placement of the cone tip in the ear, followed by removal and cleaning of the tip may have to be repeated several times before a clear picture is obtained. Because cleaning of the tip often has to be repeated many times in order to do a successful examination, the author favors the use of the less-expensive 70% alcohol for routine use. The alcohol is used liberally with each tip cleaning. It does not appear to irritate even very inflamed ears. There are various protocols for cleaning video otoscopes between patients. In the author’s clinic, where all camera’s and video otoscopes are used for only otoscopy, following the patient examination, the otoscope cone and channel are cleaned with 2% Nolvasan solution (2% chlorhexidine; diluted 50 : 50 with water for cleaning purposes). A cleaning brush is used to clean the channel. The cone and channel are then liberally rinsed with potable, high-purity water (Chlorhexidine tends to leave a sticky residue). More intense antimicrobial cleansing, utilized after known or suspected more problematic infectious problems including Pseudomonas spp. and Methicillin resistant staphylococcus spp., is provided by a quat-based product: Virex 11 256 (Diversey), followed by liberal rinsing with potable, high- purity water. Periodic cleaning with an enzymatic cleaner is done, in accordance with recommendations by the man- ufacturer (Storz). 10.6 Video Otoscopy Procedures Procedures performed through the video otoscope are done with the patient in lateral recumbency. The pinna is pulled vertically and the video otoscope is also held vertically within the ear canal. “Getting away” from vertical often results in a compromised ability to visualize well within the ear canal. Minor procedures such as grass awn foreign body removal may be done with manual restraint, although this often requires several individuals (one holding the head, one holding the rest of the body). Sedation will allow for the performance of most foreign body removals without the need for significant manual

10.6 Video Otoscopy rocedures 651 restraint. Sedation may also be adequate for other minor procedures such as flushing/suctioning or grasping and removal of larger pieces of debris from the ears or aspirating samples from deeper within the ear for purposes of cytology and/or culture and sensitivity testing. However, thoroughly cleaning debris from deep within the horizontal canal, in the area of the TM, is best done with general anesthesia. Patients are very sensitive to manipulation in the area of the TM and the stimulation of manipulation in these areas will result in head shaking which in turn hinders visualization and manipulation of instrumentation and is associated with the risk of damaging the TM and middle ear structures. Patient movement will also limit the thoroughness of the cleaning procedure. General anesthesia also requires placement of an endotracheal tube. If the TM is perforated, this will prevent aspiration of fluids that may pass through the middle ear and auditory canal into the posterior pharynx. It is possible to hold the video otoscope and pinna in one hand, leaving the other hand available to do procedures such as flushing and suctioning through a catheter or utiliz - ing grasping or biopsy forceps through the working chan - nel. The otoscopist would have to use short (e.g. 15 cm) grasping or biopsy forceps. The quickest and most effective method of doing most procedures is to use longer instru - mentation (30–34 cm) and have one individual directing the video otoscope in the ear and another utilizing the longer catheter (for flushing and suctioning), grasping or biopsy forceps through the working channel (Figure 10.28). It is important to recall that for video otoscopes that have a working channel, the channel usually exits the cone tip at 12 o’clock. Instrumentation will also exit the scope tip at 12 o’clock. This means that the otoscopist directing the scope will have to move/rotate the scope in the ear to allow for instrumentation access to the various areas of the ear. With some units, it is possible to rotate the cone on the end of the camera, to facilitate rotating the exit point and instrumenta - tion direction (Figure 10.20). The positioning of the otoscopist relative to the animal’s head while in lateral recumbency also may vary with the preference of the video otoscopist. The author prefers to manipulate the video otoscope from the back of the head (Figure 10.28). This allows for easier instrumentation access to the working channel by the individual utilizing the catheter for flushing and suction or grasping forceps, etc. Instrumentation exiting the working channel comes out at 12 o’clock which automatically directs this instrumentation into the more ventral aspects of the canal, TM, and middle ear. In the middle ear, this keeps instrumentation away from sensitive structures in the more dorsal aspects of the middle ear. Working from the back of the head will result in structures seen on the video monitor screen being upside down. Familiarity with the normal anatomy of the ear decreases any confusion when using this orientation. Continuous saline infusion, accomplished through a double port adapter, is often very valuable adjunctive to the use of manipulative instrumentation through the other port. A saline bag and IV transfer unit may be attached to one port. Saline is run into the ear by gravity flow. Greater flows, with greater pressure, can be achieved with a compression unit around the saline bag. Continuous saline infusion facilitates expansion of the ear canal, prevents fogging of the lens, and lessens debris accumulation around the tip of the otoscope. Continuous saline infusion facilitates debris removal (wax, exudate, and blood). Continuous saline infusion should be considered as an adjunctive technique when doing deep ear cleanings and biopsies or mass resections. The addition of the adapter requires the use of longer (e.g. 34 cm) grasping forceps and biopsy forceps and catheters (e.g. at least 10″/25.5 cm). 10 Video Otoscopy 652 Procedures are usually begun with a thorough examina - tion of the ear. Lens fogging or obstruction of the visual field with debris is best dealt with by removing the telescope and wiping the lens with a cotton ball soaked in 70% isopropyl alcohol. This process must usually be repeatedly done during any procedure. Images are obtained before, during, and after any procedure to document “before and after” accomplish - ments. These images are shared with the patient’s owner. 10.6.1 Deep Ear Cleaning of the Ear Canals The goal for any deep ear cleaning would be to remove all debris from the ear to the level of the TM. If the middle ear is filled with debris, a significant amount of this material can be removed from both the tympanic cavity and tympanic bulla of the dog. Only the tympanic cavity (dor - solateral chamber) of the middle ear of the cat is amenable to cleaning. Before doing a deep ear cleaning in a chronically affected ear that has significant canal wall thickening and stenosis, consideration should be given to treating the ear for one or two weeks to open up the canals and facilitate access to the deeper portions of the ear canals. This therapy usually involves use of both topical and oral glucocorticoids. Once a thorough examination of the ear has been accom- plished and baseline images of the ear have been captured, a sample of debris is aspirated from the depths of the ear canal for cytologic examination and possibly for culture and sensitivity testing. If, at any time during the ear clean- ing, the TM is noted to be perforated, samples are always taken from the middle ear for cytologic examination and for culture and sensitivity testing. Organisms from the hor - izontal canal and middle ear may differ and sensitivity pat - terns of the same organism may also differ from the canal to the middle ear. Samples obtained from the middle ear are submitted for both aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cul- tures. Cytologic examination from these areas is consid- ered mandatory, to aid in the selection of empiric therapies following cleaning procedures, and to better interpret the results of cultures. It is important to note that Malassezia sp. may be seen more readily on cytology versus culture. Prior to cleaning, a ceruminolytic may be placed in the ear and massaged in to facilitate the breakup of waxy debris. The ceruminolytic should not be potentially ototoxic. Flushing and suctioning can be done through the work - ing channel of the video otoscope using a 6.5″ “cut down” , 5 Fr polypropylene catheter, a 16-gauge, 5.5″ Teflon intra- venous catheter, a 5.5″, open-ended tomcat catheter or a 5 Fr red feeding tube attached to a 12 or 20 ml syringe. An irrigation/suction device such as the VetPump 2 (Storz) is much superior for this flushing and suctioning process (Figure 10.26). Utilizing this device, copious amounts of fluid may be continually flushed through the ear under sig - nificant amounts of pressure to facilitate debris break up. Suctioning is usually less aggressive because it will poten- tially collapse the canal. Flushing pressures are usually set at maximum when working well away from the tympa- num. They are decreased as the catheter tip approaches the tympanum. If the catheter tip is near the TM, excessive flushing or suction pressures may rupture the TM. Debris that has been lodged in the horizontal canal, just in front of the TM for long periods of time often requires protracted periods of flushing to loosen the debris (Figures 10.29– 10.31). Patience is a virtue when trying to break up this debris. Debris that is more proximal in the canals (away from the TM) and resistant to flushing may be loosened with the aid of an ear curette or cleaning brush. Grasping forceps are very effective for removing debris. Adding the Wax and exudate filling the horizontal canal, just in front of the tympanic membrane area. Occasionally, it will be the product of an ascending infection up the auditory tube, from the posterior pharynx. In this scenario, the tympanum will usually be intact. In the cat, it is more common to see ascending problems related to auditory tube dysfunction (intact tympanum). If debris has accu - mulated within the middle ear, it can be flushed and aspi - rated as outlined for the canals, either through a perforated TM or through a hole created in an otherwise intact TM. Flushing/suctioning can be done through a polypropylene catheter attached to a 12 cc syringe. 10 Video Otoscopy 654 should be “gentle.” If an irrigation/suction unit is used, both irrigation and suctioning should be set at low levels to minimize the potential of damage to sensitive struc - tures. Grasping forceps (3 Fr preferred) can be used to remove debris from the middle ear. All instrumentation should always be directed toward the ventral half of the entrance to the middle ear to avoid the sensitive structures that are present within the dorso-rostral and dorso-caudal aspects of the middle ear (Figures 10.11–10.14). In order to better access the tympanic bulla of the dog, catheter tips should be directed caudo-ventrally or caudally in the mid - dle ear. When trying to access the tympanic bulla of the dog, it is very common to have one’s catheter catch up on the bulla septum (bony ridge) that partially separates the tympanic cavity from the tympanic bulla. To facilitate better entry into the tympanic bulla, a slight curve can be given to the tip of a 16-guage Teflon catheter by placing a stylet wire through the catheter and bending the tip, then heating the catheter in boiling water. After cooling, a bend should remain within the catheter once the stylet wire is removed. Although the tip will straighten as it passes through the operating channel, it will retain its curve once it exits the scope. Large quantities of saline should be run through the middle ear as part of the management of canine otitis media. It is not uncommon to have signifi - cant amounts of epithelial debris (whitish material) per - sist in the bulla, even after cleaning. This generally does not pose a problem. In the cat, a bony plate separates the upper chamber of the middle ear (dorsolateral chamber or tympanic cavity) from the larger ventral chamber (ventro - medial chamber; tympanic bulla). It is only possible to flush the upper chamber. Techniques for “breaking down” this bony plate to access the ventromedial chamber for cleaning purposes have been described but are not deemed necessary by this author. Flushing and suctioning pres - sures should be very gentle when cleaning the middle ear of the cat. In general, it is more likely to see iatrogenic Horner’s syndrome with deep ear cleaning because, in the cat, the sympathetic nerves cover much of the dorsal half of the medial wall of the middle ear and catheters “bounc - ing” on these areas can be damaging (see Figure 10.14). The transference of inflammation and even excessive fluid pressures through the vestibular (oval) and cochlear (round) windows in the medial wall of the middle ear may also create the signs associated with otits interna (head tilts, ataxia, and nystagmus). In the dog, otitis media may be associated with a pars flaccida that is filled and widely dilated with debris. This dilated pars flaccida will often fill the entire horizontal canal and look like a mass in the ear (Figure 10.32). The pars tensa of the tympanum may or may not be intact. In either situation, the middle ear will also be filled with debris. The dilated pars flaccida will have to be opened and cleaned to facilitate access to the rest of the middle ear (Figure 10.33). The technique for dealing with such dilated pars flaccidas is addressed in Section 10.6.5. Following middle ear cleaning, depending on the results of the cytol- ogy, “safer” (no ototoxicity potential) aqueous medications such as a mix of enrofloxacin (22.7 mg/ml) and dexametha- sone sodium phosphate (4 mg/ml) at a ratio of 1 : 2 for bacterial problems or enrofloxacin (22.7 mg/ml), 1% miconazole, and dexamethasone sodium phosphate (4 mg/ ml) at a ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 for bacterial and Malassezia prob - lems, or 1% miconazole and dexamethasone sodium phos - phate (4 mg/ml) at a ratio of 1 : 1 or 1 : 2 for just Malassezia may be infused into the middle ear at the completion of the middle ear cleaning. 10.6.3 Intralesional Glucocorticoid Injections Chronic proliferative changes such as diffuse thickening of the canal walls and/or fibroproliferative nodules within the canals can be injected with glucocorticoids to facilitate shrinkage of the lesion areas. This helps reduce the amount of systemic glucocorticoid therapy necessary to achieve this shrinkage. Triamcinolone acetonide is used at a con- centration of 2 mg/ml. This is injected with a 6″, 22-gauge spinal needle. This needle passes through the operating port of the video otoscope. If there is 360° stenosis of the canal, the video otoscope is placed as deeply in the ear as Dorsal RostralRight ear Figure 10.32 Canine otitis media. 10.6 Video Otoscopy rocedures 655 possible and injections are given at the 12-, 4-, and 8-o’clock positions. 0.1–0.2 ml are administered at each injection site. Injections are repeated at about 1-cm intervals while backing the video otoscope out of the ear canal. Proliferative nodules are injected toward their base, with similar amounts of triamcinolone. 10.6.4 Laser Surgery Lasers can be used through the video otoscope to cut or vaporize masses within the ear canal, including cerumi- nous cysts, tumors, and fibroproliferative nodules. They can also be used to perform a myringotomy. A quartz diode laser fiber will pass through the 2 mm operating port of most commonly used video otoscopes. CO 2 laser tips may only readily pass through the working channel of some video otoscopes. For instance, the Vetscope Veterinary Otoendoscope (Otopet USA) will accept this tip while the The Veterinary Otoendoscope (Karl Storz Veterinary Endoscopy, America, Goleta, CA) will not. The laser tip is advanced to a point just outside the telescope tip so that it can be visualized, and the laser beam is directed at the lesion. The goal is to vaporize the mass without causing significant tissue charring. The use of a low wattage setting provides for very little smoke plume formation. The poten- tial for damaging deeper structures such as the TM can be minimized by filling part of the horizontal canal with saline or by using a small piece of moistened cotton to cover the TM. 10.6.5 Myringotomy Myringotomy (incision of the TM) is generally performed to obtain samples from the middle ear for both cytology and culture and sensitivity testing when there is suspicion of otitis media but the TM is intact. This is most commonly seen in the cat, with otitis originating from auditory tube obstruction and/or ascending infections moving up the auditory tube (Eustachian tube). It is an uncommon patho - genesis in the dog. In these scenarios, the tympanum will frequently appear abnormal (more opaque, inflamed, neo - vascularized, discolored); with a possibly dilated, thick - ened pars flaccida (Figures 10.17 and 10.19). In some cases, the TM was previously perforated but has healed. This tends to occur more commonly in dogs. Occasionally, a myringotomy may be performed to reduce the size of an air-filled or debris-filled pars flaccida to facilitate visualiza- tion of the rest of the TM area (pars tensa). Before performing a myringotomy, the horizontal canal and surface of the TM are thoroughly cleaned and then suctioned/dried. The preferred site for performing a myrin- gotomy is caudo-ventrally in the tympanum, just above the junction of the tympanum and horizontal canal wall (Figures 10.18 and 10.19). The author most commonly uses a 22-gauge, 6″ spinal needle for this purpose. An alterna- tive to this would be the Storz myringotomy needle. This will create a very small hole that will rapidly heal, espe - cially if no significant pathology is located within the mid- dle ear (i.e. no material is obtained from the middle ear). Thick, tenacious mucin fills the middle ears of affected patients and often results in severe, mucin-filled dilatation of the pars flaccida. The treatment for this problem involves initially removing mucin from the dilated pars flaccida by the techniques noted above. Once access has been allowed to the pars tensa, a hole is made in its caudoventral aspect, as out - lined above. A catheter attached to a saline-filled syringe is then advanced into the middle ear until its tip hits bone. The mucoid material is then flushed from the middle ear. Suction often does not work well to remove this material. 10.6.7 Biopsies and Mass Removals Masses are biopsied using 5 Fr biopsy forceps. Traction and avulsion followed by a 6–8 week course of oral steroid therapy is noted to cure 95% of aural polyps. A polyp snare is available (Storz) for use through the video otoscope. The author tends to use a large biopsy forceps (Storz; catalog number 69133) to grasp as much of the polyp as possible and avulse the mass in this fashion. Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/mccarthy/endoscopy 11.1 Introduction There are a number of endoscopic procedures that, although minor in case numbers, are of significant impor - tance in their application for a specific patient. These include transabdominal nephroscopy and ureteroscopy (TANU), transabdominal cholecystodocoscopy (TACCD), prepuceoscopy, fistuloscopy, laceroscopy, oculoscopy, oncoscopy, and analsacoscopy. These procedures are per - formed with smaller rigid telescopes that are used for other major endoscopies and no additional equipment is needed. 11.2 Instrumentation for Otheroscopy in Small Animals A variety of instruments are needed to perform the proce - dures in this group of techniques but no additional tele - scopes or instruments are needed beyond what has been listed in the previous chapters. The 2.7 mm diameter MPRT is the first-choice telescope for most of these techniques with the arthroscopy sheath or the operating/cystoscopy sheath (Figure 2.30 and Table 2.3). Procedures requiring a smaller telescope use the 9.5 Fr one-piece cystoscope (Figure 2.31), the 1.9 mm arthroscope with the arthroscopy sheath (Figure 2.26 and Table 2.2), or a 1.0 mm diameter semirigid miniature telescope (Figure 2.26 and Table 2.2). Those procedures requiring a longer telescope most com- monly use the 4.0 mm diameter cystoscope (Figure 2.35 and Table 6.6). Sheaths for these telescopes are shown in appropriate figures and listed in tables with the telescopes in the previous chapters. Selection of a sheath is based on the needs of the individual procedure. Sample collection and operative instruments are also presented in appropriate figures and are selected based on the needs of the specific procedure being performed. When these telescopes, sheaths, or instruments are not appropriate for a procedure being considered, perusal of endoscope catalogs or online websites will reveal many additional options. Ingenuity is often required for instru- ment selection and procedure design when performing techniques not envisioned prior to your need for the patient in front of you in immediate need of help. 11.3 Transabdominal Nephroscopy and Ureteroscopy Renal and ureteral calculi in small dogs and cats are difficult to remove surgically and the complications associated with open surgery have established conservative treatment as the procedure of choice for their management (Lulich et al. 2016). Visualization and access to renal and ureteral calculi is greatly enhanced by using a small-diameter rigid endoscope (McCarthy 2005). For years, it has been believed that the old open surgical fillet nephrotomy technique for renal calculi removal essentially destroyed the kidney lead- ing to renal failure (Gahring et al. 1977). Because of this information, renal calculi have been left untouched for many years (Ross et al. 1999). More recent studies have chal- lenged the findings of the 1977 study (Stone et al. 2002; Zimmerman-Pope et al. 2003) but there has still been resist - ance to surgical removal of renal calculi. Recent research indicating that cats with renal calculi do not live as long as cats without calculi suggests that we need to reassess leaving calculi in place (Hall et al. 2017). 11 Otheroscopies 662 approach of TANU may be an alternative approach with better long-term results. TANU has been used successfully to remove renal calculi with minimally invasive technique, minimal renal trauma, and potentially decreased loss of renal function. More recent introduction of interventional radiology, transcutaneous nephroscopy, and availability of stents present additional alternatives for minimally invasive management of urinary calculi that are recommended when these options are available. To perform TANU, the patient is placed in dorsal recum- bency and the abdomen is opened with a standard full- length ventral midline abdominal incision. Balfour retractors are placed and appropriate exposure to the kid- ney and involved portion of the ureter are established with abdominal organ retraction and packing with moistened surgical gauze sponges or laparotomy sponges. If indicated, the kidney is freed from its abdominal wall attachments, packing is placed dorsal to the kidney facilitating access, and stabilizing the kidney. Three different calculi conditions are encountered: renal and ureteral calculi, renal calculi without ureteral calculi, and ureteral calculi without renal calculi. Each is approached differently. The approach is also affected by how far the ureteral calculi have migrated down the ureter and the amount of ureteral dilation. The easiest cases are those with a single large renal calculus that is palpable within the kidney, a small stab incision is made directly over the stone, the telescope inserted into the incision with irrigation allowing visualization of the stone, and graspers or a stone basket are used to remove the stone. Cases with a single ureteral calculus that has produced significant ure - teral dilation with the calculus still close to the kidney, within the proximal 2–3 cm of the ureter, are also relatively easy to remove. With this configuration, an ureterotomy is performed proximal to the calculus on the ventromedial aspect of the convex surface where the ureter coming from the renal pelvis in a lateral-to-medial course makes the bend to its cranial to caudal course toward the bladder. This incision location allows access to both the distal ureter and to the renal pelvis. Multiple small calculi with minimal renal or ureteral dilation are the most difficult cases. For these cases, preoperative stent placement facilitates stone removal by causing compensatory ureteral dilation. Incisions are made over or proximal to the calculi. Ureterotomy closure is achieved with a double continuous pattern (baseball stitch) of 6-0 to 8-0 monofilament absorb - able suture material. An operating microscope or a VITOM video telescope system (Karl Storz) with appropriate microsurgery skills are needed for all but the easiest cases. Once access has been established, a small rigid tele - scope (1.9 mm arthroscope, 2.4 mm arthroscope, the 2.7 mm multipurpose rigid telescope with their arthroscopy or cystoscopy cannulas, or the one-piece 9.5 Fr cystoscope) is placed into the kidney or ureter and directed toward the cal - culus to be removed. Using continuous gravity flow irriga - tion with saline or Ringers solution, for distension and to maintain a clear visual field, allows accurate identification of stones. Variable size, number, and appearance of stones include single smooth (Figures 11.1 and 11.2), irregular (Figures 11.3 and 11.4), or multiple calculi (Figures 11.5 and 11.6). Calculi also cause mucosal irritation (Figure 11.21) and inflammation (Figure 11.22) that can result in ureteral strictures (Figures 11.23 and 11.24). Ureteral stents are placed following nephrotomy or uret - erotomy prior to closure to decrease the potential for leakage from incisions and to decrease the possibility for ureteral stricture formation (Figure 11.25). Success of this technique is critically dependent on removal of all ureteral calculi and patency of the ureter distal to the ureterotomy incision. If there is residual obstruction of the ureter, there will be leakage of urine from the ureterotomy closure. Excretory urography is rou- tinely performed 24–48 hours after the procedure to con- firm ureteral patency and ureterotomy closure integrity. Unusual renal abnormalities have also been evaluated and managed with this technique, but this has been rare (Figures 11.26 and 11.27). Additional applications for man - agement of renal and ureteral diseases are certainly possible. TANU is the most difficult, tedious, picky, time-consum- ing, frustrating endoscopic procedure that I have per - formed in small animal practice. It is not recommended for the beginning endoscopist. The approach in people is by retrograde cholangioscopy accessed through the duodenal lumen. The technique has been reported in research applications in various animal species (Guenther et al. 1990; Vorwerk et al. 1990, 1993) but has not been employed clinically in small animal practice. References to laparoscopic or transabdominal approaches to the biliary tree in people were not found with a computer literature search. TACCD has been effectively performed clinically in dogs and in cats as an alternative approach by passing the endoscope in a normograde fashion. With limited modification of this technique, access with laparoscopy or a laparoscopic- assisted approach seems feasible. 11 Otheroscopies 666 Transabdominal endoscopy of the gall bladder and bile ducts follows the same concept as TANU in that the abdo - men is opened with a standard ventral full-length midline incision and a rigid endoscope is used to examine these structures through a gall bladder incision or through the cystic duct after gall bladder removal. Indications for this procedure include gall stones, gall bladder or bile duct masses, bile duct obstructions, or any time that there is concern about gall bladder or bile duct pathology. Any small rigid telescope is suitable for this procedure, but the most commonly used telescope is the 2.7 mm MPRT with either the arthroscopy cannula or the operating cannula. Irrigation and suction are commonly employed to lavage the gall bladder and bile ducts for visualization and for therapeutic purposes. Diagnostic samples are collected for cultures when the biliary tract is first entered, and biopsies are collected through the biopsy channel of the operating sheath of the telescope or the gall bladder is submitted after removal. This procedure is commonly performed in association with cholecystectomy and preoperative patient prepara- tion, anesthesia protocol, operating room setup, and patient positioning are the same for this surgery. Penetrating pharyngeal foreign bodies of the type described under laceroscopy that are not identified at the time of initial injury are an additional source of chronic fistulas. In these cases, the pharyngeal lacerations have typi - cally healed, and a fistula develops in the neck. These are an ideal application of this technique. The foreign bodies are usually large and are easily identified (Figure 11.70) with extensive and reactive fistula cavities (Figure 11.71). 11.10 Oculoscopy Examination of the cornea and anterior chamber of the eye is enhanced in some cases with application of a rigid endoscopic telescope. 11 Otheroscopies 680 11.12 Oraloscopy Endoscopes are not typically needed for examination of the oral cavity but occasionally they are indicated for capturing images of pathology if other photographic equipment is not available and especially for structures in the caudal oral cavity or pharynx. Examination of the larynx and observa- tion of the laryngeal function and capture of still or video images is a particularly good application of endoscopy in this area of the body as standard photography does not achieve adequate pictures. A group of procedures are included under this title encompassing all anatomic struc- tures in the oral cavity. These areas include the teeth (Dentaloscopy), the tonsils (Tonsiloscopy), the pharynx (Pharyngoscopy), and the larynx (Laryngoscopy). 11.12.1 Dentaloscopy Examination of teeth with an endoscope is typically not necessary but the magnification is sometimes helpful and also provides an excellent method for documenting pathol- ogy. Lesions from mild insignificant calculus (Figures 11.77 and 11.78) to severe purulent gingivitis with extensive loose abscessed teeth (Figures 11.79 and 11.80) are easily identified and documented. Fractured teeth are magnified and imaged for better diagnostics and demonstration to cli- ents to encourage appropriate treatment of slab fractures (Figure 11.81) or fractures of the apex exposing tooth roots (Figure 11.82). 11 Otheroscopies 686 The normal canine larynx has sharp well-defined tight vocal folds ventrally and smooth well-defined cartilages dor - sally (Figures 11.107 and 11.108). The normal feline larynx is more difficult to define as the structures are less distinct with a typical edematous appearance (Figures 11.109– 11.111) of all cats or that any stress, manipulation, or drugs cause laryngeal edema preventing observation of the truly normal larynx. Laryngeal spasm is common in cats with the laryngeal cartilages tightly adducted to close the larynx (Figure 11.112) and this position of the laryngeal cartilages is maintained during all phases of ventilation. Everted lateral saccules, or recently termed laryngoceles, are a common laryngeal anomaly seen in brachiocephalic dogs as one part of their multilevel airway pathology. The lining of the laryngeal ventricles are everted by the excess negative pressure required for the inspiratory phase of breathing in these dogs creating tissue masses that impinge on the laryngeal airway. The classic appearance of laryngoce - les are smooth masses on both sides of the ventral laryngeal airway typically extending across the airway to contact the contralateral laryngocele and having an edematous for fluid- filled cystic character (Figure 11.113). Laryngeal collapse is seen as a progression of brachioce - phalic airway syndrome in some patients and is a severe addition to the problem requiring a more aggressive surgi- cal approach with a much worse prognosis. Documentation of the severity of this pathology is very helpful during dis - cussions with clients in preparation for surgery. The aryte - noid cartilages are deformed toward the midline bilaterally (Figure 11.121) or unilaterally (Figure 11.122) narrowing the functional laryngeal airway. Resection of the deformed cartilage is typically required for correction. Laryngeal paralysis is another common laryngeal abnor - mality with diagnosis and management benefitted by application of endoscopy. Image and video capture facili- tate communication with owners and document the extent of pathology. The most obvious abnormality observed with laryngeal paralysis is that the laryngeal cartilages do not abduct with inspiration and maintain a fixed position throughout the breathing cycle or there is paradoxical motion with abduction occurring during exhalation rather than inhalation (Video 11.1). A more subtle finding is that the vocal folds are flaccid with paradoxical motion pulling the loose tissue medially during inspiration (Figure 11.123) and pushing the tissues laterally to a more normal position during expiration (Figure 11.124). In many older dogs, the laryngeal cartilages are also fixed in a position that is narrower than normal further decreasing the airway size (Figure 11.125). These abnormalities are combined to decrease laryngeal airway size thus decreasing the ventila- tory capacity of the dog. Laryngeal paralysis is also occa- sionally seen in cats typically with normal-appearing laryngeal anatomy and dysfunction similar to that seen in dogs (Video 11.2). Laryngeal masses including benign or malignant lesions are seen in both dogs and cats. Some lesions are small inflammatory nodules that do not interfere with ventila- tion and are clinically insignificant other than that they are an indication of underlying pathology (Figures 11.126 and 11.127). Larger masses (Figure 11.128) interfere with air movement and require surgical removal (Figure 11.129) that is made easier using endoscopic guidance.
